Sketch of the manner in which the Water is filled from the Troughs into the Buckets. few brilliant exploits were succeeded by a severe overthrow; the Agrigentines lost courage, disagreed in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and humbly sued for peace to Agathocles. This commonwealth afterwards took a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with Pyrrhus; and when he left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> to the mercy of her enemies, threw itself into the arms of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. During the first Punic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRIGENTUM">Agrigentum</a> was the headquarters of the Carthaginians, and was besieged by the Roman consuls, who after eight months <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> took it by storm. It nevertheless changed matters several times during the contest between these rival states, and in every instance suffered most cruel outrages. After this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> very little mention of it occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, nor do we know the precise <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the destruction of the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the new one. See Girgenti. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> city lay in the vale; the present town, called Girgenti, occupies the mountain on which the citadel of Cocalus stood. It was difficult to be more judicious and fortunate in the choice of situation for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> city. The inhabitants were here provided with every requisite for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and comfort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wall, formed by abrupt rocks, presented a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against assailants; pleasant hills sheltered them on three sides without impeding the circulation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; before them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> plain, watered by the Acragas, gave admittance to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breeze, and to a noble prospect of that awful element; the port <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> emporium lay in view at the mouth of the river, and probably the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> across the flat was lined with gay and populous suburbs. The hospitality and parade for which the Agrigentines are celebrated in history were supported by an extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; by means of which, the commonwealth was able to refit many shocks of adversity, and always to rise again with fresh splendour. It was, however, crushed by the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>; the feeble remnants of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, which had survived so many calamities, were at length driven out of its walls by the Saracens, and obliged to lock themselves up for safety among the bleak and inaccessible rocks of the present city. At the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the ancient limits, upon some foundations of large regular <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> has been erected; a road appears hewn in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock for the convenience of the votaries who visited this temple in ancient days. It was then dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Proserpine, the peculiar patronesses of Sicily. At the south-east corner, where the ground, rising gradually, ends in a bold eminence, which is crowned with majestic columns, are the ruins of a temple said to have been consecrated to Juno. To the west of this stands the building <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Temple of Concord; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> of which, and the other buildings, is the same as that of the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and cliffs, a conglomeration of sea sand and shells, full of perforations, of a hard and durable texture, and a deep reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. This Doric temple has all its columns, entablature, pediments, and walls entire; only part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is wanting. It owes its preservation to the piety of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who have covered half the nave, and converted it into a church consecrated under the invocation of St Gregory bishop of Girgenti. Proceeding in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, you walk between rows of sepulchres cut in the rock wherever it admitted of being excavated by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or was so already by that of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Some mazes of it are hewn into the shape of coffins; others drilled full of small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> holes employed in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a>, and serving as receptacles of urns. One ponderous piece of the rock lies in an extraordinary position; by the failure of its foundation, or the shock of an earthquake, it has been loosened from the general <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, and rolled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the declivity, where it now remains supine with the cavities turned upwards. Only a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> marks the confused heap of moss-grown ruins belonging to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>. It stood on a projecting rock above a chasm in the ridge, which was cut through for a passage to the emporium. In the same tract, over some hills, is situated the building usually called the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">Tomb</a> of Thero. It is surrounded by aged olive trees, which <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a wild <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> over the ruin. The edifice inclines to the pyramidal shape, and consists at present of a triple <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLINTH">plinth</a>, and a base supporting a square pedestal; upon this plain solid foundation is raised a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order, having a window in each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and at each angle two Ionic pilasters crowned with an entablature of the Doric order. Its inside is divided into a vault, a ground room, and one in the Ionic story, communicating with each other by means of a small internal staircase. In the plain are seen the fragments of the temple of Eucleapius; part of two columns and two pilasters, with an intermediate wall, support the end of a farmhouse, and were probably the front of the cella. Pursuing the track of the walls towards the west, you arrive at a spot which is covered with the gigantic remains of the temple of the Olympian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, minutely described by Diodorus Siculus. It may literally be said that it has not one stone left upon another; and it is barely possible, with the help of much conjecture, to discover the traces of its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and dimensions. Diodorus calls it the largest temple in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>; but adds, that the calamities of war caused the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> to be abandoned before the roof could be put on; and that the Agrigentines were ever after reduced to such a state of poverty and dependence, that they never had it in their power to finish this superb monument of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and opulence of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. The length of this temple was 370 Greek feet, its breadth 60, and its height 220, exclusive of the foundations or basement story; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and solidity of its vaults and underworks were wonderful; its spacious porticoes and exquisite <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> were suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of the whole. It was not built in the usual style of Sicilian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> with a cella of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> walls and a peristyle, but was designed in a mixed style with half columns let into the walls on the outside, the inside exhibiting a plain surface. The next ruin belongs to the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>; vegetation has covered the lower parts of the building, and only a few fragments of columns appear between the vines. This was the point of the hill where the wall stood on the brink of a large fish-pond spoken of by Diodorus: it was cut in the solid rock. Agrimony 30 feet deep, and water was conveyed to it from the hills. In it was bred a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fish for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of public entertainments; swans and various other kinds of wild fowl swam along its surface, for the amusement of the citizens, and the great depth of water prevented an enemy from surprising the town on that side. It is now dry and used as a garden. On the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, are two tapering columns without their capitals, most happily placed in a tuft of carob trees. Monte Toro, where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> encamped with the Carthaginian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, before the Roman consuls drew him into an engagement that ruined his defensive plan, is a noble back-ground to this picturesque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of objects. The whole space comprehended within the walls of the ancient city abounds with traces of antiquity, foundations, brick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, and little channels for the conveyance of water; but in no part are any ruins that can be presumed to have belonged to places of public entertainment. This is the more extraordinary, as the Agrigentines were a sensual people, fond of shows and dramatic performances, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> never dwelt in any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> without introducing their <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> games. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">Theatres</a> and amphitheatres seem better calculated than most buildings to resist the outrages of time; and it is surprising that not even the vestiges of their form should remain on the ground.

or island of St Francis Xavier, in Geography, one of the Ladrones or Marian islands. It is 50 miles in circumference, is very mountainous, and has a volcano in it; situated in N. Lat. 19. 4. E. Long. 146.

AGRIGENTUM

Pages 142-142

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the site of which is now occupied by a town called Girgenti from the old name. See GIRGENTI. According to ancient authors, Dedalus, the most famous mechanician of fabulous antiquity, fled to this spot for protection against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a>, and built many wonderful edifices for Cocalus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a> after his flight, the people of Gela sent a colony hither 600 years before the birth of Christ; and from the name of a neighbouring stream called the new city Agragatis, whence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> formed their word Agrigentum. These Greeks converted the ancient abode of the Siculi into a citadel to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the magnificent city which they erected on the hillocks below. An advantageous situation, a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with all its happy effects, and an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> commercial spirit, exalted their commonwealth to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and power unknown to the other Greek settlements, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a> alone excepted. But the prosperity of Agrigentum appears to have been but of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, and tyranny soon destroyed its liberties. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a> was the first who reduced it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. His name is familiar to most readers on account of his cruelty, and the brazen bull in which he tortured his enemies. (See PHALARIS.)—Phalaris met with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fate of tyrants, and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> the Agrigentines enjoyed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> for 150 years; at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Thero usurped the sovereign authority. The moderation, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and valour of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> preserved him from opposition while living, and have rescued his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> from the obloquy of posterity. He joined his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> Gelo, king of Syracuse, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Carthaginians; in the course of which victory attended all his steps, and Sicily <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Agrigentum herself for a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> delivered from her African oppressors. Soon after his decease, his son Thrasydeus was deprived of the diadem, and Agrigentum restored to her old democratical government. Ducetus next disturbed the general tranquillity. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the mountaineers, descendants of the Siculi; and was an overmatch for the Agrigentines while they were unsupported by alliances, but sank under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of their union with the Syracusans. Some trifling alterations dissolved this union, and produced a war, in which the Agrigentines were worsted, and compelled to submit to humiliating terms of peace. Resentment led them to embrace with joy the proposals of the Athenians, then meditating an attack upon Syracuse. Their new friends soon made them feel that the sacrifice of liberty and fortune would be the price of their protection; and this consideration brought them speedily back to their old connexions. But as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it had been decreed that all friendship should be fatal to their repose, the reconciliation and its effects drew upon them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> of the Carthaginians. By this enemy their armies were routed, their city taken, their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> almost extirpated, and scarce a vestige of magnificence was left. Agrigentum lay 50 years buried under its own ruins; when Timoleon, after triumphing over the Carthaginians, and restoring liberty to Sicily, collected the descendants of the Agrigentines, and sent them to re-establish the dwellings of their forefathers. Their exertions were rewarded with astonishing success; for Agrigentum rose from its ashes with such a renewal of vigour, that in a very short time we find it engaged in the bold scheme of seizing a lucky moment, when Agathocles and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> had reduced Syracuse to the lowest ebb, and arrogating to itself supremacy over all the Sicilian republics. Xenodicus was appointed the leader of this arduous enterprise; and had his latter operations been as fortunate as his first <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a>, Agrigentum would have acquired such a preponderance of reputation and power, that the rival states would not have even dared to attack it. But a few...

AGRIMONIA

Pages 160-160

Agrimony.** See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">Hemp</a> Agrimony.** See Eupatorium, Botany Index. **<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">Water</a> Hemp Agrimony.** See Bidens, Botany Index. **AGRIONIA,** in Grecian Antiquity, festivals annually celebrated by the Boeotians in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>. At these festivals, the women pretended to search after Bacchus as a fugitive; and, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, gave over their inquiry, saying, that he had fled to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, and was concealed among them. **AGRIOPHAGI,** in Antiquity, a name given to those who fed on wild beasts. The word is Greek, compounded of ἀγελος, "wild," "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>," and φαγων, "I eat." The name is given, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, to certain people, real <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fabulous, said to have fed altogether on lions or panthers. Pliny and Solinus speak of Agriophagi in Ethiopia, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> of others in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> on this side the Ganges.

AGRIPPA

Pages 160-162

Herod,** the son of Aristobulus and Mariamne, and grandson to Herod the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, was born in the year of the world 3997, three years before the birth of our Saviour, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years before the vulgar era. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Aristobulus, his father, Josephus informs us, that Herod his grandfather took care of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and sent him to Rome to make his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> to Tiberius. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> conceived a great affection for Agrippa, and placed him near his son Drusus. Agrippa very soon won the graces of Drusus, and of the empress Antonia. But Drusus dying suddenly, all those who had been much about him were commanded by Tiberius to withdraw from Rome, lest the sight and presence of them should renew his affliction. Agrippa, who had indulged his inclination to liberality, was obliged to leave Rome overwhelmed with debts, and in a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> condition. He did not think it fit to go to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, because he was not able to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> there suitable to his birth. He retired therefore to the castle of Massada, where he lived rather like a private person than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Herod the Tetrarch, his uncle, who had married Herodias his sister, afflicted him for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with great generosity. He made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> of Tiberias, and presented him with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; but all this was not sufficient to answer the excessive expenses and profusion of Agrippa; so that Herod growing weary of afflicting him, and reproaching him with his bad economy, Agrippa took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to quit Judea, and return to Rome. Upon his arrival, he was received into the good graces of Tiberius, and commanded to attend Tiberius Nero the son of Drusus. Agrippa, however, having more inclination for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> the son of Germanicus, and grandson of Antonia, chose rather to attach himself to him; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had some prophetic views of the future elevation of Caius, who at that time was beloved by all the world. The great affluence and agreeable behaviour of Agrippa so far engaged this prince, that he kept him continually about him. Agrippa being one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> overheard by Eutyches, a slave whom he had made free, to express his wishes for Tiberius's death and the advancement of Caius, the slave betrayed him to the emperor; whereupon Agrippa was loaded with fetters, and committed to the custody of an officer. Tiberius soon after dying, and Caius Caligula succeeding him, the new emperor heaped many favours and much wealth upon Agrippa; changed his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> fetters into a chain of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; set a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> diadem upon his head; and gave him the tetrarchy which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>, the son of Herod the Great, had been possessed of, that is, Batanaea and Trachonitis. To this he added that of Lybanias; and Agrippa returned very soon into Judea to take possession of his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Caius being soon after killed, Agrippa, who was then at Rome, contributed much by his advice to maintain Claudius in possession of the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, to which he had been advanced by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. But in this affair Agrippa acted a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> wherein he showed more cunning and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> than sincerity and honesty; for while he made a show of being in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, he secretly advised Claudius to be resolute, and not to abandon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>. The emperor, as an acknowledgment for his kind offices, gave him all Judea and the kingdom of Chalcis, which had been possessed by Herod his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. Thus Agrippa became of a sudden one of the greatest princes of the east; and was possessed of as much, if not more territories Agrippa, ritories than had been held by Herod the Great his grandfather. He returned to Judea, and governed it to the great satisfaction of the Jews. But the desire of pleasing them, and a mistaken zeal for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, induced him to commit an unjust <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of which is preserved in Scripture, Acts xii. 1, 2, &c., for about the feast of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSOVER">passover</a>, in the year of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ 44, St James <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>, the son of Zebedee and brother of St John the Evangelist, was seized by his order and put to death. He proceeded also to lay <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> on St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and imprisoned him, waiting till the festival was over, that he might then have him executed. But God having miraculously delivered St Peter from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his confinement, the designs of Agrippa were frustrated. After the passover, this prince went from Jerusalem to Caesarea, and there had games performed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Claudius. Here the inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a> waited on him to sue for peace. Agrippa being come early in the morning to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to give them audience, seated himself on his throne, dressed in a robe of silver-tissue, worked in the most admirable manner. The rising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> darted on it with its rays, and gave it such a lustre as the eyes of the spectators could not endure. When therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> spoke to the Tyrians and Sidonians, the parasites around him began to say, that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of a god, and not that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Instead of rejecting these impious flatteries, Agrippa received them with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of complacency; but at the same time observed an owl above him on a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. He had seen the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> before when he was in bonds by order of Tiberius; and it was then told him, that he should be soon set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>: but that whenever he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the same thing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time, he should not live above five days afterwards. He was therefore extremely terrified; and he died at the end of five days, racked with tormenting pains in his bowels, and devoured with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>. Such was the death of Herod Agrippa, after a reign of seven years, in the year of Christ 44. Agrippa II., son of the preceding Herod, was made king of Chalcis; but three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four years after, he was deprived of that kingdom by Claudius, who gave him in the place of it other provinces. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> Vespasian carried on against the Jews, Herod <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> him a succour of 2000 men; by which it appears that though a Jew by religion, he was yet entirely devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whose affiance indeed he wanted to secure the peace of his own kingdom. He lived to the third year of Trajan, and died at Rome A.D. 100. He was the seventh and last king of the family of Herod the Great. It was before him and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERENICE">Berenice</a> his sister that St Paul pleaded his cause at Caesarea. Agrippa, Marcus Vitianus, son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to Augustus, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> birth, but one of the most considerable generals among the Romans. Augustus's victory over Pompey and Mark Antony was owing to his counsel. He adorned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with the pantheon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Germanicus, sister of Caligula, and mother of Nero; a woman of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, but excessively lewd. She was thrice married, the last time to Claudius her own uncle, whom she poisoned to make way for Nero her son. Nero afterwards caused her to be murdered in her chamber, when she bid the executioner stab her first in the belly that had brought forth Agrippina such a monster. Agrippina Colonia Ubiorum, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>: so called from Agrippina, the daughter of Germanicus, and mother of Nero, who had a colony sent thither at her request by the emperor Claudius, to honour the place of her birth. See Cologne. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRIPPINIANS">Agrippinians</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the followers of Agrippinus bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, in the third century, who first introduced and defended the practice of re-baptization. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROM">Agrom</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> frequent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> and other parts of the Indies, in which the tongue is parched, chaps, and is sometimes covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> spots. The Indians are very fearful of this disease, which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the stomach. Their remedy is, to drink some chalybeate liquor, or the juice of mint. Agrostemma, Wild Lychinis, or <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPION">Campion</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Agrostis, Bent-grass, in Botany. See Botany Index. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROSTOGRAPHIA">Agrostographia</a>, signifies the history or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of grasses. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">Aground</a>, the situation of a ship whose bottom, or any part of it, hangs, or rests upon the ground, so as to render her immovable, till a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> floats her off, or till she is drawn out into the stream by the application of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL_POWERS"><a class="xref" h</a>ref="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> powers. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRYPNIA">Agrypnia</a>, among Physicians, implies an inability to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>; a troublesome symptom of feverish and other disorders. Agrypnia, in the Greek Church, implies the vigil of any of the greater festivals. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a>, a general name for all periodical fevers, which, according to the different times of the returns of the feverish paroxysm, are denominated tertian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTAN">quartan</a>, and quotidian. See Medicine Index. ague-Cake, the popular name for a hard tumour on the left side of the belly, lower than the false ribs, said to be the effect of intermittent fevers. ague-Tree, a name given to the saffraan, on account of its fugitive qualities. Agueperse, a town of France, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, in the department of Puy-de-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">Dome</a>, about 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Clermont. aguillaneuf, or Augillaneuf, a form of rejoicing used among the ancient Franks on the first day of the year. The word is compounded of the French "a" "to," "gui" "milleto," and "l'an neuf" "the new year." Its origin is traced from a druid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>: the priests used to go yearly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, which with them was reputed a sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, to gather millet of the oak in great solemnity. The prophets marched in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, singing hymns in honour of their deities; after them came a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERALD">herald</a> with a caduceus in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; these were followed by three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> abreast, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the things necessary for sacrifice; last of all came the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> druid, accompanied with the train of people. The chief druid climbing the oak, cut off the millet with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> sickle, and the other druids received it in a white cloth; on the first day of the year it was distributed among the people, after having been blessed and consecrated it by crying "Gui l'an neuf," to proclaim... proclaim the new year. This cry is still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in Picardy, with the addition of Plantez, Plantez, to with a plentiful year. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and some other parts, the children <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the same word to beg a new-year's gift. In latter times the name Aguillaneuf was also given to a sort of begging, practised in some dioceses, for church-tapers, on new year's day, by a troop of young people of both sexes, having a chief, &c. It was attended with various ridiculous ceremonies, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> in the church, &c., which occasioned the synods to suppress it.

AGUILAR

Pages 162-162

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Navarre, about 24 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTELLA">Estella</a>. AGUILAR del Campo, a town of Old Castile, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of marquisate, about 15 leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGOS">Burgos</a>.

AGUILLON

Pages 162-162
or Aguillonius, Francis, a Jesuit, born at Bruges; he was rector of the Jesuits' college at Antwerp, and eminent for his skill in mathematics. He was the first who introduced that science among the Jesuits in the Low Countries; he wrote a book of Optics, and was employed in finishing his Coptics and Dioptrics, when he died in 1617.

AGUIRRA

Pages 162-162
Joseph Sandoval, a Benedictine, and one of the most learned men of the 17th century, was born March 24, 1630. He was censor and secretary of the supreme council of the inquisition in Spain, and interpreter of the Scriptures in the university of Salamanca. He printed three volumes in folio upon Philosophy, a commentary upon Aristotle's ten books of Ethics, and other pieces. He died at Rome in 1699.

AGUL

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a synonyme of the hedyotum. See Hedysarum, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGUR">AGUR</a>. The xxxth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the Proverbs begins with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: "The words of Agur, the son of Jakob," which, according to the signification of the original terms, may be translated, as the Vulgate has it, Verba congregantis, filii vomentis; which translation Le Clerc condemns, supposing these to be proper names which ought not to be translated. These words are rendered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> de Dieu: "the words of him who has recollected himself, the son of obedience." The generality of the fathers and commentators <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it, that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> describes himself under the name of Agur the son of Jakob; others conjecture that Agur, as well as Lemuel (in chap. xxxi. 1.) were wise men who lived in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Solomon, and were his interlocutors in the book of Proverbs; an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which F. Calmet thinks is without the least show of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, this book being nothing like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. This last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSITOR">expositor</a> thinks it probable, that Agur was an inspired author different from Solomon, whose sentences it was thought fit to join with those of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, because of the conformity of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>.

AGURAH

Pages 162-162

in Jewish Antiquity, the name of a silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, otherwise called gerah and kephira.

AGURIUM

Pages 162-162
or Agrium, in Ancient Geography, a town of Sicily in the Val di Demona, near the river Semetus. The people were called Populus Agryniensis by Cicero; Agrynius by Pliny. It was the birth-place of Diodorus Siculus, as he himself testifies; but he calls it Argyrion, as it is now called S. Philippo d'Argyron, which modern name seems to confirm that Argyrium is the true reading.

AGUSADURA

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Customs, a fee due from Agudura vassals to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> for the sharpening their ploughing tackle. Anciently the tenants in some manors were not allowed to have their rural implements sharpened by any but whom the lord appointed; for which an acknowledgment was to be paid, called agu sadura, in some places agylage: which some take to be the same with what was otherwise called reillage, from the ancient French reille, a ploughshare.

AGUSTINA

Pages 162-162

a new <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; which, as the word signifies, is taffelis, insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and when pure resembles alumina. It was discovered in the year 1800 by Trommldorff in the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERYL">beryl</a>. But as his experiments have not been repeated, the existence of this earth rests solely on his authority.

AGUTI

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the mouse, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a> glires of Linnaeus.

AGYEL

Pages 162-162

in Antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a>, sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, erected in the vestibules of houses, by way of security.

AGYNANI

Pages 162-162

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> who condemned all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, as not instituted by God, but introduced at the instigation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>. The word is compounded of the privative a and yon woman. They are sometimes also called Agynenae, and Agynei: and are said to have appeared about the year 694. It is no wonder they were of no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance. Their tenets coincide in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> with those of the Abelians, Gnostics, Cerdonians, and other preachers of chastity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>. AGYRTÉ, in Antiquity, a kind of strolling impostors running about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, to pick up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, by telling fortunes at rich men's doors, pretending to cure diseases by charms, sacrifices, and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>; also to expiate the crimes of their deceased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, by virtue of certain odours and fumigations; to torment their enemies, by the use of magical verses, and the like. The word is Greek Agorai, formed of the verb aγορα, I congregate; alluding to the practice of charlatans <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> quacks, who gather a crowd about them. Agyrta, among the Greeks, amount to the same with Euryctores among the Latins, and differ not much from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GYPSIES">Gypsies</a> among us.

AHAB

Pages 162-163

son of Omri <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel, succeeded his father A. M. 3086, and surpassed all his predecessors in impiety and wickedness. He married Jezebel the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Ethbaal king of the Zidonians, who introduced the idols of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAAL">Baal</a> and Ashtoreth among the Israelites, and engaged Ahab in the worship of these false deities. God, being provoked by the sins of Ahab, sent the prophet Elijah to him (1 Kings xvii. 1. seq.), who declared to him, that there would be a famine of three years continuance. The dearth having lasted three years, the prophet desired Ahab to gather all the people to Mount Carmel, and with them the prophets of Baal: when they were thus assembled, Elijah caused fire to descend from heaven upon his sacrifice, after which he obtained of God that it should <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>; and then the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> recovered its former fertility. Six years after this, Ben-hadad king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> (chap. xx.) laid siege to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. But God, provoked at this proud Syrian, sent a prophet to Ahab, not only Ahab, to assure him of victory, but to instruct him likewise in what manner he was to obtain it. Ahab was ordered to review the princes of the provinces, which he found to be a choice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, consisting of 232 young men, who were to command the people in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>, amounting to about 7000 men; with this small <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> Ahab was directed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOST">host</a> of the Syrians, and that at noon-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, while Ben-hadad and the 32 kings that accompanied him were drinking and making merry. Ben-hadad having notice that they were marching out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, ordered them to be brought before him alive, whatever their designs were; but the young men, followed by this small army, advanced, and killed all that opposed them. Such a panic seized the Syrian troops, that they began to fly, and even Ben-hadad himself mounted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and fled with his cavalry: which Ahab perceiving, pursued them, killed great numbers of them, and took a considerable booty. After this the prophet came to Ahab, to animate him with fresh courage, and to caution him to keep up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; assuring him, that Ben-hadad would return against him the year following. According to this prediction, at the end of the year he returned and encamped at Aphek, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to give the Israelites <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Both armies being ranged in order of battle for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days successively, at length upon the seventh day, a battle ensued, wherein the Israelites killed 100,000 of the Syrians, and the rest fled to Aphek; but as they were pressing to get into the city, the walls of Aphek fell upon them and killed 27,000 more. Ben-hadad throwing himself upon the mercy of Ahab, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> received him into his own chariot, and made an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with him. The year following, Ahab desiring to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden near his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> (chap. xxii.), requested of one Naboth, a citizen of Jezreel, that he would sell him his vineyard, because it lay convenient for him. But being refused, he returned in great discontentment to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, threw himself upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, turned towards the wall, and would eat nothing. Jezebel his wife coming in, asked the reason of his great concern; of which being informed, she procured the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Naboth, and Ahab took possession of his vineyard. As he returned from Jezreel to Samaria, the prophet Elijah met him, and said, "Hast thou killed and also taken possession? Now <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where dogs licked up the blood of Naboth, shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine. As for Jezebel, of her the Lord spoke, saying, The dogs shall eat Jezebel by the way of Jezreel." Ahab, hearing these and other denunciations, rent his clothes, put sackcloth upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and gave other indications of his sorrow and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>. But his repentance was neither sincere nor persevering. Two years after these things, Jehoshaphat king of Judah came to Samaria to visit Ahab (chap. xxiii.) at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when he was preparing to attack Ramoth-gilead, which Ben-hadad king of Syria unjustly withheld from him. The king of Israel invited Jehoshaphat to accompany him in this expedition; which that prince agreed to do, but desired that some prophet might first be consulted. Ahab therefore assembled the prophets of Baal, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> about 400; who all concurred in exhorting the king to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> resolutely against Ramoth-gilead. But Micaiah being also consulted, at Jehoshaphat's suggestion, prophesied the ruin of Ahab. Upon this, Ahab gave orders to his people to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> Micaiah, and to carry him to Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son; telling him in his name, "Put this fellow in prison, and feed him with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> of affliction, and with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of affliction, until I come in peace." But Micaiah said, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> thou return at all in peace, the Lord hath not spoken by me." Ahab, therefore, and Jehoshaphat marched up to Ramoth-gilead; and the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, "I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a> myself, and enter into the battle, but put thou on my robe:" for he knew that the king of Syria had commanded two and thirty captains that had rule over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a>, saying, "Fight neither with small nor with great, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> only with the king of Israel." These officers, therefore, having observed that Jehoshaphat was dressed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> robes, took him for the king of Israel, and fell upon him with great impetuosity: but this prince seeing himself pressed closely, cried out; and the mistake being discovered, the captains of the king of Syria gave over pursuing him. But one of the Syrian army <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> a random <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a>, which pierced the heart of Ahab. The battle lasted the whole day, and Ahab <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in his chariot with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> turned towards the Syrians. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, his blood was still issuing from his wound, and falling in his chariot; and towards the evening he died: whereupon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was made by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should return to his own city and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The king of Israel being dead, was carried to Samaria and buried: but his chariot and the reins of his horses were washed in the fountain of Samaria, and the dogs licked his blood, according to the word of the prophet. Such was the end of Ahab. His son <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AHAZIAH">Ahaziah</a> succeeded him in the year of the world 3167. AHÆTULA, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the coluber. See Coluber.

AHASUERUS

Pages 163-163
or Artaxerxes, the husband of Esther; and according to Archbishop Usher and F. Calmet, the Scripture name for Darius, the son of Hystaspes, king of Persia; though Scaliger supposed Xerxes to have been the husband of Esther, or the Ahasuerus of Scripture: and Dr Prideaux believes him to be Artaxerxes Longimanus. See History of Persia.

AHAZ

Pages 163-164
king of Judah, the son of Jotham, remarkable for his vices and impieties. One of his sons he consecrated, by making him pass through and perish by the fire, in honour of the false god Moloch; and he offered sacrifices and incense upon the high places, upon hills, and in groves. Rezin king of Syria and Pekah king of Israel invaded Judea in the beginning of the reign of Ahaz; and having defeated his army and pillaged the country, they laid siege to Jerusalem. When they found that they could not make themselves masters of that city, they divided their army, plundered the country, and made the inhabitants prisoners of war. Rezin and his part of the confederate army marched with all their spoil to Damascus; but Pekah with his division of the army having attacked Ahaz, killed 120,000 men of his army in one battle, and carried away men, women, and children, without distinction, to the number of 200,000. But as they were carrying those captives to Samaria, the prophet Oded, with the principal inhabitants of the city, came out to meet... meet them; and by their remonstrances prevailed with them to set their prisoners at liberty. At the same time, the Philistines and Edomites invaded other parts of his land, killed multitudes of the people, and carried off much booty. In this distressed condition, Ahaz finding no other remedy for his affairs, sent ambassadors to Tiglath-pileser king of the Assyrians; and to engage him to his interest, he stripped the temple and city of all the gold which he could meet with, and sent it as a present. Accordingly Tiglath-pileser marched to the assistance of Ahaz, attacked Rezin and killed him, took his capital Damascus, destroyed it, and removed the inhabitants thereof to Cyrene. The misfortunes of this prince had no influence to make him better: on the contrary, in the times of his greatest affliction, he sacrificed to the Syrian deities, whom he looked upon as the authors of his calamities, and endeavoured to render propitious to him, by honouring them in this manner. He broke in pieces the vessels of the house of God, shut up the gates of the temple, and erected altars in all parts of Jerusalem. He set up altars likewise in all the cities of Judah, with a design to offer incense on them. At length he died, and was buried in Jerusalem, but not in the sepulchres of the kings of Judah his predecessors: which honour he was deprived of, on account of his injurious course of life. Hezekiah his son succeeded him in the year of the world 3287, before Jesus Christ 726.

AHAZIAH

Pages 164-164
king of Judah, the son of Jehoram and Athaliah, succeeded his father in the kingdom of Judah, in the year of the world 3110. He walked in the ways of Ahab's house, to which he was allied. He reigned only one year. He was slain by Jehu the son of Nimshi.

AHHEAD

Pages 164-164

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, signifying further onward than the ship, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at any distance before her, lying immediately on that point of the compass to which her stem is directed. It is used in opposition to aftern, which expresses the situation of any object behind the ship.

AHIJAH

Pages 164-164

the prophet of Shilo. He is thought to be the person who spoke twice to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> from God, once while he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the temple (1 Kings vi. 11.), at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he promised his protection; and at another time (id. xi. 6.) after his falling into all his irregularities, when God expressed his indignation with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> threatenings and reproaches. Ahijah was one of those who wrote the annals <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> (2 Chr. ix. 29.) The same prophet declared to Jeroboam that he would usurp the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> (1 Kings xi. 29, &c.), and that two heifers should alienate him from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, meaning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> calves erected by Jeroboam, one at Dan, the other at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a>. About the end of Jeroboam's reign, towards the year of the world 3246, Abijah the son of that prince fell sick; upon which Jeroboam sent his wife to this prophet to inquire what would become of the child. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> therefore went to Abijah's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in Shiloh, disguised: But the prophet, upon hearing the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of her feet, said, "Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam, why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings." Then he commanded her to go and tell Jeroboam all the evil that the Lord had declared he would bring upon his house for his impurities; that so soon as she should enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> her son Abijah should die, and should be the only one of Jeroboam's house that should come to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> or receive the honours of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>. Abijah in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> survive the time of this last prophecy; but with the time and manner of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> we are not acquainted.

AHITOPHEL

Pages 164-165

a native of Gilo, was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the counsellor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, whom he at length deserted, by joining in the rebellion of Absalom. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, upon his being preferred to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> by the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Israelites, sent for Ahitophel from Gilo (2 Sam. xv. 12.) to assist him with his advice in the present state of his affairs: for at that time Ahitophel's counsels were received as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> of God himself (chap. xvi. u.l.) Nothing gave David more uneasiness than this event; and when Hushai his friend came to wait on him and attend him in his flight, he intreated him to return rather to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, make a show of offering his services to Absalom, and endeavour to frustrate the prudent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which should be proposed by Ahitophel. When Absalom was come to Jerusalem, he desired Ahitophel to deliberate with his other counsellors upon the measures which were proper for him to take. Ahitophel advised him in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to abuse his father's concubines; so that when his party should understand that he had dishonoured his father in this manner, they might conclude that there were no hopes of a reconciliation, and therefore espouse his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> more resolutely. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>, therefore, being prepared for this purpose upon the terrace of the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, Absalom, in the sight of all Israel, lay with his father's concubines. The next thing Ahitophel proposed was in the terms following: "Let me now choose out 12,000 men, and I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> arise and pursue after David this night, and I will come upon him while he is weary and weak-handed, and I will make him afraid, and all the people that are with him flee, and I will smite the king only; and I will bring back all the people unto thee; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> whom thou keepest is as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> all returned: so all the people shall be in peace." This advice was very agreeable to Absalom and all the elders of Israel. However, Abihas desired Hushai to be called to have his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>. Hushai being come, and hearing what advice <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AHITHOPHEL">Ahithophel</a> had given, said, "The counsel which Ahithophel has given is not good at this time; what, for the present, in my opinion, may do better, is this: Let all Israel be gathered unto thee, from Dan even to Beer-sheba, as the sand that is by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> for multitude, and put thyself in the midst of them, and wherever David is, we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon him, and overwhelm him with our numbers, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> falleth upon the ground." This last advice being more agreeable to Absalom and all the elders of Israel, was preferred; upon which Ahithophel saddled his ass, went to his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Gilo, hanged himself, and was buried in the sepulchre of his fathers. He foresaw, without doubt, all that would happen in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of Hushai's advice, and was determined to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> which he had deserved, and which David would probably have inflicted on him, as soon as he should be resettled on his throne.

AHMELLA

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Bidens, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. AHOLIBAH and Aholah, are two feigned names made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> (xxiii. 4.) to denote the two kingdoms of Judah and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAMARIA">Samaria</a>. Aholah and Aholibah are represented as two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> of Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. Aholah stands for Samaria, and Aholibah for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. The first signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, my tent is in her. They both profited themselves to the Egyptians and Assyrians, in imitating their abominations and idolatries; for which reason they were abandoned to those very people for whom they had thrown so passionate, and so impure an affection; they were carried into <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, and reduced to the severest servitude.

AHULLI

Pages 165-165

in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the situation of a ship when all her sails are furled on account of the violence of the storm, and when having lashed her helm on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-side, she lies nearly with her side to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and sea, her head being somewhat inclined to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the wind.

AHUYS

Pages 165-165

a town of Gothland in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. It is small, but very strong by its situation, and has a good port. It is in the principality of Gothland, in the territory of Bleckingy, near the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, about 18 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANSTADT">Christianstadt</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 14. 10. N. Lat. 56. 20.

AI

Pages 165-165

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town in Judea, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERICHO">Jericho</a>, called Ama by Josephus, and the inhabitants Ainat. Joshua having sent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of 3000 men against Ai, God permitted them to be repulsed on account of Achan's sin, who had violated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANATHEMA">anathema</a> pronounced against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Jericho. But after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIATION">expiation</a> of this offence, God commanded Joshua (chap. viii.) to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> with the whole <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of the Israelites against Ai, and treat this city and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> thereof as he had treated Jericho, with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that he gave the plunder of the town to the people. Joshua sent by night 30,000 men to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in ambush behind Ai; having first well instructed those who had the command of them in what they were to do; and the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, early in the morning, he marched against the city with the remainder of his army. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ai, perceiving them, fell hastily out of the town with all his people, and fell upon the forces of the Israelites, who, upon the first onset, fled, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had been under some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> terror. As soon as Joshua <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the enemy all out of the gates, he raised his shield upon the top of a pike, which was the signal given to the ambuscade; whereupon they immediately entered the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, which they found without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and set fire to it. The people of Ai perceiving the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> ascending, were willing to return, but discovered those who had set fire to the city in their rear, while Joshua and those who were with him <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> about, fell upon them, and cut them in pieces. The king was taken alive, and afterwards put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The chevalier Folard observes, that Joshua's enterprise on Ai, excepting in some particulars of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, is very like that of Gibeah, which is scarce anything more than a copy of it. It would appear, says that writer, by the Scripture account, that Joshua was not the author of the stratagem made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by him: for when God directs himself to Joshua, he says, "Go up against Ai; lay an ambuscade behind the town; I have delivered the king and the people of it into thine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>;" yet notwithstanding this, God might leave the whole <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> and execution of it to him, as to a great general. "Joshua arose, (says the sacred author,) and all the people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, to go up against Ai (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> 3.) and Joshua chose out 30,000 mighty men of valour, and sent them away by night," Folard remarks, that there is a manifest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> between this verse and the 14th, wherein it is said, that Joshua chose out 500 men, whom he sent to lie in ambush, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a> and Ai. How is this to be reconciled? Calmet says, that Malus allows but 5000 men for the ambuscade, and 25,000 for the attack of the city, being persuaded that an army of 600,000 men could only create confusion on this occasion, without any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> for, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> advantage in, such numbers; but the generality of interpreters, continues Calmet, acknowledge two bodies to be placed in ambuscade, both between Bethel and Ai; one of 25,000, and the other of 5000 men. With regard to the signal Joshua made to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his army which lay in ambuscade, the learned Folard embraces the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the Rabbins, who believe what is called the shield to be too small to serve for a signal: hence they make it to be the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> of one of their colours: from this, our author concludes, that the whole colours were used on this occasion; for in the Asiatic style, which is very near the poetical, the part is oftentimes to be taken for the whole.

AICHSTATT

Pages 166-166

a town of Germany, in Franconia, and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bishopric of the same name. It is remarkable for a curious piece of workmanship, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a> of the Holy Sacrament, which is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is of maffy <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and is enriched with 350 diamonds, 1400 pearls, 250 rubies, and other precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is moderately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and seated in a valley on the river Altmul, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Nieuburg, and 37 south of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 10'. N. Lat. 49° 0'. The bishopric is 45 miles in length and 17 in breadth; and the bishop is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the church of Mayence <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>.

AIDAN

Pages 166-166

a famous Scottish bishop of Lindisfarne, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOLY_ISLAND">Holy <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, in the 7th century, was employed by Oswald <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in the conversion of the English, in which he was very successful. He was a monk in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Jona, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>. He died in 651.

AIGHENDALE

Pages 166-166

the name of a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, containing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> quarts.

AIGLE

Pages 166-166

a small town in France, in Upper Normandy, 23 miles from D'Exereux, and 38 from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORNE">Orne</a>. It is surrounded with walls and ditches, and has six gates, three suburbs, and three parishes. It trades in corn, toys, and more particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a> and pins. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 5'. N. Lat. 48° 35'.

AIGUILLON

Pages 166-167

AIGUILLON, a small town of France in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guienne, and department of Garonne and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, which has a considerable trade in wines, brandy, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 22. N. Lat. 44. 25.

AIGUISE

Pages 167-167

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with its four ends sharpened, but so as to terminate in obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>.—It differs from the cross fetchees, in as much as the latter tapers by degrees to a point, and the former only at the ends.

AIKMAN

Pages 167-167

WILLIAM, a painter of considerable eminence, was born in Scotland, October 24. 1682. He was the son of William Aikman Esq. of Cairney, and was intended by his father to follow his own profession, which was that of an advocate at the Scotch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>. But the genius of the son led him to other studies. He devoted himself to the fine arts, especially that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and having for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> prosecuted his studies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in the year 1707 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, resided in Rome for three years, afterwards travelled to Constantinople and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>, and in 1712 returned to his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. About the year 1723 he fixed his residence in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he followed the profession of painting, and had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to be patronised by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Argyle, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURLINGTON">Burlington</a>, Sir Godfrey Kneller, and other liberal encouragers of the arts. He painted many portraits of persons of the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in England and Scotland; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family for the earl of Burlington, now in the possession of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, which was unfinished at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Some of his portraits painted in Scotland are in the possession of the duke of Argyle, the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> and others. Mr Aikman died in London, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 4. 1731. Six months previous to his death he had lost a son at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 17. The remains of both were removed to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and were interred in the Greyfriars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Mr Somerville the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHASE">Chase</a>, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>, Mr Allan Ramsay the Scottish poet, and Mr Thomson, were among Mr Aikman's intimate acquaintances; and the muse of each, in elegiac numbers, offered a warm tribute to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of their departed friend. The following epitaph from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> of Mr Mallet, was engraved on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>: Dear to the good and wise, disprais'd by none, Here <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> in peace the father and the son; By virtue as by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> ally'd, The painter's genius, but without the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>: Worth unambitious, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> afraid to shine, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">Honour</a>'s clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and friendship's warmth divine: The son fair rising knew too short a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>; But, oh! how more severe the father's fate! He <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him torn untimely from his side, Felt all a father's anguish—weeping and died. Mr Aikman's style of painting was an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the pleasing simplicity of nature. It is distinguished by softness of light, mellowness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, and mildness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of colouring.
