His compositions have more placid tranquillity of ease, than boldness of touch and brilliancy of effect. His portraits are supposed to have some resemblance to those of Kneller, and not only in the imitation of the dresses of the time, but in the similarity of tint and manner of working.

AILANA

Pages 167-167

AILATH, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> AHELOTH, anciently a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea, situated near the Sinus Elatites of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It was also called Eliath, and Eloth (Stephanus, Strabo, Moses). The same with Elana.

AILMER

Pages 167-167
or Æthelmaræ, earl of Cornwall and Devonshire, in the reign of King Edgar. It is not known what family he was. His authority and riches were great, and so also in appearance was his piety. He founded the abbey of Cernel, in Dorsetshire; and had so great a veneration for Eadwald, the brother of St Edmund the Martyr, who had lived a hermit in that country, near the Silver Well, as they called it, that, with the assistance of Archbishop Dunstan, he translated his relics to the old church of Cernel. In 1016, when Canute, the son of Sueno, invaded England, and found himself stoutly opposed by that valiant Saxon prince Edmund Ironside, the son of Æthelred, this Earl Ailmer, with that arch traitor Eadric Streone, earl of Mercia, and Earl Algar, joined the Dane against their natural prince, which was one great cause of the Saxon's ruin. He did not long survive this; and we find mentioned in history only one son of his, whose name was Æthelward, earl of Cornwall, who followed his father's maxims, and was properly rewarded for it. For in 1018, Canute reaping the benefit of their treasons, and perceiving that the traitors were no longer useful, he caused the infamous Eadric Streone, and this Earl Æthelward, to be both put to death.

AILRED

Pages 167-167
or EALRED, abbot of Revelby in Lincolnshire, in the reigns of Stephen and Henry II. He was born in 1109, of a noble family, and educated in Scotland with Henry the son of King David. On his return to England, he became a monk of the Cistercian order, in the monastery of Revelby, of which he afterwards was made abbot. He died on the 12th of January 1166, aged 57, and was buried in his monastery. "He was (says Leland) in great esteem during his life; celebrated for the miracles wrought after his death; and admitted into the catalogue of saints." He was author of several works; most of which were published by Gilbo the Jesuit at Douay, 1631; part of them may be also found in the Bibliotheca Cisterciensis, and Bibliotheca Patrum. His principal work is the Speculum charitatis. Leland, Bale, and Pits, mention several manuscripts which never were published.

AILSA

Pages 167-168

an inflated rock on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Scotland, between the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYRSHIRE">Ayrshire</a> and Cantire. It is two miles in circumference at the base, is accessible only at one <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and rises to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> height in a pyramidal form. A few goats and rabbits pick up a subsistence among the short <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> and furze; but the importance <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a> importance of the rock consists in the great variety and immense numbers of birds which frequent it, particularly the gannets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> folan geese, some of which are taken for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and others for the feathers. The rock is rented from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Caflillis at £31 per annum. The depth of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> around the base is from 7 to 48 fathoms. It is surrounded with excellent banks, well stocked with cod and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fish. On one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rock are the remains of an old castle, which is said to have been erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the Spanish armada invaded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>.

AILSBURY

Pages 167-167
AYLESBURY, or ALESBURY, a borough town in Buckinghamshire, consisting of about 400 houses. The streets lie round the market-place, in the middle of which is a convenient hall, where the sessions are held, and sometimes the assizes for the county. It sends two members to parliament. It is sixty miles south-east of Buckingham, and forty-four north-west of London. W. Long. o. 40. N. Lat. 51. 40.

AINSWORTH

Pages 168-170

Robert, born at Woodyale in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a> in 1660, was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a boarding school at Bethnal green, from whence he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>, and to other places in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. After acquiring a moderate fortune, he retired, and lived privately till the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1743. We are indebted to his industry for a Latin and English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, which has been much used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>: he published it in quarto 1736; and in 1752, the fourth edition, under the care of Dr <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">Ward</a> of Gresham <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, and the Rev. William Younge, was enlarged to two vols. folio. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>, in Physics, a thin, fluid, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, transparent, ponderous, compressible, and dilatable body, surrounding the terraqueous globe to a considerable height. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">Atmosphere</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PNEUMATICS">Pneumatics</a>. Air, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">Mythology</a>, was adored by the Heathens under the names of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Juno; the former representing the superior and finer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the atmosphere, and the latter the inferior and groser part. The augurs also drew prefiges from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, &c. Air, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, &c., denotes the manner and very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is that which expresses the disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>.—It is sometimes also used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with gleeure or attitude. Air, in Music, is taken in different senses. It is sometimes contrasted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; and, in this sense, it is synonymous with <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> in general.—Its proper meaning is, A tune, which is set to words, or to short pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> that are called songs. In operas, we give the name of air to such pieces of music as are formed with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> and cadences, to distinguish it from the recitative; and, in general, every piece of music is called an air, which is formed for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, or even for instruments, and adapted to stanzas, whether it forms a whole in itself, or whether it can be detached from any whole of which it forms a part, and be executed alone. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the subject admits of harmony, and is set in parts, the air is, according to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, denominated a duett, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIO">trio</a>, a quartetto, &c. We need not follow Rouffleau, and the other philologists, in their endeavours to investigate the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word air. Its derivation, though found and ascertained, would contribute little to illustrate its meaning in that remote sense, to which, through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance of time, and the various vicissitudes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, it has now passed. The curious may consult the same article in the Dictionnaire de Musique by M. Rouffleau. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> music, there are several different kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRS">airs</a>, each of which agrees to a certain kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; and from these dances the airs themselves take their specific names. The airs of our operas are, if we may be permitted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, the canvas or substratum upon which are painted all the pictures of imitative music; melody is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and harmony the colouring; every picturesque object selected from the most beautiful parts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, every reflected sentiment of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> heart, are the models which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> imitates; whatever gains <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, whatever interests the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, whatever charms the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, or causes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> in the heart, these are the objects of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. An air which delights the ear, and discovers the learning of the composer; an air invented by genius, and composed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; is the noblest effort of music: it is this which explores the compass, and displays the delicacy, of a beautiful voice; it is in this where the charms of a well conducted symphony shine; it is by this, that the passions, excited and inflamed by nice gradations, reach and agitate the soul through the avenues of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> sense. After hearing a beautiful air, the mind is agreeable and serene: the ear is satisfied, not disgusted: it remains impressed on the fancy, it becomes a part of our essence, we carry it with us, we are able to repeat it at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: without the ability acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> to breathe a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of it, we execute it in our imagination in the same manner as we heard it upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>: one sees the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, the theatre; one hears the accompaniments and the applause. The real enthusiast in music never forgets the beautiful airs which he has heard; when he chooses, he causes the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> to recommence. The words to which airs are adapted are not always rehearsed in regular succession, nor spoken in the same manner with those of the recitative; and though, in general, they are very short, yet they are interrupted, repeated, transposed, at the pleasure of the artist. They do not constitute a narrative, which once is told over: they either delineate a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, which it is necessary to contemplate in different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of view; or inspire a sentiment in which the heart acquiesces with pleasure, and from which it is neither able nor willing to be disengaged; and the different phrases of the air, are nothing else but different manners of beholding the same image. This is the reason why the subject of an air should be one. It is by these repetitions properly placed, it is by these redoubled efforts, that an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, which at first was not able to move you, at length shakes your soul, agitates you, transports you out of yourself; and it is likewise upon the same principle, that the runnings, as they are called, or those long, mazy, and inarticulated inflections of the voice, in pathetic airs, frequently seem, though they are not always so, improperly placed: for whilst the heart is affected with a sentiment equitably moving, it often expresses its emotions by inarticulate sounds, more strongly and sensibly than it could do by words themselves. The form of airs is of two kinds. The small airs are often composed of two strains, which ought each of them to be sung twice; but the important airs in operas are frequently in the form of rondellas. Air, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AYR">Ayr</a>. Air-Bladder, in fishes. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">Comparative Anatomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Air-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">Gun</a>, a pneumatic machine for exploding bullets, &c., with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> violence. See Pneumatics. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-AIR_JACKET">Air-Jacket</a>, a sort of jacket made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, in which are several bags, or bladders, composed of the same materials, communicating with each other. These are filled with air through a leather tube, having a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> stop-cock accurately ground at the extremity, by which means the air blown in through the tube is confined in the bladders. The jacket must be wet, before the air be blown into the bags, as otherwise it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immediately escape through the pores of the leather. By the help of these bladders, which are placed near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, the person is supported in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, without making the efforts used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a>. Air-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">Pipes</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> foul air out of ships, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> places, by means of fire. These pipes were first found out by one Mr Sutton, a brewer in London; and from him have got the name of Sutton's Air-pipes. The principle on which their operation depends is known to everybody, being indeed no other than that air is necessary for the support of fire; and, if it has not access from the places most adjacent, will not fail to come from those that are more remote. Thus, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, the air enters through the ash-hole; but if this is closed up, and a hole made in the side of the furnace, the air will rush in with great violence through that hole. If a tube of any length whatever be inserted in this hole, the air will rush through the tube into the fire, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> there will be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> circulation of air in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the extremity of the tube is laid. Mr Sutton's contrivance then, as communicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a>, amounts to no more than this.—"As, in every ship of any bulk, there is already provided a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> place proportionable to the size of the vessel; it is proposed to clear the bad air, by means of the fire already used under the said coppers or boiling places for the necessary uses of the ship. "It is also well known, that under every such copper or boiler, there are placed two holes, separated by a grate; the first of which is for the fire, and the other for the ashes falling from the same; and that there is also a flue from the fire-place upward, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the fire is discharged at some convenient place of the ship. "It is also well known, that the fire once lighted in these fire-places, is only preserved by the constant draught of air through the forementioned two holes and flue; and that if the said two holes are closely stopped up, the fire, though <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> ever so briskly before, is immediately put out. "But if, after stopping up the abovementioned holes, another hole be opened, communicating with any other room or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a> place, and with the fire; it is clear, the said fire must again be raised and burn as before, there being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> draught of air through the same as there was before the stopping up of the first holes; this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> differing only from the former in this, that Air-Pipes, the air feeding the fire will now be supplied from another place. "It is therefore proposed, that, in order to clear the holds of ships of the bad air therein contained, the two holes above mentioned, the fire-place and ash-place, be both closed up with substantial and tight <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> doors; and that a copper or leaden pipe, of sufficient size, be laid from the hold into the ash-place, for the draught of air to come in that way to feed the fire. And thus it seems plain, from what has been already said, that there will be, from the hold, a constant discharge of the air therein contained; and consequently, that that air, so discharged, must be as constantly supplied by fresh air <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a> or such other communications as are opened into the hold; whereby the same must be continually refreshed, and its air rendered more wholesome and fit for respiration. "And if into this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pipe so laid into the hold, other pipes are let in, communicating respectively either with the well or lower decks; it must follow, that part of the air, consumed in feeding the fire, must be respectively drawn out of all such places to which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> shall be so made." This account is so plain, that no doubt can remain concerning the efficacy of the contrivance: it is evident, that, by means of pipes of this kind, a constant circulation of fresh air would be occasioned through those places where it would otherwise be most apt to stagnate and putrefy. Several other contrivances have been used for the same purpose; and Dr Hales's ventilators, by some unaccountable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, have been reckoned superior in efficacy and even simplicity to Mr Sutton's machine, which at its first invention met with great opposition, and even when introduced by Dr Mead, who used all his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> for that purpose, was shamefully neglected. A machine capable of answering the same purpose was invented by Mr Defaguliers, which he called the ship's lungs. It consisted of a cylindrical box set up on its edge, and fixed to a wooden pedestal. From the upper edge of the box issued a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> open at the end, and communicating with the cavity of the box. Within this box was placed a cylindrical wheel <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> on an axis. It was divided into 12 parts, by means of partitions placed like the radii of a circle. These partitions did not extend quite to the centre, but left an open space of about 18 inches diameter in the middle; towards the circumference, they extended as far as possible without interfering with the case, so that the wheel might always be allowed to turn freely.—Things being thus circumstanced, it is plain, that if the wheel was turned towards that side of the box on which the trunk was, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> would push the air before it, and drive it out through the trunk, at the same time that fresh air would come in through the open space at the centre, to supply that which was thrown out through the trunk. By turning the wheel swiftly, a strong blast of air would be continually forced out through the square trunk, on the same principles on which a common fanner winnows corn. If the wheel is turned the opposite way, a draught of air may be produced from the trunk to the centre. If this machine, then, is placed in a room where a circulation of air is wanted, and the trunk made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through one of Air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">Pump</a> of the walls; by turning the wheel swiftly round, the air will be forced with great velocity out of that room, at the same time that fresh air will enter through any chinks by which it can have access to supply that which has been forced out. It is evident, that the circulation which is promoted by this machine, is entirely of the same kind with that produced by Mr Sutton's; the turning of the wheel in Mr Defagulliers's machine being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the rarefaction of the air by fire in Mr Sutton's: but that the latter is vastly superior, as acting of itself, and without intermission, requires no arguments to prove. Mr Sutton's machine has yet another convenience, of which no other contrivance for the same purpose can boast; namely, that it not only draws out putrid air, but destroys it by causing it pass through fire; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has abundantly shown, that though putrid air is thrown into a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fresh air, it is so far from losing its pernicious properties, that it often produces noxious effects. We do not say, indeed, that putrid air becomes salutary by this means; but it is undoubtedly rendered less noxious than before; though whether it is equally innocent with the smoke of a fire fed in the common way, we cannot pretend to determine. Besides this machine by Mr Defagulliers, the ventilators of Dr Hales, already mentioned, and those called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>-sails, are likewise used for the same purpose. The former of which is an improvement of the Hessian bellows; the other is a contrivance for throwing fresh air into those places where putrid air is apt to lodge; but this has the last-mentioned inconvenience in a much greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> than any of the others, as the blast of fresh air throws out that which was rendered putrid by stagnation, in such a manner as to contaminate all around it. Air-Pump, a machine by which the air contained in a proper vessel may be exhausted or drawn out. See Pneumatics. Air-Sacs, in Birds. See Comparative Anatomy. Air-Shafts, among Miners, denote holes or shafts let down from the open air to meet the adits and furnish fresh air. The damps, deficiency, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMPURITY">impurity</a> of air which occur, when adits are wrought 30 or 40 fathoms long, make it necessary to let down air-shafts, in order to give the air <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to play through the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and thus discharge bad vapours, and furnish good air for respiration: the expense of which shafts, in regard of their vast depths, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the rock, drawing of water, &c., sometimes equals, nay exceeds, the ordinary <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADIT">adit</a>. Sir Robert Murray describes a method, used in the coal-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, of working mines without air-shafts. When the miners at Mendip have sunk a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a>, they will not be at the charge of an air-shaft till they come at ore; and for the supply of air have boxes of elm exactly closed, of about six inches in the clear, by which they carry it down about twenty fathoms. They cut a trench at a little distance from the top of the groove, covering it with turf and rods disposed to receive the pipe, which they contrive to come in sidewise to their groove, four feet from the top; which carries down the air to a great depth. When they come at ore, and need an air-shaft, they sink it four or five fathoms distant, according to the convenience of the breadth, and of the same fashion with the groove, to draw ore as well as air. Air-Threads, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given to the long filaments, so frequently seen in autumn floating about in the air. These threads are the work of spiders, especially of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> called the long-legged field-spider; which, having mounted to the summit of a bush or tree, darts from its tail several of these threads, till one is produced capable of supporting the creature in the air: on this it mounts in quest of prey, and frequently rises to a very considerable height. See Aranea. Air-Trunk, is also a contrivance by Dr. Hales to prevent the stagnation of putrid effluvia in jails, and other places where a great number of people are crowded together in a small space. It consists only of a long square trunk open at both ends; one of which is inserted into the ceiling of the room, the air of which is required to be kept pure; and the other extends a good way beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. Through this trunk a continued circulation is carried on: and the reason is, that the putrid effluvia which do so much mischief when collected, being much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the pure atmosphere, arise to the top of the room; and, if they there find a vent, will continually go out through it. These effluvia arise in very considerable quantity, being calculated by the late Dr Keil at no less than 39 ounces on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in 24 hours. These trunks were first made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of by Mr Yeoman, over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Commons, where they were <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches wide within; and over the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">Court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a> in Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, where they were six inches wide. They are sometimes made wider, and sometimes narrower: but the wider they are the longer they ought to be, more effectually to promote the ascent of the vapours. The reason why vapours of this kind ascend more swiftly through a long trunk than a short one, is, that the pressure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> is always according to their different depth, without regard to the diameter of their basis, or of the vessel which contains them; and, upon this principle, a gallon of water may be made to split a strong cask. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of putrid effluvia is long and narrow, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the columns of atmosphere preëxisting on the upper end of the trunk, and that which preëxists on the lower end, is much greater than if the column of putrid effluvia was short and wide; and consequently the ascent is much swifter.—One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a> of a single <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales, which was two inches in diameter, being held within one of these trunks over the House of Commons, the force of the ascending air made it rise so as to require four grains to restore the equilibrium, and this when there was no person in the house; but when it was full, no less than 12 grains were requisite to restore the equilibrium; which clearly shows that these trunks must be of real and very great efficacy. Air-Vessels, are spiral ducts in the leaves, &c., of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, supposed to be analogous to the lungs of animals, in supplying the different parts of a plant with air. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

AIRANI

Pages 170-171

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, an obscure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, in the fourth century, who denied the consubstantiality of the Holy Ghost with the Father and the Son. They are otherwise called Airanists; and are said to have have taken their name from one <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AIRE">Aire</a>, who distinguished himself at the head of this party, in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a> and Gratian.

AIRE

Pages 171-171

a strong town in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Artois, now the department of Pas-de-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, with a castle. It was taken by the French in 1710, and was confirmed to them by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>. It is seated on the river Lis, 22 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNKIRK">Dunkirk</a>, and communicates with St Omer's by a canal cut from the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 31'. N. Lat. 50° 38'.

AIRING

Pages 171-171

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> peculiarly used for the exercising horses in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It purifies the blood; purges the body from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> humours; and, as the jockeys express it, teaches the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> how to make his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RAKE">rake</a> equally, and keep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with the other motions of his body. It also sharpens the stomach, and keeps the creature hungry; which is a thing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, as hunters and racers are very apt to have their stomach <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> off, either from want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the too violent exercise which they are often exposed to. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the horse be over fat, it is best to air him before sunrise and after sunsetting; and in general, it is allowed by all, that nothing is more beneficial to those creatures than early and late airings. Some of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> managers, however, dispute this; they say, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of these times is too great for the creature; and that if, in particular, he is subject to catarrhs, rheums, or the like complaints, the dews and cold fogs, in these early and late airings, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be apt to increase all those disorders. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>, we see, also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-beams as of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to these animals; those which are kept hardy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> out all night, always running to those places where the sunshine comes, as soon as it appears in a morning. This should seem to recommend these airings that are to be made before sunrise, and a little time after sunrise. As to the caution, so earnestly inculcated by Markham, of using these early and late airings for fat horses, it is found unnecessary by many: for they say, that the same effect may be produced by airings at warmer times, provided only that they are made longer; and that, in general, it is from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> airings that we are to expect to bring a horse to a perfect wind and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> courage.

AISNE

Pages 171-171

a river of France, which rises in Champagne, and runs west by Soisson's in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, falling into the river Oise, a little above Compiegne. It gives name to one of the five departments which comprehend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Isle of France, and contains five communal districts.

AITOCZU

Pages 171-171

a considerable river of Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, which rises in Mount Taurus, and falls into the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Euxine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

AITON

Pages 171-171

WILLIAM, an eminent botanist and gardener, was born at a village near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in Scotland, in 1731. Having been regularly trained to the profession of a gardener, he came into England in the year 1754, and soon obtained the notice of the celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Miller, then superintendent of the physic-garden at Chelsea, who engaged him as an assistant. His industry and abilities recommended him to the princess-dowager of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> as a fit person to manage the botanical garden at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEW">Kew</a>. In 1759, he was appointed to this office, in which he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and which was the source of his fame and fortune. The garden at Kew, under the auspices of his present majesty, was defined to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> repository of all the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> which could be accumulated, by regal munificence, from researches through every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the globe. These treasures were fortunately committed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Mr Aiton, whose care and skill in their cultivation, and intelligence in their arrangement, acquired him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation among the lovers of the science, and the particular esteem of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> patrons. Under his superintendence, many improvements took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and edifices of Kew-gardens, which rendered them the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of botanical culture in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In 1783, his merit was properly rewarded with the lucrative office of managing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>-gardens of Kew, which he was allowed to retain with the botanical department. In 1789, he published his Hortus Kewensis; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a Catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a> cultivated in the Royal Botanic Garden at Kew, in three vols. 8vo. with 15 plates; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which had been the labour of many years. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> contained in this work amounted to between five and six thousand, many of which had not before been described. A new and curious article in it relates to the first introduction of particular exotics into the English gardens. The system of arrangement adopted is the Linnean, with improvements, which the advanced state of botanical science required. Mr Aiton with candour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> acknowledges the affluence he received in this work from the two eminent Swedish naturalists, Dr Solander and Mr Jonas Dryander. Indeed his character was such as secured him the friendship and good offices of the most distinguished names in science of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He was for many years peculiarly honoured by the notice of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Banks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. The Hortus Kewensis was received with avidity by the botanic world, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> was soon disposed of. Notwithstanding the singular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> of Mr Aiton, he fell into that incurable malady, a schirrous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>, of which he died in 1793, in his fifty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> year. His eldest son, devoted to the same pursuits, was, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s own nomination, appointed to all his father's employments. Mr Aiton's private character was highly estimable for mildness, benevolence, piety, and every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> and social virtue. He was interred in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Kew, amidst a most respectable concourse of friends. (Gen. Biog.)

AIX

Pages 172-173

a small but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Savoy, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a marquisate. It is seated on the lake Bourget, at the foot of a mountain, between Chamberry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNECY">Annecy</a>, and Rumilly. There is here a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, but it is almost entirely ruined. The mineral waters bring a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of strangers to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The place was originally called Aquae Gratianae, from the hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> built there by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Gratian. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5. 48. N. Lat. 45. 40. Aix, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the department of the Bouches du <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>, formerly Provence, in France. This city has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of silence and gloom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> characteristic of places delitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> indultry. It is, however, well built; and most like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> of any place in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, as well for the largeness of the buildings as in respect of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a> of the inhabitants. It is embellished with abundance of fine fountains, and several beautiful squares. The Preachers <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> is on the side of a hill; it is about 160 yards in length, and is surrounded with trees, and houses built with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> three stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> is at one end of the city, and is distributed into several fine apartments: the two lowest are taken up by the board of accounts, and by the senechal; that above is designed for the sessions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. The hall of audience is adorned with the pictures of the kings of France on horseback. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a> of the city is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, but hid by the houses of the narrow street in which it is placed. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a Gothic structure, with tombs of several earls of Provence, and some good pictures by French masters. The Corfe, or Orbitelle, is a magnificent walk, above 300 yards long, formed by a triple avenue of elms, and two rows of regular and stately houses. The church of the fathers of the oratory is a handsome building; and not far from thence is the chapel of the blue penitents, which is full of paintings. The convent of preachers is very fine; in their church is a silver statue of the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> almost as big as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. There are other churches and buildings which contain a great number of rarities. The baths without the city, which were discovered not long since, have good buildings, raised at a vast expense, for the accommodation of those who drink the waters. Although Aix was the first Roman settlement in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, it is not remarkable for ancient remains. The warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, from which it is now known and frequented, induced Sextus Calvinius to found a colony here, to which he gave the name of Aquae Sextiae. They were supposed to possess particular virtues in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of debility; and several altars have been dug up sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIAPUS">Priapus</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on which indicate their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to that deity for his supposed succour and assistance. E. Long. 5. 32. N. Lat. 43. 32. Aix-la-Chapelle, a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of France, between the ile of Oleron and the continent. It is 12 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHEFORT">Rochefort</a>, and 12 fourth-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUTH">louth</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a>. W. Long. 1. 4. N. Lat. 46. 5. Aix-la-Chapelle, a fine city of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia and duchy of Juliers, and capital of the department of Roer. All authors are agreed about its antiquity, it being mentioned in Caesar's Commentaries and the Annals of Tacitus. The Romans had colonies and fortresses there, when they were at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the Germans; but the mineral waters and the hot bath so increased its fame, that, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, it was advanced to the privileges of a city, by the name of Aquaegranii, that is, the waters of Granius; that which it has now, of Aix-la-Chapelle, was given it by the French, to distinguish it from the other Aix. It is so called, on account of a chapel built in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Holy Virgin by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>; who having repaired, beautified, and enlarged the city, which was destroyed by the Huns in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTILA">Attila</a> in 451, made it the usual place of his residence. The town is seated in a valley surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and woods, and yet the air is very wholesome. It may be divided into the inward and outward city. The inward is encompassed with a wall about three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> in circumference, having ten gates; and the outward wall, in which there are eleven gates, is about a league and a half in circumference. There are rivulets which run through the town and keep it very clean, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>; besides 20 public fountains, and many private ones. They have stone quarries in the neighbourhood, which furnish the inhabitants with proper materials for their magnificent buildings, of which the Stadt-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and the cathedral are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. There are likewise 30 parochial or collegiate churches. The market-place is very spacious, and the houses round it are stately. In the middle, before the Stadt-house, is a fountain of blue <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which throws out <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, from six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, into a marble basin placed beneath, 30 feet in circumference. On the top of this fountain is placed the statue of Charlemagne, of gilt <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, holding a sceptre in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and a globe in his left. The Stadt-house is adorned with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of all the emperors since Charlemagne. This fabric has three stories, the upper of which is one entire room of 160 feet in length and 60 in breadth. In this the newly-elected emperor formerly entertained all the electors of the empire. Aix-la-Chapelle is a free imperial city, and changes its magistracy every year on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a> of St John Baptist. The mayor is in the nomination of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> palatine, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Juliers, as protector of the city. This place is famous for several councils and treaties of peace concluded here; particularly those between France and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in 1668, and between Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and France in 1748. The hot sulphurous waters for which this place has so long been celebrated, arise from several sources, which supply eight baths constructed in different parts of the town. These waters near the sources are clear and and pellucid; and have a strong sulphureous smell resembling the washings of a foul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>; but they lose this smell by exposure to air. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> is saline, bitter, and urinous. They do not contain <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. They are also neutral near the fountain, but afterwards are manifestly and pretty strongly alkaline, inasmuch that clothes are washed with them without <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>. On the vaults above the springs and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-AQUEDUCTS">aqueducts</a> of these waters is found, every year, when they are opened, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of sulphur, which has been sublimed from the waters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the water of the hottest <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, by Dr Lucas's account, raises the quicksilver of Fahrenheit's thermometer to $136^\circ$—by Mons. Monet's account, to $146^\circ$—and the heat of the fountain, where they <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> drink, by Dr Lucas's account, to $112^\circ$. Dr Simmons has given the following account of their several temperatures, as repeatedly observed by himself with a thermometer constructed by Nairne. The spring which supplies the Emperor's Bath (Bain de l'Empereur), the New Bath (Bain Neuf), and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>'s Bath (Bain de la Reine de Hongrie), - St Quirin's Bath (Bain de St Quirin) - $127^\circ$ - The Rose bath (Bain de la Rose), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">Poor</a>'s Bath (Bain des Pauvres), both which are supplied by the same spring. - $112^\circ$ - <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>'s Bath (Bain de Charles), and St Corneille's Bath (Bain de St Corneille). - $112^\circ$ The spring used for drinking is in the High Street, opposite to Charles's Bath; the heat of it at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> is - $106^\circ$ Dr Lucas evaporated the water of the hottest spring (of the Emperor's Bath), and obtained 268 grains of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> from a gallon, composed of 15 grains of calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, 10 grains of selenites, and 243 grains of a saline matter made up of natron and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. They are at first nauseous and harsh, but by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> become familiar and agreeable. At first drinking, also, they generally affect the head. Their general operation is by stool and urine, without griping or diminution of strength; and they also promote perspiration. The quantity to be drank, as an alternative is to be varied according to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and other circumstances of the patient. In general, it is best to begin with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> or half a pint in the morning, and increase the dose afterwards to a pint, as may be found convenient. The water is best drank at the fountain. When it is required to purge, it should be drank in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and often repeated draughts. In regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHING">bathing</a>, this also must be determined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, strength, &c. of the patient, and by the season. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat of the bath should likewise be considered. The tepid ones are in general the best, though there are some cases in which the hotter ones are most proper. But even in these, it is best to begin with the temperate baths, and increase the heat gradually. These waters are efficacious in diseases proceeding from indigestion and from foulness of the stomach and bowels; in rheumatism; in the scurvy, scrophula, and diseases of the skin; in hysterical and hypochondriacal disorders; in nervous complaints and melancholy; in the stone and gravel; in paralytic complaints; in those evils which follow an injudicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>; and in many other cases. They ought not, however, to be given in hectic cases where there is heat and fever, in putrid disorders, or where the blood is dissolved or the constitution much broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The time of drinking, in the first season, is from the beginning of May to the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>; and, in the latter season, from the middle of August to the latter end of September. There are galleries or piazzas under which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> walk during the time of drinking, in order to promote the operation of the waters.—The Poor's Bath is free for everybody, and is frequented by crowds of poor people. It is scarcely necessary to add, that there are all kinds of amusements common to other places of public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>; but the sharpers appear more splendid here than elsewhere, affuming titles, with an equipage suitable to them. This city was taken by the French in 1792. They lost it the year following, but retook it in 1794. Aix-la-Chapelle is 21 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPA">Spa</a>, 36 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, and 30 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>. E. Long. 5° 48'. N. Lat. 51° 53'.

AJALON

Pages 165-166

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the tribe of Dan, one of the Levitical. Another in the tribe of Benjamin, in whose valley Joshua commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to stand still, being then in her decrease, and consequently to be seen at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. AJAN, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, has the river Quilimani on the south; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> from which that river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, on the west; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ethiopia, and the strait of Babelmandel, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; and the Eastern, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, on the east. coast abounds with all necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and has plenty of very good horses. The kings of Ajan are often at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Abyssins; and all the prisoners they take sell to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Cambaya, those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, and other Arabs, who come to trade in their harbours, and give them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, coloured cloths, glass-beads, raisins, and dates; for which they also take back, besides slaves, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>. The whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coast, from Zanguebar to the strait of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BABEL">Babel</a>-mandel, is called the coast of Ajan; and a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is styled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">Desert</a> coast.

AJAZZO

Pages 166-166

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARAMANIA">Caramania</a>, anciently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean, 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Antioch and 50 west of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Ilius anciently stood, and near which Alexander fought his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 33° 10'. N. Lat. 37° 0'.

AJUTAGE

Pages 172-172
or ADJUTAGE, a kind of tube fitted to the mouth of the veifel through which the water of a fountain is to be played. To the different form and structure of ajutages is owing the great variety of fountains.

AKENSIDE

Pages 173-173

Mark, a physician, who published in Latin "A Treatise upon the Dysentery," in 1764, and a few pieces in the first volume of the "Medical Transactions" of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of physicians, printed in 1768; but far better known, and to be distinguished chiefly hereafter, as a poet. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>-upon-Tyne, November 9, 1721; and after being educated at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a>-school in Newcastle, was sent to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; at which last he took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> in physic. He was afterwards admitted by mandamus to the same degree at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; elected a fellow of the college of physicians, and one of the physicians at St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>; and, upon the establishment of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, appointed one of the physicians to her majesty. That Dr Akenside was able to acquire no other kind of celebrity than that of a scholar and a poet, is to be accounted for by the following particulars in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and conduct, related by Sir John Hawkins.—Mr Dyson and he were fellow-students, the one of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and the other of physic, at Leyden; where, being of congenial tempers, a friendship commenced between them that lasted through their lives. They left the university at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and both settled in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>: Mr Dyson took to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, and being possessed of a handsome fortune, supported his friend while he was endeavouring to make himself known as a physician; but in a short time, having purchased of Mr Hardinge his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of clerk of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons, he quitted Westminster-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>; and for the purpose of introducing Akenside to acquaintance in an opulent neighbourhood near the town, bought a house at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a>-End, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSTEAD">Hampstead</a>; where they dwelt together during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season, frequenting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-room, and all clubs and assemblies of the inhabitants. At these meetings, which, as they were not select, must be supposed to have consisted of such persons as usually meet for the purpose of gossiping, men of wealth, but of ordinary endowments, and able to talk of little else than news and the occurrences of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Akenside was for displaying those talents which had acquired him the reputation he enjoyed in other companies:

AKIBA

Pages 173-174

a famous rabbin, flourished a little after the destruction of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> by Titus. He kept the flocks of a rich citizen of Jerusalem till the 49th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and then devoted himself to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> for 24 years; and was afterwards one of the greatest matters in Israel. According to the Jewish accounts, he had 24,000 scholars. He declared for the impostor Barcochebas, whom he owned for the Messiah; and not only anointed him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, but took upon himself the office of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. The troops which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HADRIAN">Hadrian</a> sent against the Jews, who under the conduct of this false Messiah had committed horrid massacres, exterminated this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a>. Akiba was taken, and put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cruelty. He lived 120 years; and was buried with his wife in a cave upon a mountain not far from Tiberias, and his 24,000 scholars were buried round about him upon the same mountain. It is imagined he invented a supposititious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> under the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>.

AKISSAT

Pages 174-174

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Thyatira, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, situated in a plain 18 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, which produces plenty of cotton and grain. The inhabitants who are reckoned to be about 5000, are said to be all Mahometans. The houses are built of nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> turf dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and are very low and ill contrived; but there are six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> mosques, which are all of marble. There are remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> on marble in several parts of the town, which are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ruins of the ancient Thyatira. It is seated on the river Hermus, 50 miles from Pergamos. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 28° 30'. N. Lat. 38° 50'.

AKOND

Pages 174-174

an officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, who takes cognizance of the causes of orphans and widows; of contracts, and other civil concerns. He is the head of the school of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and gives lectures to all the subaltern officers; he has his deputies in all the courts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, who, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> jadra, make all contracts.

AL-TAYEFF

Pages 377-377

a town of Hejaz, a district of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix. It is situated about sixty miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, behind Mount Gazwan, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> is more intense than in any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the district, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> very wholesome. Its territory abounds in fountains, and produces excellent raisins. The town is surrounded with a wall, but is not very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>.

ALA

Pages 174-175

is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by botanists for the hollow of a stalk, which either the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the pedicle of the leaf, makes with it; or it is that hollow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a>, or sinus, placed between the stalk or branch of a plant and the leaf, whence a new offspring usually issues. Sometimes it is used for those parts of leaves otherwise called lobes, or wings. ALAE (the plural <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>) is used to signify those petals or leaves of papilionaceous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, placed between those others which are called the vexillum and carina, and which make the top and bottom of the flowers. Instances of flowers of this structure are seen in those of peas and beans, in which the top leaf or petal is the vexillum, the bottom the carina, and the side ones the ale. ALAE is also used for those extremely slender and membranaceous membranaceous parts of some seeds, which appear as wings placed on them; it likewise signifies those membranaceous expansions running along the stems of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, which are therefore called alated stalks.

ALABANDA

Pages 175-175

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, near the Meander, situated beneath eminences resembling asses with pack-faddles, which gave rise to the jest; and between Amyzo to the west and Stratonice to the east. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> they enjoyed suffrages, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a convention of jurisdiction, by Pliny reckoned the fourth in order; hence the proverb in Stephanus, expressing their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>. It was built by Alabandus, whom therefore they deemed a god. The people were called Alabandi, Alabandenses (Cicero); and Alabandei, after the Greek manner, in coins of Augustus and Claudius; they were also called Alabandeni (Livy).

ALABARCA

Pages 175-175

in Antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> among the Jews of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, whom the emperors allowed them to elect, for the superintendency of their policy, and to decide differences and disputes which arose among them.

ALABASTER

Pages 175-175

is also said to have been used for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, containing ten ounces of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the alabaster was equal to half the sextary.

ALABASTRUM DENDROIDE

Pages 175-175

a kind of laminated alabaster, beautifully variegated with the figures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, trees, &c., found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hohenstein.

ALADINISTS

Pages 175-175

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Mahometans, answering to freethinkers among us.

ALADULIA

Pages 175-176

a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATOLIA">Natolia</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Antitaurus, which separate it from Amaia on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and from Carmania on the west. It has the Mediterranean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the south; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Frat, on the east, which divides it from Diarbeker. It comprehends the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and the east part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. Formerly it had kings of its own; but the head of the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> was cut off by Selim I., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of the Turks, who had conquered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. It is now divided into two parts: the north, comprehended between Taurus, Antitaurus, and the Euphrates, is a beglerbeglic, which bears the name of Marath, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town; and the south, seated between Mount Taurus and the Mediterranean, is united to the beglerbeglic of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEPPO">Aleppo</a>. The country is rough, rugged, rugged, and mountainous; yet there are good pastures, and plenty of horses and camels. The people are hardy and thievish. The capital is Malatigah.

ALAIN

Pages 176-176

Chartier, secretary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VII, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, born in the year 1386. He was the author of several works in prose and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; but his most famous performance was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a> of King Charles VII. Bernard de Girard, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of France, styles him "an excellent historian, who has given an account of all the affairs, particulars, ceremonies, speeches, answers, and circumstances, at which he was present himself, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had information of." Giles Coroxet tells us, that Margaret, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to the king of Scotland, and wife to the dauphin, passing once through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> where Alain lay asleep, she stepped and kissed him before all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> who attended: some of them telling her, that it was strange she should kiss a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who had so few charms in his person, she replied, "I did not kiss the man, but the mouth from whence proceeded so many excellent sayings, so many wise discourses, and so many elegant expressions." Mr Fontenelle, among his Dialogues of the Dead, has one upon this incident, between the princess Margaret and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. Mr Paquier compares Alain to Seneca, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of beautiful sentences interposed throughout his writings.

ALAIS

Pages 176-176

a considerable town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GARD">Gard</a>, and formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, situated on the river Gard, at the foot of the Cevennes. The Jesuits had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and a fort was built here in 1689. It is 34 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Montpelier, and 340 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 20'. N. Lat. 44° 8'.

ALAMAGAN

Pages 176-176

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, one of the Ladrones <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Marianne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> ocean, is situated in N. Lat. 18° 5', and E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 146° 47'. It is of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> form, and about 12 miles in circumference. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in some places of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, so that it may be seen at the distance of 12 or 14 leagues. Near the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> end of the island there is a volcano which emitted an immense body of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> in the year 1799, when it was visited by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Bals. The volcano is in a mountain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, rising above its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> 1200 or 1300 feet. The high parts of the island are rugged and sterile. In the lower parts there is a profusion and luxuriance of vegetation. They abound with cocoa-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a> trees, several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> fruit, and the melon or <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-tree of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NICOBAR_ISLANDS">Nicobar islands</a>.
