Some small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes, some banana trees, and one bread-fruit tree were discovered. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIZARDS">Lizards</a>, land-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRABS">crabs</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> partridges, quails, pigeons, owls, thrushes, and bullfinches, are numerous. But no fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which was the object of Captain Bals's visit, could be found.

ALAMANDUS

Pages 176-176
Lewis, in French Aleman, archbishop of Arles, and cardinal of St Cecilia, was one of the greatest men of the fifteenth century. The cardinal presided in the council of Basil, which deposed Eugenius IV, and elected the antipope Felix V. He is much commended by Aeneas Sylvius, as a man extremely well formed for presiding in such assemblies, firm and vigorous, illustrious by his virtue, learned, and of an admirable memory in recapitulating all that the orators and disputants had said. One day, when he ranged against the superiority of the pope over the council, he distinguished himself in such an eminent Alamannic manner, that several persons went to kiss him, while others preferred even to kiss his robe. They extolled to the skies his abilities and genius, which had raised him, though a Frenchman, to a superiority over the Italians, notwithstanding all their natural subtlety and fineness. There is no need of asking, whether Pope Eugenius thundered against the president of a council which deposed him. He deprived him of all his dignities, and treated him as a son of iniquity. However, notwithstanding this, Lewis Alamandus died in the odour of sanctity, and performed so many miracles after his death, that at the request of the canons and Celestine monks of Avignon, and the solicitation of the cardinal of Clermont, legate a latere of Clement VII, he was beatified by the pope in the year 1527.

ALAMANNI

Pages 176-176
Lewis, was born at Florence, of a noble family, on the 28th of October 1495. He was obliged to fly his country for a conspiracy against Julius de Medici, who was soon after chosen pope under the name of Clement VII. During this voluntary banishment, he went into France; where Francis I, from a love to his genius and merit, became his patron. This prince employed him in several important affairs, and honoured him with the collar of the order of St Michael. About the year 1540, he was admitted a member of the Inflammati, an academy newly created at Padua, chiefly by Daniel Barbaro and Ugolin Martelli. After the death of Francis, Henry duke of Orleans, who succeeded him in 1537, showed no less favour to Alamanni; and in the year 1551, sent him as his ambassador to Genoa: this was his last journey to Italy; and being returned to France, he died at Amboise on the 18th of April 1556, being in the 61st year of his age. He left many beautiful poems, and other valuable performances, in the Italian language. We have also some notes of his upon Homer's Iliad and Odyssey; those upon the Iliad were printed in the Cambridge edition of Homer in 1689, and Joshua Barnes has also inserted them in his fine edition of Homer in 1711.

ALAMODALITY

Pages 176-176

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is the accommodating a person's behaviour, dress, and actions, to the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> times in which he lives. ALAMODALITY of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, is defined the accommodation of mental productions, both as to the choice of subject and the manner of treating it, to the genius or taste of the times, in order to render them more acceptable to the readers.

ALAMODE

Pages 176-176

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a thin glossy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, chiefly used for women's hoods and men's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> scarfs.

ALAMOS

Pages 176-177

Balthasar, a Spanish writer, born at Medina del Campo in Castile. After having studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, he entered into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Anthony Perez, secretary of state under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. He was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem and confidence with his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, upon which account he was imprisoned after the disgrace of this minister. He was kept in confinement 11 years, when Philip III. coming to the throne, set him at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, according to the orders given by his father in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. Alamos <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in a private capacity, till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Olivarez, the favourite of Philip IV., called him to public employments. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> as well as judgment, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> was superior to his tongue. He died in the 88th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His Spanish translation of Tacitus, and the aphorisms which he added in the margin, gained him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a> in 1614; and was to have been followed, as mentioned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s privilege, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>, which however has never yet appeared. The author composed the whole during his imprisonment.

ALAN

Pages 177-177
Cardinal William, was born at Rossall in Lancashire, in the year 1532. He went to Oxford at the age of 15, and in 1550 was elected fellow of Oriel college. In 1556, being then only 24 years old, he was chosen principal of St Mary's hall, and one of the proctors of the university. In 1558 he was made canon of York; but, upon Queen Elizabeth's accession to the throne, he left England, and settled at Louvain in an English college, of which he became the chief support. In 1565 he visited his native country; but, on account of his extreme activity in the propagation of the Roman Catholic religion, he was obliged to fly the kingdom in 1568. He went first to Mechlin, and then to Douay, where he was made doctor of divinity. Soon after, he was appointed canon of Cambrai, and then canon of Rheims. He was created cardinal on the 28th of July 1587, by the title of St Martin in Montibus; and obtained from the king of Spain a rich abbey in the kingdom of Naples, and afterwards the bishopric of Mechlin. It is supposed to have been by the advice and instigation of this priest, that Philip II. attempted to invade England. He died on the 20th of October 1594, aged 63; and was buried in the English college at Rome. He was a man of considerable learning, and an elegant writer. He wrote many books in defence of the Romish religion. The most remarkable are, 1. A defense of the 12 martyrs in one year. Tho. Alfstead was hanged for bringing, and publishing, this and other Alan's works, into England, in the year 1584. 2. A declaration of the sentence of Sextus V. &c. A work intended to explain the pope's bull for the excommunication of Queen Elizabeth, and to exhort the people of England to take up arms in favour of the Spaniards. Many thousand copies of this book, printed at Antwerp, were put on board the Armada; but the enterprise failing, they were afterwards destroyed. 3. Of the worship due to saints and their relics 1583. This treatise was answered by Lord Burleigh, and is esteemed the most elegant of the cardinal's writings.

ALAND

Pages 177-178

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, with its dependent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eighty, is situated between the gulfs of Bothnia and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>. These islands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between N. Lat. 59° 47' and 60° 30', and between E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 19° 17' and 22° 7'. Aland constitutes the smallest of the possessions belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. It contains about seventy-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> English miles, and is in length about twenty English miles, and fifteen in breadth. Aland has been supposed anciently to have been governed by its own monarchs; it is certain, however, that since the fourteenth century it has made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the bishoprick and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABO">Abo</a>, with the exception that in the year 1743 Aland and the other islands submitted to Ruffia, and swore <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the czarina, but were soon after restored to Sweden by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Abo. These islands in former times frequently suffered from the invasions of the Ruffians, and the inhabitants had been forced to fly from their houses and fertile plains. But in 1718 a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a> was held here for the restoration of peace, by which the enjoyment of tranquillity was secured to them. Aland and the several isles contain eight parishes, each of which has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and besides these places of worship, there are seven chapels. The Laplanders and Fins were undoubtedly the earliest inhabitants of these islands, and their residence here is plainly to be traced in the names of places which still remain. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> are met with in these islands, and but one rivulet, which however is sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, one of which is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>-mill. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are numerous; the highest of them is called Ulfdubs Klint. The revenues which the crown of Sweden receives from Aland and the other islands, amount annually to nineteen thousand <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> hundred and eighty-five rix-dollars. Two hundred and ninety-eight fallers are registered in these islands, which cost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Sweden about five thousand rix-dollars yearly. Aland contains about three thousand seven hundred and fifty acres of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> in cultivation, which produce rye, wheat, oats, and barley, in the proportion of seven for one. The annual growth of wheat is about twenty-two thousand five hundred barrels. There is one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>, which has no arable land, and in this respect resembles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>. The inhabitants of this parish employ themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>, and purchase all the corn they have occasion for of their neighbours. They catch vast numbers of pilchards, of which they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> profit, it being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> traffic of these islands. It has been in agitation to build a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Aland, but the project has not hitherto been carried into execution, owing it is said, to the difficulty of choosing a proper spot for it. The usual route from Sweden to Finland is from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> office of Grillehamn in Uppland, which is eleven and a half Swedish miles, to Eckero in Aland; and from that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> across the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to Abo, which is five miles more. A Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> makes between six and seven English miles. In the year 1792 the number of inhabitants upon the island of Aland amounted to eleven thousand two hundred and sixty, which is upwards of a thousand to every square Swedish mile; a very great number when it is considered how mountainous the island is. The inhabitants of these islands live to very great ages. From the year 1692 to the present <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, nine persons are recorded to have died at the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of one hundred years; and perhaps the number had been found greater, had it been thought worthwhile to notice this particular. In 1703 there died a woman named <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERG">Berg</a>, who was one hundred and nine years old; and at Kumlinge, in the year 1766, another person of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> died at an age of upwards of one hundred and twenty years. One fifth part of the inhabitants are above fifty years old; old; a circumstance which affords a convincing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the healthiness of the place. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> which surrounds the isle of Aland is very seldom frozen, and was less so formerly than at the present time. In 1546 it was remarked as an extraordinary event, that in that year the sea was so frozen as to be crossed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. It seems latterly that these severe frosts happened once in ten years. The winter of the year 1702 was remarkably mild, so that barley was sown on the twenty-fifth of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, at which time there was plenty of pasture for cattle: considering its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> latitude, Aland enjoys a very favourable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. In their manners and customs the inhabitants of Aland do not differ greatly from the peasants of Up-land. Their marriages and funerals are celebrated much in the same manner. The Alanders <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> nourishing food; their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is generally made of rye, even when the crops of that kind of corn have proved unfavourable. Fresh fish, and fish dried <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> salted, together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, cheese, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>-meat, are their usual fare. They make use of the flesh of seals, and prepare a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> called *fiskbroppa*, composed of collops of the flesh mixed up with flour and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, and this they reckon excellent. In their voyages by sea they lay in a good stock of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and at those times are not sparing of meat and butter. The dress of the Alanders is becoming. The men wear, in general, short jackets which on holidays are commonly of blue cloth. The young peasants commonly wear cotton stockings, and many of them have even watches. The women, when full dressed, wear a petticoat and apron of camlet, cotton, or printed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. Their dress in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a> is generally of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> silk, with a camlet petticoat. The dwellings of the peasants are very neat and convenient, kept in good repair, and well lighted. They are usually built of wood, fir, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, and covered with the bark of the birch tree, or shingles. Their out-houses are mostly thatched. As they have no running streams and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-mills, scarcely any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> is without a windmill. The Alanders are an ingenious, lively, and courteous people; and on the sea display a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of skill and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. They are far from being superstitious, but are said to be of a litigious disposition. No bears or squirrels are to be found in these islands; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">elk</a>, which formerly was uncommonly numerous, is now no longer seen in them. The animals chiefly found are wolves, (which are said to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the sea from Finland, when it has happened to be frozen over) foxes, martens, hares, ermines, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATS">bats</a>, moles, rats, mice, &c.; otters are but rarely met with: on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> are found seals, &c. Above a hundred <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of birds are found in the islands. Fish are in great abundance. The number of insects amounts to eight hundred species, some of which are extremely destructive to trees and newly built houses. The mountains are chiefly formed of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>. (Acerbi's Travels.)

ALARAF

Pages 178-178

in the Mahometian <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, the partition wall that separates heaven from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>. The word is plural, and properly written *al araf*; in the singular it is written *al arf*. It is derived from the Arabic verb *arafa*, to distinguish. Alaraf gives the denomination to the seventh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>, wherein mention is made of this wall. Mahomet seems to have copied his Alaraf, either from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of separation mentioned in the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the Jewish writers, who also speak of a thin wall dividing heaven from hell. Mahometian writers differ extremely as to the persons who are to be found on Alaraf. Some take it for a fort of limbus for the patriarchs, prophets, &c., others <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> here such whose good and evil works so exactly <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> each other, that they deserve neither reward nor <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Others imagine this intermediate space to be possessed by those who, going to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> without their parents leave, and suffering martyrdom there, are excluded paradise for their disobedience, yet escape hell because they are martyrs.

ALARBE

Pages 178-178

a name given to those Arabians who live in tents, and distinguish themselves by their dress from the others who live in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>.

ALARES

Pages 178-178

in Roman Antiquity, an epithet given to the cavalry, on account of their being placed in the two wings of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>.

ALARIC

Pages 178-178

a famous general of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>. He entered Thrace at the head of 200,000 men, and laid waste all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> through which he passed. He marched next to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Thessaly; the Thessalians met him near the mouth of the river Peneus, and killed about 3000 of his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; nevertheless he advanced into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and after having ravaged the whole country, returned to Epirus, loaded with immense spoils. After staying here five years, he resolved to turn his arms to the west. He marched through Pannonia; and, finding little resistance, entered <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the conduct of Stilicho and Aurelianus, A.D. 400. After various battles and treaties, he at last took Rome by treachery, and permitted his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to plunder it; this happened A.D. 409. Alaric, having laid waste a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Italy, intended to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>; but a storm obliging him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> again, he besieged the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Cosenza; and having taken it, he died there in 411, eleven years after he first entered Italy.

ALARM

Pages 178-178

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">Fencing</a>, is the same with what is otherwise called an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> challenge.

ALARM-POLE

Pages 178-178
or **ALARM-place**, the ground for drawing up each regiment in case of an alarm. This is otherwise called the rendezvous.

ALASCANI

Pages 178-178

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Antithenians, whose distinguishing tenet, besides their denying <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, is said to have been this, that the words, *This is my body*, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of the eucharist, are not to be understood of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, but of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> celebration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. They are said to have taken the name from one Joannes Alasco, a Polish baron, superintendent of the church of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in England. See the next article.

ALASCO

Pages 178-179

John, a Polish nobleman of the 16th century, Alatamaha century, who, imbibing the reformed opinions, was expelled his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and became preacher to a Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> at Embleton; but foreseeing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> there, came to England about the year 1551, while the reformation was carrying on under Edward the VI. The publication of the Interim driving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> to such places as afforded them toleration, 380 were naturalized here, and obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of incorporation, by which they were erected into an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> establishment, independent on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of England. The Augustinian friars church was granted them, with the revenues, for the maintenance of Alasco as superintendent, with four assistant ministers, who were to be approved by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; and this congregation lived undisturbed until the accession of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, when they were all sent away. They were kindly received and permitted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at Embleton; and Alasco at last, after an absence of 20 years, by the favour of Sigismund, returned to his own country, where he died in 1560. Alasco was much esteemed by Erasmus, and the historians of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> speak greatly in his praise; we have of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, De Cena Domini liber; Epistolae continens Summam Controversiae de Cena Domini, &c. He had some particular tenets; and his followers are called Alascani in church-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>.

ALATAMAH

Pages 179-179

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which, rising in the Appalachian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, runs southeast through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and falls into the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, below the town of Frederica.

ALATERNUS

Pages 179-179

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the rhamnus. See Rhamnus, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALAUTA

Pages 179-179

a considerable river of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, which, after watering the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Transylvania and part of Wallachia, falls into the Danube almost opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICOPOLIS">Nicopolis</a>.

ALAY

Pages 179-179

signifying in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> "The Triumph," a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> which accompanies the assembling together of the forces of that vast empire upon the breaking out of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. It consists of the most splendid festivity, and is attended with acts of the most shocking barbarity. That which took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> upon occasion of the late war between the Porte and Russia is described by Baron Tott in his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> as follows: "It consists in a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASQUERADE">masquerade</a>, in which each trade successively pretends to the spectators the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of its respective art. The labourer draws his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a>, the weaver handles his shuttle, the joiner his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>; and these different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, seated in cars richly ornamented, commence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a>, and precede the standard of Mahomet, when it is brought out of the feraglio to be carried to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, in order to insure victory to the Ottoman troops. "This banner of the Turks, which they name Sandjak-Cherif, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> The Standard of the Prophet, is so revered among them, that notwithstanding its reputation has been so often tarnished, it still retains their implicit confidence, and is the sacred signal unto which they rally. Every thing proclaims its sanctity. None but the emirs are allowed to touch it; they are its guards, and it is carried by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. The Muslims alone are permitted to look upon it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> touched by other <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, it would be defiled; if seen by other eyes, profaned. In short, it is encompassed by the most barbarous fanaticism. "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> peace had unfortunately caused the ridiculousness, and especially the danger, of this ceremony to be forgotten. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> imprudently crowded to see it; and the Turks, who, by the situation of their houses, could make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of their windows, began to profit by the advantage; when an emir, who preceded the banner, proclaimed with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, 'Let no <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> dare to profane with his presence the holy standard of the prophet; and let every Mussulman who perceives an unbeliever make it known under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>.' "From that moment no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> was to be found; even those became informers, who, by letting out their houses, had rendered themselves accomplices in the crime. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> fury seized on every mind, and put arms in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; the more atrocious the cruelty, the more was it meritorious. No regard was paid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; pregnant women, dragged by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and trodden under feet by the multitude, perished in the most deplorable manner. Nothing was respected by these monsters; and under such auspices the Turks commenced the war."

ALBA

Pages 179-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the Marsi in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the Lacus Fucinus, still retaining its name. It stands upon an eminence, and is noted in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for being the state prison where captive princes were shut up, after being barbarously dragged through the streets of Rome at the chariot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> of a triumphant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>. Perseus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Macedon terminated his wretched <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in this confinement, with his son, the last hope of an illustrious line of kings. Syphax the Numidian, and Bithynius king of the Avernii, were also condemned to this gaol by the particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, which sometimes indulged its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> disposition by putting its captives to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Alba being situated in the centre of Italy, amidst difficult mountainous passes, and far from all means of escape, was esteemed a most proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for the purpose of guarding prisoners of importance. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> strength was added to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> security by fortifications, which remain to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in a state that proves their ancient solidity. For the entertainment of the garrison, which was required in a place of such <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> was erected, of which the ruins are still valuable, as well as the foundations of a temple, and other buildings of Roman times. Lucius Vitellius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of that name, had a villa near this place, famous for the variety and excellence of its fruit trees, which he had brought from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. His gardens were the nurseries where several of the most delicious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, that are now so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. mon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, were first cultivated and multiplied. It must have been necessary at Alba to shelter trees transplanted from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and to treat them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tenderness and care, in order to rear them to perfection: for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> region is extremely rigorous in winter; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> season lasts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and is accompanied with violent storms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> and falls of snow. The lake has been often frozen entirely over.

ALBA FIRNA

Pages 180-180
or Album, in our Old Customs, denoted rent paid in silver, and not in corn, which was called black-mail.

ALBA HELVORUM

Pages 180-180
or Albaugeta, in Ancient Geography, afterwards called Vivarium, now Viviers, in the south-east of Languedoc, on the Rhone. In the lower age the inhabitants were called Albenesi, and their city Civitas Albenesium, in the Notitia Galliae. E. Long. 4. 43. Lat. 44. 50.

ALBA JULIA

Pages 180-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, now Weißenburg, a town of Transylvania, on the river Maritius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mecritus, to the west of Hermantat, supposed to be called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> Julia, after Julia Domna the mother of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARACALLA">Caracalla</a>. There are, however, several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> found at or near Weißenburg, which bear COL APUL, that is Colonia Apulensis, without the least mention of Alba julia, though <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> after Caracalla's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Add, that Ulpius, reciting the colonies of Dacia, calls this colony Apulensis, and neither Alba nor Julia. Whence there is a suspicion, that Alba Julia is a corruption of Apulum. It was also called Apulum Augustum. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 25. o. Lat. 46. 46.

ALBA LONGA

Pages 180-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a colony from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVINIUM">Lavinium</a>, in Latium, established by Alcænus the son of Æneas, at the foot of the Mons Albanus: called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sow found by Æneas, which farrowed 30 white pigs on that spot; which circumstance was interpreted to portend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> there in 30 years after (Propertius). The epithet Longa was added on account of its length. It was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence till the building of Rome, as was foretold by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHISES">Anchises</a> (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>); was destroyed by Tullius Hostilius, all but the fan <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> temple; and the inhabitants were transplanted to Rome (Strabo).

ALBA POMPEIA

Pages 180-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, on the river Ceba, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEVA">Ceva</a>, in Liguria, the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTINAX">Pertinax</a>; a colony either established at first by Pompey, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> re-established by him after having been before settled by Scipio. The inhabitants were called Albenesi Pompeiani. At this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> the town is simply called <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a>, without any epithet.

ALBA TERRA

Pages 180-180

one of the numerous names for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">ALBA</a> REGALIS. See STUHL WEISSENBURGH.

ALBAHURIM

Pages 180-180

figura sedecim laterum, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance according to astrological physicians, who built their prognostics on it.

ALBAN

Pages 180-180

St., is said to have been the first person who suffered martyrdom for Christianity in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; he is therefore usually styled the protomartyr of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. He was born at Verulam, and flourished towards the end of the third century. In his youth he took a journey to Rome, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> with Amphibalus a monk of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAERLEON">Caerleon</a>, and served <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years as a soldier under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Diocletian. At his return home, he settled in Verulam; and, through the example and instructions of Amphibalus, renounced the errors of Paganism, in which he had been educated, and became a convert to the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. It is generally agreed, that Alban suffered martyrdom during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> under the reign of Diocletian; but authors differ as to the year when it happened: Bede and others fix it in 286; some refer it to the year 296; but Usher reckons it amongst the events of 303. The story and circumstances relating to his martyrdom, according to Bede, are as follows. Being yet a Pagan (<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least it not being known that he was a Christian), he entertained Amphibalus in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The Roman governor being informed thereof, sent a party of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to apprehend Amphibalus; but Alban, putting on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of his guest, presented himself in his stead, and was carried before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>. The governor having asked him of what family he was? Alban replied, "To what purpose do you inquire of my family? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you would know my religion, I am a Christian." Then being asked his name, he answered, "My name is Alban; and I worship the only true and living God, who created all things." The magistrate replied, "If you would enjoy the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of eternal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, delay not to sacrifice to the great gods." Alban answered, "The sacrifices you offer are made to devils; neither can they help the needy, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> the petitions of their votaries." His behaviour so enraged the governor, that he ordered him immediately to be beheaded. In his way to execution, he was stopped by a river, over which was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> so thronged with spectators that it was impossible to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> it; the saint, as we are told, lifted up his eyes to heaven, and the stream was miraculously divided, and afforded a passage for himself and a thousand more persons. Bede does not indeed give us the name of this river; but, notwithstanding this omission, the miracle, we suppose, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be the least believed. This wonderful event converted the executioner upon the spot, who threw away his drawn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and, falling at St Alban's feet, desired he might have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to die with him. This sudden conversion of the headman occasioning a delay in the execution till another person could be got to perform the office, St Alban walked up to a neighbouring hill, where he prayed for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to quench his thirst, and a fountain of water sprung up under his feet; here he was beheaded, on the 23rd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. The executioner is said to have been a signal example of divine vengeance; for as soon as he gave the fatal stroke, his eyes dropt out of his head. We may see the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> on Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in regard to this narrative, in his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of England. His words are these, speaking of St Alban: "The story of whose martyrdom, foiled and worse martyred with the fabling zeal of some idle fancies, more fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> than apprehensive of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, deserves no longer digression." Between 400 and 500 years after St Alban's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, Offa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Mercians, built a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and stately <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>; and the town of St Albans in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a> takes its name from our protomartyr.

ALBANA

Pages 180-180

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBANIA">Albania</a>, on the Calpian sea, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Catus and Albanus; now called Bachu, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Bachy, giving name to the Calpian sea, viz. Mer de Babu. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 49. o. N. Lat. 40. o.

ALBANI

Pages 181-181

Francis, a celebrated painter, born in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 17, 1578. His father was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> merchant, and intended to bring up his son to that business; but Albani having a strong inclination to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, when his father died, devoted himself entirely to that art, though then but twelve years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He first studied under Denys Calvert; Guido Rheni being at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> under this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, with whom Albani contracted a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> friendship. Calvert drew but one profile for Albani, and afterwards left him entirely to the care of Guido; under whom he made great improvement, his fellow-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> instructing him with the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and good humour. He followed Guido to the school of the Caracci; but a little after their friendship for each other began to cool; which was owing perhaps to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> of Albani, who could not bear to see Guido surpass him, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the jealousy of Guido at finding Albani make such rapid progress. They certainly endeavoured to eclipse one another; for when Guido had let up a beautiful altar-piece, Albani would oppose to it some fine <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of his; thus did they behave for some time, and yet spoke of each other with the highest esteem. Albani, after having greatly improved himself under the Caracci, went to Rome, where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> many years, and married in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but his wife dying in childbed, at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> request of his relations he returned to Bologna, where he entered again into the state of matrimony. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife (Doralice) was well defended, but had very little fortune; which he perfectly disregarded, so strongly was he captivated by her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. Albani, besides the satisfaction of possessing an accomplished wife, reaped likewise the advantage of having a most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a>; so that he had now no occasion to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any other woman to paint a Venus, the Graces, Nymphs, and other deities, whom he took a particular delight in representing. His wife answered this purpose admirably well; for besides her bloom of youth, and the beauty of her person, he discovered in her so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>, so many graces and perfections, so well adapted to painting, that it was impossible for him to meet with a more refined woman. She afterwards brought him several boys, all extremely beautiful and finely proportioned; so that she and her children were the originals of his most agreeable and graceful compositions. Doralice was so conformable to his intentions, that she took a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in setting the children in different attitudes, holding them naked, and sometimes suspended by strings, when Albani would draw them in a thousand different ways. It was from them, too, that the famous sculptors Flamand and Argaldi modelled their little Cupids. Albani was of a happy temper and disposition; his paintings, says Malvasia, breathing nothing but content and joy. Happy in a force of mind that conquered every uneasiness, his poetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> carried him through the most agreeable gardens to Paphos and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYTHERA">Cythera</a>; those delightful scenes brought him over the lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a> to the delicious abodes of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>; whence what Du Fresnoy says of the famous Giulio Romano may be justly applied to Albani: Taught from a child in the bright Muses' grots, He open'd all the treasures of Parnassus, And in the lovely <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> of painting The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of Apollo has reveal'd. He died the 4th of October 1660, to the great grief of all his friends and the whole city of Bologna. Malvasia has preserved some verses of Francifco de Leme, intended for his monument; the sense whereof is, "That the mortal remains of the illustrious Albani, he who gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> interred in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> never produced so wonderful an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> equal to his immortal one; which gave colours to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and a soul to colours. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMETHEUS">Prometheus</a> animated clay, and gave life by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; but Albani animated merely by the assistance of shade." He was very famous in his lifetime, and had been visited by the greatest painters. Several princes honoured him with letters; and amongst the rest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., who invited him to England by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> signed with his own hand.

ALBANIA

Pages 181-181

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, bounded on the west by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IBERIA">Iberia</a>; on the east by the Caspian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>; on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>, and the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, now Kur; which, springing from the Mochian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> that separate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHIS">Colchis</a> from Armenia, and watering the country of Mokan, receives the Aragus and Araxes, and falls into the Caspian sea within a small distance from the southern borders of this country.—The whole country formerly called Albania, now goes under the names of Schirwan and Eoë-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and is extremely fruitful and pleasant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historians take notice of the Albanian men being tall, strong-bodied, and, generally speaking, of a very graceful appearance; far excelling all other nations in comeliness as well as stature. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> travelers take no notice of the appearance of the men; but extol the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the women, which seems to be unnoticed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The Albanians were anciently an independent and pretty powerful people; but we find no mention made of their kings till the reign of Alexander the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Albania is said to have presented a dog of an extraordinary fierceness and size.—It does not appear that the Albanians were ever conquered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, even when their power was at the greatest height; though when they ventured to engage in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with that powerful empire, they were always defeated, as might naturally be expected.

ALBANO

Pages 181-182

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, on a lake of the same name name, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> of Rome. It was called by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> Albanum Pompeii, and built out of the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> Longa, which was destroyed by Tullus Hostilius. It stands within twelve miles south-east of Rome, and for the pleasantness of its situation is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> retirement of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many Roman princes. It is likewise the see of a bishop, who is one of the six senior cardinals. The town is famous for its excellent wine, and the ruins of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, which, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the inhabitants, was made for Alcænus. The prospect from the garden of the Capuchins is extremely pleasant, taking in the Campania of Rome, and terminating in a full view of the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> by the town lies the Alban lake, of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in circumference, which, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> round it, looks like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. It abounds with excellent fish, and over against the hermitage it is said to be unfathomable. The mountain of Albano is called Monte Cavo; on the top of which was a celebrated temple dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Juno. Near the Capuchins there is another convent of Franciscans; and not far from thence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Barberini, remarkable for very pleasant gardens, with the ruins of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, and several old fragments of mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 10. N. Lat. 41. 43. Albano is also a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, remarkable for the fertility of the surrounding territory, and for the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of the inhabitants.

ALBANS

Pages 182-182

Saint, a market town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thoroughfare, accommodated with good inns, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, at the distance of 21 miles. This town sends two members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> to the noble family of Beaucherc, and has one of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for wheat in England. St Albans is seated near the ruins of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, by Tacitus called Verulam; and by the Saxons Watlingcester, because it is seated on the road called Watlingstreet. Nothing now remains of Verulam but the ruins of old walls; in the fields adjacent to which they continue to find Roman coins, as they formerly found tessellated pavements. In <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of St Alban, Offa, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Mercians, anno 795, erected an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, calling it St Albans; and near it the town of the same name was afterwards built. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the abbey is remaining to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> have made it look like <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> on the outside; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> a bit off, the redness of the brick immediately appears. When the monasteries were dissolved, the townsmen paid 400l. to prevent its being levelled with the ground, and have since converted it into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>-church, which, for its largeness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, and antiquity, claims a particular regard. It had a very noble font of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, in which the children of the kings of Scotland were used to be baptized; and was brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Lea, when the city was in flames; but in the times of the late civil wars, it was taken away. Not many years since, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> was discovered in this church, said to be that of Humphry duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>: when the leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">coffin</a> was opened, the body was pretty entire, being preserved in a sort of pickle. There was a stately <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> in the middle of the town, as there were in many other places, where <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> Eleanor's body rested when it was brought out of the north for <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a> at Westminster; but it is now demolished. W. Albans <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0. 12. N. Lat. 51. 44.

ALBANUS MONS

Pages 182-182

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Illyria, called Allius by Strabo; the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which, together with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> to the east, joining it, called Monter Berbigi, separate the farther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBURNIA">Liburnia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> from Pannonia.

ALBANY

Pages 182-182

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of one of the ten counties of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of New-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, which goes by the same name, is a well-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, conferring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Here the sachems, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the kings of the Five Nations of Iroquois, met the governors of the British plantations, when they entered into any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with them. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 44. 29. N. Lat. 42. 30.

ALBARAZIN

Pages 182-182

a strong town, and one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It is seated upon an eminence, near the river Guadalquivir, a little below its source, and on the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> and New Castile. It is the seat of a bishop, and produces the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> in all Arragon. It is about 100 miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 10. N. Lat. 40. 32.

ALBARI

Pages 182-182

in Antiquity, properly denoted those who gave the whitening to earthen vessels, &c. In which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> they stood contradistinguished from Dealbari, who whitened walls.

ALBARIUM OPUS

Pages 182-182

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the incrustation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering of the roofs of houses with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> lime. This is otherwise called opus <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUM">album</a>. It differs from Tectarium, which is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name given to all roofing or ceiling, including even that formed of lime and sand, or lime and marble; whereas Albarium was restrained to that made of lime alone.

ALBATEGNI

Pages 182-183

an Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Batan in Mesopotamia, and a celebrated astronomer, who lived about the year of Christ 880, as appears by his observations. He is also called Mubammed ben Geber, Albataani, Mahomet the son of Geber, and Mubamedes Arategenis. He made astronomical observations at Antioch, and at Racah <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Arafa, a town of Chaldea. He is highly spoken of by Dr Halley as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of admirable genius, and an excellent observer. Instead of the tables of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> which were imperfect, he computed new ones; these were adapted to the meridian of Arafa or Racah, and were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> used as the best among the Arabs. Albategni composed in Arabic a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Science of the Stars, comprising all parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, according to his own observations and those of Ptolemy. This work was translated into Latin by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIBUR">Tibur</a>, and published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> in 1537, with some additions and demonstrations of Regiomontanus. It was reprinted at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a> in 1645, with this author's notes. Dr Halley detected many faults in these editions: Philos. Trans. for 1693, No. 204. In this work, Albategni gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s apogee since Ptolemy's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as well as the motion of the stars, which he makes makes one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in 70 years. He made the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Aries to be $18^\circ 2'$; and the obliquity of the ecliptic $23^\circ 35'$. Upon Albategni's observations were founded the Alphonsine tables of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>'s motions. *(Hutton's Math. Dict.)*

ALBATRI EQUI

Pages 183-183

an appellation given to such horses, in the games of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a>, as wore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> furniture.

ALBATROSS

Pages 183-183

in *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>*, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the diomedea. See *Diomedea, Ornithology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>*.

ALBAZIN

Pages 183-183

a town of Greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, with a strong castle. It is situated upon the river Amur, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Yamour, and belongs to the Muscovites. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 103. 30. N. Lat. 54° 0'.

ALBEMARLE

Pages 183-183

the most northern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Carolina in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>.

ALBENGUA

Pages 183-183

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. It is the see of a bishop; and is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> handsome town, but not well peopled, on account of the infalibility of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. It is seated in a very beautiful plain, which is well cultivated; and the outside of the town is surrounded with olive-trees. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port, about 38 miles south-west of Genoa. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8. 13. N. Lat. 44. 4.

ALBERNUO

Pages 183-183

a kind of camlet, brought from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a> by the way of Marfelles.

ALBERONI

Pages 183-183

JULIUS**, the son of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> gardener in the suburbs of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, born in 1664; who, by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a>, rose from this low origin to the employment of first minister of state at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. He routed that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETHARGY">lethargy</a> it had sunk into for a century past; awakened the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and raised the affluence of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, by his projects; one of which was to set the Pretender on the throne of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. He was at length deprived of his employment, and banished to Rome. He died in 1752, at the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 89. His *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> Politique*, collected from his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a> and letters, was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a> in 1753.

ALBERT

Pages 183-183
Margrave of Brandenburg, and the last grand master of the Teutonic order, laid aside the habit of his order, embraced Lutheranism, and concluded a peace at Cracow in 1525, by which he was acknowledged duke of the east part of Prussia (formerly called for that reason *Ducal Prussia*), but to be held as a fief of Poland, and to descend to his male heirs. See Prussia.

ALBERTI

Pages 183-183

LEONE BATTISTA**, was descended from a noble family in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>; and was perfectly acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. He wrote of all three in Latin; but his studies did not permit him to leave any thing considerable behind him in painting. He was employed by Pope Nicholas V. in his buildings, which he executed in a beautiful manner; and his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on architecture, which consists of 10 books, is greatly esteemed. He also wrote some Alberti's treatises of morality, and a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>. He died in 1485.

ALBERTISTS

Pages 183-183

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of scholastics, so named from their leader <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBERTUS_MAGNUS">Albertus Magnus</a>.

ALBERTUS

Pages 183-183

a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth about fourteen French livres: it was coined during the administration of Albertus archduke of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>.

ALBERTUS MAGNUS

Pages 183-183

a Dominican friar, and afterwards bishop of Ratishon, was one of the most learned men and most famous doctors of the 13th century. He is said to have acted as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>-midwife; and some have been highly offended that one of his profession should follow such an employment. A book entitled *De Natura Rerum*, of which he was reputed the author, gave rise to this report. In this treatise there are several instructions for midwives, and so much skill shown in their art, that one would think the author could not have arrived at it without having himself practised: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for Albert say he was not the writer thereof, nor of that other piece *De Secretis Mulierum*; in which there are many phrases and expressions unavoidable on such a subject, which gave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> offence, and raised a clamour against the supposed author. It must be acknowledged, however, that there are, in his Comment upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">Matter</a> of Sentences, some questions concerning the practice of conjugal duty, in which he has used some words rather too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> for chaste and delicate ears; but they allege what he himself used to say in his own vindication, that he came to the knowledge of so many monstrous things at confession, that it was impossible to avoid touching upon such questions. Albert was certainly a man of a most curious and inquisitive turn of mind, which gave rise to other accusations brought against him. It is said, that he laboured to find out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER_S_STONE"><a class="xref" hre</a>f="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; that he was a magician; and that he made a machine in the shape of a man, which was an oracle to him, and explained all the difficulties he proposed. He had great knowledge in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, and by his skill in that science might probably have formed a head with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> capable of articulating sounds; like to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">machines</a> of Boetius, of which Caiusdorus has said, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">Metals</a> lowe; the birds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a> in brafs; the brazen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> hisses; counterfeited swallows chatter, and such as have no proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, from brafs send forth harmonious music." John Matthaeus de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>, in his treatise *De Rerum Inventoribus*, has attributed the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of fire-arms to Albert; but in this he is confuted by Naude, in his *Apologie des Grandes Hommes*. Albert died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1280. His works were printed at Lyons, in 1651, in 21 volumes in folio.

ALBESIA

Pages 183-183

in Antiquity, a kind of shields otherwise called Decumana. See Decumana.

ALBI

Pages 183-184

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARN">Tarn</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Albigensis, in Upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is dedicated to St Cecilia, and has one of the finest choirs in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Here is a very valuable silver shrine, of exquisite workmanship, of the mosaic kind: it contains the relics of St Clair, the first bishop of this city. The chapel of this pretended saint is magnificent, and adorned with paintings. The <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">Lice</a> is a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> walk without the city: what distinguishes this from all others, is a terrace above Albigenses, above a deep mall, which serves instead of a fossa; it is bordered with two rows of very fine trees, which are kept in excellent order. There are four gates, through which you may view all the beauties of a delightful plain. At one end of this is the convent of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMINICANS">Dominicans</a>. The archbishop's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> is very beautiful. The river washes its walls, and serves both for an ornament and defense. This city is seated on the river Tarn, 35 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, and 250 south of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 9. N. Lat. 43° 16'. The Albigeois is a small territory about twenty-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles in length, and twenty in breadth, abounding in corn, wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, saffron, plums, and sheep; and the inhabitants have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in dried prunes, grapes, a coarse sort of cloth, and wines of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAILLAC">Gaillac</a>. These wines are the only fort hereabouts that are fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a>: they are carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Bordeaux, and generally sold to the British. They have likewise several coal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>.

ALBIGENSES

Pages 184-184

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> party of reformers, about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a> and the Albigeois in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, who sprung up in the 12th century, and distinguished themselves by their opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> and ceremonies of the Roman church. This fact had their name, it is supposed, either by reason there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBI">Albi</a>, or because they were condemned by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> held in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>.
