In effect, it does not appear that they were known by this name before the holding of that council. The Albigenses were also called Albani, Albigeosi, Albi, and Albanenses, though some distinguish these last from them. Other names given to them are, Henricians, Abelardists, Bulgarians, &c.; some on account of the qualities they assumed; others on that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from whence it is pretended they were derived; and others on account of persons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> who adopted their cause, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de Bruis, Arnold de Bresse, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABELARD">Abelard</a>, Henry, &c., Berengarius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not Wickliff himself, is by some ranked in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The Albigenses are frequently confounded with the Waldenses; from whom, however, they differ in many respects, both as being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to them in point of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, as having their origin in a different country, and as being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> heresies, particularly Manicheism, from whence the Waldenses are exempt. But several Protestant writers have vindicated them from that imputation. Dr Allix shows that a great number of Manichaeans did spread over the western countries from Bulgaria; and settled in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Languedoc, and other places, where they were also Albigenses; by which means, being both under the imputation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, they came, either by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> or malice, to be confounded, and called by the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name, though in reality entirely different. Other errors imputed to them by their opponents, the monks of those days, were, That they admitted two Christs; one evil, who appeared on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the other good, who has not yet appeared: That they denied the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the body; and maintained <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> souls to be demons imprisoned in our bodies, by way of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for their sins: That they condemned all the sacraments of the church; rejected <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> as useless; held the eucharist in abhorrence; excluded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of confessions and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>; maintained <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> unlawful; laughed at purgatory; prayers for Albigenses, the dead, images, crucifixes, &c. There were likewise said to be two classes of them; the Perfect, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">Believers</a>. The perfect boasted of their living in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINENCE">continence</a>, of eating neither <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, eggs, nor cheese. The believers lived like other men, and were even loose in their morals; but they were persuaded they should be saved by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of the perfect, and that none were damned who received imposition of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> from them. But from these charges also they are generally acquitted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>; who consider them as the pious inventions of the Romish church, whose members deem it meritorious by any means to blacken heretics. However this be, the Albigenses grew so formidable, that the Catholics agreed upon a holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> or crusade against them. They were at first supported by Raymond, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Toulouse. Pope Innocent III, furious to put a stop to their progress, sent a legate into their country; which failing, he stirred up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Augustus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, and the other princes and great men of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon them. Upon this the count of Toulouse, who had sided with them, made his submission to the pope, and went over to the Catholics; but soon after, finding himself plundered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSADES">crusades</a>, he declared war against them, and was joined by the king of Arragon. His <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was defeated at the siege of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a>, where he himself was killed, and the defeat followed by the surrender of the city of Toulouse, and the conquest of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Languedoc and Provence. His son Raymond succeeded him; who agreed with the king and the pope to set up the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in his estates, and to extirpate the Albigenses. In an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> held at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, the archbishop of Toulouse drew up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> agreeable to which the count made a most ample <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> against them, which he published at Toulouse in 1253. From this time the Albigenses dwindled by little and little, till the time of the Reformation; when such of them as were left fell in with the Vaudois, and became conformable to the doctrine of Zuinglius and the discipline of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>. ALBIGENSES is also a name sometimes given to the followers of Peter Vaud, or Waldo; and hence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with what we more properly call Waldenses, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">Poor</a> Men of Lyons. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> the word is applied by Camaratus, Thuanus, and several other writers. The reason seems to be, that the two parties agreed in their opposition to the papal innovations and encroachments, though in divers other respects said to be different enough. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a> labours hard to support a distinction between the two sects, alleging that the Albigenses were heretics and Manichaeans; whereas the Waldenses were only schismatics, not heretics; being found as to articles of faith, and only separating from the church of Rome on account of forms and discipline. Dr Allix endeavours to set aside the distinction: and shows, that both of them hold the same opinions, and were equally condemned and held for heretics; and this not for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of faith, but for declaring against the papal tyranny and idolatry, and holding the pope to be the Antichrist; which last, according to M. de Meaux, constitutes nothing less than Manicheism. In this sense the Lollards and Wickliffites in England were not only Albigenses but Manichaeans.

ALBINI

Pages 185-185

in Antiquity, the workmen employed in what was called Opus Albarium. They make a different profession from the dealbatores <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> whiteners.

ALBINOS

Pages 185-186

the name by which the Portuguese call the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> Moors, who are looked upon by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> as monsters. They at a distance might be taken for Europeans; but, when you come near them, their white <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> appears like that of persons affected with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>. In Saufure's Voyages dans les Alpes, is the following account of two boys, at Chamouni, who have been called Albinos. "The elder, who was at the end of the year 1785 about twenty, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one-and-twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, had a dull look, with lips somewhat thick, but nothing else in his features to distinguish him from other people. The other, who is two years younger, is rather a more agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; he is gay and sprightly, and seems not to want <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>. But their eyes are not blue; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a> is of a very distinct rose colour; the pupil too, when viewed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, seems decidedly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; which seems to demonstrate, that the interior membranes are deprived of the uvea, and of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mucous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> that should line them. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, their eye-brows, and eye-lashes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon their skin, were all, in their infancy, of the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>-white colour, and very fine; but their hair is now of a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a>, and has grown pretty strong. Their sight too is somewhat strengthened; though they exaggerate to strangers their aversion for the light, and half shut the eye-lids, to give themselves a more extraordinary appearance. But those who, like me, have seen them in their infancy, before they were tutored to this deceit, and when too few people came to Chamouni to make this affectation profitable to them, can attest that then they were not very much offended with the light of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. At that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they were so little desirous of exciting the curiosity of strangers, that they hid themselves to avoid such; and it was necessary to do a sort of violence to them before they could be prevailed on to allow themselves to be inspected. It is also well known at Chamouni, that when they were of a proper age they were unable to tend the cattle like the other children at the same age; and that one of their uncles maintained them out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, at a time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> when others were capable of gaining a subsistence by their labour. "I am therefore of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that we may consider these two lads as true albinos; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they have not the thick lips and flat noses of the white negroes, it is because they are albinos of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, not of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. This albinism affects the eyes, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a>, and the colour of the hair; it even diminishes the strength, but does not alter the conformation of the features. Besides, there are certainly in this malady various degrees; some may have less strength, and be less able to endure the light: but these circumstances in those of Chamouni are marked with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> sufficiently strong to entitle them to the unhappy advantage of being clasped with that variety of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> denominated albinos. "When <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> presents the same appearance often, and with circumstances varied, we may at last discover some general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, or some relation which that appearance has with known causes: but when a fact is so singular and so rare, as that of those albinos, it gives but little scope to conjecture: and it is very difficult to verify those by which we attempt to explain it. "I at first imagined that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> might be referred to a particular sort of organic debility; that a relaxation of the lymphatic vessels within the eye might suffer the globules of the blood to enter too abundantly into the iris, the uvea, and even into the retina, which might occasion the redness of the iris and of the pupil. The same debility seemed also to account for the intolerance of the light, and for the whiteness of the hair. "But a learned physiologist, M. Blumenbach, professor in the university at Göttingen, who has made many profound observations on the organs of sight, and has considered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> the albinos of Chamouni, attributes their infirmity to a different cause. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARATIVE_ANATOMY">comparative anatomy</a> has furnished him with frequent opportunities of observing this phenomenon; he has found it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>, in white dogs, and in owls; he says, it is generally to be seen in the warm-blooded animals; but that he has never met with it in those with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> blood. "From his observations, he is of opinion, that the redness of the iris, and of the other internal parts of the eye, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> that accompanies this redness, is owing to the total privation of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or blackish mucus, which, about the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, covers all the interior parts of the eye in its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> state. He observes, that Simon Pontius, in his treatise de Coloribus Oculorum, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago remarked, that in blue eyes the interior membranes were less abundantly provided with this black mucus, and were therefore more sensible to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of light. This sensibility of blue eyes agrees very well, says M. Blumenbach, with northern people, during their long twilight; while, on the contrary, the deep black in the eyes of negroes enables them to support the splendour of the sunbeams in the torrid zone. "As to the connexion between this red colour of the eyes and the whiteness of the skin and hair, the same learned physiologist says, that it is owing to a similarity of structure, confusus ex similitudine fatriciae. He affirms, that this black mucus is formed only in the delicate cellular substance, which has numerous blood-vessels contiguous to it, but contains no fat; like the inside of the eye, the skin of negroes, the spotted palate of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, &c. And, lastly, he says," Albinos says, that the colour of the hair generally corresponds with that of the iris. *Gazette litt. de Gottingue*, Oct. 1784. "At the very time that M. Blumenbach was <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> this memoir to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOTTINGEN">Gottingen</a>, M. Buzzi, surgeon to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, an eleve of the celebrated anatomist Moscati, published in the *Opuscoli Scelti de Milan*, 1784, tom. vii. p. 11, a very interesting memoir, in which he demonstrates by dissection what Blumenbach had only supposed. "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> of about 30 years of age died in the hospital of Milan of a pulmonary disorder. His body, being exposed to view, was exceedingly remarkable by the uncommon whiteness of the skin, of the hair, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and of all the other covered parts of the body. M. Buzzi, who had long desired an opportunity of dissecting such a subject, immediately seized upon this. He found the iris of the eyes perfectly white, and the pupil of a rose colour. The eyes were dissected with the greatest possible care, and were found entirely destitute of that black membrane which anatomists call the *uvea*: it was not to be seen either behind the iris or under the retina. Within the eye there was only found the choroid coat extremely thin, and tinged of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> red colour, by vessels filled with discoloured blood. What was more extraordinary, the skin, when detached from different parts of the body, seemed almost entirely deprived of the *rete mucosum*: maceration did not discover the least vestige of this, not even in the wrinkles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a>, where it is most abundant and most visible. "M. Buzzi likewise accounts for the whiteness of the skin and of the hair, from the absence of the *rete mucosum*, which, according to him, gives the colour to the cuticle, and to the hairs that are scattered over it. Among other proofs of this opinion, he alleges a well-known fact, that if the skin of the blackest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> be accidentally destroyed in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, the hairs that afterwards grow on that part are always white, because the *rete mucosum* which tinges those hairs is never regenerated with the skin. "The proximate cause of the whiteness of albinos, and the colour of their eyes, seems therefore pretty evidently to depend on the absence of the *rete mucosum*: But what is the remote cause? "In the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it seems probable that men affected with this infirmity form no distinct species, for they are produced from parents that have dark skins and black eyes. What is it then that destroys the *rete mucosum* in such persons? M. Buzzi relates a singular fact, which seems to throw some light on this subject. "A woman of Milan, named Calcagni, had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons. The two eldest had brown hair, and black eyes; the three next had white skins, white hair, and red eyes; the two last resembled the two eldest. It was said that this woman, during the three pregnancies that produced the albinos, had a continual and immoderate appetite for milk, which she took in great quantities: but that when she was with child of the other four children, she had no such desire. It is not however ascertained, that this supernatural appetite was not itself the effect of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or internal disease, which destroyed the *rete mucosum* in the children before they were born. "The albinos of Chamouni are also the offspring of albinos' parents with dark skins and black eyes. They have three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> by the same father and mother, who are also brunettes. One of them that I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> had the eyes of a dark brown, and the hair almost black. They are said, however, to be all afflicted with a weakness of sight. When the lads are married, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be curious to observe how the eyes of their children will be formed. The experiment would be particularly decisive if they were married to women like themselves. But this faulty conformation seems to be more rare among women than among men; for the four of Milan, the two of Chamouni, the one described by Maupeuis, the one by Helvetius, and almost all the instances of these singular productions, have been of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>. It is known, however, that there are races of men and women affected with this disease, and that these races perpetuate themselves in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a>, &c. "Upon the whole, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGENERATION">degeneration</a> does not seem to be owing to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; for though I have traversed the greatest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, and the other mountains of Europe, these are the only individuals of the kind that ever I met with."

ALBINOVANUS

Pages 186-186

a Latin poet, whom Ovid surmised the Divine. There is now nothing of his extant, except an Elegy on Drusus, and another on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">Death</a> of Meceenas.

ALBINTEMELIUM

Pages 184-185

ALBINTEMELIUM. Albintimilium, (Tacitus); <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at full length, Alesium Intemelium, (Pliny, Strabo); now Vintimiglia, situated in the south-west of the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, near the borders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, with a port on the Mediterranean, at the mouth of the rivulet Rotta, about halfway between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONACO">Monaco</a> and S. Remo. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 40' N. Lat. 43° 17'.

ALBINUS

Pages 186-187

Bernhard Siegfried, a celebrated physician and anatomist, was born of an illustrious family at Frankfort on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ODER">Oder</a> in 1697. His father was then professor of the practice of medicine in the university of Frankfort; but in the year 1702 he repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, being nominated professor of anatomy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> in that university. Here his son had an opportunity of studying under the most eminent masters in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, who, from the singular abilities which he then displayed, had no difficulty in prognosticating his future eminence. But while he was distinguished in every branch of literature, his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> was particularly turned to anatomy and surgery. His peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to these branches of knowledge gained him the intimate friendship of Ruysh and Rau, who at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> flourished in Leyden; and the latter, so justly celebrated as a lithotomist, is said to have seldom performed a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> operation without inviting him to be present. Having finished his studies at Leyden, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, where he attended the lectures of Du Verney, Vaillant, and other celebrated professors. But he had scarce spent a year there, when he was invited by the curators of the university of Leyden, to be a lecturer in anatomy and surgery at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Though contrary to his own inclination, he complied with their request, and upon that occasion was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of physic without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. Soon after, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father, he was appointed to succeed him as professor of anatomy; and upon being admitted into that office on the 9th of November 1721, he delivered an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a>, *De vera via <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> fabriec humani corporis cognitionem ducente*; which was heard with universal approbation. In the capacity of a professor, he not only bestowed the greatest attention upon the instruction of the youth entrusted to his care, but in the improvement of the medical art. With this view, he published many important discoveries of his own; and by by elegant editions, turned the attention of physicians to works of merit, which might otherwise have been neglected. By these means his fame was soon extended over Europe; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETERBURGH">Peterburgh</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>, cheerfully received him as an associate. In 1745, he was appointed professor of the practice of medicine at Leyden, and was succeeded in the anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Frid. Bern. Albinius. He was twice rector of the university, and as often he refused that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> when it was voluntarily offered him. At length, worn out by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and intense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he died on the 9th of September 1770, in the 74th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

ALBIOECE

Pages 185-185
or ALBEOCE, (Pliny, Strabo); otherwise called Reii Apollinaris, from their superstitious worship of Apollo; also Civitas Reiensium; now Riez, in Provence, about 18 leagues to the north-east of Toulon, on the north side of the rivulet Verdon; was originally a Roman colony, (Inscription). It is sometimes written Regium. The people were called Albici, (Cæsar.) E. Long. 1° 0' N. Lat. 43° 20'.

ALBION

Pages 187-187

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. New Albion, a name given by Sir Francis Drake to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, which he discovered and took possession of in the year 1578. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Cook visited this coast in 1778, and landed in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> situated in N. Lat. 44° 33'. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 235° 20'. In the year 1792, it was again visited by Captain Vancouver, who was employed in surveying the western coast of North America. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of New Albion, according to the latter circumnavigator, is between the 30th and 40th degrees of N. Latitude.

ALBIRO

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourth magnitude, in the constellation Cygnus.

ALBIS

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, which divided ancient Germany in the middle, and was the boundary of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, so far as it was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>: all beyond they owned to be uncertain, no Roman except Drusus and Tiberius having penetrated so far as the Elbe. In the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> 744, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> about five years before Christ, Domitius Ahenobarbus, crossing the river with a few, merited the ornaments of a triumph; so glorious was it reckoned at Rome to have attempted the passage. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, however, the river that before occupied the middle of ancient Germany, became its boundary to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, from the irruptions of the Sarmatian, who possessed themselves of the Transalpine Germany. The Elbe rises in the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a> out of the Rifenberg, runs through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, Misnia, Upper <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, Anhalt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, Danneberg, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAUENBURG">Lauenburg</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLSTEIN">Holstein</a>, and after being twinned by many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and passing by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMBURG">Hamburg</a> and Glückstadt, to both which places the river is navigable by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> vessels, falls into the German or North <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

ALBISOLA

Pages 187-187

a small town belonging to the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> manufacture, and several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-houses of the Genoese <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>. It was bombarded in 1745 by the English. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 20'. N. Lat. 44° 15'.

ALBOGALERUS

Pages 187-187

in Roman Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> worn by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMEN">Flamen</a> Dialis, on the top of which was an ornament of olive branches.

ALBORAK

Pages 187-187

amongst the Mahometan Writers, the beast on which Mahomet rode in his journeys to heaven. The Arab commentators give many fables concerning this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of conveyance. It is represented as of an intermediate shape and size between an ass and a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it seems, was secured for it in paradise at the intercession of Mahomet; which, however, was in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> extorted from the prophet, by Alborak's refusing to let him mount when the angel Gabriel was come to conduct him to heaven.

ALBORG

Pages 187-187

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUTLAND">Jutland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of the same name, and a bishop's see. It has this name, which signifies eel-town, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eels taken here. It is seated on a canal, 10 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, 30 north of Viborg, and 50 north of Arhus. It has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>, and a safe and deep harbour. They have a considerable trade in herrings and corn; and a manufacture of guns, pistols, saddles, and gloves. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29° 16'. N. Lat. 56° 35'.

ALBORO

Pages 187-187

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a name by which the erythrinus, a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> fish caught in the Mediterranean, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> of Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>.

ALBRICIUS

Pages 187-187

born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a learned and able physician, and well versed in all the branches of polite literature. He lived in the 11th century, and wrote several works in Latin; particularly, 1. Of the Origin of the Gods. 2. The Virtues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">Ancients</a>. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">Poison</a>, &c.

ALBUGINEA TUNICA

Pages 187-187

in Anatomy, the third <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> innermost coat or covering of the testes; it is likewise the name given to one of the coats of the eye.

ALBUGINEUS

Pages 187-187

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> sometimes applied to the aqueous humour of the eye.

ALBUGO

Pages 187-187
or LEUCOMA, in Medicine, a distemper occasioned by a white opaque spot growing on the cornea of the eye, and obstructing vision. See Medicine Index.

ALBUM

Pages 187-187

in Antiquity, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a>, wherein the names of certain magistrates, public transactions, &c. were entered. Of these there were various sorts; as the album decurionum, album senatorum, album judicum, album praetoris, &c. Album Decurionum, was the register wherein the names of the decuriones were entered. This is otherwise called matriculatio decurionum. Album Senatorum, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of senators names, which was first introduced by Augustus, and renewed yearly. Album Judicum, that wherein the names of the persons of those decuriae who judged at certain times were entered. Album Praetoris, that wherein the formulae of all actions, and the names of such judges as the praetor had chosen to decide causes, were written. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> entered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> transactions of each year into an album, or table, which was hung up in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. Album is also used, in later times, to denote a kind of table, or pocket-book, wherein the men of letters with whom a person has conversed, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> their names with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> or motto. Album Graecum, the white dung of dogs, formerly prescribed for inflammations of the throat, &c. but now disused, and chiefly employed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-dressers to soften leather after the application of lime.

ALBUMAZAR

Pages 187-187

a learned Arabian astronomer in the tenth century, who wrote a treatise Of the Revolution of the Years.

ALBUMEN

Pages 187-188

a substance found both in animal and vegetable vegetable matters, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of eggs. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALBUQUERQUE

Pages 188-188

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, is seated on an eminence, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> miles from the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. It is commanded by an almost impregnable fortress, built on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, and serving to defend the town. It carries on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> and woollen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. It was taken by the allies of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain in 1705. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7°. N. Lat. 38°. 52'.

ALBURN

Pages 188-188

the English name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, being a mixture of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. Skinner derives the word, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, from the Latin albus, and the Italian burno, from bruno, "brown."

ALBURNUM

Pages 188-188

the soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> substance which in trees is found between the liber <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> inner bark and the wood, and in progress of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> acquiring solidity, becomes itself the wood. From its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and comparative softness, it has been styled by some writers the fat of trees, adeps arborum. The albumen is found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities in trees that are vigorous; though in such as languish, or are sickly, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of buds. In an oak six inches in diameter, this substance is nearly equal in bulk to the wood. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> of one foot diameter, it is as one to three and a half; of two and a half feet diameter, as one to four and a half, &c., but these proportions vary according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the trees.—The albumen is frequently gnawed in pieces by insects, which lodge in the substance, and are nourished from it.

ALBURNUS

Pages 188-188

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the cyprinus of Linnaeus. See Cyprinus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALCAICS

Pages 188-188

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a denomination given to several kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, from Alceus, their inventor. The first kind consists of five feet, viz. a spondee, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBIC">iambic</a>; an iambic; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a>; a dactyl; another dactyl: such is the following verse of Horace: Omnes | vol|dem cogni|nur, | omnium Verfa|tur urba |[<a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">arius</a>] | ocyus | Sors exi|tura. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind consists of two dactyls and two trochees: as, Exili|um impos|tura | cymbe. Besides these two, which are called dactylic Alcaics, there is another styled simply Alcic; consisting of an epitrite; a choriambus; another choriambus; and a bacchius: the following is of this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, Cur timet flavum Tiberim tangere, cur olivum? Alcaic Ode, a kind of manly ode composed of several strophes, each consisting of four verses; the two first of which are always Alcaics of the first kind; the third verse is a diameter hypercataleptic, or consisting of four feet and a long syllable; and the fourth verse is an Alcaic of the second kind. The following strophe is

ALCAID

Pages 188-189

ALCAIDE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ALCALDE, in the polity of the Moors, Spaniards, and Portuguese, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, or officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, answering nearly to the French provost and the British justice of peace.—The alcáid among the Moors is vested with supreme jurisdiction, both in civil and criminal <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. ALCALA de Guadeira, a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, upon the river Guadeira. Here are abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, from whence they convey <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> by an aqueduct. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 16'. N. Lat. 37° 15'. ALCALA de Henares, a beautiful and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Spain, in New Castile, seated upon the river Henares, which washes its walls. It is built in a very agreeable plain, and is of an oval <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The streets are handsome and pretty straight; one of them is very long, running from one end of the city to the other. The houses are well built; and there are several squares, the largest of which is an ornament to the city; it is surrounded on all sides with piazzas, where tradesmen have their shops, to expose several sorts of commodities to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, of which there is as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> plenty and variety as in most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Spain. The university was founded by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Ximenes, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, about the beginning of the 16th century. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> about Alcala is watered by the Henares, well cultivated, and very fruitful, while that at a distance is dry and sterile: it yields grain in plenty, very good <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a>-cattle, wine, and melons of a delicious kind. Without the walls is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, the water of which is so pure and so well tasted, that it is inclosed and shut up for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Spain's own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, from whence it is carried to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>.—This city is 10 miles south-west of Guadalajara, and 13 miles east of Madrid. W. Long. 4° 20'. N. Lat. 40° 30'. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ALCALA_REAL">ALCALA-Real</a>, a small city of Spain, in Andalusia, with a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>. It is built on the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountain, in a mountainous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to it is inconvenient, rough, and unequal; but to make amends for this, here are several kinds of exquisite fruit and wine. W. Long. 4° 15'. N. Lat. 37° 18'.

ALCANIS

Pages 189-189

a town of Arragon in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a>, 12 miles from Caffe. It was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the Moors; but being taken from them, it was made a commandery of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALATRAVA">Calatrava</a>. Here is a very remarkable fountain, which throws up <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> through 42 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>. It is surrounded with gardens and fruit trees, and defended by a good fortress. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 0'.

ALCANNIA

Pages 189-189
or ALCANNA, in Commerce, a powder prepared from the leaves of the Egyptian privet, in which the people of Cairo drive a considerable trade. It is much used by the Turkish women to give a golden colour to their nails and hair. In dyeing, it gives a yellow colour when steeped with common water, and a red one when infused in vinegar. There is also an oil extracted from the berries of alcanna, which is sometimes used in medicine.

ALCANTARA

Pages 189-189

a small, but very strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Extremadura, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It gives name to one of the three orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>. It is seated on the banks of the Tajo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a>, 21 miles from Cordova, in a very fruitful <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and is celebrated for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over that river. This was built in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, as appears by an inscription over one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, by the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUSITANIA">Lusitania</a>, who were obliged to supply the expense. It is raised 200 feet above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and though it consists but of six arches, is 670 feet in length, and 23 in breadth. At the entrance of the bridge, there is a small antique chapel hewn in a rock by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Pagans, who dedicated it to Trajan, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> did to St Julian. This city was built by the Moors, on account of the convenience of this bridge; which is at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the Tajo is very deep, running between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> steep rocks: for this reason they called it Al-Cantara, which in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies the Bridge. It was taken from them in 1214, and given to the knights of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALATRAVA">Calatrava</a>, who afterwards assumed the name of Alcantara. It was taken by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>, in April, 1706, and retaken by the French in November following. It is 45 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>, and 125 from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 12'. N. Lat. 39° 30'. Knights of Alcantara, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> order of Spain, which took its name from the above-mentioned city. They make a very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the expeditions against the Moors. The knights of Alcantara make the same vows as those of Calatrava, and are only distinguished from them by this, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> fleur de lys, which they bear over a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> cloak, is of a green <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. They possess 37 commanderies. By the terms of the surrender of Alcantara to this order, it was stipulated, that there should be a confraternity between the two orders, with the same practices and observances in both; and that the order of Alcantara should be subject to be visited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Calatrava. But the former soon released themselves from this engagement, on pretence that their grand-master had not been called to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of that of Calatrava, as had been likewise stipulated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. After the expulsion of the Moors, and the taking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, the sovereignty of the order of Alcantara and that of Calatrava was settled in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Castile by Ferdinand and Isabella.—In 1548, the knights of Alcantara sued for leave to marry, which was granted them.

ALCAREZ

Pages 189-191

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of La Mancha, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> defended by a pretty strong castle, and remarkable for an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> aqueduct. It stands near the river Guardamena, and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> about it is very fruitful. They have a breed of little running horses, which are very fleet and strong. It is 25 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, 108 south of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUENCA">Cuenca</a>, and 138 south by east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MADRID">Madrid</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 50'. N. Lat. 38° 28'. ALCASSAR do-Sal, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESTREMADURA">Estremadura</a>, which has a castle said to be impregnable. It is indeed very strong, both by art and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, being built on the top of a rock which is exceedingly steep on all sides. Here is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which produces very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> salt, from whence the town takes its name. fields produce <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of a sort of ruffies, of which they make mats, which are transported out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. W. Long. 9. 10. N. Lat. 38. 18. **Alcassar**, a city of Barbary, situated about two leagues from Larache, in Alga, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>. It was of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, and the seat of the governor of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom. It was built by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Almanzor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Fez, about the year 1180, and designed for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rendezvous for the great preparations he was making to enter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> in Spain, and to make good the footing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Almanzor had got some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before. It is said his father first invaded Spain with 300,000 men, most of whom he was obliged to bring back to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> to quell a rebellion that had broken out in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. This done, he returned to Spain again with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, as is said, of 200,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 300,000 foot. The city is now fallen greatly to decay, so that of fifteen mosques there are only two that they make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of. The reason, probably, is the bad situation of the town; for it stands so low, that it is excessively hot in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and almost overflowed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the winter. They affirm to be owing to a curse of one of their saints. Here are a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of flocks, who live very familiarly with the people, walking about the town, possessing the tops of the houses and mosques without molestation; for they esteem them sacred birds, and account it sinful to disturb them. At present, the batham of Tetuan appoints a governor to this town, which is the last of his dominions towards <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEQUINEZ">Mequinez</a>. Near this city there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ridge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, running towards Tetuan, whose inhabitants were never brought entirely under subjection; and whenever it was attempted, they revenged themselves by infesting the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, and robbing and destroying the travellers. When they were pursued, they retired into their woody mountains, where none could safely follow them. Not far from hence is the river Elmahassen, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Sebastian king of Portugal and the Moors; in which the Portuguese were defeated and their king slain. W. Long. 12. 35. N. Lat. 35. 15. **Alcavala**, in the Spanish Finances, was at first a tax of 10 per cent. afterwards of 14 per cent. and is at present of only 6 per cent. upon the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of every sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, whether moveable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> immoveable; and it is repeated every time the property is sold. The levying of this tax requires a multitude of revenue-officers sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the transportation of goods, not only from one province to another, but from one shop to another. It subjects not only the dealers in some sorts of goods, but those in all sorts, every <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a>, every merchant and shopkeeper, to the continual visits and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the tax-gatherers. Through the greater part of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in which a tax of this kind is established, nothing can be produced for distant sale. The produce of every part of the country must be proportioned to the consumption of the neighbourhood. It is to the Alcavala, accordingly, that Ufartiz attributes the ruin of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Spain. He might have imputed it to likewise the declension of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, it being imposed not only upon manufactures, but upon the rude produce of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. **Alcazar Leguer**, a town of Africa, in the kingdom of Fez, and in the province of Ifrout. It was taken by Alphonso, king of Portugal, in 1468; but soon after that, it was abandoned to the Moors. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the straits of Gibraltar. W. Long. 3. 50. N. Lat. 38. 0. **Alcazer**, a town of Spain, in New Castle, seated on the river Guardamena, which has a fortress on a high hill for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, and lies in a very fruitful country. It is 100 miles north-west of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>. W. Long. 2. 10. N. Lat. 38. 15. **Alce**, **Alces**, or **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELK">Elk</a>**, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the cervus, belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a> pecora. See Cervus. **Alcea**, the Holly-Hock. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Alcedo**, or Kingfisher. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> Index. **Alchemilla**, or Ladies-mantle. See Botany Index. **Alchemist**, a practitioner in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCHEMY">alchemy</a>. **Alchemy**, that branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a> which had for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objects the transmutation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>; the panacea, or universal remedy; an alkali, or universal menstruum; an universal ferment; and many other things equally ridiculous. Kircher, instructed in all the secrets of chemistry, has fully exposed the artifices and impostures of alchemists. An alchemist puts into a crucible the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> which is to be converted into gold: this he sets on the fire, blows it, stirs it with rods; and, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> operations, gold is found at the bottom of the crucible, instead of the matter first put in. This there are a thousand ways of effecting, without any transmutation. Sometimes it is done by dextrously dropping in a piece of gold concealed between the fingers, sometimes by casting in a little of the dust of gold or silver disguised under the appearance of some elixir, or other indifferent matter; sometimes a crucible is used which has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> bottom, and gold put between the two; sometimes the rod used to stir the matter is hollow, and filled with the dust of the metal desired; at other times there is metal mixed with the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>, the ashes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a>, or the like. Mr Harris very properly distinguishes alchemy from chemistry; and defines the former to be *ars sine arte*, cujus principium est mentiri, medium laborare, et finis mendicare; and the Italians have a proverb, *non ti fidare al alchemista povero o medico amato*. The ruin which has attended this delusion has occasioned several states to make severe laws against pretences to alchemy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> formerly banished all such as professed it; and the sacred canons likewise directed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of their censure against them. Diocletian and Caesar directed all books which treated of this subject to be burnt. Rymer furnishes us with a license for practising alchemy, with all kinds of metals and minerals, granted to one Richard Carter in 1476; Rymer, tom. xii. Nevertheless, we have had severe laws against alchemy, and multiplying of metals, as much so as against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> itself. **Alchornea**. See Botany Index. **Alciat** or **Alciate**, Andrew, a great lawyer, who flourished in the 16th century, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. He mixed much of polite learning in the explication of the laws, and happily drove out the barbarity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> which till then had reigned in the lectures and writings of lawyers; for which Thuanus highly praises. <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCIBIADES">Alcibiades</a> praises him. He published a great many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>-books, and some notes upon Tacitus. His Emblems have been much admired, and translated into French, Italian, and Spanish; and several learned men have written commentaries on them.

ALCEUS

Pages 188-188

a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> lyric poet, born at Mitylene, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESBOS">Lesbos</a>. Horace seems to think him the inventor of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>: Now the Roman muse inspire, And warm the song with Grecian fire. Francis. He flourished in the 44th Olympiad, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAPPHO">Sappho</a>, who was likewise of Mitylene. Alceus was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy to tyrants, but not a very brave soldier. He was present at an engagement, wherein the Athenians gained a victory over the Lebians; and here, as he himself is said to have confessed in one of his pieces, he threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his arms, and saved himself by flight. Horace, who, of all the Latin poets, most resembled Alceus, has made the like confession: With thee I <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> Philippi's plain, Its fatal rout, a fearful <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>! And dropp'd, alas! th' inglorious shield, Where valour's self was forc'd to yield; Where foil'd in dust the vanquish'd lay, And breath'd th' indignant <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> away. Francis. The poetical abilities of Alceus are indisputable; and, though his writings were chiefly in the lyric strain, yet his muse was capable of treating the sublimest subjects with a suitable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. Hence Horace says, Alceus strikes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> strings, And seas, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and exile, sings. Thus while they strike the various lyre, The ghosts the sacred sounds admire; But when Alceus lifts the strain To deeds of war and tyrants slain, In thicker crowds the shadowy throng Drink deeper down the martial song. Francis. Alceus, an Athenian tragic poet, and, as some think, the first composer of tragedies. He renounced his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> Mitylene, and passed for an Athenian. He left 16 pieces, one of which was Paphia, that which he produced when he disputed with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, in the 9th year of the 97th Olympiad. There is another Alceus mentioned in Plutarch, perhaps the same whom Porphyrius mentions as a composer of satirical lambics and epigrams, and who wrote a poem concerning the plagiarist of Euphorus the historian. He lived in the 14th Olympiad. We are told likewise of one Alceus, a Messenian, who lived in the reign of Vespasian and Titus. We know not which of these it was who suffered for his lewdness a very singular kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which gave occasion to the following epitaph: Αλκευς ταφος γυνης, &c. This is Alceus's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>; who died by a radish, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and punisher of adulterers. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on adulterers, was thrusting one of the largest radishes up the anus of the adulterer: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, for want of radishes, they made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a fish with a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> head, which Juvenal alludes to: Quodam macbos et mugillis intrat. Sat. x. The mullet enters some behind. Hence we may understand the menace of Catullus, Ah! tum te miserum, malique fati, Quem attrahit pedibus, patente porta, Percurrent raphanique, mugilisque. Epig. xv. Ah! wretched thou, and born to luckless fate, Who art discover'd by the unholy gate! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> once, alas! the jealous husband come, The radish or the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-fish thy doom.

ALCIBIADES

Pages 191-191

an Athenian general. It was the fate of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to live at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of confusion. The Greeks, grown insolent from their conquests in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, turned their armies against each other, and banded together under the conduct of the two most opulent states, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Macedon. Alcibiades, in the midst of an expedition he had planned against the enemies of his country, was recalled home to answer some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of a private <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; but fearing the violence of his enemy, instead of going to Athens, he offered his services at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, where they were readily accepted. By his advice the Macedonians made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with Persia, which gave a very favourable turn to their affairs. But his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in the republic raising jealousies against him, he privately reconciled himself to his country, and took again the command of an Athenian <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Here victory, waiting as it were at his command, attended all his motions. The loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> battles obliged the Spartans to sue for peace. He enjoyed his triumphs, however, only a short time at Athens. One unsuccessful event made him again obnoxious to the malice of his citizens; and he found it expedient to retire from Athens. In his absence the Spartans again took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and at the fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Eges entirely subdued the Athenian power. Alcibiades, though an exile, endeavoured to restore the power of his country; of which the Spartans having intelligence, procured him to be assassinated. He was a man of admirable accomplishments, but indifferently principled; of great parts; and of an amazing versatility of genius.

ALCINOUS

Pages 191-191
king of the Phaeacians, in the island now called Corfu, was son of Nautilus, and grandson of Neptune and Peribea. It is by his gardens this king has chiefly immortalized his memory. He received Ulysses with much civility, when a storm had cast him on his coast. The people here loved pleasure and good cheer, yet were skilful seamen; and Alcinous was a good prince.

ALCMAN

Pages 191-191

a lyric poet, who flourished in the 27th Olympiad, about 670 years before Christ. He was born at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>; and composed several poems, of which only some fragments are remaining, quoted by Athenaeus and some other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. He was very amorous; accounted the father of gallant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; and is said to have been the first that introduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of singing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> songs in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. He is reported to have been one of the greatest eaters of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; upon which Mr Bayle remarks, that such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> would have been extremely inconvenient, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> poetry had been at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> upon such a footing, as it has been often since, not able to procure the poet <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. He died of a strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>; for he was eaten up with <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-LICE">lice</a>.

ALCMANIAN

Pages 191-191

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Lyric <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> consisting of two dactyls and two trochees; as, Virginius puerique cantos. The word is formed from Alcman, the name of an ancient Greek poet, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> esteem for his erotics <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> amorous compositions.

ALCMENA

Pages 191-191

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Eleotheo <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Mycenae, and wife of Amphitryon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> putting on the shape of her husband while he was abroad in the wars, begot <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> upon her: he made that night as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as three ordinary ones.

ALCOCK

Pages 191-191

JOHN, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws, and bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a> in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VII. Was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERLEY">Beverley</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>. He was first made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of Wellsminster, and afterwards appointed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls. In 1471, he was consecrated bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>; in 1476, he was translated to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>; and in 1486, to that of Ely, in the room of Dr John Morton, preferred to the see of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. He was a prelate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning and piety; and so highly esteemed by King Henry, that he appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, and afterwards lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England. Alcock founded a school at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>, and built the spacious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> belonging to the episcopal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> at Ely. He was also the founder of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in Cambridge, for a master, six fellows, and as many scholars. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was formerly a nunnery, dedicated to St Radegund; and, as Godwin tells us, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> being greatly decayed, and the revenues reduced almost to nothing, the nuns had all forsaken it, except two; whereupon Bishop Alcock procured a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and converted it into a college. But Camden and others tell us, that the nuns of that house were notorious for their incontinence, that King Henry VII. and Pope Julius II. consented to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a> accordingly calls this nunnery "spiritualium meretricum cenobium," "a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> of spiritual harlots." Bishop Alcock wrote several pieces; among which are the following: 1. Mons Perfectionis. 2. In Psalmorum Petentiales. 3. Homiliae Vulgares. 4. Meditationes Pia. He died October 1, 1500; and was buried in the chapel he had built at Kingston upon Hull.

ALCOHOL

Pages 191-192
or ALKOHOL, in Chemistry, spirit of wine highly rectified. It is also used for any highly Alcohol rectified spirit.—Alcohol is extremely light and inflammable: It is a strong antiseptic, and therefore employed to preserve animal substances. See Chemistry Index. Alcohol is also used for any fine impalpable powder.

ALCOHOLIZATION

Pages 192-192

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of rectifying any spirit. It is also used for pulverization.

ALCOR

Pages 192-192

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a small <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> adjoining to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> bright one in the middle of the tail of ura <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>.—The word is Arabic. It is a proverb among the Arabs, applied to one who pretends to see small things, but overlooks much greater: Thou canst see Alcor, and yet not see the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>.

ALCORAN

Pages 192-196
or Al-koran, the scripture, or bible of the Mahometans. The word is compounded of the Arabic particle al, and coran or koran, derived from the verb caraar or karaa, to read. The word therefore properly signifies, the reading; or rather, that which ought to be read. By this name the Mahometans denote not only the entire book or volume of the Koran, but also any particular chapter or section of it; just as the Jews call either the whole Scripture, or any part of it, by the name of Karab, or Mikra, words of the same origin and import. Besides this peculiar name, the Koran is also honoured with several appellations common to other books of Scripture: as, al Farqan, from the verb faraka, to divide or distinguish; not, as the Mahometan doctors say, because those books are divided into chapters or sections, or distinguish between good and evil; but in the same notion that the Jews use the word Perak, or Pirka, from the same root, to denote a section or portion of Scripture. It is also called al Mojsaf, the volume, and al Kitab, the book, by way of eminence, which answers to the Bibliia of the Greeks; and al Dhikr, the admonition, which name is also given to the Pentateuch and Gospel. The Koran is divided into 114 larger portions of very unequal length, which we call chapters; but the Arabs jowar, in the singular jowa, a word rarely used on any other occasion, and properly signifying a row, order, or a regular series; as a course of bricks in building, or a rank of soldiers in an army; and is the same in use and import with the Sura, or Tora, of the Jews, who also call the fifty-three sections of the Pentateuch Sedarim, a word of the same signification. These chapters are not, in the manuscript copies, distinguished by their numerical order, but by particular titles, which are taken sometimes from a particular matter treated of, or person mentioned therein; but usually from the first word of note, exactly in the same manner as the Jews have named their Sedarim; though the word from which some chapters are denominated be very far distant, towards the middle, or perhaps the end, of the chapter; which seems ridiculous.
