There are five gates, which are open from sunrise till sun-setting; and seven forts or castles without the walls, the greatest of which is on the mole without the gate, all of which are well supplied with great guns. There are 10 large mosques and 50 small ones; three great colleges or public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and a great number of petty ones for children. The houses are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and built of stone and brick, with a square court in the middle, and galleries all around. There are said to be about 100,000 inhabitants in the city, comprehending 5000 Jewish families, besides Christians. There are four fundics or public inns, such as are in Turkey; and six causeries, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, for the unmarried Turkish soldiers, which will hold 600 each. There are no inns for Christians to lodge at; but only a few tippling huts kept by slaves, for the accommodation of Greeks and the poorer sort of travellers, where anything may be had for money. Here are bagnios or public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, in the same manner as in Turkey, at a very moderate rate. The women have baths of their own, where the men dare not come. Without the city there is a great number of sepulchres, as also cells or chapels, dedicated to marabouts or reputed saints, which the women visit every Friday. The Turkish soldiers are great tyrants; for they not only turn others out of the way in the streets, but will go to the farmhouses in the country for 20 days together, living at free quarters, and making use of every thing, not excepting the women. The Algerines eat, as in Turkey, sitting <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged round a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> about four inches high, and use neither knives nor forks. Before they begin, every one says Be yme Allah, "In the name of God." When they have done, a slave pours water on all their hands as they sit, and then they wash their mouths. Their drink is water, sherbet, and coffee. Wine is not allowed, though drank immoderately by some. The prospect of the country and sea from Algiers is very beautiful, it being built on the declivity of a mountain; but the city, though for several ages it has braved some of the greatest powers in Christendom, it is said, could make but a faint defence against a regular siege; and that three English fifty-gun ships might batter it about the ears of its inhabitants from the harbour. If so, the Spaniards must have been very deficient either in courage or conduct. They attacked it in the year 1775, by land and by sea, but were repulsed with great loss; though they had near 20,000 foot and 2000 horse, and 47 king's ships of different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> and 346 transports. In the years 1783 and 1784, they also renewed their attacks by sea to destroy the city and galleys; but after spending a quantity of ammunition, bombs, &c., were forced to retire without either its capture or extinction. The mole of the harbour is 500 paces in length, extending from the continent to a small island where there is a castle and large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a>. E. Long. 2. 12. N. Lat. 36. 49. ALGOA Bay, or Zwart-bops, in southern Africa, is situated in S. Lat. 33. 56. E. Long. 26. 53. and 500 miles distant from the Cape of Good Hope. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, who visited this place, found, in an adjoining valley, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of antelope, called the rietjok, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-goat, previously unknown to naturalists. He also mentions that great advantages might accrue to the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> Company from the erection of an establishment at this place, for the purpose of preparing salted beef and fish, in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>-pans, and the abundance of large bullocks in the vicinity; together with great numbers of excellent fish with which the coast abounds.

ALGOL

Pages 310-310

a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the third magnitude, called <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>'s Head, in the constellation Perseus. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> is 21° 50' 42" of Taurus, and its latitude 23° 23' 47" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; according to Flamsteed's catalogue. For an account of its changes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and other circumstances, see <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALGONQUINS

Pages 310-310

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who formerly possessed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tracts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> along the north shore of the river St Lawrence. For a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they had no rivals as hunters and warriors, and were long in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Iroquois; whom they agreed to protect from all invaders, and to let them have a share of their venison. The Iroquois, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, were to pay a tribute to their allies, out of the culture of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and to perform for them all the menial duties, such as flaying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, curing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, and dressing the skins. By degrees, however, the Iroquois associated in the hunting matches and warlike expeditions of the Algonquins; so that they soon began to fancy themselves as well qualified, either for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hunting, as their neighbours. One winter a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DETACHMENT">detachment</a> of both nations having gone out a hunting, and secured, as they thought, a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of game, fix young Algonquins and as many Iroquois were sent out to begin the slaughter. The Algonquins, probably becoming a little jealous of their associates, upon seeing a few elks, desired the Iroquois to return on pretence that they would have sufficient employment in flaying the game they should kill; but after three days hunting, having killed none, the Iroquois exulted, and in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two privately set out to hunt for themselves. The Algonquins were fo exasperated at seeing their rivals return laden with game, that they murdered all the hunters in the night time. The Iroquois dissembled their resentment; but in order to be revenged, applied themselves to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the art of war as practised among those <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nations. Being afraid of engaging with the Algonquins, at first they tried their prowess on other inferior nations, and, when they thought themselves sufficiently expert, attacked the Algonquins with such diabolical fury, as showed they could be satisfied with nothing less than the extermination of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; which, had it not been for the interposition of the French they would have accomplished.—The few Algonquin nations, that are now to be seen, seem entirely ignorant of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>, and subsist by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and hunting. They allow themselves a plurality of wives; notwithstanding which, they daily decrease in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, few or none of their nations containing above 6000 souls, and many of them not 2000. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is one of the three radical ones in North America, being understood from the river St Lawrence to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>.

ALGOR

Pages 310-310

with Physicians, an unusual coldness in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body.

ALGUAZIL

Pages 310-311

ALGUAZIL, in the Spanish polity, an officer whose business it is to see the decrees of a judge executed.

ALHAMA

Pages 311-311

a very pleasant town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated in the midst of some craggy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, about 25 miles S.W. of Granada, on the banks of the Rio Frio, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 26' N. Lat. 36° 39' and having the finest warm <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> in all Spain. It was taken from the Moors in 1481. The inhabitants, though surprised, and the town without a garrison, made a gallant defense; but being at length forced to submit, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was abandoned to the pillage of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, who, not satisfied with an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and jewels, made slaves of upwards of 3500 of the inhabitants.

ALHAMBRA

Pages 311-314

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> fortress and residence of the Moorish monarchs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>. It derives its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the materials which it was originally built with, Alhambra signifying a red <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It appears to a traveller a huge heap of ugly buildings as can well be seen, all huddled together, seemingly without the least intention of forming one habitation out of them. The walls are entirely unornamented, all gravel and pebbles, daubed over with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> by a very coarse <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; yet this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the Moorish kings of Granada, indubitably the most curious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> within that exiles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, perhaps in the world. In many countries may be seen excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> as well as ancient <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, both entire and in ruins; but nothing to be met with anywhere else can convey an idea of this edifice, except the decorations of an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the tales of the genii. Paffing round the corner of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s palace, one is admitted at a plain unornamented door in a corner. On my first visit, says Mr Swinburne, I confess I was struck with amazement, as I swept over the threshold, to find myself on a sudden transported into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">fairy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The first place you come to is the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> called the communa or del melicar, that is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bath; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with a deep basin of clear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the middle; two flights of marble steps leading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the bottom; on each side a parterre of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, and a row of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> trees. Round the court runs a peristyle paved with marble; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> bear upon very slight pillars, in proportions and style different from all the regular orders of architecture. The ceilings and walls are incrusted with fretwork in stucco, so minute and intricate, that the most patient draughtsman would find it difficult to follow it, unless he made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. This would facilitate the operation exceedingly; for all this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is frequently and regularly repeated at certain distances, and has been executed by means of square <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> applied successively, and the parts joined together with the utmost nicety. In every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> are Arabic sentences of different lengths, most of them expressive of the following meanings: "There is no conqueror but God;" or, "Obedience and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> Abouabdoulah." The ceilings are gilt or painted; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> has caused no diminution in the freshness of their colours, though constantly exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the walls is mosaic, disposed in fantastic knots and festoons. A work so <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a>, so exquisitely finished, and so different from all that he had ever seen, must afford a stranger the most agreeable sensations while he treads this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> ground, Alhambra. The porches at the ends are more like grotto-work than any thing else to which they can be compared. That on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand opens into an octagon vault, under the emperor's palace, and forms a perfect whispering gallery, meant to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the offices of both houses. Opposite to the door of the communa through which you enter, is another leading into the quarto de los leones, or apartment of the lions; which is an oblong court, 100 feet in length and 50 in breadth, environed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONNADE">colonnade</a> 7 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> on the sides and 10 at the end. Two porticoes or cabinets about 15 feet square, project into the court at the two extremities. The square is paved with coloured tiles; the colonnade with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble. The walls are covered five feet up from the ground with blue and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tiles, disposed chequerwise. Above and below is a border of small escutcheons, enamelled blue and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with an Arabic motto on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>; signifying, "No conqueror but God." The columns that support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> and gallery are of white marble, very slender, and fantastically adorned. They are 9 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, including base and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and 8½ inches diameter. They are very irregularly placed; sometimes singly, at others in groups of three, but more frequently two together. The width of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> arches above them is four feet two inches for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ones, and three for the smaller. The ceiling of the portico is finished in a much finer and more complicated manner than that of the communa, and the stucco laid on the walls with inimitable delicacy; in the ceiling it is so artfully frosted and handled as to exceed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. The capitals are of various designs, though each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> is repeated several times in the circumference of the court, but not the least <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> has been paid to placing them regularly or opposite to each other. Not the smallest representation of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> can be discovered amidst the varieties of foliage, grotesques, and strange ornaments. About each <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> is a large square of arabesques, surrounded with a rim of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, that are generally quotations from the Koran. Over the pillars is another square of delightful filigree work. Higher up is a wooden rim, or kind of cornice, as much enriched with carving as the stucco that covers the part underneath. Over this projects a roof of red tiles, the only thing that disfigures this beautiful square. This ugly covering is a modern addition made by a late prime minister, who a few years ago gave the Alhambra a thorough repair. In Moorish times, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> was covered with large painted and glazed tiles, of which some few are still to be seen. In the centre of the court are twelve ill-made lions muzzled, their fore parts smooth, their hind parts rough, which bear upon their backs an enormous bafon, out of which a lesser rises. While the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> were kept in good order, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> volume of water was thrown up, that, falling down into the bafons, palled through the beasts, and issued out of their mouths into a large reservoir, where it communicated by channels with the jet d'eau in the apartments. This fountain is of white marble, embellished with many festoons and Arabic ditiches, thus translated: "Seest thou not how the water flows copiously like the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>?" This resembles a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> washing over its shores, threatening shipwreck to the mariner. This water runs abundantly, to give drink to the lions. Terrible as the lion is our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The Nile gives <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to the king, and the lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> proclaim it. This garden is fertile in delights: God takes care that no noxious animal shall approach it. The fair princess that walks in this garden, covered with pearls, augment its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> so much, that thou mayst doubt whether it be a fountain that flows, or the tears of her admirers. Palling along the colonnade, and keeping on the south side, you come to a circular room occupied by the men as a place for drinking coffee, &c. A fountain in the middle refreshed the apartment in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. The form of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, the elegance of its cupola, the cheerful distribution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from above, and the exquisite manner in which the stucco is designed, painted, and finished, exceed all powers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>. Every thing in it inspires the most pleasing voluptuous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>: yet in this sweet retreat they pretend that Abouabdoulah assembled the Abencerrages, and caused their heads to be struck off into the fountain. Continuing your walk round, you are next brought to a couple of rooms at the head of the court, which are supposed to have been tribunals or audience chambers. Opposite to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALA">Sala</a> de los Abencerrajes is the entrance into the Torre de las dos hermanas, or the tower of the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; so named from two very beautiful pieces of marble laid as flags in the pavement. This gate exceeds all the rest in profusion of ornaments, and in beauty of prospect which it affords through a range of apartments, where a multitude of arches terminate in a large window open to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In a gleam of sunshine, the variety of tints and lights thrown upon this enfilade are uncommonly rich. The first hall is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a>-room, where the women sit; the musicians played above in four balconies. In the middle is a jet d'eau. The marble pavement is equal to the finest existing, for the size of the flags and evenness of the colour. The two sisters which give name to the room, are slabs that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> 15 feet by 7½, without flaw or stain. The walls, up to a certain height, are mosaic, and above are divided into very neat compartments of stucco, all of one design, which is also followed in many of the adjacent halls and galleries. The ceiling is a fretted cove. To preserve this vaulted roof, as well as some of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cupolas, the outward walls of the towers are raised 10 feet above the top of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a>, and support another roof over all, by which means no damage can ever be caused by wet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> or excessive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. From this hall you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> round the little myrtle garden of Lindaraza, into an additional building made to the east end by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. The rooms are small and low. His dear motto, Plus oultre, appears on every beam. This leads to a little tower, projecting from the line of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> wall, called el recador, or the dressing-room of the sultana. It is a small square cabinet, in the middle of an open gallery, from which it receives light by a door and three windows. The look-out is charming. In one corner is a large marble <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, drilled full of holes, through which the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of perfumes ascended from furnaces below; and here, it is presumed, the Moorish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> was wont to sit to fumigate and sweeten her person. The emperor caused this pretty room to be painted with representations of his wars, and a great variety of grotesques, which appear to be copies, or at least imitations, of those in the loggie of the Vatican. From hence you go through a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> passage to the hall of ambassadors, which is magnificently decorated with innumerable varieties of mosaics, and the mottos of all the kings of Granada. This long narrow antechamber opens into the commun on the left hand, and on the right into the great audience-hall in the tower of Comares; a noble apartment, 36 feet square, 36 high up to the cornice, and 18 from thence to the centre of the cupola. The walls on three sides are 15 feet thick, on the other 9; the lower range of windows 13 feet high. The whole wall is inlaid with mosaic of many colours, disposed in intricate knots, stars, and other figures. In every part various Arabic sentences are repeated. Having thus completed the tour of the upper apartments, which are upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the offices of the new palace, you descend to the lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a>, which consisted of bedchambers and summer-rooms; the back stairs and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a>, that facilitated the intercourse between them, are without <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>. The most remarkable room below is the king's bedchamber, which communicated by means of a gallery with the upper story. The beds were placed in two alcoves, upon a raised pavement of blue and white tiles; but as it was repaired by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> V, who passed some time here, it cannot be said how it may have been in former times. A fountain played in the middle, to refresh the apartment in hot weather. Behind the alcoves are small doors, that conduct you to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. These consist of one small closet with marble cisterns for washing children, two rooms for grown-up persons, and vaults for boilers and furnaces that supplied the baths with water and the stoves with vapours. The troughs are formed of large slabs of white marble; the walls are beautified with party-coloured earthen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>; light is admitted by holes in the coved ceiling. Hard by is a whispering gallery, and a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABYRINTH">labyrinth</a>, said to have been made for the diversion of the women and children. One of the passages of communication is fenced off with a strong <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> grate, and called the prison of the Sultana; but it seems more probable that it was put up to prevent any body from climbing up into the women's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. Under the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>-room is a long flue, called the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; and adjoining to it are several vaults, said to be the place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> of the royal family. In the year 1574, four sepulchres were opened; but as they contained nothing but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and ashes, were immediately closed again. This description of the Alhambra may be finished by observing how admirably every thing was planned and calculated for rendering this palace the most voluptuous of all retirements; what plentiful supplies of water were brought to refresh it in the hot months of summer; what a free circulation of air was contrived, by the judicious disposition of doors and windows; what shady gardens of aromatic trees; what noble views over the beautiful hills and fertile plains! No wonder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> wondered the Moors regretted Granada; no wonder that they still offer up prayers to God every Friday for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, which they regard as a terrestrial paradise! Ali, the son of Abu Taleb, is one of the most celebrated characters in Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> to Mahomet; and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fourteen engaged with youthful ardour in his cause. When Mahomet first revealed his prophetic character to his friends, and inquired who among them would undertake to be his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, Ali exclaimed, "O Prophet, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be thy attendant; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to rise against thee I will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> his legs, pluck out his eyes, dash out his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and even rip up his belly." Mahomet accepted his services, and honoured him with the titles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, vicegerent, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> to a new Moses. He was remarkable both for eloquence and valour; and the latter obtained him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of "the Lion of God, always victorious." He succeeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of the renowned house of Hashem, and was also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of the temple and city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. Mahomet gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Fatimah in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and the grandfather lived to embrace the children of his daughter. These advantages induced Ali to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> a wilful eye towards the regal succession; however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABUBEKER">Abubeker</a>, Omar, and Othman reigned before him. But after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the latter he was saluted caliph by the chiefs of the tribes, and the companions of the Prophet, when he was repairing to the mosque of Medina at the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, A.D. 655. Hegir. 35. Ayetha, the widow of the Prophet, strenuously opposed his succession; and under her influence two powerful chiefs soon raised the standard of rebellion. Ali greatly increased his difficulties by the imprudent removal of all the governors of provinces from their station. Telha and Zobeir, two chiefs of great influence, collected a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and induced Ayetha to attend them to the field of battle; but Ali gained a complete victory and took Ayetha prisoner. Telha fell in the field, and Zobeir was affiliated after surrendering upon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of quarter. This dastardly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was severely reprehended by Ali. He likewise kindly treated the captive widow, and sent her back to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the Prophet. Ali next attacked Moawiyah, who had been proclaimed caliph, and strongly supported by a powerful and numerous party. When the two armies approached each other, Ali proposed to decide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBAT">combat</a>, but to this his opponent would not agree. Several skirmishes were fought with considerable loss on both sides; but at length a pious fraud produced a division of sentiment in the army of Ali. They fixed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of lances a number of copies of the Koran, carried them before the troops, and exclaimed, saying, "This is the book which forbids Muslims to shed each other's blood, and ought therefore to decide our disputes." Ali was constrained to yield, and umpires were mutually chosen; on the side of Ali, Abu Moulla; Amru, the conqueror of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, on the part of Moawiyah. The day of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> decision arrived. Abu Moulla ascended the pulpit, and cried, "As I draw this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> from my finger, so I depose both Ali and Moawiyah from the caliphate." When Amru ascended, he cried, "As I put on this ring, so I invest Moawiyah with the caliphate, and also depose Ali." He also added, that Othman the former caliph had declared Moawiyah both his successor and avenger. Thus began that memorable contest among the Mahometans which was long agitated with considerable violence by both parties. Ali was highly enraged at this injustice; but, constrained for the present to yield, he retired to <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KUFA">Kufa</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of enthusiasts called the Kharejites revolted against Ali; but he quickly reduced them to subjection, and again obtained possession of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, and Egypt fell to the share of his rival. An unexpected event terminated the existing disputes. Three Kharejites one day converging together concerning the blood which had been shed, and the impending calamities, resolved to assassinate Ali, Moawiyah, and Amru, the three authors of the present disasters. They provided themselves with poisoned swords, and hastened to accomplish their purpose. Moawiyah was wounded, but the wound did not prove fatal. A friend of Amru fell in his stead. Ali was fatally wounded at the door of the mosque, and in the sixty-third year of his age, he expired on the fifth day after his wound, A.D. 660. A.Hegir. 40. Ali had eight wives besides Fatimah, and left a numerous family who were very remarkable for their valour. He also rose to high eminence for learning and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and of his works there are still extant a hundred maxims, a collection of verses, and a prophecy of all the great events which are to happen to the end of time. One of his sayings may be quoted as an example. "He who would be rich without wealth, powerful without subjects, and a subject without a master, has only to forsake sin, and serve God." The Mussulmans <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> Ali the heir of Mahomet, and the accepted of God, and his particular followers have possessed various states in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the Persian part of the Ufhe Tartars; and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>-reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> are at present of the feet of Ali. A monument is raised upon his tomb near Kufa, which the kings of Persia have successively decorated and religiously revered. Near the ruins of Kufa a city named Meftied Ali has been built to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Some of his deluded followers imagine that he is still alive, and that he will revisit the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> and fill the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. A green turban still continues to distinguish the descendants of Ali. (Gen. Biog.) Ali Bey, an eastern adventurer, is said to have been a native of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a>, and about the age of twelve or fourteen he was sold for a slave in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. The two Jews who became his masters presented him to Ibrahim, then one of the most respectable men in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In the family of this powerful man he received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of literature, and was also instructed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art. Both in letters and military skill he made a rapid improvement. He gradually gained the affection of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that he gave him his freedom, permitted him to marry, promoted him to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of governor of a district; and afterwards by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> he was raised to the elevated station of one of the governors of provinces. Deprived of his protector by death, and engaging in the dangerous intrigues that pave the way to power in that unstable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he procured his own banishment to Upper-Egypt. Here he spent two years in maturing... his schemes for future greatness, and in 1766, returning to Cairo, he either flew or expelled the beys, and seized the reins of government. Emboldened by success, he refused himself from the power of the Porte, coined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in his own name, and boldly assumed the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of Egypt. Occupied in more important concerns, the Porte made no vigorous opposition to his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and Ali Bey seized this favourable opportunity to recover a part of the Sûd or Upper Egypt, which had been taken by an Arab sheik. Next he sent out a fleet from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUEZ">Suez</a>, which seized upon Djedda, entered the port of Mecca; while a body of cavalry, commanded by Mohammed Bey his favourite, took and plundered Mecca itself. A young Venetian merchant laid before him a plan of reviving the ancient trade to the East Indies through the Mediterranean and Red Seas. Having formed an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, in 1772, with one Sheik Daher, a rebel against the Porte in Syria, he aimed at the conquest of all Syria and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>. He first endeavoured to secure Gaza; then his army forming a junction with that of Daher at a place called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">Acre</a>, advanced to Damascus. On the 6th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1771, a battle was fought at this place with the Turkish pachas, and Mohammed and Daher the commanders of Ali Bey routed them with great slaughter. They instantly took possession of Damascus, and the castle itself had also capitulated, when all on a sudden Mohammed hastened back to Egypt with all his Mamelukes. Some ascribe this strange conduct to an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> made upon Mohammed by the Turkish agents, and others to a report of the death of Ali Bey. Although unsuccessful, Ali Bey never lost sight of his favourite object, and Mohammed losing his confidence was forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his life by exile. Mohammed, however, quickly returned with an army and drove Ali Bey from Cairo. In this unfortunate state of affairs Ali Bey fled to Daher, and combining their forces, they attacked the Turkish commander at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a>, and came off victorious, although the Turkish army was three times their number. After a siege of eight months they next took the town of Jaffa. Deceived by letters from Cairo which were only intended to enflame him, and stimulated with recent victories, he returned to Cairo. Entering the deserts which divide Gaza from Egypt, he was furiously attacked by a thousand chosen Mamelukes led on by Murad Bey, who was enamoured with the beauty of Ali Bey's wife, and had obtained the promise of her, provided that he could take Ali Bey captive. Murad wounded and made Ali Bey prisoner, and carried him to Mohammed, who received him with affected respect; but in three days, either in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> or the effects of his wounds, Ali breathed his last. Ali Bey was certainly a singular production in the school of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarity, and displayed a very great degree of original vigour of character and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> penetration of mind. He is blamed for engaging in enterprises beyond his power to accomplish; but he is acknowledged to have been very favourable to the Franks, and to have governed Egypt with no small degree of steady moderation. He is also <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with devolving too much upon his lieutenants, and not being sufficiently attentive to the exactions made by his officers. Among his failings may also be ranked that of an unbounded confidence in his favourite. Generosity Aljameia and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of justice were not wanting in his character, although his morals, under the sanction of his clads and country, were strongly tainted with perfidy and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> in the pursuit of his ambitious plans. (Gen. Biog.) ALJAMEIA is a name which the Moriscos in Spain give to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the Spaniards. Among other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> agreed on by the junto, which was appointed by the emperor Charles V. in 1526, in favour of the Moriscos, this was one, that the Moriscos should no longer speak Algavareia, i.e. Moorish, or Arabic; but should all speak Aljameia, i.e. Spanish, as it was called by the Moors, and all their writings and contracts should be in that language.

ALIAS

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> farther writ issued from the courts of Westminster, after a copias, &c. sued out without effect.

ALIBI

Pages 314-314

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes the absence of the accused from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where he is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with having committed a crime; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> his being elsewhere, as the word imports, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> specified.

ALICANT

Pages 314-314

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, and territory of Segura. It is seated between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and the sea, and has a castle deemed impregnable. The port is defended by three bastions furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. To prevent the visits of the Algerine pirates, watch-towers were built to give notice of the approach of an enemy's ship. It was taken from the Moors in 1264. The castle was taken by the English in 1706, and held out a siege of two years before it was retaken by the French and Spaniards, and at last surrendered upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> terms, after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the rock was blown up on which the castle stood, and the governor killed. The houses are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and well built; and a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade is carried on here, particularly in wine and fruit. It is seated on the Mediterranean, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the same name, 37 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, and 75 south of Valencia. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 36'. N. Lat. 38° 24'.

ALICATA

Pages 314-314

a mountain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, near the valleys Mazara and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOTO">Noto</a>, upon which was situated (as is generally thought) the famous Dedalion, where the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHALARIS">Phalaris</a> kept his brazen bull. ALICATA Chlamys, was a sort of vest with sleeves worn by the Roman boys till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of thirteen, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they put on the pretexta.

ALIEN

Pages 314-315

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, implies a person born in a strange <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, not within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>; in contradistinction to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENIZEN">denizen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> subject. The word is formed from the Latin alius, "another;" q.d., one born in another country. An alien is incapable of inheriting lands in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> till naturalized by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. No alien is entitled to vote at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of members of parliament; nor can he enjoy any office, or be returned on any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, unless where an alien is party in a cause, when the inquest is composed of an equal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of denizens and aliens. The reasons for establishing these laws were, that every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is professed to bear <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and country where he received protection during his infancy. ALIEN; and that one prince might not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> spies in another's country; but chiefly that the rents and revenues of the country might not be drawn to the subjects of another. Some have thought that the laws against aliens were introduced in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Henry II. when a law was made at the parliament of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALLINGFORD">Wallingford</a>, for the expulsion of strangers, in order to drive away the Flemings and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PICARDS">Picards</a> introduced into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> by the wars of King Stephen. Others have thought that the origin of this law was more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>; and that it is an original branch of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a>: for by that law no man can purchase any lands but he must be obliged to do fealty to the lords of whom the lands are holden; so that an alien who owed a previous faith to another prince, could not take an oath of fidelity in another sovereign's dominions. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> only the Cives Romani were effectually freedmen; but when their territories increased, all the Italians were made free under the name of Latins, though they had not the privilege of wearing <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> rings till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>. Afterwards all born within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> of the empire were considered as citizens. ALIEN-Duty, an impost laid on all goods imported by aliens, over and above the customs paid for such goods imported by Britons, and on British bottoms. ALIENS-Duty is otherwise called petty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> duty.—Fish dried or salted, and cod-fish or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> not caught in British vessels and cured by British subjects, pay a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> aliens-duty.—On what footing aliens are permitted to import foreign commodities into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Britain, see Duty. ALIEN-Priories, a kind of inferior monasteries, formerly very numerous in England, and so called from their belonging to foreign abbeys.

ALIENATION

Pages 315-315

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of making over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> in lands, tenements, &c., to another person. ALIENATION in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTMAIN">mortmain</a>, is making over lands, tenements, &c., to a body politic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, for which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s licence must first be obtained, otherwise the lands, &c., alienated <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be forfeited. ALIENATION in fee is the selling the fee-simple of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> or other incorporeal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>. All persons who have a right to lands may generally alien them to others; but some alienations are prohibited; such as alienations by tenants for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, &c., whereby they incur a forfeiture of their estate. By the statute of Edward I., a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> was put to alienations by what we call entails, which is an expedient for procuring perpetuities in families; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>-expedients were devised to defeat this intent, and a practice was introduced of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off entails by fines, and of barring remainders and reversions by recoveries. The statute for alienations in Henry VII.'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> effect on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; as, among other regulations of that reign, it tended to throw the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of power more into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the people. By the stat. 12 Car. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 24, fines for alienations are taken away. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a> lands are only alienable under a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Lateran, held in 1123, forbids any clerk to alienate his benefice, prebend, or the like. By the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Jews, lands could only be alienated for the space of 50 years. At each return of the jubilee all returned again to the primitive owners, or their descendants, to whom the lands were originally allotted at the first distribution of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANAAN">Canaan</a>. ALIENATION Office, is an office to which all writs of covenants and entry, upon which fines are levied, and recoveries suffered, are carried, to have fines for alienation set and paid thereon.

ALIMENT

Pages 315-316

implies food both <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> and liquid: from which, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of digestion, is prepared a very mild, sweet, and whitish liquor, resembling <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, and distinguished by the name of chyle; which being absorbed by the lacteal veins, by them conveyed into the circulation, and there assimilated into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of blood, affords that supply of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUTRITION">nutrition</a> which the continual waste of the body is found to require.—Next to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, food is the most necessary thing for the preservation of our bodies; and as on the choice thereof our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> greatly depends, it is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> importance to understand, in general, what is the proper diet for our nourishment; and, in particular deviations from health, what is the best adapted to restore us. The blood and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> naturally incline to waste and diminish: fresh chyle, duly received, prevents this waste and diminution, and preserves in them that mild state which alone consorts with health. An animal diet affords the most of this bland nutritious mucilage; watery fluids <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> the too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> parts, and carry off what is become unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. It is only the small portion of jelly which is separated from the farnaceous parts of vegetables, that, after being much elaborated, is converted into the animal nature; yet the use of vegetables prevents both repletion and a too great tendency to a putrefactive acrimony of the blood. In hot climates, as well as against the constitutional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of particular persons, vegetables are demanded in the largest proportion. Animal substances afford the highest relish while our appetite continues; but <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> satiate the appetite before the stomach is duly filled. Vegetables may be eaten after either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fish: few herbs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> satiate so much as that the stomach may not be filled with them, when it is already satisfied with flesh or fish; whence it may be observed, that no diet which is very nourishing can be eaten to fulness, because its nutritious parts are oily and satiating. Health depends almost wholly on a proper draft of the blood; and to preserve this a mixture of vegetables in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> is always required, for a loathing is soon the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of animal food alone: hot acid habits, too, receive from milk and vegetables the needful for correcting their excesses; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, pituitous, and nervous habits, who want most nourishment from least digestion, and from the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of food, animal diet is to be used more freely. Thus much being offered as general principles with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of our aliment, the valetudinarian may easily regulate his diet with some advantage to himself by an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the few ensuing particulars. In winter, eat freely, but drink sparingly: roast meat is to be preferred, and what is drunk should be stronger than at other seasons. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, let thirst determine the quantity to be drunk; cold stomachs never require much: boiled meats and vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not otherwise contraindicated, may now be more freely used. Lax habits require the winter's diet to be <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> all the year, and rigid ones should be confined to that of summer. Fat people should fast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">ALI</a> Aliquot at times, but the lean should never do so. Those who are troubled with eruptions occasioned by their food should drink but little, and use some unaccustomed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. The thirsty should drink freely, but eat sparingly. In general, let moderation be observed; and though no dinner hath been had, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> is at all times to be preferred. After very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> seasoned meats, a glass of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> acidulated with the acid elixir of vitriol, or in very weak stomachs the sweet elixir of vitriol, is far more afflignant to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of digestion than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> method of taking brandy. See further Food and Drink. Obligation of Aliment, in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> obligation on parents to provide their children with the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, &c. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Alimentarii Pueri, &c., were certain children maintained and educated by the munificence of the emperors, in a sort of public places, not unlike our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>.—Trajan was the first who brought up any of these alimentary boys. He was imitated by Adrian. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a> did the same for a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of maids, at the solicitation of Faustina; and hence, in some medals of that empress, we read PVEILLAE FAVSTINIANAE.—Alexander Severus did like at the request of Mamaea; and the maids thus educated were called Mammeae. Alimentary Duct or Canal, is a name given by Dr Tylor and some others to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body through which the food passes from its reception into the mouth to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXIT">exit</a> at the anus; including the gula, stomach, and intestines. See Anatomy. This duct has been said to be the true characteristic of an animal, or (in the jargon of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>) in proprium quarto modo; no animal being without it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a> receive their nourishment by the numerous fibres of their roots; but have no common receptacle for digesting the food received, or for carrying off the recrements. But in all, even the lowest degree of animal life, we may observe a stomach and intestines, even where we cannot perceive the least formation of any organ of the senses, unless that common one of feeling, as in oysters. Phil. Trans. No. 269, p. 770, et seq. Dr Wallis brings an argument from the structure of the alimentary tube in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, to prove that he is not naturally carnivorous; to which Dr Tyton makes some objections. Vid. Phil. Trans. No. 269, p. 777. Alimentarii Lex, lex alimentaria, was an old law among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, whereby children were obliged to find sustenance for their parents.

ALIMONY

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, implies that allowance which a married woman dues for, and is entitled to, upon any occasional separation from her husband. See Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALIPERIUM

Pages 316-316

an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a>, in Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> palestrae, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> were anointed before their exercises.

ALIPILARIUS

Pages 316-316
or Alipilus, in Roman Antiquity, a servant belonging to the baths, whose business it was, by means of waxen plasters, and an instrument called volfella, to take off the hairs from the arm pits, and even arms, legs, &c., this being deemed a point of cleanliness.

ALIQUANT PART

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">Arithmetic</a>, is that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> which cannot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> any other exactly without some remainder. Thus 7 is an aliquant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of 16; for aliquot twice 7 wants two of 16, and three times 7 exceeds 16 by 5.

ALIQUOT PART

Pages 316-316

is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> exactly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> it without any remainder. Thus 2 is an aliquot part of 4, 3 of 9, 4 of 16, &c.

ALISONTIA

Pages 316-316
or Alisuntia, in Ancient Geography, a river of Belgic Gaul, now Alfis; which, rising on the borders of Lorraine, and running through that duchy, waters the city of Luxemburg, and, swelled by other rivulets, falls into the Seine.

ALITES

Pages 316-316

in Roman Antiquity, a designation given to such birds as afforded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of auguries by their flight.

ALKADARII

Pages 316-316

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> among the Mahometans who deny any eternal, fixed, divine decrees, and are adherents of free-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. The word is formed from the Arabic alkadar, which signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a>." The Alkadari are a branch of Mozazalites, and stand opposed to the Algiabarii. See Algiabarii.

ALKAHEST

Pages 316-316
or Alkahest, among Alchemists, derived from a word which signifies spirit of salt, or all-spirit, was supposed to be an universal menstruum capable of resolving all bodies into their first principles. Van Helmont pretended he was possessed of such a menstruum.—It is likewise used by some authors for all fixed salts volatilized.

ALKALLI

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, denotes a particular class of salts. The word alkali is of Arabian origin, and was introduced into chemistry after it had been applied to a plant which still retains the name of kali. When this plant is burnt, the ashes walked in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the water evaporated to dryness, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> substance remains, which was called alkali. According to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBERTUS_MAGNUS">Albertus Magnus</a>, who uses the word, it signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> amaritudinis, "the dregs of bitterness." Alkali may be obtained from other substances besides kali. Chemists gradually discovered that bodies, differing from one another in several of their properties, had been confounded together under the same name. The word, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, became general, and is now applied to all bodies which possess the following properties: 1. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INCOMBUSTIBLE">Incombustible</a>. 2. A hot caustic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. 3. Volatilized by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. 4. Soluble in water even when combined with carbonic acid. 5. Capable of converting vegetable blues to green. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a> at present known are three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTASH">Potash</a>; 2. Soda; 3. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIA">Ammonia</a>. The two first are called fixed alkalies, because they require a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> heat to volatilize them; the last is called volatile alkali, because it readily assumes a gaseous form, and consequently is dissipated by a very moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat. See Chemistry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. "Alkali, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Sal Kali. See Salicornia, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. ALKANET. See Anchusa, Botany Index.

ALKEENGI

Pages 316-316

the trivial name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of phyllis. See Physalis, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ALKENNA. See Lawsonia, Botany Index.

ALKERMES

Pages 316-316

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> cordial medicine made in the form of a confection, deriving its name from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KERMES">kermes</a> berries used in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>.

ALKORAN

Pages 316-317
ALL-Saints, in the Kalendar, denotes a festival celebrated on the first of November, in commemoration of all the saints in general; which is otherwise called All-Hallows. The number of saints being so excessively multiplied, it was found too burdensome to dedicate a feast day to each. In reality, there are not days enough, scarce hours enough, in the year, for this purpose. Hence an expedient was had recourse to, by commemorating such in the lump as had not their own days. Boniface IV, in the ninth century, introduced the feast of All-Saints in Italy, which was soon after adopted into the other churches. All-Saints, islands near Guadaloupe, in the West Indies. All-Saints, a parish in Georgetown district, South Carolina, containing 2225 inhabitants, of whom 429 are whites, and 1795 slaves. It sends a member to each house of the state legislature. All-Saints Bay, a spacious harbour near St Salvador in Brazil, in S. America, on the Atlantic ocean, W. Long. 40°, S. Lat. 12°. All-Saints Bay, a captainship in the middle division of Brazil, so called from the harbour of that name, bounded on the north by the Rio Real; on the south by that of Las Ilheos; on the east by the ocean; and on the west by three unconquered nations of Indians. It is reckoned one of the richest and most fertile captainships in all Brazil, producing great quantities of cotton and sugar. The bay itself is about two and a half leagues over, interspersed with a number of small but pleasant islands, and is of prodigious advantage to the whole country. It has several cities and towns, particularly St Salvador, which is its capital. All-Saints Bay lies in S. Lat. 12. 3. W. Long. 40. 10. See Salvador. All-Souls, in the Kalendar, denotes a feast-day, held on the second of November, in commemoration of all the faithful deceased.—The feast of All-Souls was first introduced in the eleventh century, by Odilon abbot of Cluny, who enjoined it on his own order; but it was not long before it became adopted by the neighbouring churches. All-Spice. See Myrtus and Calycanthus, Botany Index.

ALLAHABAD

Pages 317-318

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hindostan, about 162 miles in length, and 120 in breadth. Its eastern boundaries meet the province of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAHAR">Bahar</a>, the southern Berar, the western Malwa and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGRA">Agra</a>, and the northern Oude. According to the distribution of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Akbar, recorded in the Ayeen Akberry; it contains 10 circars <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> counties, which are divided into 1777 pargunahs or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>. According to the statement of Maurice, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> antiquities, it affords a revenue of 3,310,695 seca rupees. It contributes to the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> 323 elephants, 237,870 infantry, and 11,375 cavalry. Azuh Dowlia, a tributary ally of Allamanda the British power, possesses the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of this province. Allahabad, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENARES">Benares</a>, and Iconpour, are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cities. Allahabad, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the above province, is situated at the confluence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Jumna and Ganges. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is divided into two parts, called the Old and the New Town: The old is situated upon the Ganges, and the new upon the Jumna. The emperor Akbar erected a strong fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which occupies a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> space in this city, and from him it received its present name. Of this fortress, Mr Hodges, in No IV. of his select views in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, gives an accurate and elegant delineation. A pillar consisting of one stone 40 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, ascribed by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> to Bima, one of the heroes of Mahabarat, wholly covered with illegible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a>, and the elegant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> Khurfu, are excellent specimens of Mahometan <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">Devotion</a> has fixed her residence, and flourishes to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> in this city, that it hath obtained the appellation of "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of worshipped places." According to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the Ayeen-Akberry, the adjacent territory, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of 40 miles, is deemed holy ground. In such veneration is this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> held by the Hindoos, that when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> dies here, they believe he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> obtain the utmost of his wishes in his next regeneration. They deem it a meritorious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for a man to slay himself, although they teach that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUICIDE">suicide</a> will be punished with torments in a future state. In and about this city there are various objects of veneration, which immense numbers of pilgrims continue to visit with great devotion. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Rennel has placed Palibothra on the same site with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>; but Dr Robertson is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Palibothra is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> city of Allahabad. N. Lat. 25. 27. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 82. 5. Allamanda, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Allan, a river of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a>, in Scotland, which passes by Dunblane, and falls into the Forth near Stirling. Allantois, or Allantoides, a thin transparent bag investing the fetus of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, as cows, goats, sheep, &c., filled with an urinous liquor conveyed to it from the bladder of the young animals by means of the urachus. See Anatomy Index. Allatius, Leo, keeper of the Vatican library, a native of Scio, and a celebrated writer of the 17th century. He was of great service to the gentlemen of Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> in the controversy they had with M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> touching the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of the Greeks with regard to the eucharist. No Latin was ever more devoted to the see of Rome, or more inveterate against the Greek schismatics, than Allatius. He never was married; nor did he take orders; and Pope Alexander VII. having asked him one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, why he did not enter into orders? he answered, Because I would be free to marry." The pope rejoined, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> so, why do you not marry?" "Because," replied Allatius, "I would not be at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to take orders." Thus, as Mr Bayle observes, he passed his whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, wavering betwixt a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> and a wife; forry, perhaps, at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, for having chosen neither of them; when, if he had fixed upon one, he might have repented his choice for 30 or 40 years.—If we believe John Patricius, Allatius had a very extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>, with which, and no other, he wrote Greek for 40 years; at the loss of which, he was so grieved. Allay grieved as to lament it with tears. He published several <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>, several translations of Greek authors, and several pieces of his own composing. In his works he discovers more erudition and industry than found judgment. His manner of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> is diffuse and perplexed, making frequent digressions from one subject to another. He died at Rome in 1669, aged 83. ALLAY. See Allay.

ALLECTUS

Pages 318-318

the prime minister and confidential friend of Carausius, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. In order to avoid the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to the several enormous crimes with which he was chargeable, he fell upon the desperate expedient of murdering his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and usurping the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, which he maintained for three years. With a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of recovering Britain, Constantius about this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> fitted out a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> squadron, which being assembled in the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, the command was devolved upon the prefect Asclepiodotus. The fleet of Allectus was stationed off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Wight to receive them; but under the cover of a thick fog, the invaders escaped their notice, and landed in safety on the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and, according to Gibbon, convinced the Britons "that a superiority of naval strength <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not always protect their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> from a foreign invasion." No sooner had the intrepid commander disembarked his forces, than he set fire to his ships, and marched forward to meet the enemy. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of an attack from Constantius, who commanded the fleet off <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>, the usurper had taken his station in the vicinity of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but informed of the defeat of Asclepiodotus, he made forced marches to oppose his progress.
