Allectus attacked the imperial troops, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> being reduced to a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fatigued and dispirited men, he fell in the field, and his forces received a total defeat. Thus, in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and by a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the fate of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was decided; and Britain, after a separation of 10 years, was restored to the Roman empire, A.D. 297. Constantius landing on the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, was saluted with the loud applause and unanimous acclamations of obedient subjects, and welcomed to the British <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>.

ALLEGAS

Pages 318-318
or ALLEGAS, a fluff manufactured in the East Indies. There are two sorts of them; some are of cotton, and others of several kinds of herbs, which are spun like flax and hemp. Their length and breadth are of eight ells, by five, fix, or seven eighths; and of twelve ells, by three-fourths or five-eighths.

ALLEGATA

Pages 318-318

a word anciently subscribed at the bottom of recripts and constitutions of the emperors; as signata, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> tektata, was under other infrumens.

ALLEGHANY

Pages 318-318

is the most western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARYLAND">Maryland</a>, and has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. The windings of the Patowmac river separate it from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a> on the south, and Sideling-hill Creek divides it from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a> county on the east. It contains 4809 inhabitants, including 258 slaves. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> is its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town. Alleghany County, in Pennsylvania, extends from the junction of the river of that name with the Ohio, where its chief town, Pittsburgh, is situated, to the New-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a> line. It contains 10,309 inhabitants, including 159 slaves. Alleghany <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, between the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> river, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, are a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> range of mountains, made up of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ridges, extending north-easterly and south-Alleghany, westerly, nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, about 900 Alleghany miles in length, and from 60 to 150 and 250 miles in breadth. Mr. Evans observes, with respect to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of these mountains which he travelled over, viz., in the back parts of Pennsylvania, that scarcely one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a> in ten is capable of culture. This, however, is far from being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in all parts of this range. Numerous tracts of fine arable and grazing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> intervene between the ridges. The different ridges which compose this immense range of mountains, have different names in the different states, viz., the Blue Ridge, the North Mountain, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> North Ridge, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a>'s Back-Bone, Laurel Ridge, Jackson's Mountains, and Kittatinny Mountains. All these different and immense ridges, except the Alleghany, are broken through by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, which appear to have forced their way through <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rocks. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ridge is more immediately called Alleghany, and is descriptively named the Backbone of the United States. From these several ridges proceed innumerable branches, or spurs. The general name of the whole range, taken collectively, seems not yet to have been determined. Mr. Evans calls them the Endless Mountains; others have called them the Appalachian Mountains, from a tribe of Indians who live on a river which proceeds from this mountain, called the Appalachiola; but the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> name is the Alleghany Mountains, so called, probably, from the principal ridge of the range. These mountains are not confusedly scattered, rising here and there into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> peaks, towering each other; but run along in uniform ridges, scarcely half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> high. They spread as you proceed south, and some of them terminate in high perpendicular bluffs; others gradually subside into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, giving rise to the rivers which run southerly into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. Alleghany River, in Pennsylvania, rises on the western side of the Alleghany mountains, and after running about 200 miles in a south-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, meets the Monongahela at Pittsburg, and both united form the Ohio. The lands on each side of this river, for 150 miles above Pittsburg, consist of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> oak and chestnut ridges, and in many places of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> pitch pines, interspersed with tracts of good land, and low meadows. This river, and the Ohio likewise, from its head waters until it enters the Mississippi, are known and called by the name of Alleghany River, by the Seneca, and other tribes of the Six Nations, who once inhabited it.

ALLEGIANCE

Pages 318-320

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the tie, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ligamen, which binds the subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, in return for that protection which the king affords the subject. The thing itself, or substantial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, is founded in reason and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; the name and the form are derived to us from our Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. Under the feudal system, every owner of lands held them in subjection to some superior or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, from whom or from whose ancestors the tenant or vassal had received them; and there was a mutual trust or confidence subsisting between the lord and vassal, that the lord should protect the vassal in the enjoyment of the territory he had granted him; and, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, that the vassal should be faithful to the lord, and defend him against all his enemies. This obligation on the part of the vassal was called his fidelitas. Allegiance, fidelitas or fealty; and an oath of fealty was required by the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a> to be taken by all tenants to their landlord, which is couched in almost the same terms as our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> oath of allegiance; except that, in the usual oath of fealty, there was frequently a favoring or exception of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> due to a superior lord by name, under whom the landlord himself was perhaps only a tenant or vassal. But when the acknowledgment was made to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> superior himself, who was vassal to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, it was no longer called the oath of fealty, but the oath of allegiance; and therein the tenant swore to bear faith to his sovereign lord, in opposition to all men, without any favoring or exception. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a> held by this exalted <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fealty, was called feudum ligium, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEGE">liege</a> fee; the vassals homines ligii, or liege men; and the sovereign, their dominus ligius, or liege lord. And when sovereign princes did homage to each other for lands held under their respective sovereignties, a distinction was always made between simple homage, which was only an acknowledgment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>; and liege homage, which included the fealty before mentioned, and the services consequent upon it. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, it becoming a fettered principle of tenure, that all lands in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> are holden of the king as their sovereign and lord paramount, no oath but that of fealty could ever be taken to inferior lords; and the oath of allegiance was necessarily confined to the person of the king alone. By an easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of allegiance was soon brought to signify all other engagements which are due from subjects to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, as well as those duties which were simply and merely territorial. And the oath of allegiance, as administered in England for upwards of 600 years, contained a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> "to be true and faithful to the king and his heirs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and faith to bear of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and limb and terrene <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, and not to know or hear of any ill or damage intended him, without defending him therefrom." But, at the Revolution, the terms of this oath being thought perhaps to favour too much the notion of non-resistance, the present form was introduced by the convention <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, which is more general and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> than the former; the subject only promising "that he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be faithful and bear true allegiance to the king," without mentioning "his heirs," or specifying in the least wherein that allegiance confits. The oath of supremacy is principally calculated as a renunciation of the pope's pretended authority; and the oath of abjuration, introduced in the reign of King William, very amply supplies the loose and general texture of the oath of allegiance; recognizing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his majesty, derived under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of settlement; engaging to support him to the utmost of the juror's power; promising to disclose all traitorous conspiracies against him; and expressly renouncing any claim of the defendants of the late pretender, in as clear and explicit terms as the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> can furnish. This oath must be taken by all persons in any office, trust, or employment; and may be tendered by two justices of the peace to any person whom they shall suspect of disaffection. And the oath of allegiance may be tendered to all persons above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twelve years, whether natives, denizens, or aliens. But, besides these express engagements, the law also holds that there is an implied, original, and virtual allegiance, owing from every subject to his sovereign, antecedently to any express promise, and although the subject never swore any faith or allegiance in form. Thus Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> very justly observes, that "all subjects are equally bounden to their allegiance as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had taken the oath; because it is written by the finger of the law in their hearts, and the taking of the corporal oath is but an outward <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the same." Allegiance, both express and implied, is however distinguished by the law into two sorts or species, the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, the other local; the former being also perpetual, the latter temporary. Natural allegiance is such as is due from all men born within the king's dominions immediately upon their birth. For, immediately upon their birth, they are under the king's protection; at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> too, when (during their infancy) they are incapable of protecting themselves. Natural allegiance is, therefore, a debt of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>; which cannot be forfeited, cancelled, or altered, by any change of time, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, or circumstance, nor by anything but the united concurrence of the legislature. A Briton who removes to France, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, owes the same allegiance to the king of Britain there as at home, and 20 years hence as well as now. For it is a principle of universal law, That the natural born subject of one prince cannot by any act of his own, no, not by swearing allegiance to another, put off or discharge his natural allegiance to the former; for this natural allegiance was intrinsic and primitive, and antecedent to the other; and cannot be divested without the concurrent act of that prince to whom it was first due. Local allegiance is such as is due from an alien, or stranger born, for so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time as he continues within, the king's dominion and protection; and it ceases the instant such stranger transfers himself from this kingdom to another. Natural allegiance is therefore perpetual, and local temporary only; and that for this reason, evidently founded upon the nature of government. That allegiance is a debt due from the subject, upon an implied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the prince; that so long as the one affords protection, so long the other will demean himself faithfully. The oath of allegiance, or rather the allegiance itself, is held to be applicable, not only to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> capacity of the king, or regal office, but to his natural person and blood <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>; and for the misapplication of their allegiance, viz. to the regal capacity or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, exclusive of the person of the king, were the Spencers banished in the reign of Edward II. And from hence arose that principle of personal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> and affectionate loyalty, which induced our forefathers (and, if occasion required, would doubtless induce their sons) to hazard all that was dear to them, life, fortune, and family, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> and support of their liege lord and sovereign. It is to be observed, however, in explanation of this allegiance, That it does not preclude resistance to the regal and regal king, when his misconduct or weakness is such as to make resistance beneficial to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. It seems fairly presumable, that the convention parliament, which introduced the oath of allegiance in its present form, did not intend to exclude all resistance: since the Allegory. very authority by which the members sat together, was itself the effect of a successful opposition to an acknowledged sovereign. Again: The allegiance above described can only be understood to signify obedience to lawful commands. If, therefore, the king should issue a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a>, levying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> or imposing any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> or restraint upon the subject, beyond what the law authorized, there would exist no sort of obligation to obey such a proclamation, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of having taken the oath of allegiance. Neither can allegiance be supposed to extend to the king after he is actually and absolutely deposed, driven into exile, or otherwise rendered incapable of exercising the regal office. The promise of allegiance implies, that the person to whom the promise is made continues king; that is, continues to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the power, and afford the protection, which belong to the office of king; for it is the possession of these which makes such a particular person the object of the oath.

ALLEGORY

Pages 320-320

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">Composition</a>, consists in choosing a secondary subject, having all its properties and circumstances resembling those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> subject, and describing the former in such a manner as to represent the latter. The principal subject is thus kept out of view, and we are left to discover it by reflection. In other words, an allegory is, in every respect, similar to a hieroglyphical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, excepting only that words are used instead of colours. Their effects are precisely the same: A hieroglyphic raises two images in the mind; one seen, that represents one that is not seen: An allegory does the same; the representative subject is described, and the resemblance leads us to apply the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> to the subject represented. There cannot be a finer <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more correct allegory than the following, in which a vineyard is made to represent God's own people the Jews: "Thou hast brought a vine out of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>; thou hast <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> out the heathen, and planted it. Thou didst cause it to take deep root, and it filled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. The hills were covered with its shadow, and the boughs thereof were like the goodly cedars. Why hast thou then broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> her hedges, so that all that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> do pluck her? The boar out of the wood doth waste it, and the wild beast doth devour it. Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine and the vineyard thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> hath planted, and the branch thou madest strong for thyself." Psa. lxxx. Nothing gives greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> than an allegory, when the representative subject bears a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>, in all its circumstances, to that which is represented. But most writers are unlucky in their choice, the analogy being generally so faint and obscure, as rather to puzzle than to please. Allegories, as well as metaphors and similes, are unnatural in expressing any fervent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> which totally occupies the mind. For this reason, the following speech of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a> is justly condemned by the learned author of the Elements of Criticism: Methought I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> cry, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">Sleep</a> no more! Macbeth doth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> Sleep; the innocent sleep; Sleep that knits up the ravell'd sleeve of Care, The birth of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, fore Labour's bath, Balm of hurt minds, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> course, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">Chief</a> nourisher in life's feast. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a> ii. Sc. 3. But see this subject more fully treated under the article <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHOR">METAPHOR</a> and Allegory.

ALLEGRI

Pages 321-321

Gregorio, an ecclesiastic by profession, and a celebrated composer of music of the 17th century, was a native of Rome. He was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Nanni, the intimate friend and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTRINA">Palestrina</a>. His abilities as a singer were not remarkable, but he was deemed an excellent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; and so much respected by all the musical professors of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, that the pope, in the year 1629, appointed him to be one of the singers of his chapel. To his uncommon merit as a composer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> music, he united an excellent moral character, exhibiting in his actions the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> and benevolence of his heart. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> crowded daily to his door, whom he relieved to the utmost of his ability; and not content with these beneficent actions, he daily visited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> of Rome, in order to relieve the most deserving and afflicted objects which were immured in these dreary mansions. With such divine simplicity and purity of harmony, did he compose many parts of the church <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, that his lofs was feverishly felt and sincerely lamented by the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of singers in the papal service. He died Feb. 18, 1652, and was interred in the Chiesa Nuova, in a vault destined for the reception of deceased singers in the pope's chapel, before the chapel of S. Filippo Neri, near the altar of annunciation. Among his other musical works preserved in the pontifical chapel, is the celebrated miérere, which, for 170 years, has been annually performed at that chapel on Wednesday and Good Friday, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">Passion</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, by the choral band, and the best singers in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. It is, however, generally believed, that it owes its reputation more to the manner in which it is performed, than to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> itself. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and effect of the music is not discernible upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, but the fingers have, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, certain customs, expressions, and graces of convention, which produce wonderful effects. Some of the effects produced may be justly attributed to the time, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and the solemnity of the ceremonials observed during the performance. "The pope and conclave are all prostrated on the ground, the candles of the chapel and the torches of the balustrade are extinguished one by one, and the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of this psalm is terminated by two choirs; the maglia di capello <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> time slower and slower, and the fingers diminishing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather extinguishing the harmony by little and little, to a perfect point." Padre Martini says, that there were never more than three copies made by authority, "one of which was for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Leopold, one for the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and the other for himself; but a very complete one was presented by the pope himself to King George III., as an inestimable curiosity." (Gen. Biog.)

ALLEGRO

Pages 321-322

in Music, an Italian word, denoting Allein, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is to be played in a sprightly, brisk, lively, and gay manner. [Merged from PIU ALLEGRO, p.322] u Allegro signifies, that the part it is joined to should be sung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> played quicker; as Poco piu Allegro intimates, that the part to which it refers ought to be played or sung only a little more briskly than allegro alone requires. Allein, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, the son of Tobias Allein, was born in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol7.html#article-DEVIZES">Devizes</a>, in Wiltshire, in 1633, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. In 1655, he became afflant to Mr Newton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAUNTON">Taunton</a> Magdalen, in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOMERSETSHIRE">Somersetshire</a>; but was deprived for nonconformity. He died in 1668, aged 35. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning, and greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>; preserving, though a nonconformist, and a severe sufferer on that account, great respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and loyalty to his sovereign. He wrote several books of piety, which are highly esteemed; but his Alarm to unconverted sinners is more famous than the rest. There have been many editions of this little pious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of which has been very great; of the edition 1672, there were 20,000 sold; of that of 1675, with this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, A sure guide to heaven, 50,000. There was also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of it with its first title, in 1720. Allein, Richard, an English nonconformist divine, a native of Ditchet, in Somersetshire, was born in the year 1611. His father was rector of Ditchet, and conducted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of his son, until he was prepared for the university. There he soon obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts, and after he entered into holy orders, first as an afflant to his father, and afterwards as rector of Batcomb, in Somersetshire, he discharged the duties of a clergyman with great industry and singular fidelity. From his education, he conceived an early predilection for the sentiments of the Puritans, and consequently, in the contest between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he firmly adhered to the latter. Having adopted these sentiments, he sometimes received a little disturbance from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s forces, but he never carried his opposition to any undue length. He, along with several others, signed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, entitled "The Testimony of the Ministers of Somersetshire to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of Christ," in which their declared principles and becoming candour were amply displayed. Along with his father, he was employed by the commissioners appointed by parliament for ejecting scandalous ministers; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> which was executed with rigour, and originated in intolerance. Upon the Restoration he manifested a disposition to loyalty, but unable with a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to unite in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of conformity, he resigned his living after enjoying it for 20 years, and ranked with the meritorious band of sufferers, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 2000, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> denominated the ejected ministers. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Mr More who had been a member of the parliament, he exercised the duties of his ministerial office under the penalties of that act, and was consequently reprimanded by the magistrates and imprisoned; but his piety and exemplary conduct, procured him a mitigation of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. But no dangers could deter him from duty; for although constrained to remove from that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the "five-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> act," he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in the discharge of his ministerial office at Frome Selwood. Here he remained until he terminated his labours by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in 1681. Piety, boldness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and candour, shone in the character of Richard Allein. He was admired as a pathetic and practical preacher, and justly respected for the diligence with which he discharged the public and private duties of his profession. Mr Jenkins, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> where he resided, preached his funeral sermon, and bore an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> testimony to his activity, moderation, and piety. Richard Allein, similar to his nonconformist brethren, closely confined his studies and publications to subjects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. His works are strongly marked with the peculiar features of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> character then prevalent among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NONCONFORMISTS">nonconformists</a>. They have been frequently reprinted, and very much perused. His most celebrated work is "Vindicatio Pietatis, or a Vindication of Godliness in its greatest Strictness and Spirituality, with directions for a godly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>;" this book was published in 1665, without a printer's name; and being unlicensed, the copies of it were seized and sent to the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> for wafer paper. The other productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> are, "Heaven opened, or a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and plain discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of God's Covenant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">Grace</a>;" printed in 1665. "The World Conquered;" published in 8vo, in 1674. "Godly Fear;" printed in 8vo, in 1674. "A Rebuke to Backsliders, and a Spur for Loiterers;" printed in 8vo in 1677. "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">Companion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">Prayer</a>;" in 12mo, 1680. "A brief character of Mr Joseph Allein;" and "Instructions about heart-work, what is to be done on God's part and ours for the cure and keeping of the heart;" a posthumous piece published in 8vo, by Dr Annelley in the year 1681. (Gen. Biog.) Alleluia, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALLELUJAH">Hallelujah</a>, a word signifying, praise the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, to be met with either at the beginning or end of some psalms: such as psalm cxlv. and those that follow to the end. Alleluia was sung upon solemn days of rejoicing, Tobit xiii. 12. St John in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> (xix. 1, 3, 4, 6.) says, that he heard a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of much people in heaven, who said, Alleluiah; and the four and twenty elders, and the four beasts, fell <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and worshipped God that sat on the throne, saying, Alleluiah." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> of joy and praises was transferred from the synagogue to the church. St Jerome tells us, that at the funeral of Fabiola several psalms were sung with loud alleluias; and that the monks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> were awakened at their midnight watchings, with the ringing of alleluias. So much energy has been observed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> church thought proper to preserve it, without translating it either into Greek or Latin, for fear of impairing the genius and softness of it. The fourth <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> has prohibited the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of it in times of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">Lent</a>, or other days of fasting, and in the ceremonies of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOURNING">mourning</a>: and, according to the present practice of the Roman church, this word is never repeated in Lent, nor in the obsequies of the dead; notwithstanding which, it is used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> for the dead, according to the Moarabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a>, at the introit, when they sing, Tu es portio mea, Domine, Alleluia, in terra viventium, Alleluia, Alleluia. The ringing alleluia was oftentimes an invitational or call to each other to praise the Lord. Allemaengel, a small Moravian settlement on Swetara river, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>. Allemand, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> solemn music, with good

ALLEMANNIC

Pages 322-323

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes anything belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans. Thus, we meet with Allemannic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, Allemannic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, Allemannic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, &c.

ALLEN

Pages 323-323

Thomas, a famous mathematician of the 16th century, born at Uxeter in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a> the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1542. He was admitted scholar of Trinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, the 4th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1561; and in 1567 took his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts. In 1570 he quitted his college and fellowship, and retired to Gloucesterhall; where he studied very closely, and became famous for his knowledge in antiquity, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. Having received an invitation from Henry <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of the mathematicians, he spent some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at the earl's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where he became acquainted with those celebrated mathematicians Thomas Harriot, John <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, Walter Warner, and Nathaniel Torporley. Robert earl of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEICESTER">Leicester</a> had a particular esteem for Mr Allen, and would have conferred a bishopric upon him, but his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of solitude and retirement made him decline the offer. His great skill in the mathematics made the ignorant and vulgar look upon him as a magician <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> conjuror; the author of a book entitled Leicester's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">Common</a>-wealth, has accordingly accused him with using the art of figuring, to procure the earl of Leicester's unlawful designs, and endeavouring by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> art to bring about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> betwixt him and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>. But without pretending to point out the absurdity of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, it is certain that the earl placed such confidence in Allen, that nothing material in the state was transacted without his knowledge; and the earl had constant information, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> from Mr Allen, of what passed in the university. Mr Allen was very curious and indefatigable in collecting scattered <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> relating to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, antiquity, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, philosophy, and mathematics; these collections have been quoted by several learned authors, &c. and mentioned to have been in the Bibliotheca Allemanna. He published in Latin the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third books of Claudius <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> of Peleusium, Concerning the Judgment of the Stars, or, as it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called, of the Quadrupartite <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a>, with an exposition. He wrote also notes on many of Lilly's books, and some on John <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALE">Bale</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> De Scriptoribus M. Britanniae. Having lived to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he died at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> on the 30th September 1632.

ALLENDORF

Pages 323-323

a small town in the circle of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, and in the landgraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, remarkable for its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works and three <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bridges. It is seated on the river Weser, 15 miles east of Cassel. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10° 5'. N. Lat. 51° 26'.

ALLENTOWN

Pages 323-323

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, on the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> formed by Jordan's creek, and the Little Lehigh. It contains about 90 houses, and an academy.

ALLER

Pages 323-323

good, in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Writers. The word aller serves to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of superlative signification. So, aller-good is the greatest good. Sometimes it is written aller.

ALLERION

Pages 323-323
or Alerion, in Heraldry, a sort of eagle without beak or feet, having nothing perfect but the wings. They differ from martlets by having their wings expanded, whereas those of the martlets are close; and denote imperialists vanquished and disarmed: for which reason they are more common in French than in German coats of arms.

ALLESTRY

Pages 324-324
Jacob, an English poet of the last century. He was the son of James Allestry, a bookeller of London who was ruined by the great fire in 1666. Jacob was educated at Westminster School, entered at Christ-church, Oxford, in the a.d. term 1671, at the age of 18, and was elected student in 1672. He took the degree of arts; was music reader in 1679, and terne filius in 1681; both which offices he executed with great applause, being esteemed a good philologist and poet. He had a chief hand in the verses and pastorals spoken in the theatre at Oxford May 21, 1681, by Mr William Saville second son of the marquis of Halifax, and George Cholmondeley second son of Robert Viscount Kells (both of Christ-church), before James duke of York, his duchess, and the lady Anne; which verses and pastorals, were afterwards printed in the "Examen Poeticum." He died October 15, 1686, and was buried in St Thomas's churchyard.

ALLEVEURE

Pages 324-324

a small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, worth about ½d. English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>.

ALLEVIATION

Pages 324-324

denotes the making a thing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a>, and easier to bear <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> endure. It stands opposed to aggravation.

ALLEY

Pages 324-325

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">Perspective</a>, that which, in order to have a greater appearance of length, is made wider at the entrance than at the termination.

ALLEYN

Pages 325-326

Edward, a celebrated English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the reigns of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James, and founder of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> at Dulwich in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURREY">Surrey</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of St Botolph, Sept. 1, 1566, as appears from a memorandum of his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. Dr Fuller says, that he was bred a stage-player; and that his father would have given him a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, but that he was not turned for a ferious course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He was, however, a youth of an excellent capacity, a cheerful temper, a tenacious <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, a sweet elocution, and in his person of a stately port and aspect: all which advantages might well induce a young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to take to the theatrical profession. By several authorities we find he must have been on the stage some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before 1592; for at this time he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> favour with the town, and greatly applauded by the best judges, particularly by Ben Jonson. Haywood, in his prologue to Marlowe's Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, calls him Proteus for shapes, and Roscius for a tongue. He usually played the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> parts, and was one of the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in Shakespear's plays; in some of Ben Jonson's he was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performer: but what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> he personated in either of these poets, it is difficult now to determine. This is owing to the inaccuracy of their editors, who did not print the names of the players opposite to the characters they performed, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> is; but gave one general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of actors to the whole set of plays, as in the old folio edition of Shakespear; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> divided one from the other, setting the dramatic personae before the plays, and the catalogue of performers after them, as in Jonson's. It may appear surprising how one of Mr Alleyn's profession should be enabled to erect such an edifice as Dulwich college, and liberally endow it for the maintenance of so many persons. But it must be observed that he had some paternal fortune, which, though small, might lay a foundation for his future affluence; and it is to be presumed, that the profits he received from acting, to one of his provident and managing disposition, and one who by his excellence in playing drew after him such crowds of spectators, must have considerably improved his fortune: besides he was not only an actor, but <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> built at his own expense, by which he is said to have amassed considerable wealth. He was also keeper of the king's wild beasts, or master of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> bear-garden, which was frequented by vast crowds of spectators; and the profits arising from these sports are said to have amounted to £500 per annum. He was thrice married; and the portions of his two first wives, they leaving him no issue to inherit, might probably contribute to this benefaction. Such kind of donations have been frequently thought to proceed more from vanity and ostentation than real piety; but this of Mr Alleyn has been ascribed to a very singular cause, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a> has been said to be the first promoter of it. Mr Aubrey mentions a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, "that Mr Alleyn playing a demon, with six others, in one of Shakespear's plays, was, in the midst of the play, surprised by an apparition of the devil; which so worked on his fancy, that he made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a>, which he performed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> Dulwich college." He began the foundation of this college, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Inigo Jones, in 1614; and the buildings, gardens, &c. were finished in 1617, in which he is said to have expended about £10,000. After the college was built, he met with some difficulty in obtaining a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> for settling his lands in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTMAIN">mortmain</a>: for he proposed to endow it with £800 per annum, for the maintenance of one master, one warden, and four fellows, three whereof were to be clergymen and the fourth a skillful organist; also five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> men and as many women, besides twelve poor boys to be educated till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fourteen or fifteen, and then put out to some trade or calling. The obstruction he met with arose from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who wished King James to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of those lands for the support of two academical lectures; and he wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, dated August 18, 1618, entreating him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> with his majesty for that purpose. Mr Alleyn's solicitation was however at last complied with, and he obtained the royal license, giving him full power to lay his foundation, by his majesty's letter patent, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1619; by virtue whereof he did, in the chapel of the said new <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Dulwich, called The College of God's Gift, on the 13th of September following, publicly read and publish a quattuorpartite writing in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>, whereby he created and established the said college; he then subscribed it with his name, and fixed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> to several parts thereof, in presence of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> persons, and ordered copies of the writings to four different parishes. He was himself the first master of his college; so that to make use of the words of Mr Haywood, one of his contemporaries, "He was so mingled with humility and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, that he became his own penitent, humbly submitting himself to that proportion of diet and clothes which he had bestowed on others." We have no reason to think he ever repented of this distribution of his substance; but on the contrary, that he was entirely satisfied, as appears from the following memorial in his own writing, found amongst his papers: "May 26, 1620.—My wife and I acknowledged the fine at the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, of all our lands to the college: blest be God that he has given us life to do it." His wife died in the year 1623; and about two years afterwards he married <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCE">Constance</a> Kinchtoe, who survived him, and received remarkable... remarkable proofs of his affection, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> at least we may judge of it by his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, wherein he left her considerably. He died Nov. 25, 1626, in the 61st year of his age, and was buried in the chapel of his new college, where there is a tombstone over his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, with an inscription. His original Diary is also there preserved. The subjoined anecdote is entertaining in itself, and shows the high esteem in which Mr Alleyn was held as an actor: "Edward Alleyn, the Garrick of Shakespeare's time, had been on the most friendly footing with our poet, as well as Ben Jonson. They used frequently to spend their evenings together at the sign of the Globe, somewhere near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Friars, where the playhouse then was. The world need not be told, that the convivial hours of such a triumvirate must be pleasing as well as profitable, and may truly be said to be such pleasures as might bear the reflections of the morning. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of one of these meetings, the following letter was written by G. Peele, a fellow of Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> college, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and a dramatic poet, who belonged to the Club, to one Marle, an intimate of his: 'Friend Marle, 'I must desire that my sister may watch, and the cookery book you promised, may be sent by the man.—I never longed for thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> more than last night: we were all very merry at the Globe, when Ned Alleyn did not scruple to affirm pleasantly to thy Friend Will, that he had stolen his speech about the Qualities of an actor's excellency in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a> his Tragedy, from conversations many-fold which had passed between them, and opinions given by Alleyn touching the subject.—Shakespeare did not take this talk in good part; but Jonson put an end to the strife with witty remarks: This affair needeth no Contention; you stole it from Ned, no doubt; do not marvel: Have you not seen him at times out of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>?—Believe me most sincerely, yours, G. Peele.'

in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is applied to any kind of union <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> connexion; thus we say, there is an alliance between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and state. ALLIARIA. See Erysimum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALLIER

Pages 326-326

a department of France, formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Bourbonnois, is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the departments of Saone and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, Nievre and Cher; on the east by those of Saone and Loire and the Loire; on the south by those of the Loire, Puy de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">Dome</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREUSE">Creuse</a>; and on the west by those of Creuse and Cher. It contains 1,454,341 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> acres; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants is about 266,105; and it is divided into four communal districts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULINS">Moulins</a>.

ALLIGATI

Pages 326-326

in Roman Antiquity, the basest kind of slaves, who were usually kept fettered. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had three degrees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> orders, of slaves or servants; the first employed in the management of their estates; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the menial or lower functions of the family; the third called alligati, above mentioned.

ALLIGATION

Pages 326-328

the name of a method of solving all questions that relate to the mixture of one ingredient with another. Though writers on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> generally make alligation a branch of that science; yet, as it is plainly nothing more than an application of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> properties of numbers, in order to solve a few questions Alligation questions that occur in particular branches of business, we choose rather to keep it distinct from the science of arithmetic. Alligation is generally divided into medial and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a>. **Alligation Medial**, from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a> and quantities of the simples given, discovers the rate of the mixture. **Rule.** As the total <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the simples, To their price <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> value; So any quantity of the mixture, To the rate. **Examp.** A grocer mixeth 3cbl. of currants, at 4d. per lb. with 10lb. of other currants, at 6d. per lb.: What is the value of 1lb. of the mixture? **Ans.** 4½d. | lb. | d. | |-----|----| | 30 | 4 | | 10 | 6 | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a> 1. When the quantity of each simple is the same, the rate of the mixture is readily found by adding the rates of the simples, and dividing their sum by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of simples. Thus, Suppose a grocer mixes several sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and of each an equal quantity; viz. at 5gs. at 54s. and at 60s. per cwt. the rate of the mixture <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 54s. 8d. per cwt.; for \[ \frac{50 + 54 + 60}{3} = 54.8 \] Note 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it be required to increase or diminish the quantity of the mixture, say, As the sum of the given quantities of the simples, to the several quantities given; so the quantity of the mixture proposed, to the quantities of the simples sought. Note 3. If it be required to know how much of each simple is an assigned portion of the mixture, say, As the quantity of the mixture, to the several quantities of the simples given; so the quantity of the assigned portion, to the quantities of the simples sought. Thus, Suppose a grocer mixes 10lb. of raisins with 30lb. of almonds and 40lb. of currants, and it be demanded how many ounces of each sort are found in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> or in every 16 ounces of the mixture, say, | oz. | 80 : 10 :: 16 : 2 raisins. | |-----|--------------------------| | | 80 : 30 :: 16 : 6 almonds. | | | 80 : 40 :: 16 : 8 currants. | <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">Proof</a> 16 Note 4. If the rates of two simples, with the total value and total quantity of the mixture, be given, the quantity of each simple may be found as follows: viz. Multiply the lesser rate into the total quantity, subtract the product from the total value, and the remainder will be equal to the product of the excess of the higher rate above the lower, multiplied into the quantity of the higher-priced simple; and consequently the said remainder, divided by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the rates, Alligation, will quote the said quantity. Thus, Suppose a grocer has a mixture of 400lb. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, that cost him 7l. 10s. confiting of raisins at 4d. per lb. and almonds at 6d. how many pounds of almonds were in the mixture? | lb. | Rates. | |-----|-------| | 400 | 6d. | | 7 | 10 = 1800 | | 1600 | 1600d. | 2)200(100lb. of almonds at 6d. is 2 10 And 300lb. of raisins at 4d. is 5 0 Total 400 Proof 7 10 **Alligation Alternate**, being the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> of alligation medial, from the rates of the simples, and rate of the mixture given, finds the quantities of the simples. **Rules.** I. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> the rate of the mixture on the left side of a brace, as the root; and on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> side of the brace set the rates of the several simples, under one another, as the branches. II. Link or alligate the branches, so as one greater and another less than the root may be linked or yoked together. III. Set the difference betwixt the root and the several branches right against their respective yoke-fellows. These alternate differences are the quantities required. Note 1. If any branch happen to have two or more yoke-fellows, the difference betwixt the root and these yoke-fellows must be placed right against the said branch, one after another, and added into one sum. 2. In some questions, the branches may be alligated more ways than one: and a question will always admit of so many answers as there are different ways of linking the branches. Alligation alternate admits of three varieties, viz. 1. The question may be unlimited, with respect both to the quantity of the simples and that of the mixture. 2. The question may be limited to a certain quantity of one or more of the simples. 3. The question may be limited to a certain quantity of the mixture. **Variety I.** When the question is unlimited, with respect both to the quantity of the simples, and that of the mixture, this is called **Alligation Simple**. **Examp.** A grocer would mix sugars at 5d. 7d. and 10d. per lb. so as to sell the mixture or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> at 8d. per lb.: What quantity of each must he take? | Ib. | |-----| | 8 | | 7 | | 10 | Here the rate of the mixture 8 is placed on the left side of the brace, as the root; and on the right side of the same brace are set the rates of the several simples, viz. 5, 7, 10, under one another, as the branches; according to Rule I. The branch 10 being greater than the root, is alligated or linked with 7 and 5, both these being less than the root; as directed in Rule II. The difference between the root 8 and the branch 5, viz. 3, is set right against this branch's yoke-fellow 10. The difference between 8 and 7 is likewise set right against Alligation against the yoke-fellow 10. And the difference betwixt 8 and 10 viz. 2, is set right against the two yoke-fellows 7 and 5; as prescribed by Rule III. As the branch 10 has two differences on the right, viz. 3 and 1, they are added; and the answer to the question is, that 2lb. at 5d., 2lb. at 7d. and 4lb. at 10d. will make the mixture required. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and reason of the rules will appear by considering, that whatever is lost upon any one branch is gained upon its yoke-fellow. Thus in the above example by selling 4lb. of 10d. sugar at 8d. per lb. there is 8d. lost; but the like sum is gained upon its two yoke-fellows; for by selling 2lb. of 3d. sugar at 8d. per lb. there is 6d. gained; and by selling 2lb. of 7d. sugar at 8d. there is 2d. gained; and 6d. and 2d. make 8d. Hence it follows, that the rate of the mixture must always be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> or middle with respect to the rates of the simples; that is, it must be less than the greatest, and greater than the least; otherwise a solution would be impossible. And the price of the total quantity mixed, computed at the rate of the mixture, will always be equal to the sum of the prices of the several quantities <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> up at the respective rates of the simple. Variety II. When the question is limited to a certain quantity of one or more of the simples, this is called Alligation Partial. If the quantity of one the simples only be limited, alligate the branches, and take their differences, as if there had been no such limitation; and then <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> by the following proportion: As the difference right against the rate of the simple, whose quantity is given, To the other differences respectively; So the quantity given, To the several quantities sought. Example. A distiller would, with 40 gallons of brandy at 12s. per gallon, mix rum at 7s. per gallon, and gin at 4s. per gallon: How much of the rum and gin must he take, to sell the mixture at 8s. per gallon? \[ \begin{align*} \text{Gal.} & \\ 8 & \quad 12 & \quad 14 & \quad 5 & \quad 40 \text{ of brandy.} \\ 7 & \quad 4 & \quad 4 & \quad 4 & \quad 32 \text{ of rum.} \\ 4 & \quad 4 & \quad 4 & \quad 4 & \quad 32 \text{ of gin.} \end{align*} \] The operation gives for answer, 5 gallons of brandy, 4 of rum, and 4 of gin. But the question limits the quantity of brandy to 40 gallons; therefore say, If \(5 : 4 :: 40 : 32\) The quantity of gin, by the operation, being also 4, the proportion needs not be repeated. Variety III. When the question is limited to a certain quantity of the mixture, this is called Alligation Total. After linking the branches, and taking the differences, work by the proportion following: As the sum of the differences, To each particular difference; So the given total of the mixture, To the respective quantities required. Example. A vintner hath wine at 3s. per gallon, and would mix it with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so as to make a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of 144 gallons, worth 2s. 6d. per gallon: How much wine, and how much water, must he take? \[ \begin{align*} \text{Gal.} & \\ 30 & \quad 36 & \quad 30 & \quad 120 \text{ of wine.} \\ & \quad 6 & \quad 24 \text{ of water.} \\ 36 & \quad 144 \text{ total.} \\ 120 \times 36 = 4320 \\ 24 \times 6 = 0 \end{align*} \] Proof \(144)4320(30\) As \(36 : 30 :: 144 : 120\) As \(36 : 6 :: 144 : 24\). There being here only two simples, and the total of the mixture limited, the question admits but of one answer.

ALLIOTH

ALLITERATION

Pages 328-329

an ornament of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and consisting in the repetition of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> at certain intervals. We do not remember to have ever seen any satisfactory account of alliteration in the writings of the critics. They seem to have passed it over in contemptuous silence; either as a false refinement <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> trifle. It perhaps deserves a better fate. Many chapters have been composed on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> resulting from different arrangements of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables, and on the powers of pauses as they are variously placed, without a word of alliteration. This is the more extraordinary, as one should think it impossible for any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to examine minutely, and, as it were, dissect a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of verses, without perceiving the vast abundance of this ornament. It is as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> an anatomist should publish a complete <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, and affect never to have seen a vein or a nerve: for it may be affirmed, with small danger of mistake, that if you examine any number of verses, remarkable either for sweetness or for energy, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> alliterative. We do not pretend to say, that the sweetness and energy of versification depends chiefly on this circumstance, yet we cannot help believing that it may claim some share: for it is a constant appearance, as far as we have ever observed, that the poets whose fame is highest for versification, have been attentive to alliteration. The very trifling appearance of the ornament itself, upon a superficial view, and the frequent abuse of it, are circumstances indeed which give no encouragement to a serious inquiry into its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and operation. How <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> is it for writers, who affect to be comic, when in want of other means for raising a smile, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> affected alliteration with success? But, in the fine arts, no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> is beyond the power of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>. The noblest attitudes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> have been rendered laughable by caricature. St Paul preaching at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of Raphael, appears elegant, noble, and in some degree awful. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a>, represented by Hogarth, in nearly the same attitude, pleading before fore the governor Felix, seems altogether ridiculous. So the language and versification of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in the Paradise Lost appear only proper for the most elevated subjects. In the Splendid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">Shilling</a> of Philips, they appear equally proper for the lowest. So fares it also with alliteration. Nor ought we to be mortified at the discovery, that much of the delight afforded by versification arises from a cause so pitiful as the repetition of the same letter twice, or oftener, on the accented parts of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>; for there are many other causes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, which, when thus detected and taken to pieces, seem equally contemptible. We apprehend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> operation of this ornament to be quite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>. It is easier for the organs of speech to resume, at short intervals, one certain conformation, than to throw themselves into a number of different ones, unconnected and discordant. For example, a succession of labials, interperated at regular distances with dentals and gutturals, will be more easily pronounced than the succession of all the three at random. Sounds of which the articulation is easiest, are most completely in the power of the speaker. He can pronounce them slowly or rapidly, softly or with force, at pleasure. In this we imagine the power and advantage of alliteration are founded; for we would not lay any stress on the pleasure which can result to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> from the repetition of the same letter. It has been compared to the frequent returns of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in a musical strain; but that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> is extremely faint. The ear, we presume, can be pleased with alliteration only in so far as it contributes to the superior easiness of recitation; for what is recited with ease must be heard with pleasure. These remarks might be confirmed and illustrated by numberless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> from the best poets. Some few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> will suffice, taken from Gray, who seems to have paid particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to this grace. He professed to have learned his versification from Dryden, as Dryden did from Spenner; and these three abound in alliteration above all the English poets. We choose Gray for another reason, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of what we mentioned before, that alliteration contributes not only to the sweetness, but also to the energy, of versification; for he uses it chiefly when he aims at strength and boldness. In the Silver Odes (as Dr Johnson styles them), almost every strophe commences and concludes with an alliterative line. The poet, we suppose, wished to begin with force, and end with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. "Ruin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> thee, ruthless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>." "To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-born Hoel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>, or soft Llewelyn's lay." "Weave the warp, and weave the woof." "Stamp we our vengeance deep, and ratify his doom." "Regardless of the sweeping whirlwind's sway." "That hush'd in grim repose, expects his ev'ning prey." It must be observed here, that we hold a verse alliterative which has a letter repeated on its accented parts, although those parts do not begin words; the repeated letter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a strong analogy to the bars in a musical phrase. Gray seems to have had a particular liking to these sort of balanced verses, which divide equally, and of which the opposite sides have an alliterative resemblance. "Eyes that glow, and fangs that grin." "Thoughts that breathe, and words that burn." "Hauberk crash, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>." All these lines appear to us to have a force and energy, arising from alliteration, which renders them easy to be recited; or, if the reader pleases, mumbled. For the same reason the following passage appears sad and solemn, by the repetition of the labial liquid. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, ye mourn in vain," "Mordred, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> song,"—&c. If alliteration thus contributes to enforce the expression of a poetical sentiment, its advantages in poetry must be considerable. It is not, therefore, unworthy a poet's regard in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. If two words offer of equal propriety, the one alliterative, the other not, we think the first ought to be chosen. We would compare this to the practice of fuguing in music. A composer who aims at expression will not hunt after fugues; but if they offer, if they seem to arise spontaneously from the subject, he will not reject them. So a good poet ought not to select an epithet merely for beginning with a certain letter, unless it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> his purpose well in every other respect; for the beauty of alliteration, when happy, is not greater than its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> when affected. A couplet from Pope will exemplify both; the first line being bad, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> good: "Eternal beauties grace the shining <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, Fields ever fresh, and groves for ever green."

ALLIX

Pages 329-330
PETER, a French Protestant divine, was born at Alençon in France, in the year 1641. He became a learned divine of the English church, and a strenuous defender of the Protestant faith. At the time when the edict of Nantes tolerated and protected the Protestants of France, he entered upon his clerical profession, and remained minister of Rouen until the thirty-fifth year of his age. In this period he wrote several pieces upon the controversy between the Papists and the Protestants, which obtained him great fame among his own party. He removed to Charenton in the vicinity of Paris, which was the principal church among the reformed, and frequented by persons of the first rank in France, who professed the Protestant faith. Here Allix preached a course of excellent sermons in defence of the Protestant religion, some of which were afterwards printed in Holland, and added to his increasing fame. The chief object of these sermons was to repel the attack of the bishop of Meaux, the most ingenious and able opponent of the Reformation at that time. The unwise revocation of the edict of Nantes drove Allix and many others to seek refuge in England. Three years after his arrival in England, he had made himself so perfectly master of the English language as to be able to write very correctly a "Defence of the Christian Religion." This work he dedicated to James II., in testimony of gratitude for his kind reception of the distressed refugees of France. In justice to the memory of James, and as a specimen of the talents of Allix, it may be proper to give an extract from this curious dedication. "As your majesty continues still to give such illustrious instances of your clemency and royal protection to those of your nation; so I confess, Sir, I thought myself under an obligation to lay hold upon this opportunity of publishing what all those who find so sure a protection in your majesty's dominions feel and think as much as myself upon these new testimonies of your royal bounty. When your majesty had taken us into your particular care, and had granted us several privileges, and so made us sharers in all the advantages which those who live under your government enjoy; your majesty did yet something more, and inspired all your subjects with the same compassion towards us, with which your royal breast was already touched. You saw our miseries, and resolved to give us ease; and this generous design was executed, and your royal clemency diffused in the hearts of all your subjects. The whole world, Sir, which has received upon all its coasts some remainders of our shipwreck, is filled with admiration of the unexampled effects of your majesty's clemency.
