I could wish, Sir, that this work which I now present to your majesty might be so happy as to pass to posterity with this character of our acknowledgment, and that it might stand as a faithful record for ever to perpetuate the memory of that lively sense of your bounty which is imprinted on all our hearts." Not long after his arrival in England, he was honoured with the title of doctor of divinity, and also received the more substantial honour of being appointed treasurer of the church of Salisbury. Allix still maintained the station of a champion for the Protestant cause, and in opposition to the bishop of Meaux, proved that the charge of heresy justly belonged to the Papists, and not to their opponents, because they had introduced new doctrines into the church. After having with much industry and learning exercised his talents in defence of Protestantism, he employed his pen to support the doctrine of the Trinity against the Unitarians, who contended that the idea of Christ's divinity could be traced up no higher than the time of Justin ss="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr. With a great display of erudition, he attempted to prove that the Trinitarian doctrine was believed by the Jewish church. But the reputation which he had acquired for learning and ability was somewhat diminished by the ridicule which he brought upon himself in attempting to fix the precise time of Christ's second coming to the year 1720, or at the very latest, to the year 1736. He died at London in the year 1717, after his studious life had been protracted to the length of 76 years. He left behind him numerous proofs of his great talents, extensive learning, uncommon industry, and zealous attachment to the doctrines of the church of England. (Gen. Biog.)

ALLOA

Pages 330-330
or Alloway, a sea-port town in Scotland, seated on the Forth, about 20 miles higher up the river than Leith, and five miles east of Stirling. It is a populous place; has two market days in the week; and is remarkable for its fine castle, the seat of Mr Erskine of Mar, and for the coal mines near it. The harbour is extremely commodious, with great depth of water; and vessels are expeditiously loaded with coals from the pits by an uncommon waggon-way, on which one horse draws with ease three waggons at once, each waggon containing a ton and a half. An excellent dry dock has also lately been erected here, capable of receiving ships of the greatest burden. There is likewise a large glas-house for blowing bottles, of which vessels are supplied with any quantity upon the shortest notice. The tower and lands of Alloa were exchanged by David II, king of Scots, anno 1365, with Thomas Lord Erskine, for the lands and estate of Strathgarnet in Perthshire; and since that time the castle of Alloa has been the favourite residence of the family of Mar. The situation is uncommonly beautiful. The gardens here were the first that were laid out on a great scale in Scotland; and, with the advice of Le Naute, were indebted to the taste of John the late earl of Mar, who began to plant them in the year 1706. They contain about forty acres, in which there is some very fine timber, near a century old. The tower of Alloa is 89 feet in height, with walls of 11 feet in thickness; and was built in the end of the 13th century. In this residence of the family of Erskine many of the Scottish princes received their education, having been for more than two centuries, the wards of the Lords Erskine and Earls of Mar; who held generally the castle of Stirling, and frequently the three principal fortresses of the kingdom, Edinburgh, Stirling, and Dumbarton. The last heir of the Scottish monarchy who was nurtured there was Henry prince of Wales; whose cradle, golf-clubs, and other infantine and youthful remains, are preserved by the heir of the earls of Mar, in remembrance of that spirited and promising prince; of whom Dr Birch has preserved several anecdotes, connected with the Erskines and his residence at Alloa. Among other remains of antiquity preserved at Alloa, in remembrance of the confidence and affection which subsisted always betwixt the Stuarts and the Erskines, is the private signet of the unfortunate Mary, which she gave to the regent Mar, after she was obliged by the treaty of Edinburgh to desist from wearing the arms of England in the first quarter; the child's chair of James VI, her son; and the effigy chair of Thomas Lord Erskine the second earl of Mar of the name, with the fashionable grace carved on it, Soli Deo Honor et Gloria. ALLOBROGES (Inscriptions, Livy, Velleius, Florus); from Allobroges (Horace): a people of Gallia Narbonensis, situated between the rivers Ilara and Rhodanus, and the Lacus Lemanus; commanded by Cicerro for their fidelity; but reproached by Horace on account of their fondness for novelty. Novisque rebus infidelis Allobroges. Epod. 16.

ALLOCATION

Pages 330-330

N denotes the admitting <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> allowing of an article of an account, especially in the exchequer. Hence ALLOCATIONS Facienda, is a writ directed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, or barons of the exchequer, commanding them to allow an accountant such sums as he has lawfully expended in the execution of his office.

ALLOCUTIO

Pages 330-330

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> speech of a general addressed to his soldiery, to animate them to fight, to appease sedition, or to keep them to their duty. A mound of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was raised upon the occasion, as it were a kind of a tribunal of turf. From this the general pronounced his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, which was ranged...

ALLODIUM

Pages 330-331
or Alleud, denotes lands which are the absolute property of their owner, without being obliged to pay any service or acknowledgment whatever to a superior lord. See Fee and Fodal System.

ALLOTTING

Pages 331-331
or Allotment of Goods, in matters of commerce, is when a ship's cargo is divided into several parts, bought by divers persons, whose names are written on as many pieces of paper, which are applied by an indifferent person to the several lots or parcels; by which means the goods are divided without partiality, every man having the parcel which the lot with his name appropriates. ALLOWAY Creek, in Salem county, New-Jersey, empties into the Delaware. It is navigable 16 miles, interrupted, however, by several draw-bridges.

ALLOY

Pages 331-331
or Allay, properly signifies a proportion of a baser metal mixed with a finer one. The alloy of gold is estimated by carats, that of silver by pennyweights. In different nations different proportions of alloy are used; whence their moneys are said to be of different degrees of fineness or baseness, and are valued accordingly in foreign exchanges. The chief reasons alleged for the alloying of coin are: 1. The mixture of the metals, which, when melted from the mine, are not perfectly pure. 2. The saving the expense it must otherwise cost if they were to be refined. 3. The necessity of rendering them harder, by mixing some parts of other metals with them, to prevent the diminution of weight by wearing in passing from hand to hand. 4. The melting of foreign gold or coin which is alloyed. 5. The charges of coinage, which must be made good by the profit arising from the money coined. 6. Lastly, the duty belonging to the sovereign, on account of the power he has to cause money to be coined in his dominions. In a more general sense, the word is employed in chemistry to signify the union of different metallic matters.—As an infinity of different combinations may be made according to the nature, the number, and the proportions of the metallic matters capable of being alloyed, we shall not here enter into the detail of the particular alloys, all which are not yet nearly known. Those which are used, as Bronze, Tombac, Brass, White Copper, &c., may be found in the article Chemistry, and what is known concerning other alloys will be treated of along with the metals in the same article. See Chemistry Index. ALLUM. See Alum.

ALLUMINOR

Pages 331-331

from the French allumer, "to lighten," is used for one who colours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> paints upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARCHMENT">parchment</a>; and the reason is, because he gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and ornament by his colours to the letters or other figures. Such ornaments are styled illuminations. The word is used in stat. i R. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 9. But now such a person is called a limner.

ALLUSH

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>. The Israelites being in the wilderness of Shur, departed from Dophkah, and went to Allush, from whence they proceeded to Rephidim; Num. xxxiii. 13, 14. Eusebius and St. Jerome fix Allush in Idumea, about Gabala <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Petra, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea. In the accounts of the empire, it is situated in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; and by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, among the cities of Idumea.

ALLUSION

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> by which something is applied to, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> understood of, another, on account of some similitude between them.

ALLUVION

Pages 331-331

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, denotes the gradual increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> on banks of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>.

ALMACARRON

Pages 331-331

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, at the mouth of the river Guadalentin. It is about twenty miles west of Cartagena, and is remarkable for the prodigious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> found in its territory. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 15. N. Lat. 37° 40'.

ALMADEN

Pages 331-331

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of La Mancha, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Castile, situated upon the top of a mountain, where are the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as well as the richest silver <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>.

ALMADIE

Pages 331-331

a kind of canoe, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> small vessel, about four fathoms <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made of bark, and used by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">negroes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. ALMADIE is also the name of a kind of long boats, fitted out at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALICUT">Calicut</a>, which are eighty feet in length, and six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> in breadth. They are exceedingly swift, and are otherwise called catburi.

ALMAGEST

Pages 331-331

in Matters of Literature, is particularly used for a collection <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> book composed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, containing various problems of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> both in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. ALMAGEST is also the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of other collections of this kind. Thus, Riccioli has published a book of astronomy, which he calls the New Almagest; and Plukenet, a book which he calls Almagestum Botanicum.

ALMAGRA

Pages 331-331

a fine deep <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> ochre, with some admixture of purple, very heavy, and of a dense yet friable structure, and rough dusty surface. It adheres very firmly to the tongue, melts freely and easily in the mouth, is of an astringent and strongly astringent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and stains the skin in touching. It is the Sil Atticum of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>; it ferments very violently with acid menstruums; by which single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, it is sufficiently distinguished from the Sil Syricum, to which it has in many respects a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a>. It is found in immense quantities in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a> there are in a manner whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of it. It is used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, and in medicine as an astringent.

ALMAGRO

Pages 331-334

a fortress of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of one of the districts of La Mancha. It was built by the archbishop Roderic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, who finished it in 1214, and put a considerable garrison into it to restrain the incursions of the Moors. This was hardly done, when the fortress was besieged by an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 5000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot, under the command of a Moorish officer of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation; but the prelate, its founder, took care to supply those within with such plenty of necessaries, that at length the enemy found themselves obliged to raise the siege and retire with great loss. Almagro, Diego De, a Spanish commander, was... of such obscure birth and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> parentage, that he derived his name from the village where he was born, in 1463. Deprived of the means of early instruction, he could neither read nor write, but nevertheless, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his improvements in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, he formed an afflication with Pizarro and de Luque, for the purpose of discoveries and conquest upon the Peruvian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The governor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANAMA">Panama</a> having sanctioned their enterprise, they devoted their united exertions to that undertaking. Pizarro directed the conquest, and Almagro was appointed to conduct the supplies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and reinforcements. In the two first unsuccessful attempts, he performed this office with persevering fidelity and uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. His perseverance was followed with complete success; for they at last discovered the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and landed at Tumbez, distinguished by its temple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the incas <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sovereigns, and situated about three degrees south of the line. Pizarro was sent over to Spain to solicit farther powers, after the three adventurers had previously adjusted their future preferences, and agreed that Pizarro should be governor, Almagro <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-governor, and Luque bishop. In this negociation, Pizarro obtained the clerical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> for Luque; but chiefly concerned about his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, he neglected the preference of Almagro. On his return, Almagro was so enraged, that he refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with such a perfidious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, and resolved to form a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. Pizarro, for the present artfully endeavoured to avert the indignation of Almagro, and gradually soothed the rage and disappointment of the folder. The union was renewed upon the former terms; and it was solemnly stipulated that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> expense and a common advantage should take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In February 1531, leaving Almagro at Panama, to supply provisions and reinforcements, Pizarro set sail for Peru. He attacked a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlement of the natives, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Coaque, obtained immense spoil, and made such ample remittances to Almagro, as enabled him to complete his reinforcement, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 1532, he arrived at St Michael with a body of men, which nearly doubled the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those which Pizarro had along with him. The Spaniards about this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> took captive the unfortunate Inca Atahualpa; and after they had received an immense sum for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a>, they barbarously put him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Pizarro sailed for Spain with the news of their success, and with remittances to a great amount; and consequently Almagro gained that elevated station he so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and eagerly desired. But no sooner had Almagro received the intelligence of his promotion by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a>, than he attempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> Cuzco, the imperial residence of the incas, under pretence that it lay within his defined territory. This produced a new quarrel; but peace was restored upon the determination of Almagro to attempt the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, and likewise to have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the territory of Peru. In 1535, he accordingly set out at the head of 570 Europeans, and in crossing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, he suffered great hardships and losses by mistaking the route, but at length he descended into the plains of that devoted region. Here he met with a more vigorous resistance from the natives than the Spaniards had ever experienced in other countries. He had, however, made some progress, when he was recalled to Peru by the news of the natives having risen in great numbers, and attacked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMA">Lima</a> and Cuzco. He purified a new route, and marching through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plains on the coast, he suffered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and drought calamities not inferior to those which he had endured from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and famine on the summit of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>. Arriving at a favourable moment, he resolved to hold the place both against the Indians and his Spanish rivals. He attacked the Peruvian army with great vigour, and making a great slaughter, he proceeded to the gates of Cuzco without any farther interruption. The open, affable, and generous temper of Almagro, gained over to his side many of the adherents of the Pizzaros, who were disgusted with their harsh and opprobrious conduct. With their aid, he advanced towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> by night, surprized the sentinels, and surrounded the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> where the two brothers resided, who were compelled, after an obstinate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>. A form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was settled in the name of Almagro, and his jurisdiction over Cuzco was universally acknowledged. This was the origin of a civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; the beginning of which was very advantageous to Almagro, who by skilful manoeuvres entirely routed a body of Spanish troops advancing to the relief of Cuzco, and made Alvarado their commander prisoner. But instead of improving these advantages, he unwisely marched back to Cuzco, and there awaited the arrival of Pizarro. Pizarro, convinced of his own feeble resources, proposed an accommodation, and with his usual art protracted the negociation until he found himself in a condition to meet his antagonist in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Meanwhile Alvarado and one of the Pizzaros, by bribing their keepers, found means to escape, and persuaded 60 of the men who guarded them to attend them in their flight; and the governor released the other Pizarro. When Pizarro thought himself sufficiently prepared to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the dominion of Peru, he marched with an army of 500 men to Cuzco. Almagro, previous to this, worn out with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> and infirmity, resigned the command to Orgognez. A fierce and bloody battle ensued, in which Almagro was made prisoner, his army defeated, and the commander wounded. About 140 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> fell in the field, and Orgognez, along with several others, was massacred in cold blood. During that fatal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, Almagro, placed in a litter, which was stationed on an eminence, beheld from thence the total defeat of his troops, and felt all the indignation of a folder who had seldom experienced defeat. He was taken prisoner, remained several months in confinement, and afterwards was tried, and condemned to death. In the view of an ignominious death, the courage of the veteran forsook him, and he unsuccessfully supplicated for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in a manner unworthy of his former character. All the arguments he could employ were ineffectual. The Pizzaros remained unmoved by all his entreaties. As soon, however, as Almagro <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> that his fate was inevitable, he refused his courage, and exhibited all his usual dignity and fortitude. In the year 1538, and in the 7th year of his age, he was strangled in prison, and afterwards beheaded. He left one son by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> woman of Panama; and in consequence of a power which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> had granted, he declared his son his successor in Almagro, in the government, although he was then a prisoner in Lima. With the qualities of intrepid valour, indefatigable activity, and infurmountable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>, he blended the more amiable dispositions of frankness, generosity, and candour. These qualities rendered him beloved by his followers; and his misfortunes excited their sympathy and pity, so that his death was universally regretted, and particularly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Indians, who deemed him their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> and protector against the cruel and unfeeling Pizarro. Upon the whole review of his character, it appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> to conclude, that he was, although of inferior abilities, a more amiable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> than his rival. (Gen. Biog.) Almagro the Younger, by his courage, generosity, and other accomplishments, was placed at the head of the party after the death of his father. The father, conscious of his own inferiority from the total want of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, used every possible mean to improve the mind and embellish the manners of his son; so that he soon acquired those accomplishments which rendered him respected by illiterate adventurers, who cheerfully ranged around his standard; and, by his dexterity and skill, fought deliverance from the oppressions of Pizarro. Juan de Herrera, an officer of great abilities, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> still to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his counsels and to regulate his enterprises; and, while Pizarro confined in his own security, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> was formed against him, which terminated in his death. The afflains, exulting in their success, and waving their bloody swords, halted to the street, proclaimed the death of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a>, and compelled the magistrates and principal citizens of Lima to acknowledge Almagro as lawful successor to his father. But his reign was of short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>; for, in 1541, Vaca de Castro, arriving at Quito, produced the royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, appointing him governor of Peru, together with all the privileges and authority of Pizarro. The talents and influence of the new governor soon overpowered the interest of Almagro, who, perceiving the rapid decline of his influence, hastened with his troops to Cuzco, where his opponents had erected the royal standard under the command of Pedro Álvarez Falgén. Herrera the guide of his counsels died during his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>; and from that time his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were conspicuous for their violence, concerted with little ingenuity, and executed with little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>. On September 16, 1542, at length the forces of Almagro and Vaca de Castro met, and victory long remained doubtful; till at last it declared for the new governor. The followers of Almagro displayed uncommon valour, and Almagro conducted the military operations of that fatal day with a gallant spirit, worthy of a better cause and deserving of a better fate. In proportion to the number of combatants the carnage was very great. Of 1500 men 500 fell in the field, and many more were wounded. Almagro escaped, but being betrayed by some of his own officers, he was publicly beheaded at Cuzco, and in him the name and spirit of the party of Almagro became extinct. (Gen. Biog.) <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALMAMON">Almamon</a>, or Mamon, also named Abdallah, caliph of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, was born A.D. 785. His elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Al Amin succeeded to the caliphate on the death of his father, and Almamon at that time was governor of Chorasan. As by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the father it Almamon provided, that his three sons should succeed to the caliphate in order, Almamon ordered his elder brother to be proclaimed caliph throughout his government. But his brother repaid his friendship and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his interest with open expressions of hatred, and unjust attempts to exclude him from the defined succession. Almamon was thus forced to consult measures for his own safety and promotion, by causing himself to be proclaimed caliph. After various struggles, his general, Thalier, in the year 813 took possession of Bagdad, pursued Al Amin to his retreat, and caused him to be assassinated, so that Almamon remained without a competitor. Various rebellions disturbed the tranquillity of the first years of his reign; but by his prudent administration and vigorous exertions, these were at length extinguished. Incited by the advice of his vizier, he soon after raised greater commotions, and exposed his dignity to greater dangers, by countenancing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>. He invited to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> Imam Rizza, gave him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and even declared him his successor in the empire. He assumed the green turban, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the house of Ali, and obliged his courtiers and soldiers to imitate his example. Alarmed at these proceedings, the orthodox Mussulmans, and the house of Abbas, excited a great revolt in Bagdad, and proclaimed Ibrahim, Almamon's uncle, caliph. A civil war was just about to commence when Fadel the vizier was assassinated and Rizza died. The people of Bagdad then depoed Ibrahim, and returned to their former <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>. Taking the advantage of Almamon's absence, Thalier his general seized upon the government of Chorasan, where he founded a dynasty which existed during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of 16 years. Almamon employed the period of tranquillity that followed in the introduction and improvement of literature into his dominions, which constitutes the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of his reign. During the days of his father he discovered an ardent thirst after knowledge, by forming a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in Chorasan, adorned with the most eminent men of various countries; and appointed Mefue, a famous Christian physician of Damascus, for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. When his father remonstrated against conferring such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> upon a Christian, he reminded him, that the most learned men and the most skilful artists in his dominions were Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; and added, that he had chosen Mefue as a preceptor in science and useful arts, and not as a teacher of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Under his auspices Bagdad became the seat of literature, of private and academical instruction, and the habitation of men of eminence from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Many valuable books in the Greek, Persian, Chaldean, and Coptic languages, among which were the works of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> and Galen, were translated into the Arabic at his own expense. The caliph himself deemed it an honour to set an example to others of the becoming respect due to mental cultivation, by visiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and treating the professors with great regard. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, he made a rapid and extensive progress. He was the author of astronomical tables, which on account of their accuracy have been much admired. By these various exertions the character of the Saracens was suddenly changed from... Almamon, a rude and ferocious to a polite and civilized people, while the most powerful and extensive of the European states were involved in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> and barbarism. Literature has sustained some irreparable losses from his too great partiality to the Arabic writers, which induced him to destroy the originals of the translated <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a>. He is represented by the Sonnites or orthodox Mahometans as little better than an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">Infidel</a>, because of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to philosophy and letters. His conduct, however, shows that he was not sufficiently careful to preserve a philosophical mean between the different <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> parties during the time of his administration, as he openly manifested a predilection to the doctrines of the Motaellis, who asserted the free will of man, and denied the eternity of the Koran. Some allege, that on account of the murmurs which arose against him, he was induced to exhibit too great a zeal by establishing a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a>, to compel all his subjects to profess <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAM">Islam</a>. The experiment, however, soon terminated in the better and juster expedient of universal toleration; and it is abundantly evident, that the Christians in his dominions never felt the power of his inquisition. The public transactions of his reign are in themselves important. In the year 822 he sent a body of his troops to the assistance of Thomas, a Greek, who made war on Michael the Stammerer, the emperor of Constantinople, and besieged his capital. This expedition, which on the part of the caliph seems to have been founded in injustice, proved unsuccessful; Thomas was taken prisoner, and suffered death. In the years 829 and 830 he commenced open hostilities upon the Greeks, rendered himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of many places, and carried devastation into their territories. He was successful in suppressing a revolt in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> in the year 831. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> he was led to discover a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> buried under two columns by Merwan, the last caliph of the house of Ommiiah. In repairing a decayed masonry or measuring pillar, and erecting a new one for determining the gradation of the increase of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, Almamon displayed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science. In the year 833 he again visited Egypt; on his return he penetrated into the territories of the Greek emperor, even into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CILICIA">Cilicia</a>. Returning home he encamped on the banks of a river, and, excited by thirst, drank too freely of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and at the same time indulged himself immoderately in eating a particular kind of dates, which brought on a complaint in his stomach, and reduced him to the most imminent danger. Sensible of his approaching <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a>, he wrote letters into all the provinces, announcing his brother Motafem his successor; and then patiently awaited the event. After a tedious struggle under the prelure of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and while uttering this ejaculation; "O thou who never died, have mercy on me, a dying man!" he expired at the age of forty-eight or forty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years. He reigned 20 years and some months, and was buried at Tarbus, which some religious zealots interpreted as a mark of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this caliph affords an illustrious instance of the meliorating effect of science and literature upon the conduct and temper of rude and uncultivated men. Under the milder features of a liberal, virtuous, and benevolent sovereign, the usual cruelty of a Saracen and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a> seemed entirely lost. He displayed Almamon, an uncommon greatness of mind and an unusual example of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> in his conduct towards his rival and uncle Ibrahim. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> concealed himself in some sequestered corner of Bagdad. The place of his concealment being at length discovered, he was instantly brought before the caliph, and informed that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> had unanimously condemned him to death. "Your counsellors (said Ibrahim) have judged, according to the customary rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> government; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> me, you will not, indeed, judge according to precedent, but you will have no equal among sovereigns." The caliph rose up and embracing him tenderly, with great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, said, "Uncle be of good cheer; I will not do you the least injury;" and he added to forgive us a fortune suitable to his birth and former elevated station. When Almamon's courtiers complimented him on this generous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, he exclaimed, "O! did men but know the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> I feel in pardoning, all who have offended me would come and confess their faults." To the same generosity of disposition may be ascribed his strong predilection to the oppressed house of Ali, which filled the beginning of his reign with political troubles. By his frequent intercourse with men of enlightened minds, and of different religious sentiments, he acquired a liberality very unusual in a Mussulman; and his preference to some particular opinions seems to have originated from his own vigour of mind, and his knowledge of these opinions. (Gen. Biog.)

ALMANACK

Pages 334-336

a book <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> of days and months, the rising and setting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, the eclipses of both luminaries, &c.—Authors are divided with regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word; some deriving it from the Arabic particle al and manach, to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a>; some from almanach, new-year's gifts, because the Arabian astrologers used at the beginning of the year to make presents of their ephemerides; and others, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> almanen achte, observations on all the months. Dr Johnson derives it from the Arabic particle al, and the Greek μήν, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. But the most simple etymology appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPELLING">spelling</a>; the word being composed of two Arabic ones, Al Manack, which signify the Diary. All the classes of Arabs are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> much given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and astrology; to both which a pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and a sort of husbandry, not only incline them, but afford <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and opportunity to cultivate them. They neither sow, reap, plant, travel, buy or sell, or undertake any expedition or business, without previously consulting the stars, or, in other words, their almanacks, or some of the makers of them. From these people, by their vicinity to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, this art, no less useful in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> than trifling and ridiculous in another, hath passed over hither; and those astronomical compositions have still everywhere not only retained their old Arabic name; but were, like theirs, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while, and still are among many European nations, intermixed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of astrological rules for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a>, sowing, bleeding, purging, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and paring of the nails.—Regiomontanus appears to have been the first in Europe, however, who reduced almanacks into their present form and method, gave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of each Almanack each year and month, foretold the eclipses and other phases, calculated the motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, &c. His first almanack was published in 1474. The essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an almanack is the calendar of months and days, with the risings and settings of the sun, age of the moon, &c. To these are added various parerga, astronomical, meteorological, chronological, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a>, rural, &c., as calculations and accounts of eclipses, solar ingresses, prognostics of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, tables of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>, terms, &c., lists of posts, offices, dignities, public institutions, with many other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> political as well as local, and differing in different countries. A great variety are annually published in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>; some for binding, which may be denominated book almanacks; others in loose papers, called sheet almanacks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> almanack answers to the Fasti of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. See FASTI. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of Almanacks. The first thing to be done is, to compute the sun's and moon's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the year, or it may be taken from some ephemerides and entered into the almanack; next, find the dominical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>, and, by means thereof, distribute the calendar into weeks; then, having computed the time of Easter, by it fix the other moveable feasts; adding the immovable ones, with the names of the martyrs, the rising and setting of each luminary, the length of day and night, the aspects of the planets, the phases of the moon, and the sun's entrance into the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the ecliptic, i.e. the two equinoxes and solstices. (See ASTRONOMY, paffim.) By the help of good astronomical tables or ephemerides, the construction of almanacks is extremely easy. For every almanack or calendar for one year or less, a stamp duty of 8d. must be paid. And for every almanack serving more than a year, the same duty is paid for each year. Perpetual almanacks pay for three years only. All books and pamphlets serving chiefly the purpose of almanacks, are <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> as such. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> any almanack contains more than one sheet, one sheet only need be stamped; and every almanack required by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to be so printed, that some part of the print shall be upon the stamp. Selling unstamped almanacks incurs the same penalty as for selling unstamped newspapers. Almanacks in bibles and common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> books are exempted. Almanack, among Antiquaries, is also the name given to a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, usually of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> with various figures and Runic characters, and representing the order of the feasts, dominical letters, days of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> number, with other matters necessary to be known throughout the year used by the ancient northern nations, in their computations of time, both civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a>. Almanacks of this kind are known by various names, among the different nations wherein they have been used; as rimlocks, primasters, runflocks, runstaffs, Scipiones Ravici, Baculi Annales, clogs, &c. They appear to have been used only by the Swedes, Danes, and Norwegians. From the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> of these people, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> was introduced into England, whence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> remains of them in the counties. Dr Plot has given the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of one of these clogs, found in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of The Perpetual Staffordshire Almanack. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> figure and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of these calendars appear to have been various. Sometimes they were cut on one or more wooden leaves, Almanor bound together after the manner of books; sometimes on the scabbards of swords, or even on daggers; sometimes on tools and implements, as portable steelyards, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HAMMERS">hammers</a>, the halves of hatchets, flails, &c. Sometimes they were made of braids or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; sometimes of the skins of eels, which being drawn over a stick properly inscribed, retained the impressions of it. But the most usual form was that of walking staves, or sticks, which they carried about with them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, market, &c. Each of these staves is divided into three regions; whereof the first indicates the signs, the second the days of the week and year, and the third the golden number. The characters engraved on them are, in some, the ancient Runic; in others the later Gothic characters of Ulphilus. The saints' days are expressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, significant either of some endowment of the saint, the manner of his martyrdom, or the like. Thus, against the notch for the first of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, or St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>'s day, is represented a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARP">harp</a>; against the 23rd of October, or Crispin's day, a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes; against the 12th of August, or St Lawrence's day, a gridiron; and lastly, against New-year's day, a horn, the symbol of liberal potations, which our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> indulged in at that season. ALMANSOR the Victorious, the second caliph of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Al Abbas, succeeded his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Abul Abbas Al Safah, in the year 753, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 136, and in the following year was inaugurated at Al Hashemiyah. Although Al Safah had declared him presumptive heir of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and he had been proclaimed caliph in the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANBAR">Anbar</a>, yet immediately upon his inauguration, his uncle Abdallah ibn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> had sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to cause himself to be proclaimed caliph at Damascus. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, and Mesopotamia, he collected a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and arrived at the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, near Nisibis, where he encamped, ready to dispute his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCLAMATION">acclamation</a> by arms. Almanor collected an immense army in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, Khorasan, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRAK">Irak</a>, and gave the command of it to Abu Moflem, who harassed his uncle's troops for five months, and at last totally defeated him, A.D. 754. Notwithstanding the services which Abu Moflem had rendered to the family of Al Abbas, after this victory he became an object of jealousy, and was affianced in the presence of Almanor himself, by his express order. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Abu Moflem, the standard of rebellion was raised by Sinon a Magian, who seized on the treasures of the deceased governor of Khorasan, and excited the people of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to a general revolt; but this insurrection was suddenly quelled by the general of Almanor, Jamhur ibn Morad. The caliph avengingly seized the spoils of this victory, which so incensed Jamhur that he immediately turned his arms against his royal <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>; but he was soon defeated by the caliph's forces. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of Antioch was about this time detected in an illicit correspondence with the Grecian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, and consequently was banished into an obscure part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in the dominions of the caliph were prohibited from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> or repairing any churches, and also were laid under several other severe restraints. Almanor sent a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> army into Cappadocia in the year 757, fortified the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALATIA">Malatia</a> or Melitene, Almanfor, litene, and deposited in it a great part of his treasures. But in this year he was attacked by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">believers</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEMPSYCHOSIS">metempsychosis</a>, called the Rawandians. This sect assembled at Al Hashimiyyah the residence of the caliph, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of going in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> round his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, intimated their purpose of invoking him as a deity, and paying him divine homage. Incensed by their impiety, the caliph ordered several of these sectaries to be imprisoned, which roused their resentment, and led them to form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of his assassination. The generous interposition of Maan ibn Zaidet an Ommiyan <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, who had been under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of concealing himself from the caliph's resentment, however defeated their intention. This insult received in his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, induced him to build the city of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, and to fix his residence there, A.D. 762. In the preceding year a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was formed to dethrone him; but it being discovered, he severely punished all who were either directly or indirectly concerned in it. Abdallah his uncle shared the fate of other rebels: for being allured to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and protection, he was placed in a building which was so constructed that it immediately fell and crushed him in its ruins. Not long after his residence at Bagdad, he was seized with a disorder of which he was cured by the advice of a famous Christian physician, whose name was George ibn Baktifluwa Al Jondaburi. The caliph, previously informed that he was married to a wife old and infirm, as a compensation presented him with three beautiful Greek girls, and a considerable sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; the girls, to the caliph's surprise, were sent back, with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> on the part of George, that it was not lawful for a Christian to have more wives than one at a time. The conduct of the physician, on this occasion, raised him in the esteem of the caliph, and procured him a greater profusion of favours. In his succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> transactions, Almanfor was generally victorious. His conduct to his Christian subjects was rigorous and severe. He set out on a pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> in the year 774, and being seized on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> with a dangerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, he sent for his son and intended successor Al Mohdi, and gave him some salutary advice. "I command you," said he, "to treat publicly your relations with the greatest marks of distinction, since this conduct <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> reflect no small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> upon yourself. Increase the number of your freedmen, and treat them with all kindness, as they will be of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to you in your adversity; but neither this, nor the other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INJUNCTION">injunction</a> will you fulfil. Enlarge not that part of your capital erected on the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Tigris, as you will never be able to finish it; but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> I know you will attempt. Never permit any of your women to intermeddle in affairs of state, or to have any influence over your counsels; but this advice I know you will not take. These are my last commands; or, if you please, my dying advice; and to God I now recommend you." In parting they both gave vent to their feelings in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> of tears. He pursued his journey to Bir-Maimun, i.e., the well of Maimun, where he died in the 63rd year of his age and the 20th of his reign, and his remains were interred at Mecca. The character of Almanfor was formed of very different and even contradictory qualities. His temper conciliated affection and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> in private life, but in his public character his aspect and demeanour inspired terror. He was well acquainted with the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; he was prudent and brave, but perfidious, covetous, cruel, and implacable; and amid such a variety of character, it is singular that he should have displayed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of study and literature, and particularly of astronomy. (Gen. Biog.)

ALMANZA

Pages 336-336

a little town of New Castile, on the frontiers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 19. N. Lat. 38. 54. It is remarkable for the defeat of the allies in 1707, under the marquis de las Minas and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALWAY">Galway</a>. In the beginning of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> the English troops penetrated through the centre of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but the Portuguese cavalry being broken by the Spanish, and the French infantry making a dreadful fire on their flanks, the allied army was at last broken, and began their retreat when it was almost dark. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Hill carried off the remains of thirteen battalions towards the river Xucar, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they could have paused, they might have been safe; but being very much fatigued, they were obliged to halt; by which means they were surrounded, and forced to surrender prisoners of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, the allies lost 120 standards, together with all their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> and baggage; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> were killed, and several thousands taken prisoners. The Marquis de las Minas was dangerously wounded; and his mistress, in the garb of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMAZON">amazon</a>, killed by his side. The earl of Galway had two cuts across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, which, though not dangerous, had prevented him from seeing, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> giving orders properly.

ALME

Pages 336-337
or ALMA, singing and dancing girls in Egypt, who, like the Italian Improvisatori, can occasionally pour forth "unpremeditated verse." They are called Almé, from having received a better education than other women. They form a celebrated society in that country. To be received into it, according to M. Savary, it is necessary to have a good voice, to understand the language well, to know the rules of poetry, and be able to compose and sing couplets on the spot, adapted to the circumstances. The Almé know by heart all the new songs. Their memory is furnished with the most beautiful tales. There is no festival without them; no entertainment of which they do not constitute the ornament. They are placed in a rostrum, from whence they sing during the repast. They then descend into the falcon, and form dances which have no resemblance to ours. They are pantomime ballets, in which they represent the usual occurrences of life. The mysteries of love, too, generally generally furnish them with scenes. The suppleness of their bodies is inconceivable. One is astonished at the mobility of their features, to which they give at pleasure the impression suited to the characters they play. The indecency of their attitudes is often carried to excess. Their looks, their gestures, every thing speaks, but in so expressive a manner, that it is impossible to mistake them. At the beginning of the dance, they lay aside with their veils the modesty of their sex. A long robe of very thin silk goes down to their heels, which is slightly fastened with a rich girdle. Long black hair, plaited and perfumed, is flowing on their shoulders. A shift, transparent as gauze, scarcely hides their bosom. As they put themselves in motion, the shapes, the contours of their bodies, seem to develop themselves successively. Their steps are regulated by the sound of the flute, of cattanets, the tambour de basque, and cymbals, which accelerates or retards the measure. They are still further animated by words adapted to such scenes. They appear in a state of intoxication. They are the Bacchants in a delirium. It is when they are at this point, that throwing off all reserve, they abandon themselves totally to the disorder of their senses; it is then that a people far from delicate, and who like nothing hidden, redouble their applause. These Almé are sent for into all the harems. They teach the women the new airs; they amuse them with amorous tales, and recite in their presence poems, which are so much the more interesting, as they furnish a lively picture of their manners. They initiate them into the mysteries of their art, and teach them to contrive lascivious dances. These girls, who have cultivated understanding, are very agreeable in conversation. They speak their language with purity. The habit of dedicating themselves to poetry renders the softest and most sonorous expressions familiar to them. They repeat with a great deal of grace. In singing, nature is their only guide. Sometimes two of them sing together, but always with the same voice. It is the same with an orchestra, where all the instruments playing in unison execute the same part. The Almé assist at the marriage-ceremonies, and march before the bride, playing on instruments. They make a figure likewise at funerals, and accompany the procession, singing sorrowful airs. They break forth into groans and lamentations, and give every sign of grief and despair. These women are paid very high, and seldom appear but amongst the grandees and rich men. The common people have also their Almé. They are girls of the second class, who try to imitate the former; but they have neither their elegance, their graces, nor their knowledge. They are everywhere to be met with. The public places and the walks about Grand Cairo are full of them. As the populace require allusions still more strongly marked, decency will not permit the relation to what a pitch they carry the licentiousness of their gestures and attitudes.

ALMEDIA

Pages 337-337

a frontier town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Tralos Montes, on the confines of Leon, where there was a very brisk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> between the French and Portuguese in 1663; 17 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIUDAD_RODRIGO">Ciudad Rodrigo</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 7° 10'. N. Lat. 42° 41'.

ALMEHRAB

Pages 337-337

in the Mahometan Customs, a niche in their mosques, pointing towards the kebla <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> temple of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>, to which they are obliged to bow in praying. See KEBLA.

ALMEISAR

Pages 337-337

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Arabs, performed by a kind of casting of lots with arrows, strictly forbidden by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of Mahomet, on account of the frequent quarrels occasioned by it. The manner of the game was thus: A young camel being brought and killed, was divided into a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parts. The adventurers, to the number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, being met, 11 arrows were provided without heads <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> feathers; seven of which were marked, the first with one notch, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> with two, the third with three, &c. the other four had no marks. These arrows were put promiscuously into a bag, and thus drawn by an indifferent person. Those to whom the marked arrows fell, won shares in proportion to their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>; the rest to whom the blanks fell, were entitled to no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the camel, but obliged to pay the whole price of it. Even the winners tasted not of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> themselves more than the losers, but the whole was distributed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>.

ALMENE

Pages 337-337

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of two pounds used to weigh saffron in several parts of the continent of the East Indies.

ALMERIA

Pages 337-338

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, pleasantly situated on a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> at the mouth of the river Almeria, on the Mediterranean. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 20'. N. Lat. 36° 51'. This town is by some thought to have risen upon the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDERA">Abdera</a>, and was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. It was taken from the Moors in 1147, by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> III., in conjunction with the French, Geneoese, and Pisans. It was at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the strongest place in Spain held by the Infidels; from which their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIVATEERS">privateers</a>, which were exceedingly numerous, not only troubled the sea-coasts inhabited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, but gave equal disturbance to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> provinces of France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> being well fortified, having a strong castle, a numerous garrison, and being excellently provided with everything necessary, made a vigorous resistance; but was at last taken by storm, when the victor put to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all the inhabitants who were found in arms, distributing the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the plunder among his allies, whom he sent away thoroughly satisfied. The Geneoese, particularly, acquired here that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a> vessel which still remains in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, and is deemed invaluable. Upon its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> by the Christians, Almeria became a bishopric; but is at present very little better than a village, indifferently inhabited, and has nothing to tellify so much as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> of its former greatness, except certain circumstances which cannot be effaced even by the indolence of the Spaniards themselves. What these are, Udal ap Rhys, a Welshman, thus describes, in his Tour through Spain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. "Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> (says he) is so peculiarly blest, that one really wants words to express its charms and excellence. Its fields and meads are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> all the year round; they are adorned also with palms, myrtles, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> trees, oranges, and olives; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> and promontories near it are as noted for their producing a great variety of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, inasmuch that the next promontory to it is called the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Gates, which is a corruption from the word agates, the hills..." Almiggim hills thereabouts abounding in that fort of precious stones, as well as in emeralds and amethysts, garnets <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> coarse rubies, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> curious alabaster in the mountains of Filaures." ALMIGGIM. See ALMUGGIM.

ALMEYDA

Pages 338-338
DON FRANCIS, was the son of the Count d'Abrantes, a grandee of Portugal, who served with great distinction in the war of Ferdinand of Castile with Granada; and in consequence of his important services he became highly esteemed in the court of his sovereign. Without any solicitation on his part he was nominated the first governor general and viceroy of the newly conquered countries in the East Indies; and set sail from Lisbon in March 1505-6 with a powerful fleet. To give dignity and influence to his elevated station, a body of guards was appointed to attend his person, several chaplains were assigned him, together with every other appendage of grandeur. He touched at the Cape Verde islands, doubled the Cape at a considerable distance to the south, and arrived at Gulloa. From thence he proceeded to Mombaza, a well fortified city in an island, which he reduced, and proceeded to the Angediva islands not far from Goa, where he built a fort; he likewise erected and garrisoned another fort at Cannanor, and arriving at Cochin, he secured it to the Portuguese interest. The island of Madagascar was discovered during his government, and his son Don Lorenzo first surveyed the Maldives islands; and about the same time discovered the fine island of Ceylon, the principal sovereign of which he brought under submission to the crown of Portugal. Returning from this expedition, while employed in the fleet destined against Calicut, he lost his life in a sea-fight against the Zamorin. His father sustained his loss with a heroic firmness, saying, "that Lorenzo could not die better than in the service of his country." On the arrival of Alphonso d'Albuquerque, who was destined to be his successor, Almeida yielded to the impressions of jealousy; and under the pretence of misconduct he confined him in the citadel of Cannanor. He engaged in 1508, the whole force of the Mahommedans in the port of Diu; and, gaining a complete victory, facilitated the enterprises of Albuquerque his successor, by contributing to break that formidable league by which the Zamorin was in hopes of being able to compel the Portuguese to abandon their Indian conquests. Returning home with the great riches which he had acquired, he unfortunately touched at Saldanha Point on the coast of Africa, where some of the sailors, in quest of water, quarrelled with the natives, who attacked and drove them to their ships. With a view to revenge this pretended affront, they persuaded Almeida himself to go ashore, with a body of 150 men, armed only with swords and lances. While stepping into the boat, Almeida exclaimed, "whither do you carry my 60 years?" The Portuguese furiously rushed on to attack the natives, whose numbers were greatly augmented, and Almeida with 57 of his men were killed in this rash and unprovoked attempt. (Gen. Biog.)

ALMISSA

Pages 338-338

a small but strong town at the mouth of the Cetina, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, famous for its piracies; ten miles east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPALATRO">Spalatro</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 18. 14. N. Lat. 43. 56.

ALMOHEDES

Pages 338-339

the name of a dynasty, which, in the commencement of the twelfth century, succeeded Almoravides in Barbary. It derived its name from an obscure founder called Al Mohedi, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Al Mohedes, and it rose into public notice in the 25th year of the reign of Al <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, or Brahem, who succeeded his father <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, A.D. 1115. This person was a Bereber, and was a famous preacher of the tribe of Muzamada, which was settled along Mount <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>. His scheme was the exertion of ingenuity, and it was executed with unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. In order to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> and success, he assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Mohdi or Mohedi, and claimed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of leader of the orthodox, or unitarians, and, by his preaching they became so numerous, that he even dared to let the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> power at defiance. Confident of security, and immersed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, Brahem looked with a contemptuous eye upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INFRACTION">infraction</a> of a party composed of such persons. They increased in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and strength, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> was at last roused from his indolence, and prepared for his own security and their subjection. In the first engagement he was defeated, being overpowered with superior numbers. The artful Abdallah took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, so that Brahem, pursued as a fugitive by Abdolmumen, one of the party, sought refuge in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>. The gates were shut against him; but they were opened to admit his pursuers. He next took refuge in the city of Auran, or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>; but he was pursued by Abdolmumen, who threatened to destroy the city with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; and the magistrates, unable to defend themselves, urged him to leave the town, and provide for his own safety. Concealed by the darkness of the night, he escaped with his favourite wife on horseback behind him; but being closely pursued by the enemy, rather than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, he rushed over a precipice, and, along with his wife, he was dashed to pieces. Such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, which put a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to the empire of the Almoravides. When the death of Brahem was known, Abdolmumen was chosen by the chiefs of that party his successor, and proclaimed king of the Almohedes, under the title of Al Emir Al Mumin Abdallah Mohammed Abdal Mumin Ebn Abdallah Ibbi Ali, i.e. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">Chief</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> of the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEVERS">Believers</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Mohammed Abdal Mumin, the son of Abdal Mumin, the son of Abdallah, of the lineage of Ali. Abdallah, during his reign, enacted prudential laws for the establishment of his new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and the regulation of the conduct of his followers. He appointed a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of forty of his disciples, all of whom were preachers. Some of these were commissioned to regulate all public affairs; and at proper seasons they went forth as itinerant preachers for the purpose of strengthening their party, and spreading their doctrines, and fifteen of their number acted as secretaries.
