As both the regal and pontifical dignities were united in the same person, the king was chosen from both of these two classes. The disciples of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> were denominated Mohammedin, or Ali Mohaddin; but the Arabian writers only style them preachers, and the Spanish Al Mohedes. The descendants and successors of that tribe <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to retain the appellation of Emir Al Muminin, or chiefs of the faithful believers, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as their dynasty lasted; and they became very powerful both in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. By their invectives against the Almohades, the tyranny of the Almoravides, and their loud clamours for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, they induced the greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdom to revolt, and to embrace their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> doctrines. The chief thing in them was their specious pretence to orthodoxy, and strict adherence to the unity of the Godhead, which they inculcated with the greatest zeal and diligence. On his accession to power, the new sovereign extinguished all the unhappy remains and steady adherents of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, by strangling Ifaac the son of Brahem. The Almoravides governor taking advantage of the general tumult and distraction that prevailed, constituted their governments into independent principalities and petty kingdoms; and they who inhabited the mountainous parts, established under their own chevys a variety of lordships. The Libyans and Nubians took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and the states of Barbary, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAIRWAN">Kairwan</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, Algiers, Tremecen, and Bujeyah, followed their example. Abdolmumun, however, successfully pursued his conquests; and in a few years he reduced to his subjection the Numidians and Galatians in the west, and the kingdoms of Tunis, Tremecen, and the greatest part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a> and Tingitana. He expelled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> of Mohedia, the chief city of Africa, and some others on the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>; and likewise made conquests both in Spain and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. He died in the seventh year of his reign, and was succeeded, A.D. 1156, by his son Yulef or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Yulef proved a valiant and martial prince, and in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> he first established the kings of Tunis and Bujeyah in their respective dominions, as his tributaries and vassals; and then by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> solicitation he embarked for Spain to assist the Moorish princes. Yakub or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, or the conqueror, succeeding him after providing for his own safety against the revolted and plundering Arabs, pursued his conquests with such success, that he soon became <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> lying between <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a> and the entire length of the Barbary coasts, from Tripoli to the boundaries of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. Thus he was acknowledged as sovereign by most of the Arabian Moorish princes in his Spanish dominions; but also extended his territory above 1200 leagues in length, and 480 in breadth. The remaining part of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this prince is involved in obscurity. About the year 1206, he quelled a revolt in Morocco, but violated his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> with the governor of the capital, which he reduced, and in a cruel and perfidious manner he extirpated all his adherents. Touched, it is said, with remorse, he disappeared, and, according to report, wandered about obscure and unknown, until he died in the humble condition of a baker at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. His son Mohammed, named Al Naker, succeeded his father; and, on his accession to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, he passed over into Spain with an immense <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 120,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and 300,000 foot, and engaging the whole force of the Christians on the plains of Tholofa, received a total defeat, with the loss of above 150,000 foot, 30,000 horse, and 50,000 prisoners. According to Spanish and other historians, this famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was fought in 617, A.D. 1220; but according to the Arabian writers, it was in the year of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 629, A.D. 1212. Returning home to Africa, he was received with coldness and disgust by his subjects, on account of his defeat; and soon after died of vexation, having appointed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>- fon Zeyed Arrax his successor. A descendant of the Abdolwates, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monarchs of the kingdom, named Gamarazan Ebn Zezen, of the tribe of the Zeneti, caused him to be assassinated. With him terminated the dynasty or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Almohades, having possessed it for about 170 years, which gave <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to that of the Benimerini, another branch of the Zeneti. These having enlarged their conquests, and enriched themselves by frequent inroads, not only into the neighbouring kingdoms, but even <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUBIA">Nubia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, and Numidia, were at length lost in the general prevalence of Mohamedism, after having existed 117 years. (Mod. Univ. Hist.)

ALMOND

Pages 339-339

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by which the Portuguese sell their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>: 26 almonds make a pipe.

ALMONDBURY

Pages 339-339

a village in England, in the west riding of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>.

ALMONDS

Pages 339-339

among Lapidaries, signify pieces of rock-crystal, used in adorning branch-candlesticks, &c., on account of the resemblance they bear to the fruit of that name. ALMOND <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FURNACE">Furnace</a>, among Refiners, that in which the flags of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>, left in refining silver, are reduced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> again by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a>.

ALMONEER

Pages 339-339

in its primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes an officer in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, to whom belonged the management and distribution of the alms of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> canons, all monasteries were to spend at least a tenth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their income in alms to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The almoner of St Paul's is to dispose of the moneys left for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>, according to the appointment of the donors, to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the poor who die in the neighbourhood, and to breed up eight boys to singing, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the choir. By an ancient canon, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> are required to keep almoners. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Almoner, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Almoner of England, is an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> officer, generally a bishop, who has the forfeiture of all deadlands, and the goods of felons de se, which he is to distribute among the poor. He has also, by virtue of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, the power of giving the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> to whatever poor person he pleases, or, instead of it, an alms in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Almoner, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Almonier, in France, before the revolution, was the highest ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. To him belonged the superintendency of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> and houses of lepers. The king received the sacrament from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>; and he sat mats before the king in all grand ceremonies and solemnities. Almoner is also a more fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> given by some writers to chaplains. In this sense we meet with almoner of a ship, almoner of a regiment.

ALMONRY

Pages 339-339
or Aubury, the office or lodgings of the almoner; also the place where alms are given. See Aubury.

ALMORAVIDES

Pages 339-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, the name of an Arab tribe, who took possession of a district of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, with the pretence of living in retirement, that their minds might not be distracted from the rigid observance of the precepts of the Koran. Hence they assumed the name of Morabites, which was changed by the Almoravi- the Spaniards into that of Almoravides. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABUBEKER">Abubeker</a> ben Omar, called by the Spanish authors Abu Texe- fien, was the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of this tribe. Supported by a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of malecontents from the provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, which was assembled by the influence of the Morabites, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Marabouts, he founded the dynasty of the Almoravides in Barbary, in the year 1051. Texeifen was succeeded by his son Yufc or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, who, after having reduced to a state of vassalage the kingdoms of Tremecen, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>, passed over into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the civil wars, vigorously repulsed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and soon <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURCIA">Murcia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, Cordova, Leon, and some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, subjected to his power. He then returned into Africa, and left his newly acquired dominions, with a considerable army, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of his nephew Moham- med. On his arrival in Africa, with a view to prosecute and extend his conquests in Spain, he announced, in a public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, a general gazie, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; assembled a numerous army, with which he embarked at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CEUTA">Ceuta</a>; and rejoining his nephew in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, soon laid waste that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> with fire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. In the year 1107, five years afterwards, he undertook another invasion, penetrated into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and reduced the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, with a considerable part of the kingdom. At this time he lost the cities of Alguazir and Gibraltar, which he had formerly taken. On his return to Barbary, he was defeated at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. This induced him to propose a truce, which was agreed to only on condition of his submitting to become the tributary of the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. Indignant at these humiliating terms, Yufc made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> that he would never desist in his attempts, till he had utterly rooted out the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> in Spain. He made preparations accordingly for a fresh invasion, embarked his army, and landing at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALAGA">Malaga</a>, marched into the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. His progress was rapid; but his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> were inconsiderately planned and rashly executed. In the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Counts, he was indeed victorious, but after a terrible slaughter, and the loss of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of his army. This disastrous victory obliged him to return to Africa; and he died soon after at his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> his son, succeeded to the sovereignty in 1110. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who seems to have been of a less warlike disposition than his father, neglecting his Spanish conquests, turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the arts of peace, and erected many sumptuous buildings, and in particular the great mosque of Morocco. Alphonso, then king of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, retook from him some considerable cities; which obliged him to undertake an expedition to Spain in support of the Moorish princes. But all his attempts proved unfortunate; and in his last enterprise, though powerfully assisted by the Moorish chiefs, with the loss of 30,000 men he was defeated and slain by Alphonso, in the sixth year of his reign. He was succeeded by his son Al <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, who devoted himself entirely to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. His subjects were harassed and oppressed with heavy taxes, which excited discontent and open rebellion. A revolution was soon effected, and in the 25th year of his reign, the government transferred from the tribe of the Almoravides to the Almohades. (Mod. Univ. Hist.)

ALMS

Pages 340-340

also denotes lands <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other effects left to churches or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, on condition of praying for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of the donor. Hence, Free ALMS, that which is liable to no rent or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>. Reasonable ALMS, a certain portion of the estates of intestate persons, allotted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. ALMS-Box, or Cheft, a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, or coffer, called by the Greeks κάστρον, wherein anciently the alms were collected, both at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and at private houses. The almshoest, in English churches, is a strong box, with a hole in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, having three keys, one to be kept by the parson or curate, the other two by the church-wardens. The erecting of such alms-chest in every church is enjoined by the book of canons, as also the manner of distributing what is thus collected among the poor of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. ALMS-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, a petty kind of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, for the maintenance of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of poor, aged, or disabled people.

ALMUCANTAR'S-STAFF

Pages 340-340

is an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> usually made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>-tree <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> box, having an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of 15 degrees; used to take observations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of its rising and setting, in order to find the amplitude, and consequently the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the compass.

ALMUCANTARS

Pages 340-340

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, an Arabic word denoting circles of the sphere passing through the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the horizon, being the same as PARALLELS OF <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">ALTITUDE</a>.

ALMUCIUM

Pages 340-340

M denotes a kind of cover for the head, worn chiefly by monks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>. It was of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> form, and seems to have given rise to the bonnets of the same shape still retained in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> and cathedrals.

ALMUGGIM

Pages 340-341

ALMIGGIM, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ALMUG TREE, a certain kind of wood mentioned in the first book of Kings (x. 11.), which the Vulgate translates ligna thyma, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> wrought wood. The Rabbins generally render it coral; others, ebony, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">brazil</a>, or pine. But it is observed, that the almug tree can by no means be coral, because that is not fit for the purpose that the Scripture tells us the almug tree <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALNWICK">Alnwick</a> was used, such as musical instruments, flutes, &c. The word *thyrsus* is a name for the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a> tree, known by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and very much esteemed for its sweet odour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>. It came from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>. The almug tree, or *almugim*, *algumim*, or simply *gumim*, taking *al* for a kind of article, is therefore by the best commentators understood to be an oily and gummy sort of wood; and particularly that sort of tree which produces the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> ammoniac, which is also thought to be the same with the Shittim wood, whereof there is such frequent mention made by Moses.

ALMUNECAR

Pages 341-341

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated on the Mediterranean, with a good harbour, defended by a strong castle, 20 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALHAMA">Alhama</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 45'. N. Lat. 36° 50'.

ALNAGE

Pages 341-341
or **ALNAG**, the measuring of woollen manufactures with an ell. It was at first intended as a proof of the goodness of that commodity; and accordingly a seal was invented as a mark that the commodity was made according to the statute; but, being now possible to purchase these seals, they are affixed, whenever the vender pleases, to all cloths indiscriminately, to the great prejudice of our woollen manufactures.

ALNAGER

Pages 341-341

**ALNEGER**, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> **ALNEGER**, q.d. measurer by the ell, signifies a sworn public officer, who, by himself or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>, is to look to the assize of woollen cloth made throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, i.e. the length, width, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> thereof; and to the seals for that purpose ordained. The office of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s alnager seems to have been derived from the statute of Richard I. A.D. 1197, which ordained, that there should be only one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and that the custody of the assize, or standard of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, should be committed to certain persons in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and borough. His business was, for a certain fee, to measure all cloths made for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>, till the office was abolished by the statute 11 and 12 W. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 20.

ALNUS

Pages 341-341

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-THEATRES">Theatres</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which was most distant from the stage.

ALNWICK

Pages 341-341

a thoroughfare town in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to Scotland. Here Malcolm, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Scotland, making an inroad into Northumberland, was killed, with Edward his son, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> defeated by Robert Moubray, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, anno 1102. Likewise William, king of Scotland, in 1174, invading England with an army of 80,000 men, was here encountered, his army routed, and himself made prisoner. The town is populous, and in general well built; it has a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-sessions and county-courts are held, and members of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> elected. It has a spacious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, in which a market is held every Saturday. Alnwick appears to have been formerly fortified, by the vestiges of a wall still visible in many parts, and three gates which remain almost entire. It is governed by four chamberlains, who are chosen once in two years out of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, consisting of 24 members. It is ornamented by a stately old Gothic castle, which has been the seat of the noble family of Percy, earls of Northumberland. As the audits for receipt of rents have ever been in this castle, it has always been kept in tolerable repair; and not many years ago, it was repaired and beautified by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Northumberland, who made very considerable alterations, upon a most elegant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, with a view to reside in it some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season. The manner of making freemen is peculiar to this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and indeed is as ridiculous as singular. The persons who are to be made free, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as the phrase is, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> the well, assemble in the market-place, very early in the morning, on the 25th of April, being St Mark's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. They appear on horseback, with every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> by his side, dressed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and with white nightcaps, attended by the four chamberlains and the castle <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, mounted and armed in the same manner; from hence they proceed, with music playing before them, to a large dirty pool, called Freeman's-well, where they dismount, and draw up in a body, at some distance from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and then rush into it all at once, and scramble through the mud as fast as they can. As the water is generally very foul, they come out in a dirty condition; but taking a dram, they put on dry clothes, remount their horses, and ride full gallop round the confines of the district; then re-enter the town, sword in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and are met by women dressed in ribbons with bells and garlands, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> and singing. These are called *<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-wrights*. The houses of the new freemen are on this day distinguished by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> holly bush, as a signal for their friends to assemble and make merry with them after their return. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is owing to King John, who was mired in this well, and who, as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> for not mending the road, made this a part of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. Alnwick is 310 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by west from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 33 north of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, and 29 south of Berwick. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 10'. Lat. 55° 24'.

ALOGIANS

Pages 341-341

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who denied that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ was the Logos, and consequently rejected the gospel of St John. The word is compounded of the privative *a* and *λόγος*, q.d. Without Logos <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Word. Some ascribe the origin of the name, as well as of the sect of Alogians, to Theodore of Byzantium, by trade a currier; who having apostatized under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus, to defend himself against those who reproached him therewith, said, that it was not God he denied, but only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Whence his followers were called in Greek *άλογοι*, because they rejected the Word. But others, with more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, suppose the name to have been first given them by Epiphanius in the way of reproach. They made their appearance toward the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century.

ALOGOTROPHIA

Pages 341-341

among Physicians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> signifying the unequal growth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> nourishment of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body, as in the rickets.

ALOOF

Pages 341-342

has frequently been mentioned as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>; but whether justly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not, we shall not presume to determine. It is known in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> discourse to imply at a distance; and the resemblance of the phrase "keep aloof," and keep a *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUFF">luff</a>*, or keep the *luff*, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> gave rise to this conjecture. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it was really a ALPESE <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-phrase originally, it seems to have referred to the dangers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEE">lee</a>-shore, in which situation the pilot might naturally apply it in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> understood, viz. keep all off, or quite off; it is, however, never expressed in that manner by seamen now. See LUFF. It may not be improper to observe, that besides using this phrase in the same sense with us, the French also call the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>-side of a ship, and the weather-clue of a course, le lof.

ALOPECE

Pages 342-342

ALOPECIA, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> placed by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> at the mouth of the Tanais, and called the island Tanais: now l'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> des Renards (Baudrandt). Also an island of the Bosphorus Cimmerius (Pliny); and another in the Ægean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, over against <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">Smyrna</a>.

ALOPECIA

Pages 342-342

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used among physicians to denote a total falling off of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> from certain parts, occasioned either by the defect of nutritious juice, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by its vicious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> corroding the roots of it, and leaving the skin rough and colourless. The word is formed from ἀλοπεξ, vulpes, "a fox;" whose urine, it is said, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> occasion baldness, because it is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to that creature. It is directed to wash the head every night at going to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> with a ley prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the ashes of vine branches in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine. A powder made by reducing hermodactyls to fine flour is also recommended for the same purpose. In <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where the baldness is total, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the finest burdock roots are to be bruised in a marble <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>, and then boiled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wine until there remains only as much as will cover them. This liquor, carefully strained off, is said to cure baldness, by washing the head every night with some of it warm. A ley made by boiling ashes of vine branches in common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is also recommended with this intention. A fresh cut onion, rubbed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> until it be red and itch, is likewise said to cure baldness. A multitude of such remedies are everywhere to be found in the works of Valescus de Taranta, Rondeletius, Hollerius, Trincavellius, Celsius, Senertay, and other practical physicians.

ALOPEX

Pages 342-342

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANIS">canis</a>, with a straight tail and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> tip. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the field fox.

ALOSA

Pages 342-342

the shad, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mother of herrings, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the clupea. See Clupea, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALOST

Pages 342-342

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, seated on the river Dender, in the midway between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> and Ghent. It has but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is collegiate, and has a provost, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a>, and 12 canons. Here is a convent of Carmelites, another of Capuchines, another of barefooted Carmelites, three nunneries, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a>, and a convent of Guillelmus, in which is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of Theodore Martin, who brought the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> out of Germany into the Low Countries. He was the friend of Erasmus, and wrote his epitaph. Alost was taken and dismantled by Marshal Turenne in 1667; and after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a> in 1706, was abandoned to the allies. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 56'. N. Lat. 49° 35'.

ALP ARSLAN

Pages 342-343

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a> of the dynasty of Seljuk in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> grandson of Seljuk the founder of the dynasty. He Alp Arslan, was born in the year 1039, of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a> 421. In <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Ibrahîm, which was his original name, he assumed that of Mohammed, when he embraced the Muslim <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, and he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a>, Alp Arslan, which in the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> signifies a valiant lion, on account of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> prowess. Having held the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> command in Khorasan for ten years as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of his uncle Toghrul Beg, he succeeded him in the year 1063, and at the commencement of his reign <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> himself sole monarch of Persia, from the river Amu to the Tigris. When he assumed the reins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACTION">faction</a> and open rebellion prevailed in his dominions, in subduing of which he was ably assisted by Nadham al Molk his vizir, one of the most distinguished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and integrity in the administration of the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> proved of most essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and to his successor. Peace and security being established in his dominions, he convoked an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states; and having declared his son Malek Shaw his heir and successor, seated him on a throne of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, and exacted an oath of fidelity to him from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of the empire. With the hope of acquiring immense booty in the rich temple of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in Caesarea, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Cappadocia, he placed himself at the head of the Turkish cavalry, crossed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, and entered and plundered that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He then marched into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, which in the year 1065 he finally conquered. In the former <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the very name of a kingdom and the spirit of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> were totally extinguished. But the native Georgians who had retired to the woods and valleys of Mount <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAUCASUS">Caucasus</a> made a more vigorous resistance. They too, however, overpowered by the arms of the sultan and his son Malek, were forced to submission, and reduced to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>. To punish them for the brave <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> which they had made, and as a badge of their humiliating condition, Alp Arslan obliged them to wear at their ears huge thorns of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. Some, to escape this mark of cruelty and ignominy, professed to embrace the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Mahomet. In the year 1068 Alp Arslan invaded the Roman empire, the seat of which was then at Constantinople. Eudocia, the reigning empress, saw and dreaded the progress of his arms. To avert the threatened danger, she married Romanus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOGENES">Diogenes</a>, a brave soldier, who was accordingly associated with her in the government, and raised to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. The new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, during the exhausted state of their resources, sustained the Roman power with surprising valour and invincible courage. His spirit and success animated his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> in the field to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> with fortitude and firmness, inspired his subjects with hope, and struck terror in his enemies. In three severe campaigns his arms were victorious; and the Turks were forced to retreat beyond the Euphrates. In the fourth he advanced with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 men into the Armenian territory for the relief of that country. Here he was met by Alp Arslan with 40,000 cavalry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to some authors, a much smaller <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>; and the sultan having proposed terms of peace which were insultingly rejected by the emperor, a bloody and decisive engagement took place. Alp Arslan, it is said, when he saw that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> was inevitable, wept at the thought that so many of his faithful followers must <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in Alp Arlan, in the struggle; and after offering up a devout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a>, granted free permission to all who chose it to retire from the field. Then with his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> he tied up his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s tail, exchanged his bow and arrows for a mace and scimitar, and robed himself in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> garment perfumed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, resolved to perish on the spot unless he came off victorious. The skilful movements of the Turkish cavalry soon made an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on the superior numbers of the Greeks, who were thrown into great disorder, and after a terrible slaughter, were totally routed. Romanus, deserted by the main body of his army, with unshaken courage kept his station, till he was recognized by a slave, taken prisoner, and conducted into the presence of Alp Arlan. In the Turkish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVAN">divan</a>, the captive emperor was commanded to kiss the ground as a degrading mark of submission to the power and authority of the sultan, who, it is said, leapt from his throne and set his foot on his neck. But this is scarcely probable or consistent with the generous and respectful treatment which he otherwise experienced. For the sultan instantly raised him from the ground, embraced him tenderly, and assured him that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and dignity should remain inviolate under the protection of a prince who had not forgotten the respect due to the majesty of his equals, and the vicissitudes of fortune. When the terms of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> were about to be settled, Romanus was asked by Alp Arlan what treatment he expected to receive. To this question the emperor, with seeming indifference, replied, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> you are cruel, you <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> take my life; if you follow the dictates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a>, you will drag me at your chariot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>; if you consult your <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, you will accept a ransom, and restore me to my country." "But what?" says the sultan, "would you have done in such circumstances?" "Had I been victorious," said the insolent Romanus, "I would have inflicted on thy body many a stripe." The conqueror smiled at the fierce and unsubdued spirit of his captive; observed that the Christian precepts strongly inculcated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of enemies and the forgiveness of injuries; and, with a noble greatness of mind, declared that he would never imitate an example which he disapproved. A ransom of a million, an annual tribute of 3000 pieces of gold, an intermarriage between the families, and the deliverance of all the captive Muslims in the power of the Greeks, were at last agreed to as the terms of peace and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the emperor. Romanus was now dismissed loaded with presents, and respectfully attended by a military <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>. But the distracted state of his dominions, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a revolt of his subjects, precluded him from fulfilling the terms of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, and remitting the stipulated price of his ransom. The sultan seemed disposed to favour and support the declining fortunes of his ally; but the defeat, imprisonment, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Romanus interrupted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of his generous, or rather ambitious, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. At this time the dominion of Alp Arlan extended over the fairest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; 1200 princes, sons of princes, surrounded his throne; and 200,000 soldiers were ready to execute his commands. He now meditated a greater enterprise, and declared his purpose of attempting the conquest of Turkestan, the original seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>. After great preparations for the expedition, he marched with a powerful army, and arrived at the banks of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OXUS">Oxus</a>. Before he could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the river with safety, it was necessary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> possession of some fortresses in its vicinity; one of which was for several days vigorously defended by the governor, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Cothul, a Circassian. He was, however, obliged to surrender, and was carried a prisoner before the sultan, who, being enraged at his obstinacy and presumption, addressed him in very reproachful terms. Joseph replied with so much spirit, that he roused the resentment of Alp Arlan, and was commanded instantly to be fastened by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet to four stakes, to suffer a painful and cruel death. Joseph, on hearing this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, became furious and desperate; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a dagger which he had concealed in his boots, rushed towards the throne to stab the sultan; the guards raised their battle-axes, and moved forward to defend their sovereign; but Alp Arlan, the most expert archer of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, checking their zeal, forbade them to advance, and drew his bow; his foot slipped, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARROW">arrow</a> missed Joseph, who rushed forward, and plunging his dagger in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of the sultan, was himself instantly cut in pieces. The wound proved mortal, and the sultan expired in a few hours after he received it, in the year 1072. When he found his end approaching, he addressed himself in these words to his attendants: "In my youth," said he, "I was advised by a wise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to humble myself before God, never to confide in my own strength, or to despise the most contemptible enemy. These <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> I have neglected, for which I have now met deserved <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. Yesterday, when I beheld from an eminence the number and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of my troops, I said in the confidence of my heart, 'What power on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> can oppose me? what man <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to attack me?' To-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, vainly trusting to my own strength and dexterity, I foolishly checked the prompt zeal and alacrity of my guards for my safety, and now I have fallen by the hand of an afflatus! But I perceive that no force or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> can resist fate." He died in the 10th year of his reign, at the age of 44. He was buried at Maru, one of the four cities of Khorasan, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the Seljukian dynasty. On his tomb was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> the following epitaph: "All you who have beheld the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a> of Alp Arlan exalted to the heavens, come to Maru, and you will see it buried in the dust." This prince was distinguished for his valour, liberality, and piety. He was patient, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>, and sincere. His stature, aspect, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, commanded the respect of all who approached him. He had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> whiskers, and usually wore a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> turban in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He was succeeded by his son Malek Shaw, who had been proclaimed and acknowledged sultan of the Turks during his life. (Mod. Univ. Hist. Gibbon's Hist.)

ALPHA

Pages 343-344

the name of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>, answering to our A. As a numeral, it stands for one, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the first of any thing. It is particularly used, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, to denote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of his class or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the word stands contradistinguished from beta, which denotes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> person. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> was called the Alpha of the wits: Eratosthenes, keeper of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> library, whom some called a Second Plato, is frequently named Beta. Alpha is also used to denote the beginning of any thing. In which sense it stands opposed to omega, which Alphabet, which denotes the end. And these two letters were made the symbol of Christianity; and accordingly were engraven on the tombs of the ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, to distinguish them from those of idolaters. Moralez, a Spanish writer, imagined that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> only commenced since the rise of Arianism; and that it was peculiar to the orthodox, who hereby made confession of the eternity of Christ; but there are tombs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Constantine whereon the two letters were found, besides that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned bore them on his labarum before <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a> appeared.

ALPHABET

Pages 344-355

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> customary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the several letters of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> (see LANGUAGE and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">WRITING</a>). The word is formed from alpha and beta, the first and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> letters of the Greek alphabet. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of letters is different in the alphabets of different languages. The English alphabet contains 24 letters; to which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we add j and v consonant, the sum <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 26; the French contains 23; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Chaldee, Syriac, and Samaritan 22 each; the Arabic 28; the Persian 31; the Turkish 33; the Georgian 36; the Coptic 32; the Mufcorite 43; the Greek 24; the Latin 22; the Sclavonic 27; the Dutch 26; the Spanish 27; the Italian 20; the Ethiopic and Tartarian, each 20; the Indians of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> 21; the Baramele 19. The Chinese have, properly speaking, no alphabet, except we call their whole language by that name; their letters are words, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, amounting to about 80,000. It has been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of considerable dispute whether the method of expressing our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> by visible symbols called letters be really a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; or whether we ought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> an art so exceedingly useful to an immediate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> from the Deity.—In favour of the latter <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> it has been urged, 1. The five books of Moses are universally acknowledged to be the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> compositions as well as the most early specimens of alphabetical writing we have. If, therefore, we suppose writing to be the result of human ingenuity, it must be different from all other arts, having been brought to perfection at once; as it seems impossible to make any real improvement on the Hebrew alphabet. It may indeed be replied, that alphabetical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> perhaps have existed many ages before the writings of Moses, though the more ancient specimens have perished. This, however, being a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> unsupported assertion, without any historical testimony to corroborate it, cannot be admitted as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Again, Setting aside the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> to be derived from Scripture on this subject, the simplicity of manners predominant in the early ages, the small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the intellectual powers of mankind, and the little intercourse which nations had with one another, which would seem more particularly to render writing necessary, can scarcely allow us to suppose that such a complex and curious contrivance as alphabetical writing could be invented by a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of men whose wants were so few, their advantages so circumscribed, and their ideas so limited. 2. If alphabetical writing were a mere human invention, it might be expected that different nations would have fallen upon the same expedient independent of each other during the compass of so many ages. But no such thing has taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; and the writing of every people on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> may be referred to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> original. If this can be proved, the argument from Alphabet, successive derivation, without a single instance of independent discovery, must be allowed to amount to the very highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> in favour of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, which will now rest on the evidence for or against this fact; and which may be summed up in the following manner. Among the European nations we find none who can pretend any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the discovery of letters. All of them derived the art from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, excepting only the Turks, who had it from the Arabians. The Romans never laid claim to the discovery; but confessed that they derived their knowledge from the Greeks, and the latter owned that they had it from the Phoenicians; who, as well as their colonists the Carthaginians, spoke a dialect of the Hebrew scarcely varying from the original. The Coptic, or Egyptian, resembles the Greek in most of its characters, and is therefore to be referred to the same original. The Chaldee, Syriac, and latter Samaritan, are dialects of the Hebrew, without any considerable deviation, or many additional words. The Ethiopic differs more from the Hebrew, but less than the Arabic; yet these languages have all issued from the same stock, as the similarity of their formation, and the numberless words common to them, all sufficiently evince; and the Peric is very nearly allied to the Arabic. Alterations indeed would naturally be produced, in proportion to the civilization of the several nations, and their intercourse with others; which will account for the superior copiousness of some above the rest. It appears then, that all the languages in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> amongst men that have been conveyed in alphabetical characters, have been the languages of people connected ultimately or immediately with the Hebrews, who have handed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the earliest specimens of writing to posterity; and we have therefore the greatest reason to believe, that their method of writing, as well as their language, was derived from the same source. This proposition will be farther confirmed from considering the famelics of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> denominations of the letters in the Oriental, Greek, and Latin languages, accompanied also by a similar arrangement, as alpha, beta, &c. It may still be objected, however, that the characters employed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to discriminate their letters are entirely dissimilar. Why should not one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, it may be urged, adopt from the other the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of expressing the art as well as the art itself? To what purpose did they take the trouble of inventing other characters? To this objection it may be replied, 1. From the influence of our own language we know what diversities may be introduced in this respect merely by length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and an intercourse with neighbouring nations. And such an effect would be more likely to take place before the art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> had contributed to establish an uniformity of character: For when every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was transcribed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, we may easily imagine how many variations would arise from the fancy of the scribe, and the mode of writing so constantly different in individuals. 2. This diversity might sometimes arise from vanity. When an individual of another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a> had become acquainted with this wonderful art, he might endeavour to recommend himself as the inventor; and, to avoid detection, might invent other characters. 3. The char- racters of the alphabet might sometimes be accommodated as much as possible to the symbolical marks already in use amongst a particular people. These having acquired a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of sanctity by the use of many generations, would not easily be superseded without the aid of some such contrivance. 4. This is supported by the testimony of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>; who informs us, "that those Phoenicians who came with <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADMUS">Cadmus</a> introduced many improvements among the Greeks, and alphabetical writing too, not known among them before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. At first they used the Phoenician character; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> altered, the standard of the letters was also changed. The Ionian Greeks inhabited at the time the parts adjacent to Phoenicia: who having received the art of alphabetical writing from the Phoenicians, used it, with an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of some few characters, and confessed ingenuously, that it was called Phoenician from the introducers of it." He tells us that he had himself seen the characters of Cadmus in the temple of Iphigenia <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> at Thebes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, engraven upon tripods, and very much resembling the Ionian characters. 5. The old Samaritan is precisely the same as the Hebrew language: and the Samaritan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a> does not vary by a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in twenty words from the Hebrew: but the characters are widely different: for the Jews adopted the Chaldaic letters during their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a> instead of the characters of their forefathers. 3. What we know of those nations who have <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> for many centuries unconnected with the rest of the world, strongly militates against the hypothesis of the human invention of alphabetical writing. The experiment has been fairly made upon the ingenuity of mankind for a longer period than that which is supposed to have produced alphabetical writing by regular gradations; and this experiment determines peremptorily in their favour. The Chinese, a people famous for their discoveries and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> turn of genius, have made some advances towards the delineation of their ideas by arbitrary signs, but have nevertheless been unable to accomplish this exquisite device; and after so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> to no purpose, we may reasonably infer, that their mode of writing, which is growing more intricate and voluminous every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, would never terminate in so clear, so comparatively simple, an expedient as that of alphabetical characters. The Mexicans, too, had made some rude attempts of the same kind; but with less success than the Chinese. We know also, that hieroglyphics were in use among the Egyptians <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> to the practice of alphabetical writing by the Jews; but whether the epigraphy, as it is called, of the former people, which was in vogue during the continuance of the hieroglyphics, might not possibly be another name for alphabetical writing, cannot be decided. 4. We shall consider the argument on which the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> received supposition entirely depends: that is, the natural gradation, through the several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of symbols acknowledged to have been in use with various people, terminating at last, by an easy transition, in the detection of alphabetical characters. The strength of this argument will be best understood from the following representation. 1. The first method of embodying ideas would be by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a representation of the objects themselves. The imperfection of this method is very obvious, both on account of its tediousness and its inability of going beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearances to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> ideas of the mind. 2. The next method would be somewhat more general, and would substitute two or three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> circumstances for the whole transaction. So two kings, for example, engaging each other with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> weapons, might serve to convey the idea of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> between the two nations. This abbreviated method would be more expeditious than the former; but what it gained in conciseness would be lost in perspicuity. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> more compendious indeed, but still a description of outward objects alone, by drawing their resemblance. To this head may be referred the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>-writing of the Mexicans. 3. The next advance would be to the use of symbols; the incorporation, as it were, of abstract and complex ideas in figures more or less generalized, in proportion to the improvement of it. Thus, in the earlier stages of this device, a circle might serve to express the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; which is only a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of the foregoing method. This symbol writing in its advanced state would become more refined, but enigmatical and mysterious in proportion to its refinement. Hence it would become less fit for common use, and therefore more particularly appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. Thus, two feet standing upon <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> served to express an impossibility; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> denoted the oblique trajectories of the heavenly bodies; and the beetle, on account of some supposed properties of that insect, served to represent the sun. The Egyptian hieroglyphics were of this kind. 4. This method being still too subtle and complicated for common use, the only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> to be pursued was a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the first stage of the preceding method. Thus a dot, instead of a circle, might stand for the sun; and a similar abbreviation might be extended to all the symbols. On this scheme every object and idea would have its appropriated mark: these marks, therefore, would have a multiplicity proportionable to the works of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and the operations of the mind. This method was likewise practised by the Egyptians; but has been carried to greater perfection by the Chinese. The vocabulary of the latter is therefore infinite, or at least capable of being extended to any imaginable length. But if we compare this tedious and awkward contrivance with the astonishing brevity and perspicuity of alphabetical writing, we must be persuaded that no two things can be more dissimilar; and that the transition from a scheme constantly enlarging itself, and growing daily more intricate, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of every possible idea by the modified arrangement of four-and-twenty marks, is not so very easy and perceptible as some have imagined. Indeed this seems still to be rather an expression of things in a manner similar to the second stage of symbol writing than the notification of ideas by arbitrary signs." To all this we shall subjoin the following remarks, which seem to give additional force to the foregoing reasoning. 1. Pliny asserts the use of letters to have been eternal; which shows the antiquity of the practice to extend beyond the era of authentic <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>. 2. The cabalistical doctors of the Jews maintain, that alphabetical writing was one of the ten things which God created on the evening of the Sabbath. 3. Most of the profane authors of antiquity ascribe the first use of alphabetical characters to the Egyptians, who, according to some, received them from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; and, according to others, from their god Teuth. 4. There is very little reason to suppose that even language itself is the effect of human ingenuity and invention." Thus we have stated the arguments in favour of the revelation of alphabetical writing; which are answered, by those who take the contrary side, in the following manner. 1. Moses nowhere says that the alphabet was a new thing in his time; nor does he give the least hint of his being the inventor of it. The first mention we find of writing is in the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Exodus; where Moses is commanded to write in a book; and which took place before the arrival of the Israelites at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SINAI">Sinai</a>. This shows that writing did not commence with the delivery of the two tables of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, as some have supposed. Neither are we to conclude that the invention had taken place only a short time before; for the writing in a book is commanded as a thing commonly understood, and with which Moses was well acquainted. It is plain, from the command to engrave the names of the twelve tribes of Israel upon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> like the engravings of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIGNET">signet</a>, that writing had been known and practised among them, as well as other nations, long before. We must also remember, that the people were commanded to write the law on their door posts, &c. so that the art seems not only to have been known, but universally practised among them. But had writing been a new discovery in the time of Moses, he would probably have commemorated it as well as the other inventions of music, &c. Nor is there any reason to suppose that God was the immediate revealer of the art; for Moses would never have omitted to record a circumstance of such importance, as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of it would have been one of the strongest barriers against idolatry. Again, though several profane writers attribute the origin of letters to the gods, or to some divine person, yet this is no proof of its being actually revealed; but only that the original inventor was unknown. The learned bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLOUCESTER">Gloucester</a> observes, that the ancients gave nothing to the gods of whose original they had any records; but where the memory of the invention was lost, as of seed-corn, wine, writing, civil <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, &c. the gods seized the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, by that kind of right which gives stays to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a>. As neither the sacred nor profane historians, therefore, have determined anything concerning the invention of letters, we are at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to form what conjectures we think most plausible concerning the origin of them; and this, it is thought, might have taken place in the following manner. 1. Men, in their rude uncultivated state, would have neither leisure, inclination, nor inducement, to cultivate the powers of the mind to a degree sufficient for the formation of an alphabet; but when a people arrived at such a pitch of civilization as required them to represent the conceptions of the mind which have no corporeal forms, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> would occasion further exertions, and urge them to find out a more expeditious manner of transacting their business than by picture-writing. 2. These exertions would take place whenever a nation began to improve in arts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; and the greater genius such a nation had, the more improvements would be made in the notation of their language; whilst those people who had made less progress in civilization and science, would have a less perfect system of elementary characters; and perhaps advance no farther for many ages than the marks or characters of the Chinese. Hence we may see, that the business of princes, as well as the manufactures and commerce of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, would produce the necessity of devising some expeditious manner of communicating information to one another. The art of writing, however, is of so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, and the early history of most nations so full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a>, that it must be extremely difficult to determine what nation or people may justly claim the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the invention. But as it is probable that letters were the produce of a certain degree of civilization among mankind, we must therefore have recourse to the history of those nations who seem to have been first civilized. The Egyptians have an undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> to a very Claim of early civilization; and many learned men have attributed the invention of letters to them. The late bishop of Gloucester contends, that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> of all the learning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and was referred to by all the Grecian legislators, naturalists, and philosophers; and endeavours to prove that it was one of the first civilized countries on the globe. Their writing was of four kinds: 1. Hieroglyphic; 2. Symbolic; 3. Epitaphic; and, 4. Hierogrammatic. In the most early ages they wrote, like all other infant nations, by pictures; of which some traces yet remain amongst the hieroglyphics of Horapollo, who informs us, that they represented a fuller by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s two feet in water; fire, by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> ascending, &c. But to render this rude invention less inconvenient, they soon devised the method of putting one thing of similar qualities for another. The former was called the curiologic, the latter the tropical hieroglyphic; which last was a gradual improvement on the former. These alterations in the manner of delineating hieroglyphic figures produced and perfected another character, called the running-hand of the hieroglyphics, resembling the Chinese writing; which having been first formed by the outlines of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, became at length a kind of marks; the natural effects of which were, that the constant use of them would take off the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> from the symbol and fix it on the thing signified. Thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of symbolic writing would be much abbreviated; because the writer or decipherer would have then little to do but to remember the power of the symbolic mark; whereas before, the properties of the thing or animal delineated were to be learned. This, together with the other marks by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, to denote mental conceptions, would reduce the characters to a similar state with the present Chinese; and these were properly what the ancients called hieroglyphical.
