We are informed by Dr Robert Huntingdon, in his account of the Porphyry pillars, The sacred book or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> of the Egyptians, according to Apuleius, was written partly in symbolic and partly in these hieroglyphic characters, in the following manner: "He (the hierophant) drew out certain books from the secret repositories of the sanctuary, written in unknown characters, which contained the words of the sacred formula compendiously expressed, partly by figures of animals, and partly by certain marks or notes intricately knotted, revolving in the manner of a wheel, crowded together, and curled inward like the tendrils of a vine, so as to hide the meaning from the curiosity of the profane." But though letters were of great antiquity in Egypt, there is reason to believe that they were not first invented in that country. Mr Jackson, in his Chronological Antiquities, has endeavoured to prove, that they were not invented or carried into Egypt by Taaut or Thoth, the first Hermes, and son of Misfram, who lived about 300 years after the deluge; but that they were introduced into that country by the second Hermes, who lived about 400 years after the former. This second Hermes, according to Diodorus, was the inventor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> and music, and added many words to the Egyptian language. According to the same author also, he invented letters, rhythm, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of sounds. This was the Hermes so much celebrated by the Greeks, who knew no other than himself. On the other hand, Mr Wile affirms that Moses and Cadmus could not learn the alphabet in Egypt; and that the Egyptians had no alphabet in their time. He adduces several reasons to prove that they had none till they received what was called the Coptic, which was introduced either in the time of the Ptolemies or under Plammitichus or Amasis; and the oldest alphabetic letters which can be produced as Egyptian, appear plainly to have been derived from the Greek. Herodotus confesses, that all he relates before the reign of Plammitichus is uncertain; and that he reports the early transactions of that nation on the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the Egyptian priests, on which he did not greatly depend; and Diodorus Siculus is said to have been greatly imposed upon by them. Manetho, the oldest Egyptian historian, translated the sacred registers out of Egyptian into Greek, which are said by Synecus to have been written in the sacred letters, and to have been laid up by the second Mercury in the Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>. He allows the Egyptian gods to have been mortal men; but his history was very much corrupted by the Greeks, and hath been called in question by several writers from the account which he himself gave of it. After Cambyses had carried away the Egyptian records, the priests, to supply their loss, and to keep up their pretensions to antiquity, began to write new records; wherein they not only unavoidably made great mistakes, but added much of their own invention, especially as to distant times. The Phoenicians have likewise been supposed the inventors of letters; and we have the strongest proofs of the early civilization of this people. Their most ancient historian, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANCHONIATHO">Sanchoniatho</a>, lived in the time of Abibalus, father of Hiram <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. He informs us, that letters were invented by Taaut, who lived in Phoenicia in the 12th and 13th generations after the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. "Milon (says he) was the son of Hamyn; the son of Misfr was Taaut, who invented the first letters for writing." The Egyptians call him Thoth; the Alexandrians Thoyth; and the Greeks Hermes, or Mercury. In the time of this Taaut or Mercury, (the grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">Ham</a> the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOAH">Noah</a>,) Phoenicia and the adjacent country was governed by Uranus, and after him by his son <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> or Cronus. He invented letters either in the reign of Uranus or Cronus; and itaid in Phoenicia with Cronus till the 32d year of his reign. Cronus, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father Uranus, made several settlements of his family, and travelled into other parts; and when he came to the south country, he gave all Egypt to the god Taautus, that it should be his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Sanchoniatho began his history with the creation, and ended it with placing Taautus on the throne of Egypt. He does not mention the deluge, but makes two more generations in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIN">Cain</a>'s line from Protagonus to Agrovenus (or from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> to Noah than Moses. As Sanchoniatho has not told us whether Taaut invented letters either in the reign of Uranus or Cronus, "we cannot err much (says Mr Jackson) if we place his invention of them 550 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, or 20 years after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, and 2619 years before the Christian era, and fix, or perhaps ten years, before he went into Egypt." This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> and his posterity reigned at Thebes in Upper Egypt for 15 generations. Several Roman authors attribute the invention of letters to the Phoenicians. Pliny says (A), the Phoenicians were famed for the invention of letters, as well as for astronomical observations and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVEL">novel</a> and martial arts. Curtius informs us, that the Tyrian nation are related to be the first who either taught or learned letters; and Lucan says, that they were the first who attempted to express sounds or words by letters. Eusebius also tells us from Porphyry, that "Sanchoniatho studied with great application the writings of Taaut, knowing that he was the first who invented letters." The Greeks, as we have already observed, knew no older Hermes than the second, who lived about 400 years after the Mezrite Taaut or Hermes. This second Hermes is called by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> Thoeuth, and counsellor or sacred scribe to King Thanus; but it is not said that he ever reigned in Egypt: but the former Taaut, or Athothes, as Manetho calls him, was the immediate successor of Menes the first king of Egypt. This second Mercury, if we may believe Manetho, composed several books of the Egyptian history, and having improved both the language and letters of that nation, the Egyptians attributed the arts and inventions of the former to the latter. The Phoenician language is generally allowed to have been a dialect of the Hebrew; and though their alphabet does not entirely agree with the (4) He says in another place, that the knowledge of letters is eternal. What dependence can we put in the opinion of a writer who thus contradicts himself? the Samaritan, yet there is a great similarity between them. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a> were much cultivated among them in the most early ages; their fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, purple, and glass, were much superior to those of other nations; and their extraordinary skill in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> and other arts was such, that whatever was great, elegant, or pleasing, whether in buildings, apparel, or toys, was distinguished by the epithet of Tyrian or Sidonian; these being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> cities of Phoenicia. Their great proficiency in learning and arts of all kinds, together with their engrossing all the commerce of the western world, are likewise thought to give them a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> claim to the invention of letters. The Chaldeans also have laid claim to the invention of letters; and with regard to this, there is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> among the Jews, Indians, and Arabians, that the Egyptians derived their knowledge from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>, who was a Chaldean. This tradition is in some degree confirmed by most of the western writers, who ascribe the inventions of arithmetic and astronomy to the Chaldeans. Josephus positively affirms, that the Egyptians were ignorant of the sciences of arithmetic and astronomy before they were instructed by Abraham; and Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton admits, that letters were known in the line of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> for many centuries before Moses. The Chaldaic letters appear to have been derived from the Hebrew or Samaritan; which are the same, or nearly so, with the old Phoenician. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EZRA">Ezra</a> is supposed to have exchanged the old Hebrew characters for the more beautiful and commodious Chaldee, which are still in use. Berossus, the most ancient Chaldean historian, who was born in the minority of Alexander the Great, does not say that he believed his countrymen to have been the inventors of letters. The Syrians have also laid claim to the invention of letters. It is certain indeed, that they yielded to no nation in knowledge and skill in the fine arts. Their language is said to have been the vernacular of all the oriental tongues, and was divided into three dialects. 1. The Aramean, used in Mesopotamia, and by the inhabitants of Roha and Edefa of Harram, and the Outer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. 2. The dialect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; spoken by the inhabitants of Damascus, Mount Lebanon, and the Inner Syria. 3. The Chaldee or Nabatean dialect, the most polished of the three; and spoken in the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and the villages of Irac or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. It has been generally believed, that no nation of equal antiquity had a more considerable trade than the Syrians; they are supposed to have first brought the commodities of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> into the west of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>; and they seem to have carried on an inland trade by engrossing the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>, whilst the Phoenicians traded to the most distant countries. Notwithstanding these circumstances, however, which might seem to favour the claim of the Syrians, the oldest characters they have are but about three centuries before Christ. Their letters are of two sorts. 1. The Estrangelo, which is the more ancient; and, 2. The Fhito, the simple or common character, which is the more expeditious and beautiful. We must next examine the claims of the Indians, whose pretensions to antiquity yield to no other nation on earth. Mr Halhed, who has written a grammar of the Sanskrit language, informs us, that it is not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> literature, but the parent of almost every dialect from the Persian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> to the Chinese seas, and which is said to be a language of the most venerable antiquity. At present it is appropriated to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> records of the Brahmans, and therefore shut up in their <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>; but formerly it appears to have been current over the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the eastern world, as traces of its extent may be found in almost every district of Asia. Mr Halhed informs us, that "there is a great similarity between the Sanskrit words and those of the Persian and Arabic, and even of Latin and Greek; and these not in technical or metaphorical terms, but in the main groundwork of language; in monosyllables, the names of numbers, and the appellations of such things as would be first discriminated on the immediate dawn of civilization. The resemblance which may be seen of the characters on the medals and signs of different parts of Asia, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> they reciprocally throw upon one another, and the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> which they all bear to the grand prototype, affords another ample field for curiosity. The coins of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSAM">Assam</a>, Nipal, Cashmiria, and many other kingdoms, are all stamped with Sanskrit letters, and mostly contain allusions to the old Sanskrit <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>. The same conformity may be observed in the impressions of seals from Bootan and Thibet." The country between the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDUS">Indus</a> and Ganges still preserves the Sanskrit language in its original purity, and offers a great number of books to the perusal of the curious; many of which have been handed down from the earliest periods of human civilization. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> different sorts of Indian hand-writings, all comprised under the general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of Naagoree, which may be interpreted writing. The Brahmans say that letters were of divine origin; and the elegant Sanskrit is styled Dael-naagoree, or the writings of the Immortals, which might not improbably be a refinement from the more simple Naagoree of former ages. The Bengal letters are another branch of the same stock. The Brahmans of Bengal have all their Sanskrit books copied in their national alphabet, and they transcribe into them all the Dael-naagoree <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> for their own perusal. The Moorish dialect is that species of Hindustanic which we owe to the conquests of the Mahometans. The Sanskrit language contains about 700 radical words; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> part being divided into three classes, viz. 1. Dhata, or roots of verbs; 2. Shubd, or original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>; 3. Etya, or particles. Their alphabet contains 50 letters; viz. 34 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSONANTS">consonants</a> and 16 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOWELS">vowels</a>. They assert that they were in possession of letters before any other nation in the world; and Mr Halhed conjectures, that the long boasted original civilization of the Egyptians may still be a matter of dispute. The rajah of Kishinagar affirms, that he has in his possession Sanskrit books, where the Egyptians are constantly described as disciples, not as instructors; and as seeking in Hindostan that liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and those sciences, which none of their own countrymen had sufficient knowledge to impart. Mr Halhed hints also, that the learning of Hindostan might have been transplanted into Egypt, and thus have become familiar to Moses. Several authors, however, are of opinion, that the ancient Egyptians possessed themselves of the trade of the East by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and that they carried carried on a considerable traffic with the Indian nations before the time of Sesostris; whom they suppose to have been <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Abraham, though Sir Isaac Newton conjectures him to have been the Shihak who took <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> in the time of Rehoboam. In the year 1769, one of the sacred books of the Gentoos called Bagavadam, translated by Meridas Poule, a learned man of Indian origin, and chief interpreter to the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Pondicherry, was sent by him to M. Bertin in France. In his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> he says, that it was composed by Vialfar the son of Brahma, and is of sacred authority among the worshippers of Vishnu. This book claims an antiquity of 5000 years; but M. de Guines has shown, that its pretensions to such extravagant antiquity are entirely inconclusive and unsatisfactory: whence we may conclude, says Mr. Ayle, that though a farther inquiry into the literature of the Indian nations may be laudable, yet we must by no means give too easy credit to their relations concerning the high antiquity of their manuscripts and early civilization. It is not pretended that the Persians had any great learning among them till the time of Hyrcanus the father of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIUS">Darius</a>. The former, we are told, travelled into India, and was instructed by the Brahmins in the sciences for which they were famed at that time. The ancient Persians despised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> and commerce, nor had they any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> among them till after the conquest of Lydia. It appears by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> taken from the ruins of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of Persepolis, which was built near 700 years before the Christian era, that the Persians sometimes wrote in perpendicular columns like the Chinese. This mode of writing was first made use of on the items of trees, pillars, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBELISKS">obelisks</a>. As for those simple characters found on the west side of the staircase of Persepolis, some have supposed them to be alphabetic, some hieroglyphic, and others antediluvian. Dr. Hyde pronounces them to have been mere whimsical ornaments, though the author of Conjectural Observations on Alphabetic Writing supposes them to be fragments of Egyptian antiquity brought by Cambyses from the spoils of Thebes. The learned are generally agreed, that the Persians were later in civilization than many of their neighbours; and they are not supposed to have any pretensions to the invention of letters. As the Arabians have been in possession of the country they now inhabit for upwards of 3700 years, without being intermixed with foreign nations, or subjugated by any other power, their language must be very ancient. The two principal dialects of it were that spoken by the Hamyarites and other genuine Arabs; and that of the Koreish, in which Mahomet wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCORAN">Alcoran</a>. The former is named by oriental writers, the Arabic of Hamyar; the latter, the pure or defected Arabic. Mr. Richardson observes, as a proof of the richness of this language, that it consists of 2000 radical words. The old Arabic characters are said to have been of very high antiquity; for Ebn Hafhem relates, that an inscription in it was found in Yemen as old as the days of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Hence some have supposed, that the Arabians were the inventors of letters; and Sir Isaac Newton is of opinion, that Moses learned the alphabet from the Midianites, who were Arabians. The alphabet of the Arabs consists of 28 letters similar to the ancient Cufic, in which the first copies of the Alcoran were written. The present Arabic characters were formed by Ebn Mokiah, a learned Arabian who lived about 300 years after Mahomet. The Arabian writers themselves inform us, that their alphabet is not very ancient, and that they received it only a short time before the introduction of Islamism. On this account of the pretensions of different nations to the invention of letters, Mr. Ayle makes the following reflections: "The vanity of each nation induces them to pretend to the most early civilization: but such is the uncertainty of ancient history, that it is difficult to determine to whom the honour is due. It should seem, however, that the contest may be confined to the Egyptians, the Phoenicians, and the Chaldeans. The Greek writers, and most of those who have copied them, decide in favour of Egypt, because their information is derived from the Egyptians themselves. The positive claim of the Phoenicians does not depend entirely upon the testimony of Sanchoniatho; the credibility of his history is so well supported by Philo of Byblus, Phoenicia's translator, Porphyry, Pliny, Curtius, Lucan, and other ancient writers, who might have seen his works entire, and whose relations deserve at least as much credit as those of the Egyptian and Greek writers. It must be allowed, that Sanchoniatho's history contains many fabulous accounts; but does not the ancient history of the Egyptians, the Greeks, and most other nations, abound with them to a much greater degree? The fragments which we have of this most ancient historian are chiefly furnished by Eusebius, who took all possible advantages to represent the Pagan writers in the worst light, and to render their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> absurd and ridiculous. "The Phoenician and Egyptian languages are very similar; but the latter is said to be more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and full, which is an indication of its being of a later <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a>. The opinion of Mr. Wile, however, that the ancient Egyptians had not the knowledge of letters, seems to be erroneous; as they had commercial intercourse with their neighbours the Phoenicians, they probably had the knowledge of letters, if their policy, like that of the Chinese at this day, did not prohibit the use of them. "The Chaldeans, who cultivated astronomy in the most remote ages, used symbols or arbitrary marks in their calculations; and we have shewn that these were the parents of letters. This circumstance greatly favours their claim to the invention: because Chaldea, and the countries adjacent, are allowed by all authors, both sacred and profane, to have been peopled before Egypt; and it is certain, that many nations said to be descended from Shem and Japheth, had their letters from the Phoenicians, who were descended from Ham. "It is observable that the Chaldeans, the Syrians, Phoenicians, and Egyptians, all bordered upon each other; and as the Phoenicians were the greatest as well as the most ancient commercial nation, it is very probable that they communicated letters to the Egyptians, the ports of Tyre and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIDON">Sidon</a> being not far distant from each other. "Mr. Jackson is evidently mistaken when he says that letters were invented 2619 years before the birth of Christ. The deluge recorded by Moses was 2349 years..." years before that event; and if letters were not invented till 550 years after, as he affirms, we must date their discovery only 1799 years before the Christian era, which is 410 years after the reign of Menes, the first king of Egypt, who, according to Syncellus and others, is said to have been the same person with the Mitor of Sanchoniatho, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIZRAIM">Mizraim</a> of the Scriptures, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a> of the Egyptians; but whether this be true or not, Egypt is frequently called in Scripture the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of Mizraim. This Mizraim, the second son of Amyn or Ham, seated himself near the entrance of Egypt at Zoan, in the year before Christ 2188, and 160 years after the flood. He afterwards built Thebes, and some say <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMPHIS">Memphis</a>. Before the time that he went into Egypt, his son Taaut had invented letters in Phoenicia; and if this invention took place ten years before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of his father into Egypt, as Mr. Jackson supposes, we may trace letters as far back as the year 2178 before Christ, or 150 years after the deluge recorded by Moses; and beyond this period, the written annals of mankind, which have been hitherto transmitted to us, will not enable us to trace the knowledge of them; though this want of materials is no proof that letters were not known until a century and a half after the deluge. As for the pretensions of the Indian nations, we must be better acquainted with their records before we can admit of their claim to the first use of letters; especially as none of their manuscripts of any great antiquity have as yet appeared in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. That the Arabians were not the inventors of letters, has appeared by their own confession. Plato somewhere mentions Hyperborean letters very different from the Greek; these might have been the characters used by the Tartars, or ancient Scythians. It may be expected that something should be said concerning those books mentioned by some authors to have been written before the deluge. Amongst others, Dr. Parsons, in his Remains of Japheth, p. 346, 359, supposes letters to have been known to Adam; and the Sabaeans produce a book, which they pretend was written by Adam. But concerning these we have no guide to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> us any more than concerning the supposed books of Enoch; some of which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> tells us, were found in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Felix, in the dominions of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Saba. Tertullian affirms, that he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and read several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> of them; and, in his treatise De Habitui Mulierum, he places those books among the canonical; but St Jerome and St Austin look upon them to be apocryphal. William Pottellius pretended to compile his book, De Originibus, from the book of Enoch; and Thomas Bangius published at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, in 1657, a work which contains many singular relations concerning the manner of writing among the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTEDILUVIANS">Antediluvians</a>, which contains several pleasant stories concerning the books of Enoch. With regard to this patriarch, indeed, St Jude informs us that he prophesied, but he does not say that he wrote. The writings, therefore, attributed to the Antediluvians, must appear quite uncertain; though it might be improper to assert that letters were unknown before the deluge recorded by Moses. Our author proceeds to show, that all the alphabets in the world cannot be derived from one original; because there is a variety of alphabets used in different parts of Asia, which vary in name, number, figure, order, and power, from the Phoenician, ancient Hebrew, or Samaritan. In several of these alphabets also, there are marks for sounds peculiar to the language of each, which are not necessary to be employed in the notation of the languages of Europe. None of the alphabets to the east of Persia have any connexion with the Phoenician or its derivatives, except where the Arabic letters have been introduced by the conquests of the Mahometans. The foundation of all the Indian characters are those called Shanfcrir or Sungferir. This signifies something brought to perfection, in contradistinction to Prakrit, which signifies vulgar or unpolished. Hence the refined and religious language and characters of India are called Sungferir, and the more vulgar mode of writing and expression Prakrit. From this Shanfcrir are derived the sacred characters of Thibet, the Cashmirian, Bengalese, Malabarese, and Tamoul; the Singalese, Siamese, Maharattn, Concaneese, &c. From the same source we may derive the Tartaric or Tartar characters, which are similar in their great outlines to the Shanfcrir; though it is not easily determined which is derived from the other. The common Tartar is generally read, like the Chinese, from top to bottom. There are, however, several alphabets used in different parts of Asia, entirely different not only from the Shanfcrir and all those derived from it, but also from the Phoenician and those which proceed from it. Some of these are the alphabet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEGU">Pegu</a>, the Batna characters used in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, and the Barman or Roman characters used in some parts of Pegu. The names and powers of the letters of which these alphabets are composed, differ entirely from the Phoenician, or those derived from them. It is impossible to assimilate their forms; and indeed it is by no means easy to conceive how the 50 letters of the Shanfcrir language could be derived from the Phoenician alphabet, which consisted originally only of 13; though it is certain, that by far the greater number of alphabets now in use are derived from the ancient Hebrew, Phoenician, or Samaritan. Mr. Ashle next proceeds to consider what alphabets are derived from the Phoenician. These he supposes to have been immediately the ancient Hebrew or Samaritan; the Chaldaic; the Bafulian (a) or Spanish Phoenician; the Punic; Carthaginian, or Sicilian; and the Pelagian. From the ancient Hebrew proceeded the Chaldaic or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> Hebrew; the round Hebrew; and what is called the running hand of the Rabbins. The Pelagian gave birth to the Etrurcan, Eugubian or Umbrian, Ofcan, Samnie, and Ionic Greek, written from the left. From the Chaldaic or square Hebrew are derived the Syriac, and the ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Arabic. The Syriac is divided into the Estrangelo and (a) The Bafuli are said to have been a Canaanitish or Phoenician people who fled from Joshua, and settled afterwards in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. Alphabet, and Mendelean, and the modern Arabic has given rise to the Persian and Turkish. From the ancient Arabic are derived the Cufic or Oriental, the Mauritanian or Occidental, the African or Saracen, and the Moorish. The Ionic Greek gave rise to the Arcadian, Latin, ancient Gaulish, ancient Spanish, ancient Gothic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Runic, Illyrian or Slavonic, Bulgarian, and Armenian. From the Roman are derived the Lombardic, Visigothic, Saxon, Gallican, Franco-Gallic or Merovingian, German, Caroline, Capetian, and modern Gothic. The Punic letters are also called Tyrian, and were much the same with the Carthaginian or Sicilian. The Punic language was at first the same with the Phoenician; it is nearly allied to the Hebrew, and has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with the Chaldee and Syriac. Some remains of it are to be met with in the Maltese. To make a complete Punic, Carthaginian, or Sicilian alphabet, we must admit several pure Phoenician letters. The Pelagii were likewise of Phoenician origin; and, according to Sanchoniatho, the Dioecuri and Cabiri wrote the first annals of the Phoenician history, by order of Taaut, the inventor of letters. They made ships of burthen; and being <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> near Mount Cænus, about 40 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELUSIUM">Pelusium</a>, where they built a temple in the second <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> after the deluge related by Moses, they were called Pelagii, from their passing by sea, and wandering from one country to another. Herodotus informs us, that the Pelagii were descendants of the Phoenician Cabiri, and that the Samothracians received and practised the Cabiric mysteries from them. The Pelagian alphabet prevailed in Greece till the time of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEUCALION">Deucalion</a>, when the Pelagii were driven out of Thessaly or Oenotria by the Hellenes; after which some of them settled at the mouth of the Po, and others at Croton, now Cortona in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>. Their alphabet consisted of 16 letters, and the Tyrrhenian alphabet, brought into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> before the reign of that prince consisted of no more than 13. Deucalion is said to have reigned about 820 years after the deluge, and 1529 before the Christian era. That the Tyrrheni, Tyrfeni or Hetrufi, settled in Italy long before this period, appears from the testimony of Herodotus, who informs us, that a colony went by sea from Lydia into Italy under Tyrrhenus; and Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a> proves that many authors called them Pelagii. He then cites Hellanicus Leficus, an author somewhat more ancient than Herodotus, to prove, that they were first called Pelagii Tyrrheni; and when they passed into Italy, they settled in that part of it called Etruria. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> took place about the year of the world 2011, or 1993 years before the Christian era, which is 350 years before the Pelagii left Greece. Bishop <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> adduces many proofs to show that the Tyrrhenians originally came out of Lydia into Italy. Several Roman authors also speak of this Lydian colony; and Horace compliments his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> Maecenas upon his Lydian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>: Lydomum quicquid Etruscum Incoluit fines, nemo generosior est. The Etruscan letters are Pelagian, and several of the Etruscan inscriptions are written in the Pelagian language. The Roman letters are Ionic. The Oscan Vol. I. Part II. Language was a dialect of the Etruscan; their characters are nearer the Ionic or Roman than the Etruscan. There is also very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the Pelagian, Etruscan, and most ancient Greek letters, which are placed from right to left. The Arcadians were ancient Greeks, and used the Ionic letters; but at what time they began to write from left to right is not known, as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a> is very uncertain. The Etruscan, Oscan, and Samnite alphabets, are derived from the Pelagian; they differ from each other more in name than in form; but a far greater number are derived from the Ionic Greek, namely, the Arcadian, the Latin or Roman, and the others already enumerated.—The Runic is immediately derived from the Gothic. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, the first Greek colony which came into Italy consisted of Arcadians, under the conduct of Oenotrus, the son of Lycaon, and fifth in descent from Phoroneus, the first king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a>, who reigned about 566 years before the taking of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>, and 1750 years before the Christian era. These Oenotrians were called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>; and after they had been engaged for many years in a war with the Siculi, entered into an <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with a colony of the Pelagii, who came out of Thessaly into Italy, after having been driven from the former country. About 1476 B.C., another colony of the Pelagii, who had been driven out of Thessaly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURETES">Curetes</a> and Leleges, arrived in Italy, where they assisted the Aborigines to drive out the Siculi, possessing themselves of the greatest part of the country between the Tiber and the Liris, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> several cities. Sozomenus and Pliny tell us, that the Pelagii first carried letters into Italy; and the latter distinguishes between the Pelagian and the Arcadian; so the letters first carried into Italy were not the Ionic Greek, but those more ancient Pelagian characters which the Pelagii carried with them before Deucalion and Cadmus are said to have come into Boeotia and Thessaly. The story of Cadmus is much involved in fable; but it is agreed by most of the ancients, that the children of Agenor, viz., Cadmus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPA">Europa</a>, Phoenix, and Cilix, carried with them a colony, composed of Phoenicians and Syrians, into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, Greece, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>, where they introduced letters, music, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and other arts, sciences, and customs, of the Phoenicians. Dionysius enumerates the following Greek colonies which came into Italy: 1. The Aborigines under Oenotrus, from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. 2. The Pelagian colony, which came from Eremonia or Thessaly. 3. Another Arcadian colony, which came with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVANDER">Evander</a> from Palantium. 4. Those who came from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>; and 5. Those who came with Æneas from Troy. It is not easy to discover when the Ionic way of writing from left to right was introduced into Italy; but it is certain, that it did not universally prevail even in Greece till several ages after it was found out. The Athenians did not comply with it till the year of Rome 350; nor was it practised by the Samnites even in the 6th century of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, or 230 years before Christ: for M. Gaebelein, Vol. VI. Pl. 2. gives us the Samnite alphabet of that century, wherein the letters are placed from right to left; although the Ionic way of writing prevailed in some parts of Italy in the third century of Rome. "In time (says Pliny) the tacit consent of all nations..." nations agreed to use the Ionic letters. The Romans consented to this mode about the time of Tarquinius Priscus, their fifth king. The letters brought by Demaratus the Corinthian, the father of Tarquin, Mr Wife thinks, must have been the new or Ionic alphabet, and not the same with that brought by Evander 500 years before. After the Romans had established the use of the Ionic letters, they seem not to have acknowledged the Pelasgian and Etruscan to have been Greek alphabets: the most learned of them knew none older than the Ionic, as appears from the Greek Farnese inscriptions of Herodes Atticus. This learned man, out of a regard to antiquity, caused the oldest orthography to be observed in the writing, and the letters to be delineated after the most antique forms that could be found; and they are plainly no other than the Ionic or right-handed characters. The ancient Gaulish letters are derived from the Greek, and their writing approaches more nearly to the Gothic than that of the Romans: this appears by the monumental inscription of Gordian, messenger of the Gauls, who suffered martyrdom in the third century, with all his family. These ancient Gaulish characters were generally used by that people before the conquest of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> by Caesar; but after that time the Roman letters were gradually introduced. The ancient Spaniards used letters nearly Greek before their intercourse with the Romans. The ancient Gothic alphabet was very similar to the Greek, and is attributed to Ulpilas, bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, who lived in Moesia about 370 years after Christ. He translated the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a> into the Gothic tongue. This circumstance might have occasioned the tradition of his having invented these letters; but it is probable that these characters were in use long before this time. The Runic alphabet is derived from the ancient Gothic. The Coptic letters are derived immediately from the Greek. Some have confounded them with the ancient Egyptian; but there is a very material difference between them. The Ethiopic alphabet is derived from the Coptic. The alphabet proceeding from that of the Scythians established in Europe, is the same with what St Cyril calls the Servien. The Ruthenian, Illyrian, or Slavonic, and the Bulgarian, are all derived from the Greek. The Armenian letters differ very much from the Greek, from which they are derived, as well as from the Latin. With regard to the alphabets derived from the Latin, the Lombardic relates to the manuscripts of Italy; the Visigothic to those of Spain; the Saxon to those of England; the Gallican and Franco-Gallic or Merovingian to the manuscripts of France; the German to those of that country; and the Caroline, Capetian, and Modern Gothic, to all the countries of Europe who read Latin. The first six of these alphabets are before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, the last three posterior to it. They are more distinguished by their names than the forms of their characters; and the former indicate all of them to have been of Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>. Each nation, in adopting the letters of the Romans, added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and manner peculiar to itself; which obviously distinguished it from the writings of all other people; whence arose the differences between the writings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, Spaniards, French, Saxons, Germans and Goths, and all the strange terms observable in the writings of the Francie Gauls or Merovingians; and those of the Carlovingians, their successors, may be traced from the same source. From these distinctions the name of national writing was derived. The writing of Italy was uniform till the irruption of the Goths, who disfigured it by their barbarous taste. In 569, the Lombards, having possessed themselves of all Italy, excepting Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, introduced that form of writing which goes under their name; and as the popes used the Lombardic manner in their bulls, the name of Roman was sometimes given to it in the 11th century; and though the dominion of the Lombards continued no longer than 206 years, the name of their writing continued in Italy from the 7th to the 13th century, and then ceased; when learning, having declined in that as well as in other countries, the manner of writing degenerated into the modern Gothic. The Visigoths introduced their form of writing into Spain, after having overrun that country; but it was abolished in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, held at Leon in 1091, when the Latin characters were established for all public instruments, though the Visigothic were used in private writings for three centuries afterwards. The Gauls, on being subjected by the Romans, adopted their manner of writing; but by subsequent additions of their own, their characters were changed into what is called the Gallican or Roman Gallic mode. This was changed by the Franks into the Franco-Gallie or Merovingian mode of writing, being practised under the kings of the Merovingian race. It took place towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fifth century, and continued till the beginning of the ninth. The German mode of writing was improved by Charlemagne; and this improvement occasioned another distinction in writing, by introducing the alphabet named Caroline, which declined in the 12th century, and was succeeded in the 13th by the modern Gothic. In France it had degenerated by the middle of the 10th century, but was restored in 897 by Hugh Capet, whence it obtained the name of Capetian. It was used in England, as well as Germany and France. The modern Gothic, which spread itself all over Europe in the 12th and 13th centuries, is improperly named, as not deriving its origin from the writing anciently used by the Goths. It is, however, the worst and most barbarous way of writing, and originated among the schoolmen in the decline of the arts; being indeed nothing else than Latin writing degenerated. It began in the 12th century, and was in general use, especially among monks and schoolmen, in all parts of Europe, till the restoration of arts in the 15th century, and continued longer in Germany and the northern nations. Our statute books are still printed in Gothic letters. The most barbarous writing of the seventh, eighth, and ninth centuries, was preferable to the modern Gothic. It is diversified in such a manner as can scarce admit of description; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBREVIATIONS">abbreviations</a> used by the writers were so numerous, that it became very difficult to read it; which was one of the great causes of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of those times. Along with this, however, Alphabet, however, the Lombardic, Gothic, Roman, Caroline, and Capetian modes of writing, were occasionally used by individuals. The idea that all the alphabets above mentioned are derived from the Roman, tends to prove the distinction of national writing, and is of great use in discovering the age of manuscripts: for though we may not be able exactly to determine the time when a manuscript was written, we may be able nearly to ascertain its age. For example, if a writing is Merovingian, it may be declared not to be posterior to the 6th, nor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the 5th century. If another be Lombardic, it may be affirmed to be posterior to the middle of the 6th, and prior to the 13th. Should it be Saxon, it cannot be of an earlier date than the 7th, nor later than about the middle of the 12th. Having considered whence the alphabets now in use throughout the various nations of the world are derived, it remains to say something concerning them as the elements of words, or how far they are capable of expressing those sounds which, by proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> and arrangement, constitute articulate language. The number of simple sounds in any language cannot be very numerous; and it is plainly these simple sounds alone that we have occasion to represent by alphabetical characters. Hence the person who first invented letters must have been capable of analyzing language in a manner which seems by no means easy to do, and concerning which even the learned among ourselves are not yet agreed. It is this difficulty which has produced the great diversity in the number of alphabetical characters used by different nations; and where we see a vast number of them used, we may account the writing not the better, but much the worse for it; and whoever the pretended inventor was, it is more reasonable to suppose that he disfigured an alphabet already invented, by unnecessary additions, than that he was the author of one himself. When we consider alphabetical characters as thus resulting from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of language, it will by no means appear probable that it was derived from a gradual and progressive operation of the human mind through many ages. There is not the least affinity between representing any object by a picture and finding out the sounds which compose the word by which it is expressed: nor, though a nation had been in use to represent things either in this method, or by any kind of arbitrary marks, for thousands of years, could the one ever have led to the other. Arbitrary marks must always be the same with pictures in this respect, that they must always be fixed to particular objects, and thus be increased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> infinitum. Letters, on the other hand, are indifferent to all objects; and therefore, by their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, which are more numerous than as many arbitrary marks as we could remember, may express all the objects in nature. This might furnish an argument of some strength for the divine revelation of writing, were it not that other arts, seemingly as useful, and as difficult to be invented, had not been expressly ascribed to particular persons whom we cannot suppose to have been divinely inspired. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">metallurgy</a>, music, the keeping of cattle, and use of tents, are all ascribed to a single family; and though writing be not expressly mentioned as an invention in Scripture, there is no reason to have recourse to a revelation for it as long as the human faculties are known to have been sufficient for the invention of it. Nevertheless, if we take a review of the different arts which mankind have invented, we shall find, that few of them resulted from any gradual progress or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a> of the powers of the human mind, but rather by some sudden and almost unaccountable turn of thought in an individual. Thus, the art of printing, little inferior in its utility to that of writing, lay hid for ages, and was at last invented we scarcely know how; so that if one inclined to suppose this a divine revelation, he could be at little loss for arguments to support his hypothesis. This was what all the inventions and evolutions of human powers since the creation had never been able to accomplish; yet nobody believes that it required supernatural abilities to be the author of this art, because we see plainly that it might have occurred to the human mind from various sources, and are surprised that it did not occur long before. In like manner, the method of accounting for the celestial motions by the united forces of projection and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVITATION">gravitation</a>, was no result of the progress that mankind had made in science, but luckily occurred to Mr Horrox, without any thing that we know to direct him, or perhaps from causes almost unknown to himself. Thus, also, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> engine, aerostation, &c., were suddenly invented only by a slight review of principles well known before, and which had been a thousand times overlooked by those who might have invented both. Alphabetical writing, therefore, might have been no deduction from hieroglyphic or picture writing, from which it is essentially different; and it seems to be some <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of this, that all nations who ever pretended to the invention of letters, have ascribed it to the labours of one particular person, without taking notice of the progress made towards it in preceding ages. The learned author of Hermes informs us, that to Of the about 20 plain elementary sounds we owe that variety of articulate voices which have been sufficient to explain the sentiments of such an innumerable multitude as all the past and present generations of men. Mr Sheridan says, that the number of simple sounds in our tongue is 28; while Dr Kenrick says, that we have only 11 distinct species of articulate sounds, which even by contraction, prolongation, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, are increased only to the number of 16; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> or articulate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> in our language being one of the number. Bishop Wilkins and Dr William Holder speak of 33 distinct sounds. After the analysis or decomposition of language into the elementary sounds, the next towards the notation of it by alphabetical characters, would be the delineation of a separate mark or letter to represent each sound; which marks, though few in number, would admit of such a variety of arrangements and combinations, as might be capable of producing that infinity of articulate sounds which compose language. The ingenious Wachter, in his Nature et Scripture <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCORDIA">Concordia</a>, p. 64, endeavours to show, that ten marks or characters are sufficient for this purpose. His scheme is as follows: \[ \text{A Z 2} \] Genus. If this is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, then the most simple alphabet, which consists only of 13 letters, must have been abundantly sufficient to answer all the purposes of mankind, and much of our twenty-four letter alphabet may appear superfluous. That able mathematician Tacquet has calculated the various combinations of the 24 letters, even without any repetition, to amount to no fewer than $629,448,401,733,239,439,360,000$; while Clavius makes them only $5,852,616,738,497,664,000$. Either of these numbers, however, is infinite to the human conceptions, and much more than sufficient to express all the sounds that ever were articulated by man. As there are more sounds in some languages than in others, it follows of course, that the number of elementary characters or letters must vary in the alphabets of different languages. The Hebrew, Samaritan, and Syriac alphabets, have 22 letters; the Arabic 28; the Persian, and Egyptian or Coptic, 32; the present Russian 41; the Shanshiri 50; while the Cashmirian and Malabar are still more numerous. The following is the scheme of the English alphabet, as given by Mr Sheridan in his Rhetorical Grammar, p. 9. Number of simple sounds in our tongue 28. | Genus | Figura | Poteftas | |-------|--------|----------| | Vocal | O | a. e. i. o. u. | | Guttural | O | k. c. ch. q. g. h. | | Lingual | L | l. | | Lingual | Z | d. t. | | Lingual | R | r. | | Dental | N | f. | | Labial | 3 | b. p. | | Labial | N | m. | | Labial | R | s. ph. v. w. | | Nasal | A | n. | Number of letters in different alphabets. | Number of letters | |------------------| | Hebrew | | Samaritan | | Syriac | | Arabic | | Persian | | Egyptian | | Coptic | | Russian | | Shanshiri | | Cashmirian | | Malabar | Consonants divided into Mutes and Semivowels. 6 Mutes, eb ed eg ek ep et. 3 Pure Mutes, ck ep et. 3 Impure, eb ed eg. 13 Semivowels or liquids, ef el em en er es ev ez eth ing. 9 Vocal, el em en er ez eth ing. 4 Aspirated, ef els eth efh. Divided again into 4 Labial, eb ep ev ef. 8 Dental, ed et eth eth ez els ezh efh. 4 Palatine, eg ek el er. 3 Nasal, em en ing. Mr Sheridan observes, that our alphabet is ill calculated for the notation of the English tongue, as there are many sounds for which we have no letters or marks; and there ought to be <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> more characters or letters to make a complete alphabet, in which every simple sound ought to have a mark peculiar to itself. The reason of the deficiency is, that the Roman alphabet was formerly adopted for the notation of the English language, though by no means suited to the purpose. It now remains only to take some notice of the forms of the different letters; some knowledge of which is absolutely necessary for ascertaining the age and authenticity of inscriptions, manuscripts, charters, and ancient records. Many authors are of opinion, that letters derive their forms from the positions of the organs of speech in their pronunciation. Van Helmont has taken great pains to prove, that the Chaldaic characters are the genuine alphabet of nature; because, according to him, no letter can be rightly founded without disposing the organs of speech into a uniform position with the figure of each letter; and in support of this system, he has anatomized the organs of articulation. Mr Nelme has endeavoured to show, that all elementary characters or letters derive their forms from the line and the circle. His alphabet consists of 13 radical letters, four diminished and four augmented.—The radicals are L, O, S, A, B, C, D, N, U, I, E, M, R.—H, according to him, is derived from A; P from B; T from D; and F from U: they are called diminished letters. The augmented ones are, Z from S; G from C; W from U; and Y from I. He proves that his characters are very similar to those of the ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ETRUSCANS">Etruscans</a>; but all characters are composed either of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> and circles of the former, or of parts of the latter.—Mr Gebelin deduces them from hieroglyphic representations; and has given several delineations of human figures, trees, &c., in confirmation of his hypothesis. One of the most simple alphabets has been formed by making two perpendicular and two <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> lines: \[ \begin{<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>}{ccc} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \\ \end{array} \] Thus, \( \begin{array}{ccc} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \\ \end{array} \) From which may be deduced nine different characters or letters: Thus, \[ \begin{array}{cccccc} a & b & c & d & e & f \\ g & h & i & j & k & l \\ \end{array} \] | Phoenicum | Hbr. ex Mediat. | Bastulam | Etruscam | Graecum | Graecum | Latinum | Runicum | Gothicum | Copticum | Teutonicum | |-----------|-----------------|----------|----------|---------|---------|---------|---------|----------|----------|-----------| | Α | Χ | ΛΙ | Α | Α | Α | Α | Α | Λ | Λ | Α | | Β | Β | Ι | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | Ξ | | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | Χ | | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Ω | Plate XV.

ALPHABETUM ANTIQUISSIMA

Pages 355-359

a dextra <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">ad</a> sinistram exaruit. a sinistra ad dextram. | Panicum | Pelasguum | Oscan | Arcadian | Galli antiqui | Phenicium libri antiqui sive Samaritarum | generalis Etruscorum | |---------|-----------|-------|----------|--------------|----------------------------------------|---------------------| | A | Ἀ | Α | Α | Α | Α | Α | | B | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | Β | | Gh | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | Γ | | D | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | Δ | | E | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | Ε | | V | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | Φ | | Z | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | Ζ | | H | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | Η | | Th | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | Θ | | I | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | Ι | | K | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | Κ | | L | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | Λ | | M | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | Μ | | N | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | Ν | | S | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | | O | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | Ο | | P | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | Π | | T | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | | Q | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | Ψ | | R | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | Ρ | | Sch | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | Σ | | T | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | Τ | | V | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | Υ | <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ALPHENIX">Alphenix</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> more may be made by adding a point to each, \[ k \mid l \mid m \] and as many more as \( n \mid o \mid p \) may be sufficient for the \[ q \mid r \mid s \] notation of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, by adding two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> to each character. Though these <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> are not calculated for despatch; yet they may be made as expeditiously, or more so, than the Tartar, the Bramin, the Cashmirian, or many others. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">Writing</a> composed of these characters, is at first sight somewhat like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>.—Mr Dow, author of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Indostan, lately formed a new language and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a>. This language, and the characters formed for its notation, were so easy, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> of his acquaintance acquired the knowledge of them in three weeks, and corresponded with him therein during their intimacy. ALPHÆNIX, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> barley-fugar, to which is given an extraordinary name, to render it more valuable. This fugar, which is thought good for colds, is made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, which is boiled until it becomes easy to crack, when they pour it upon a marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, greased with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of sweet almonds, and mould it into various figures with a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> crochette. It is easily falsified with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>.

ALPHERY

Pages 359-359

Mixipher, an English divine, was born in Russia, and of the imperial line. When that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was distracted by intestine commotions, in the latter end of the 16th century, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> particularly was so feverishly persecuted by impostors, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> and his two brothers were sent over to England, and recommended to the care of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Bidell a Russia merchant. Mr Bidell, when they were of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> fit for the university, sent them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where the smallpox unhappily prevailing, two of them died of it. We know not whether this surviving <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> took any degrees <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not, but it is very probable he did, since he entered into holy orders; and in the year 1618, was presented to the rectory of Wooley in Huntingdonshire, a living of no very considerable value, being rated under 10l. in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books. Here he did his duty with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> cheerfulness and alacrity; and although he was twice invited back to his native country by some who would have ventured their utmost to have fet him on the throne of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, he chose rather to remain with his flock, and to serve God in the humble station of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. Yet in 1643, he underwent the severest trials from the rage of the fanatics; who, not satisfied with depriving him of his living, insulted him in the most barbarous manner; for, having procured a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> of musqueteers to pull him out of his pulpit, as he was preaching on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUNDAY">Sunday</a>, they turned his wife and small children into the street, into which also they threw his goods. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in this distress raised a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> under some trees in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, over against his house, where he and his family lived for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> having gotten a few eggs, he picked up some rotten wood and dry sticks, and with these made a fire in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> porch, in order to boil them; but some of his adversaries, to show how far they could carry their rage against the church (for this poor man was so harmless they could have none against him), came and kicked about his fire, threw <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a>, and broke his eggs. After this, having still a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, he made a small Alpheus purchase in that neighbourhood, built a house, and lived there some years. He was encouraged to this by the Presbyterian minister, who came in his room, who honestly paid him the fifth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the annual income of the living, which was the allowance made by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> to ejected ministers, treated him with great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and did him all the favours in his power. It is a great misfortune that this gentleman's name is not preserved, his conduct in this respect being the more laudable, because it was not a little singular. Afterwards, probably on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> or removal of this gentleman, Mr Alpher left Huntingdonshire, and came and resided at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMMERSMITH">Hammersmith</a> till the Restoration put him in possession of his living again. He returned on this occasion to Huntingdonshire, where he did not stay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>; for being upwards of 80, and withal very infirm, he could not perform the duties of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a>. Having, therefore, settled a curate, he retired to his eldest son's house at Hammersmith, where soon after he died, much honoured and respected, and affording a remarkable instance of the vicissitudes of the world.

ALPHEUS

Pages 359-359

(Strabo); ALPEUS, (<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a noted and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> river of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>; which, rising in, and after several windings running through <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>, and by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OLYMPIA">Olympia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>, with a south-west course, falls into the Sinus Cheloniotes, about ten miles to the south of Olympia. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> with the Eurotas, at the foot of Mount Parthenius, near the village Alea, (Strabo.) The Alpheus and Eurotas mix and run together for 20 stadia; after which, they enter a subterraneous passage at Mantinea; then again emerge, the Eurotas in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, and the Alpheus in the territory of Megalopolis, (Pausanias.) The poets' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> (strange things of this river, particularly, that out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NYMPH">nymph</a> Arethusa, it runs under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and bursts out at the fountain of that name in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRACUSE">Syracuse</a>, (<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.) Its waters were reckoned good in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEPROSY">leprosy</a>, which is called Αλφειος by the Greeks; and hence the name Alpheus. On the banks of this river the Olympic games were celebrated, to which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PINDAR">Pindar</a> alludes. "Alpheus, thy immortal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, On his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>'s triumphant brows The Olympic wreath bestow'd."

ALPHONSIN

Pages 359-367

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for extracting bullets out of gunshot wounds. This instrument derives its name from the inventor Alphonso Ferrier, a physician of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. It consists of three branches, which are closed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a>. When closed and introduced into the wound, the operator draws back the ring towards the handle, upon which the branches... Alphonso branches opening take hold of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>; and then the ring is pulled from the haft, by which means the branches grasp the ball so firmly as to extract it from the wound. ALPHONSO I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, son of Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Portugal, grandson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Alonso king of Leon and Castile, who, as the dowry of his wife Theresa, received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Portugal. One Egas Munitz had the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> from his father, the duties of which he executed with fidelity and success. In the year 1112 his father died, leaving him a boy only three years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when the reins of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the care of the infant son fell to his mother Theresa. At the age of 18 he assumed the sovereign authority by the advice of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> of Portugal, who were highly offended at the growing partiality of his mother for Don Ferdinand Perez, count of Trastamara; for it was suspected that she intended to marry him. But Theresa was little disposed to resign the reins of government. Her party raised an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which took the field to oppose the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> who supported Alphonso; but her adherents were defeated, herself taken prisoner, and kept in confinement during the remainder of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after his accession to the throne, his abilities both to govern and to conquer received a severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, in several arduous enterprises, as well against the king of Leon and Castile as against the Moorish princes, who then possessed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and Portugal. The Moorish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> in Barbary having sent a strong reinforcement to the princes, they were enabled to take the field with an army far superior to that of Alphonso's; yet he valiantly met them in the plains of Ourique, and totally defeated their forces. Thus <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> conferred such a signal favour on the Christian arms as procured a residence for Christianity in those parts. The ambitious king of Leon and Castile assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of emperor of the Spaniards, and entered Portugal to waste and destroy; but after the emperor had received a temporary check, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> was accommodated, and he withdrew his army. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the victory obtained on the plains of Ourique, Alphonso was instantly proclaimed king; but the form and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a> was not settled until the nobility, prelates, and commons had assembled at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAMEGO">Lamego</a> for that purpose in the year 1145. The conquest of Santarem preceded this event, and was sanctioned by the unanimous concurrence of the states. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of crowning the king was conferred upon the archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGA">Braga</a>; and it was legally provided, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> succession should descend with an uninterrupted succession to the heirs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> of Alphonso. The prelates and nobility, with the concurrence of the people, instituted a code of laws consisting of 18 statutes, for the government of the kingdom. It being proposed whether it was their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that the king should go to Leon and do homage to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to any other, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, exclaimed, "We are free, and our king is free, and we owe our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to our courage; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he shall at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> submit to such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, he deserves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and shall not either reign over us or among us." The year after his coronation he was married to Matilda, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Amadeus, count of Maurienne and Savoy; and he recovered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a> from the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Moors, in the year 1147. A multitude of adventurers being assembled at the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAGUS">Tagus</a> in their progress to the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a>, greatly assisted him in this conquest. After having added six other provinces to his dominions, he wisely began with industrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> to regulate the affairs of his kingdom. In all his great and benevolent designs he was vigorously seconded by Matilda, a princess equally celebrated for her great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, mental vigour, and singular piety. With the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of the statesman, and the benevolence of the man, he laboured as much for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of his acquired territories as for their increase. The conjugal felicity of this prince and princess was greatly enhanced by a numerous offspring, which enabled him, by great alliances, to strengthen his interests. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> daughter was married to Don Ferdinand, king of Leon, who, notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a>, generously made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> on his father-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and took him prisoner in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; but released him, on the humiliating condition of coming in person to do homage for his dominions at Leon. In the latter part of his reign, his son Don Sancho, who inherited all his father's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> talents, took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> on several occasions; and in the year 1180, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>, king of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, and emperor of the Almohades, advanced with an army as far as Santarem, and there gained a glorious victory over him. Such was the contumacy of the infidels, in consequence of this defeat, that they left the Portuguese at liberty to improve the interior part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and to fortify their frontiers during the whole of the next year. Worn out with care and intense application, Alphonso needed repose, and had retired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIMBRA">Coimbra</a>, where, after a reign of 37 years, and in the 76th year of his age, he died. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> at Coimbra his remains were deposited with great funeral solemnity.
