He was no less than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and his gigantic size and his martial ardour have given occasion to many absurd and incredible stories concerning his military achievements, so that, in the annals of chivalry, as well as in the records of martial exertions, he attains a very high <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. Two orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, that of the Wings, and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVIS">Avis</a>, were instituted by him; and they still continue to flourish in that kingdom. At the age of 31, when all the faculties of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind are in full vigour, Don Sancho, his son, succeeded him. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) ALPHONSO II. distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of the Fat, was the third king of Portugal, and succeeded his father at the age of 27 years, in 1212. His accomplished education and his military and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> talents were tarnished by his great neglect and hatred of his brothers and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>, which involved him in many troubles. He, however, commenced his reign with two very popular actions. The one was, sending a body of infantry to the assistance of the king of Castile, who fought with uncommon bravery in the renowned battle of Navas de Tolosa. The other was, his donation of the Castle of Avis to the knights of that order, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> removed from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EVORA">Evora</a>, and took up his habitation in that castle. During the life of his father, he discovered his aversion to the rest of the family, which induced him to secure the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of his children from the effects of his resentment. Alphonso, as much as in his power, by conferring upon them <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> and jewels, and some of the best parts of the kingdom. After the death of his father, however, Alphonso strenuously laboured to convince them that it was not in the power of his father to separate or give away any part of his dominions; but all his urgent eloquence proving unsuccessful, he had recourse to arms. The two princesses, his sisters, who had received by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of their father very extensive and valuable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, upon being attacked by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, implored the interference of the pope, and also applied to the king of Leon, to grant his protection, so that they made a very vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. The pope granted the request of the young princesses, and threatened to excommunicate Alphonso; and from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALICIA">Galicia</a>, Don Ferdinand entered the dominions of Portugal to ravage and destroy; but the king prepared to defend himself against the arms of the king of Leon, and by specious pretences to evade the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> of the pope. Authors are not agreed with respect to the success of this war, but it is generally supposed that, by the interference of these two powerful persons, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> affairs of that <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> were restored to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tranquillity; however, the departure of the infant Don Ferdinand to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Castile, and of Don Pedro to another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, strongly indicate that the reconciliation was far from being perfect. The conduct of the king, however, produced much diversity of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of Portugal. Some were induced, by the arguments of the king, to conclude that it was not in the power of Don Sancho, the late king, to dismember his kingdom; and others very properly suspected the kindness of a prince to his people who displayed such uncommon and such unfathomable hatred to his own relations; at the same time, those nobles whom the father had solemnly sworn to carry his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> into execution, regarded the sacred <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> to such a degree as induced them to operate against the reigning prince. The displeasure of the pope, however, was not to be endured. The mind of Alphonso seemed indeed to be of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> which little regarded the displeasure or thunders of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a>; but the effects of his threatenings were very different upon the public mind, consequently the king was constrained to seek the favour of the pope, to retain the obedience of his subjects. The king therefore sent deputies to Rome, who argued, that the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> his father wore was the purchase of the blood and valour of the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and therefore not in his power to alienate; that it was a dangerous precedent, and obviously tended to subvert the sovereignty of a state; that the diminution of the kingdom would tend to promote the cause of the infidels; and, in fine, that his disputes with his sisters had no connexion with <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> matters. The pope, however, was as well qualified to discern the nature of these specious arguments as the prince was qualified to urge them, consequently he remained unmoved; and Alphonso, in order to have the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of excommunication removed which had been pronounced upon him, was reluctantly induced to be reconciled to his sisters. His holiness informed of the reconciliation, with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> revoked his curse and excommunication from the king and his subjects. But the reign of this prince was destined to troubles; for no sooner was this domestic broil terminated, than the Moors rushed into the plain country in such prodigious numbers, that the king found it very difficult to repel them, or to drive them back to their own country. A favourable occurrence, however, enabled him to complete his object, by the taking of a fortress seated on a rock which was deemed impregnable, in the following manner. The Germans and Flemings had equipped an immense fleet destined for the Holy Land, consisting of 300 sail, with a numerous army on board. In consequence of tempestuous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, their fleet was so disabled that they were forced to put into the harbour of Lisbon to refit, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the time when Alphonso was preparing an army to attack the Moors. The king instantly sent some of the most respectable men of his court to solicit their aid against the Moors, alleging that it was perfectly consistent with their vows to fight against the Moors in Portugal, as well as in the Holy Land. William <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and many other generals, were convinced by this argument, and cheerfully engaged to join him against the infidels; but about a third part of the fleet refused to join, and proceeded on their voyage. It happened, however, that they were driven by a violent storm into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where they wintered. The greater part of the nobility and gentry landed under the conduct of William earl of Holland; and it was resolved that they should proceed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> up Alcacer-do-Sal, the fortress already mentioned, while the army of Alphonso, reinforced by a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, should <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> by land; and thus attack the place both by land and sea at once. The Moors, convinced of the importance of this place, brought an army into the field consisting of 50,000 men; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> raised the siege, gave them battle, and routed them with great slaughter; and some of the chiefs of the Moors fell in the field. The fortresses surrendered on the 21st of October 1217, and was conferred upon the order of St James; but notwithstanding of very urgent entreaties, the pope would not permit the army to winter in Portugal. He was furious of having these troops and their generals removed to a greater distance. The writers of that nation affirm that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> experienced supernatural aid in this battle, and that the banner of the cross was actually displayed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. But civil animosity succeeded to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> war. The archbishop of Braga was highly offended that the clergy were forced to pay money and furnish troops to carry on the war against the infidels; and the people severely complained of the strictness of the laws. To chastise the rebellious clergy, the king seized upon the revenues of the bishop, and forced him to fly from his dominions. Enraged at this impious conduct, the pope excommunicated the king, and laid his kingdom under an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> consequence was, that all things were thrown into confusion and consternation, and perplexity universally prevailed; so that Alphonso was obliged to consult <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> to quell the rising discontent. It happened, however, that in the midst of these negotiations he was removed by death, and not only died under the papal malediction, but left his kingdom under the same curse. He was interred without royal honours in the conventual church. Alphonso church of Alcobaça. His person was above the common size; he was brave and strong, but not devoid of many qualities worthy of blame. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) Alphonso III. Don, king of Portugal, succeeded his brother Don Sancho II, in the year 1248. In the course of a war with the Moors, which he engaged in at the beginning of his reign, he considerably extended the Portuguese dominions. He took possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Fara, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Moorish kingdom, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Algarve. Loula, another Moorish town, which was carried by storm, also fell into his hands. His power was thus extended abroad by the success of his arms, and the administration of his affairs at home became prosperous and popular by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and prudence. But the tranquillity and prosperity of the kingdom were somewhat disturbed by an interdict which it was put under by Pope Alexander IV, whose displeasure he had incurred by marrying Donna Beatrix, the natural daughter of Don Alfonso the Wise, king of Castile, while his first wife was living. In 1262, when his first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> died, the interdict was removed by Pope Urban, a dispensation was granted, and the children of Donna Beatrix were legitimated. Hitherto frequent disputes had occurred between the kings of Portugal and Castile relating to the boundaries of the two kingdoms. To terminate all differences on this subject, and to prevent them in future, commissioners were appointed to define and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> the limits of their respective dominions; and these were agreed to and acknowledged by a solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>. Encouraged by the prosperity of his kingdom, and by the success which had attended his enterprises, Alphonso made an attempt to extend the influence of the crown, by obliging the clergy to contribute to the welfare of the state. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, as might have been expected, was not quietly submitted to. It occasioned the revival of old disputes, the pope interfered, and in 1268 the kingdom was again laid under an interdict. He succeeded, by the wisdom of his negotiations, in obtaining from Castile an exemption of all claims upon the crown of Portugal, and in procuring an acknowledgment that its monarchs were entirely relieved from the performance of every kind of homage. He died in the year 1279, in the 60th year of his age, and in the 31st of his reign. Before his death, he was reconciled to the pope and clergy, having made a full and ample submission. This prince was tall in stature, of a prepossessing aspect, and of engaging manners. Alike removed from a disposition to extravagant expense or fond avarice, in times of peace and prosperity, he could indulge in magnificence; but when his affairs required it, he failed not to regulate them by frugality and economy. To the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> he was a sincere friend. In a time of scarcity, he pawned his crown to provide them with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. His steady and vigorous administration secured to him the respect of the nobles and the obedience of the clergy. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) Alphonso IV. king of Portugal, surnamed the Brave, was the son of King Denis. Inflamed, it is said, by the queen dowager of Castile, and moved with jealousy against his natural brother Alphonso Sanchez, he revolted against his father, and commenced a civil war. In this unnatural and baleful war, he was justly unsuccessful; but although he was reduced to subjection, yet his haughty and ungovernable temper broke out in many occurrences, until he succeeded his father in 1324. Hunting was his favourite amusement at the time when he ascended the throne; and one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> entertaining his counsellors with a narrative of his sporting adventures during a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, one of them ventured to remonstrate against his conduct, and even proceeded to threaten, that if the grievances of his subjects were not speedily redressed, they would be forced to look out for a better king. Alphonso was greatly enraged; but suddenly recollecting himself, he said, "I perceive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of your remark; he cannot long have subjects who will not be a king. Remember that from this day, you have nothing to do with Alphonso the sportman, but with Alphonso the king of Portugal." To this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> he strictly adhered, and exercising the power of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESPOT">despot</a>, he overawed his subjects, without conciliating their favour or procuring their esteem. He displayed a conduct very singular in a young man, regarding those who had so vigorously opposed him when at war with his father, as friends to the crown, although enemies to the young ambitious prince. He commenced his reign with devising plans for the security of his family in the government, and the good of the kingdom; he likewise manifested a strong benevolence of heart, in his affection for his consort queen Beatrix, and his dutiful conduct towards his mother. Notwithstanding all these amiable qualities, he persecuted his brother Alonzo Sanchez, and wished to inflict the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to him as a profligate traitor; which drove the desperate Alonso to open rebellion. But, however, the natural good qualities of the heart of the king rose superior; so that his persecuted brother was again received into favour. Not long after he engaged in war with Alonso XI, king of Castile, and which, after several severe struggles with varying success on both sides, terminated in an alliance, and in effectual assistance against the Moors. The artful and cruel part which he acted towards Donna Agnes de Castro, the mistress and concealed wife of his son, reflected the greatest disgrace upon his character. It is proper, however, to remark, that he was implicated to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of this princess by his courtiers. It was not therefore to be wondered at if his son was induced by this act to rise up in open rebellion against him, but the arms of his father were too formidable; and after his submission, his father treated him with particular marks of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Instructed by the growing infirmities of years, he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the termination of his reign and his life approaching. He began to compensate for his past errors and faults, by establishing acts of piety and benevolence, by redressing grievances, by restraining immorality through the establishment of pious laws, by dictating salutary maxims for the government of the state, by removing those from the seats of power, who were the most likely to become the objects of resentment after his death; he thus laboured to efface from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his son the insult which he had received. While concerting these conciliating measures, he died in May 1357, in the 32d year of his reign, and the 67th of his age, "with the character of an undutiful son, an unnatural brother, and a cruel father." But in many respects he deserves the character "of a great man and a great king, brave and fortunate in war, but artful and indirect in his political measures, attached to his subjects," Alphonso subjects, strict in the administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, attentive to the public welfare, and affilious in encouraging industry, and enriching his people." But after all, it must be acknowledged, that although he was feared and even esteemed, he was not much honoured nor beloved, but was rather reverenced for a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of power, than relied upon as a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. His character is perhaps expressed in his device, which was an eagle on the wing, with the following motto, *aliae peto*, "I aim at higher things." **Alphonso V. Don**, king of Portugal, was born in 1432, and on account of his heroic deeds, obtained the surname of the African. At the age of six years, he succeeded his father King Edward. The administration of the affairs of the kingdom during his minority, was entrusted to his uncle Don Pedro, who, although his public conduct met with general approbation, was persecuted as a traitor at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of his regency, and with several persons who were attached to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and involved in his misfortunes, was put to death. The young king had married the daughter of the regent; but even his influence, which was overpowered by the regent's enemies, could not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> him from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. Afterwards indeed he did justice to his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and discovered an unusual mark of respect and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to his queen, by abstaining from all connexion with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> after her death, which happened in 1455, and it has been supposed, was occasioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a>, administered by the enemies of her father. Alphonso aspired to the acquisition of military <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. In the year 1458, he made great preparations to attack the Moors in Barbary. He assembled an army of 20,000 men, and equipped a fleet of 200 sail. He first directed his arms against Alcazar, which soon fell into his hands; and to maintain the footing which he had gained, he furnished this place with a strong garrison. For 12 years he prosecuted the war in Barbary with various success, in that time reduced Arzila and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANGIER">Tangier</a>, and in 1740, returned to Portugal loaded with honours. It was then he obtained the surname of African, and to the titles which he derived from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, added that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the coasts on both seas. And with a view to perpetuate the memory of these exploits and conquests, he caused a representation of them to be wrought in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, a monument purely constructed of very frail materials, but not less durable than many which have been erected by ambition and vanity. During the war in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, a military order denominated the knights of the sword was founded. Alphonso was less successful in supporting the claim of his niece Donna Joanna to the crown of Castile against Ferdinand and Isabella. Finding his own resources unequal to the contest in which he was engaged, he took a journey to France to solicit the aid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> XI. But his solicitations proved fruitless; and the mortification which he experienced from this faithless monarch, filled him with melancholy, and induced him to resign his crown for the purpose of making a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. The administration of affairs during his absence, was committed to the hands of his son Don Juan, who governed the kingdom with great ability. When the king returned, he was joyfully received by the prince, and reinstated in his authority. But the mind of Alphonso had lost its wonted vigour, and was unfit to resume the arduous duties of government. Oppressed still with a deep melancholy, he determined at length to withdraw from the cares of a kingdom, and to end his days in the repose and quiet of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. But on his journey to the place of his retirement, he was seized with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> at Cintra, where he died in the year 1481, in the 43rd year of his reign, and the 49th of his age. The moderation, the wisdom and prudence which this prince exhibited in his public conduct, were not more powerful in conciliating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and veneration of his subjects, and of all good men, than were the amiable virtues of his private character. He was distinguished for his affability and condescension, his benevolence and bounty, and especially for his unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of this latter virtue, he was honoured with the title of redeemer of the captives, in consequence of his having procured the freedom of many prisoners, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> he cheerfully paid. Nor was he less eminent for his chastity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, his attachment to letters, and his love and encouragement of learning. The first library in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the kings of Portugal was founded in his time. He established and vindicated against the pretensions and hostile attempts of the Spaniards, a very profitable trade on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, which country was discovered during his reign, under the auspices of his uncle Don Henry, a celebrated character of that age. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) **Alphonso VI. Don Enriques**, king of Portugal, ascended the throne when only a child of thirteen years of age. It is not easy to conceive a kingdom in a more perilous situation than this at the death of Don John. The young king was remarkable for weakness of body, and imbecility of mind; the regency in the hands of a woman, and that woman a Castilian; the nation involved in war, and this reflecting the title to the crown; many of the nobility engaged in feuds and contentions with each other, and some of them secretly disaffected to the reigning family; so that the queen scarcely knew to whom she could trust, or by whom she was to be obeyed. A very indecent joy was manifested by the people on the king's death, as if his death was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of government: but the great abilities of the queen, and the vigorous measures which she adopted, soon changed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of affairs. For her own safety, and the prosperity of the kingdom, she appointed Don Francisco de <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARO">Faro</a>, count of Odemira, of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAGANZA">Braganza</a>, governor to the king, and one of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ministers of state; and she made choice of Don Antonio de Meneses, count de Caltenheda, to be his coadjutor. The former was a person in high repute among the nobility, in great favour with the people, entirely devoted to the interests of the queen, possessed of a large estate, and far advanced in years; the latter was also an aged man of great talents, and equally capable to preside in the cabinet, and to command in the field. As might naturally be expected, these men sometimes differed in opinion; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> never hurt the cause of the queen. Seconded, protected, and counselled by such able men, the nation began to feel the effects of the queen's firmness and superior talents. The first important exertion of the queen was, to Alphonso send express orders to the count de San Lorenzo, who commanded on the frontiers, to act offensively; but the measure, though prudent in itself, was not attended with the desired success. About this time, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de St Germain, an Italian officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Spain, entered Portugal, besieged and took Olivenza and the castle of Moran. In consequence of this, the general was dismissed, and his place was filled by Juan Mendez Valencelles, a man in great favour with the troops, and universally popular. He engaged to act also upon the offensive, but being unsuccessful, he was only saved from punishment by his simple and candid defence; in which he says, "that he had undertaken the siege in obedience to the order of the queen, and for the honour of the nation; and that he had raised it without orders, for the preservation of the army: that he knew the hazard he ran when he did it, but that it gave him pleasure to think, that at the hazard, or even the loss, of his reputation and life, the troops of Portugal had been saved." He was declared innocent and worthy of the queen's favour, by the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of war who presided. Don Sancho Manuel, who commanded in Elvas, and defended it with equal bravery and conduct, shewed himself to be an officer of considerable degree of judgment, by his hazarding nothing more when he had performed his service, upon which the very being of the state depended; but it was the count de Caftanheira who raised that siege, and forced the army of Spain in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. After some other political measures, some of them more, and some of them less important; the queen regent finished in a manner, her administration, with the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of her only daughter, the princess Catharine, once intended for Lewis XIV. with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. king of Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, one of the most fortunate events that ever happened for Portugal; since it immediately procured them the protection of the English fleets, reinforcements of some thousands of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> and foot; besides adding much reputation to their affairs throughout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; which was the reason that the Spanish court opposed it with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, or rather, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. By the vigorous exertions and fortunate victories of Montefelos, the war was soon terminated to the honour of Portugal. The fifth and last victory in the course of 28 years, was obtained by the Marquis de Marialva, which was chiefly owing to unforeseen accidents, and the determined courage of foreign troops, and to the great abilities of Schomberg. This victory determined the fate of the kingdom, though not of the sovereign; and it was easy to be seen by the more intelligent sort of people in Portugal, that the king would sooner or later be depoed. Alphonso being struck with the palsy while a child, rendered it necessary to treat him with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>, on account of his weak state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>; consequently, as he rose to maturity, his want of parts, and the defects in his education, were very perceptible. It is alleged that a greater affection was thrown by the queen his mother, to the infant Don Pedro, and that she endeavoured at the time of their father's decease, to infuse into the nobles an idea of preferring him; but they universally declined to make a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> in the succession, declaring it was difficult to make an estimate of the powers of a king who was then only a child. The queen yielded, and endeavoured by every proper means to make him worthy of a crown, which, by birth, he was entitled to wear. The count de Odenira, who was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with his education, found it a very difficult task to manage the young prince, who, forgetful of his birth and destination, was prone only to those amusements which the youth of his age were accustomed to. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> and preceptor struggled with this disposition, and even ventured to take some pretty severe measures; but to his great mortification, it proved entirely abortive. Education can only improve, but can never confer mental abilities. Yet he was quick enough to perceive he was a king, which proved very fatal to him. Those who approached his person complied with his follies, and, even commended the most absurd actions; and those who were independent of the court inveighed against him in the strongest terms, and, because guilty of some childish actions, they ascribed to him all the cruel and foolish accidents which happened in Lisbon. Unfortunately, however, for his adversaries, many of these actions, such as fighting of dogs, scouring the streets, encountering three men alone, running at a bull, and such like, indicate no want of strength or courage. A variety of facts that might be mentioned, are sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that his natural dispositions were weak, wild, refractory, and unteachable; and that although he was born to reign, yet he was destitute of the qualities absolutely necessary in a prince. The direful consequences of this having been for some time experienced by the nation, the nobles at last were driven to the revolution of deposing the king, and exalting Don Pedro to the regency. In the morning of the next day after the determination, the marquis de Calcaes, at the head of the council, went to the palace to propose the resignation to the king. The king was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> and fast asleep; the marquis ordered him to be awakened, and knocked violently at the door for that purpose; and when he had obtained admission, he is said to have upbraided him in very coarse terms for his laziness and inattention to public affairs at so critical a conjuncture; adding, that since he must be sensible of his want of abilities to govern a kingdom, the wisest method he could adopt was, to resign it in favour of his brother. The king absolutely refused to consent, but not long after, Don Pedro coming to the palace, ordered him to be confined in his apartment, where one of his favourites persuaded him, in the hope of being set at liberty, to make a short renunciation of the crown in favour of his brother Don Pedro, and his lawful issue, referring the house of Braganza and its dependencies, together with 100,000 crowns out of the revenue of the crown. Nor was this deemed sufficient: for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> was presented to him, making him avow, that for want of consummation, his marriage was null. This he at first declined; but, by the advice of some divines, he was prevailed on to subscribe the deed. When evening drew on, the unhappy king then perceived he was a prisoner; upon which he sent to request his brother to let him have John, who managed his dog-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a>, to keep him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>. When Don Pedro heard it, losing his usual calmness, he burst into a violent fit of passion, and instantly gave orders, that those who were the most agreeable to him, should remain in his apartment. Such was the situation of affairs until the meeting of the States. But in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, the unfortunate Don Alonzo died, after he had been a prisoner near fifteen years, suddenly in the castle of Cintra, on the 12th of September, when he had borne the title of king almost twenty-seven, and had lived about forty years. It is reported, that he said in his last agonies, "I am now going; but it will not be long before the queen shall follow me, to give an account, at the most awful tribunal, of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a> she has done me." (Mod. Univ. Hist.) Alphonso III. the Great, king of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTURIAS">Asturias</a>, was born in 847, and succeeded his father Ordoño in 865. In consequence of the rebellion of Don Froila, not long after his accession to the throne, he was forced to leave his kingdom; but that usurper being affianced, with universal applause he returned to his throne. In many successful enterprises against the Moors, in which he greatly enlarged his territories, he soon displayed the talents of a warlike and able prince. He formed a powerful alliance against the Moors, by marrying Ximene or Chimene, descended from the house of Navarre, which paved the way for a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of victories. The great attention which he paid to the comfort and welfare of the common people, greatly disgusted his haughty nobles; which excited them to revolt against him in the advanced part of his life. Enjoying a small <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of tranquility from the distraction and tumults of war, he called a general council of the clergy and nobility, enacted some useful regulations, and directed their attention to several other subjects, which contributed to the honour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his kingdom. Whilst he was busily occupied in repairing some of those <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> which he had taken from the Moors, he was suddenly interrupted by them, and was under the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of defending himself with a considerable army, which he did with such success, that they were defeated with great loss. The unnatural rebellion of his son Don Garcias, at this time, greatly disturbed his government; but by the diligence of the father, this unnatural rebellion was soon quelled. The confinement of Garcias, and the new imposition of taxes, produced general murmurs among the people; which induced Alphonso, now worn out with years and incessant contentions, to assemble the states, and resign the reins of government into the hands of his son Don Garcias. He gave to his other son Don Ordoño the province of Galicia. The ambitious and military spirit which Don Garcias discovered in his father's reign, soon displayed itself in an attack on the Moors. By the advice of his father, to which he prudently listened, he was taught that these new conquests tended more to enrich the soldiers, than to the advantage of the crown. Alphonso, although far advanced in years, took upon himself the command of the army raised for new operations, and returned to Zamora loaded with spoils, and with increased reputation and fame, in the year 912. He died <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 20th, 912, two years after his abdication, 49 years from the time of his being associated with his father in the government, and when he was about 63 or 65 years of age. His great learning, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> he gave to literature, his distinguished piety and virtue, and other princely qualities, raised this king high in the estimation of mankind. Some writers affirm that he composed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> of the Spanish affairs, from the death of Receifuintho, to that of his own father Don Ordoño, which has been incorrectly published by Sandovel, Alphonso, and the later editions has sustained considerable injury. The bishop of Orenfa, at whose request it was originally composed, published it in his own name to the world. (Gen. Biog.) Alphonso X the Wise, king of Leon and Castile, succeeded his father Ferdinand in the year 1252. He obtained the appellation of wise, not for his political knowledge as a king, but his erudition as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. In consequence of the general opinion of his princely qualities, and his uncommon generosity, he ascended the throne with universal approbation. The ill-concerted projects of his ambition, however, disturbed the prosperity of his reign. Pretending a better right than Henry III of England to that territory, he directed his first attempt against Gascony. The arms of England, however, proved too formidable; and he was compelled to renounce his claim, on condition that Henry's son, afterwards King Edward I, should marry his sister Eleonora. At an expense which drained his treasuries, and obliged him to debauch his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, he prepared for an expedition against the Moors in Barbary; but his maternal right to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Swabia, which he was called to defend, diverted him from it. Thus he formed a connexion with the German princes; and became a competitor, with Richard earl of Cornwall, for the imperial crown, in quest of which they both expended immense sums of money. The claims of several of the princes of the blood, gave exercise to his military talents; and he was successful both in opposing and defeating them. He formed the romantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of visiting Italy in the year 1268; but the states firmly remonstrating, he was obliged to relinquish it. But, although he abandoned the design, yet it produced such discontentments both among the common people and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> among the nobles, that it required considerable exertion before the king could allay the ferment. Alphonso, still anxious of ascending the imperial throne, attempted it after the death of Richard earl of Cornwall, and even after Rodolph of Hapsburg was actually elected emperor of Germany, and for that purpose took a journey to Beaucaire to obtain an interview with the pope, in order to prevent him from confirming the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. The Moors, ever ready to draw the sword against him, took this opportunity of entering his dominions for the purpose of ravaging them. This ambitious journey, undertaken at so vast an expense, and productive of so much confusion in his kingdom, proved unsuccessful; for the pope would not realize his claim, or alter the former election. But his excessive ambition was soon punished by domestic calamity; for his eldest son died in this interval, and his second son Don Sanchez, having obtained great reputation in opposing the infidels, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of his brother's children, laid claim to the crown. This claim was admitted by the states of the kingdom; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> king of France, supporting the cause of the children, whose mother was his sister Blanche of France, involved Alphonso in a war; and it occasioned the retreat of his own queen Yolande or Violante to the court of her father, the king of Arragon. While thus harassed with dissensions, he proclaimed war against France, and by the authority of the pope he renewed the war with the Moors, which proved to unfortunate, that he reluctantly concluded a truce with them, and engaged in a contest Alphonso, with the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>. These various measures exhausted his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, taxes were multiplied, and the affairs of the kingdom were in such confusion, that he was under the disagreeable necessity of calling an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the states, which was held at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVILLE">Seville</a> in the year 1281, where, on the king's proposal, the states consented to give a currency to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> money. In consequence of the intrigues of Don Sanchez his son, another assembly of the states was held at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a> A.D. 1282, which deprived Alphonso of the regal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and appointed Sanchez regent. Reduced to almost insurmountable difficulties, Alphonso solemnly cursed and disinherited his son, and by his last will, in the year 1283, confirmed the act of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>, and appointed, for the succession, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> de la Cerda, and upon the failure of their heirs the kings of France; and at the same time supplicated the affiance of the king of Morocco against the power of his son. At the commencement of the next year, when Alphonso received information, from <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, that Sanchez was dangerously ill, his heart relented. He pardoned his son, revoked his curses, and then died on the 4th of April 1284 in the 81st year of his age. His remains were interred in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of Seville; and he left behind him the character of a learned man, but a weak king. Alphonso has been charged with irreligion and impiety, chiefly on account of a well-known saying of his, viz., "if he had been of God's privy-council when he created the world he could have advised him better." The various contradictory accounts, given by different writers render the truth of this doubtful; but if ever such a horrible saying dropt from his lips, it must unquestionably be declared inconsistent with the character of an enlightened philosopher; and that reverence of the Creator, which an enlarged <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of his works naturally inspires. "An indecent astronomer is mad," Young. He was an eminent proficient in science, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of literature. He concluded that book of laws, known by the title of Las Partidas, which his father had begun; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> displayed the abilities of a politician as well as those of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. By obliging his subjects to use their own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he redressed the confusion in law proceedings occasioned by intermixing Latin with the vulgar tongue. Under his patronage a general <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Spain was composed, which he took great pains in polishing; he also corrected many errors in the statutes of the university of Salamanca. <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> being his favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, he chiefly directed his attention to the improvement of that science; so that, even during the life of his father, he assembled at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a> a number of the most celebrated astronomers of his time, Christians, Jews, and Arabs, from all parts of Europe, for the purpose of examining the astronomical tables of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, and correcting their errors. The completion of these tables employed them about four years, and in 1252, the first year of Alphonso's reign, they were completed; and they were called Alphonso Tables from the name of this prince, who encouraged the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of them by his unbounded liberality. It is reported that 400,000 ducats were expended on them, or, according to others, 40,000. Some have ascribed the principal management of this work to the Jewish Rabbi <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Aben-Said; others, pretending to derive information from the MSS. of Alphonso, refer it to Aben-Ragée and Alcabitius. The other astronomers who were employed on this occasion were Aben-Mufa Mohammed, Joseph Ben-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Abuena, Arabians: if there were any Christians, their names are unknown. The 30th of May 1252, which was the day of his accession to the throne, was fixed as the epoch of these tables. A book, entitled "The Treasure," is also ascribed to him, containing treatises of rational <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, physics, and ethics. He is likewise said to have been well acquainted with astrology and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>; in which last science, he is said to have compiled two volumes in cipher, which are extant, and to be found full in his Catholic Majesty's library. But this work must be more curious than useful, if we consider the state of this science at that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. (Gen. Biog.) Alphonso V. king of Arragon and Naples, succeeded his father in the year 1416. As the father had formerly been honoured with the appellation of Just, so the son was honoured with that of Magnanimous. The conspiracy of some of his own nobles against his life, together with the insolence of Pope Benedict XIII., greatly disturbed the tranquillity of his reign. Fortunately this conspiracy was discovered just when it was about to be carried into execution; and instead of proceeding with rigour against the conspirators, he generously tore a paper containing their names without <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a> it, and added, "that he would at least force them to acknowledge, that he had a greater regard for their lives than they had for his." After quelling a disturbance in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, he was just making preparations to advance to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, when Joan of Naples offered, if he would assist her against the pope, the duke of Anjou, and the comte Sforza, who had formed a confederacy to depose her, to adopt him as her son and heir. He readily accepted the proposal, and with a powerful army soon raised the siege of Naples, and was immediately declared heir apparent of her kingdom, and duke of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. But as the queen was unfaithful, and did not fulfil her engagements, Alphonso took possession of Naples, and expelled her from it; but when the duke of Anjou again entered her territories, and made himself master of great part of them, she was obliged to renew her solicitations to Alphonso; who, in the year 1434, involved himself in a quarrel with the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> and the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, by besieging <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a> in a second attempt to conquer Naples. The Genoese fleet engaged Alphonso; and all his ships were dispersed or destroyed, and himself taken prisoner. But such was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> of this prince, that when carried to Milan a prisoner, he there ingratiated himself to much into the duke's favour, that he became his friend and ally, and soon rose to greater power than formerly. He got possession of Naples in 1443; and in an assembly of the states held at Beneventum, and then transferred to Naples, his sovereignty was recognized, and his son, Don Ferdinand, declared successor to the throne, and in consequence of this elevation he was deemed the sole arbiter of peace and war through all Italy. Naples became the residence of Alphonso during the remainder of his life; but his declining years were much disquieted by political dissensions and intrigues. The natural attendant of jealous old age at Alphonso last feigned him; and in conformation and dread, he was removed from one castle of Naples to another, until he breathed his last on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1468, bequeathing to his natural son Ferdinand the kingdom of Naples, and to his brother Don Juan, king of Navarre, the kingdoms of Arragon, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, Sardinia, Sicily, and the principality and dependencies of Catalonia. Alphonso was not only deemed the ablest statesman, and the most renowned military commander in that age, but also the greatest prince that ever occupied the throne of Arragon. He was a distinguished patron of learning, and opened an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for the Greek literati expelled from Constantinople. His device was an open book. He frequently uttered this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, "That an unlettered prince was but a crowned ass." He was brave and liberal; and in all his negotiations he disdained the mean arts of intrigue and dissimulation. It is reported that his personal Quintus Curtius cured him of a disorder with which he was attacked at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>. Such was his familiar intercourse with his subjects, and his affection towards them, that he walked unarmed and unaccompanied in his capital; and was wont to say, "that a father has nothing to fear in the midst of his children." While he was besieging Gaeta he dismissed the women and children that were turned out of the town without any injury, saying, "That he had rather lose any city in his dominions than lose the reputation of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>." He leaped into a shallop for the relief of one of his galleys, which with its whole crew and soldiers was just about to perish, exclaiming, "I had rather share than witness their calamity." Such was his generosity, that upon hearing an officer who saw his treasure bringing him 10,000 ducats, exclaiming, "I should only with that sum to make me happy." "You shall be so," said Alphonso, and gave him the money in a present. He deemed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> a certain degree of madness; but was strongly addicted to women, which involved him in many dishonourable intrigues, and justly entailed upon him the disgrace of an unfaithful husband to a kind and affectionate queen. (Mod. Univ. Hist.)

ALPHONSUS TOSTATUS

Pages 367-367

bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVILA">Avila</a>, a learned and voluminous Spanish writer. He flourished about the middle of the 15th century, and by his uncommon abilities rose to the highest offices both in the civil and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> departments of the state. At the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 22 years he finished his studies at the university of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, having made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in every branch of learning then in estimation. He was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, and was afterwards promoted to the bishopric of Avila. He died at the age of 40 years, in 1454, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Avila. The following epitaph, expressive of his great erudition, was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> on his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>. Hie stupor est mundi qui scibile discebit omne. "This is the wonder of the world who treated of everything that could be known." The numerous productions of Alphonsus are sufficient proofs of his laborious industry: during his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he wrote no less than 27 volumes in folio, of which 24 are commentaries on the Scriptures; the rest are on theological subjects. By the order of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Ximenes they were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1530, and in 1596; and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a> in 1612. Several of his pieces on ecclesiastical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, science, and literature in general, were separately printed at Salamanca in 1560, and also his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> upon the Chronicon of Eusebius. Although <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> encomiums have been bestowed upon his works, they have nevertheless in the current of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> improvement fallen into oblivion. (Dupin.)

ALPINI

Pages 367-368

PROSPERO, in Latin, Prosper Alpinus, a celebrated physician and botanist, was born at Marofica in the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in November 1553. In his early years his inclination led him to the profession of arms, and he served some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the Milanese. By the encouragement and persuasion of his father, who was a physician, he retired from the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to literature. To prosecute his studies with more advantage, he went to the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, where he was soon after elected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the rector and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNDIC">syndic</a> to the students. But in the discharge of his official duties which was distinguished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, he was not prevented from pursuing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of physic which he had chosen. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his medical studies with zeal and success; and after having acquired the necessary qualifications, he was admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine in 1578. Soon after he left the university, and settled as a physician in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of an invitation from the citizens in Campo San Pietro, a small town in the Paduan territory. In the course of his studies he had paid particular attention to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and had become an enthusiast in botanical science. The sphere of his present practice was too limited to afford him much opportunity of prosecuting his favourite study. He wished particularly to extend his knowledge of exotic plants; and the only means to attain this, he thought, was to study their economy and habits in their native <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. And to gratify this laudable curiosity an opportunity soon presented itself. George Emo, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> for the Venetian republic in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, appointed Alpini his physician. They sailed from Venice in September 1580; and after having experienced a tedious and dangerous voyage, arrived at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a> in the beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> the following year. Alpini spent three years in Egypt, and by his industry and assiduity, greatly improved his botanical knowledge. With this view he travelled along the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>, visited every <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and consulted every person from whom he expected any new information. From a practice in the management of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> trees which he observed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, Alpini seems to have deduced the doctrine of the sexual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of plants which was adopted as the foundation of the celebrated system of Linnaeus. He says, "That the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> date trees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> palms, do not bear fruit, unless the branches of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and female plants are mixed together; or, as is generally done, unless the dust found in the male sheath, or male <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, is sprinkled over the female flowers." When Alpini returned to Venice in 1586 he was appointed physician to Andrea Doria <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Melfi, and during his residence at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, acquired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> a name as to be esteemed the first physician of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. The Venetians became jealous that the Genoese state should <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> among its citizens a person of such distinguished merit and reputation, whose services might be: Alpini be essentially beneficial, and whose fame might be highly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> to his native country. In the year 1593, he was recalled to fill the botanical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> in the university of Padua, with a salary of 200 florins, which was afterwards augmented to 750. He discharged the duties of his professorship for many years with great reputation, till his declining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> interrupted his labours. He died in the year 1617, in the 64th year of his age, and was succeeded as botanical professor by one of his sons. Alpini wrote the following works in Latin: 1. *De Medicina Ægyptiorum, libri iv.* "Of the Physic of the Egyptians, in four books;" printed at Venice, 1591, in 4to. 2. *De Plantis Ægypti liber:* "A treatise concerning the plants of Egypt;" printed at Venice, 1592, in 4to. 3. *De Balsamo Dialogus:* "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a> concerning the Balm of Gilead;" printed at Venice, 1529, in 4to. 4. *De Praefagienda vita et morte ægrotantium libri vii:* "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> books concerning the method of forming a judgment of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of patients;" printed at Venice, 1601, in 4to. 5. *De Medicina medica,* libri xiii: "Thirteen books concerning methodical Physic." Padua, 1611, folio; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>, 1719, in 4to. 6. *De Rhapontico Disputatione:* "A disputation held in the school at Padua concerning the Rhaponticum;" Padua, 1612, and 1629, in 4to. 7. *De Plantis Exoticis, libri ii:* "Of exotic plants, in two books;" Venice, 1699, in 4to. He left several other works, which have never been printed; particularly, 8. The fifth book concerning the physic of the Egyptians. 9. Five books concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of things observed in Egypt, adorned with figures of plants, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and animals. (Biog. Diet.) ALPINIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ALPINUS. See Alpini.

ALPISTE

Pages 368-368
or ALPIA, a sort of feed used to feed birds with, especially when they are to be nourished for breeding. The alpiste seed is of an oval figure, of a pale yellow, inclining to an Isabel colour, bright and glossy. It is an article of the corn-chandlers and seedmen's trade.

ALPS

Pages 368-371

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a range of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, separating <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> and Germany, in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a>. They take their rise from the Vada Sabatia, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVONA">Savona</a>; and reach to the Sinus Flavianicus (now Golfo di Carnaro of the Adriatic), and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the river Colapis (now the Kulpe); extending, according to Livy, 2000 stadia in length, or 250 miles: they are divided into several parts, and accordingly have different names. From Savona to the springs of the Varus, where the Alps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, they are called Maritima, now le Montagne di Tenda. These extend from south to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, between Gaul to the west, and Genoa to the east, beginning at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONACO">Monaco</a> on the Mediterranean; then running out through the east of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Nice, and between that and the marquisate of Saluzzo, terminate at length at Mount Vilo, between Dauphiné and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. Hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSA">Susa</a> run the Alpes Cottiae (Sueton.) Cotane (Tacitus); mountains extremely high, separating Dauphiné from Piedmont, and extending from Mount Vilo to Mount Cenis, between the Alpes Maritimae to the south, and the Graiae to the north. The Alpes Graiae (Pliny), so called from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, begin from Mount Cenis, where the Cottiae terminate; and run out between Savoy and the Tarentese to the west, and Piedmont and the Duché d'Aouife to the east, quite to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> St Bernard, where the Alpes Pennine begin. They are also called by some Graiae Alpes, and Graiae Mons (Tacitus); which extend from west to east, between St Bernard and the Adula, or St Gothard; and thus they run out between the Valais to the north, and the Milanese to the south. With these are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the Alpes Rhaetiae, to the head of the river Piave; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of which are the Alpes Tridentinae, to the north of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>. To these join the Alpes Noricae, reaching to Doblach in Tyrol, to the north of the river Tajamento: thence begin the Alpes Carnicae, or of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARNIOLA">Carniola</a>, extending to the springs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">Save</a>: and the last, called Alpes Pannonicae, and Julie, extend to the springs of the Kulpe. Some, however, extend the Alps to the north of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>; others, again, to Thrace and the Euxine. But their termination at the Kulpe, as above, is more generally received. They were formerly called Albia, and Alpionia (Strabo). Through these mountains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> forced his passage into Italy, by pouring <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a> on the rocks, heated by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> piles of wood on them, by which means they became crumbled, (Livy). They are covered with perpetual snow. The Alps are the highest mountains in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; being, according to some geometricians, about two miles in perpendicular height. They begin at the Mediterranean; and stretching northward, separate Piedmont and Savoy from the adjacent countries; whence directing their course to the east, they form the boundary between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and Italy, and terminate near the extremity of the Adriatic sea, north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. It was over the western part of those mountains, towards Piedmont, that Hannibal forced his passage into Italy. The prospect from many parts of this enormous range of mountains is extremely romantic, especially towards the north-west. One of the most celebrated is the Grande <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARTREUSE">Chartreuse</a>, where is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> founded by St Bruno about the year 1084. From Echelles, a little village in the mountains of Savoy, to the top of the Chartreuse, the distance is six miles. Along this course, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> runs winding up, for the most part not five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. On one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> is the rock, with woods of pine trees hanging over head; on the other a prodigious precipice almost perpendicular; at the bottom of which rolls a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a>, that sometimes tumbling among the fragments of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> which have fallen from on high, and sometimes precipitating itself <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> vast descents with a noise like <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, rendered yet more tremendous by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECHO">echo</a> from the mountains on each side, concurs to form one of the most solemn, the most romantic, and most astonishing scenes in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. To this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> may be added the strange views made by the crags and cliffs, and the numerous cascades which throw themselves from the very summit down into the vale. On the top of the mountain is the convent of St Bruno, which is the superior of the whole order. The inhabitants consist of 100 fathers, with 300 servants, who grind their corn, press their wine, and perform every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> office, even to the making of their clothes. In the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBUM">Album</a> of the fathers is an admired alcaic ode, written by the late ingenious Mr Gray when he visited the Chartreuse, and which has since been published among his works. The glaciers of Savoy are also justly reckoned among the the most stupendous works of nature. These are immense masses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, lodged upon the gentler declivities amidst the Alps, and exhibiting representations beyond <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> fantastic and picturesque. In the extraordinary narrative of M. Bourrit's journey hither, we meet with the following account of the Prieuré, in the valley of Chamouni. "We had (says he) the magnificent prospect of a chain of mountains, equally inaccessible, and covered with ice; and above the rest that of Mount Blanc, whose top seemed to reach, and even pierce, the highest region of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>. The chain upon which this mountain looks down like a giant, is composed of masses of rocks, which terminate in pikes or spires, called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a>, and which are ranged like tents in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>. Their sides appear <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> and more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIRY">airy</a>, from the ornament of several hollow breaks and furrows fretted in the rock itself, as well as from the different streaks and panes of ice and snow, which, without changing the general character of their form, or the majesty of their appearance, give them a picturesque variety. Lower down, the eye surveys with ravishment the gills of ice, and the several glaciers, extending almost into the plain, whilst this appears like an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> garden, embellished with the mixture of a variety of colours. We have a picturesque opposition to this chain, which is formed by innumerable mountains at the distance of near 50 leagues, between whose tops we have a glimpse of those several plains which they environ." M. de Saufure, who had visited those mountains about two months before M. Bourrit, felt himself naturally electrified in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. This extraordinary phenomenon seems not to have been experienced by the latter or his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; but they heard a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>-continued rumbling noise like that of thunder, which was rendered more awful by the silence of the place where they stood. This noise proceeded from the subsequent causes, viz. the avalanches of snow, which separated from the tops of the mountains, and rolled down to the bottom; considerable fragments of the rocks which followed them, overturning others in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; and muddy blocks of ice, which precipitated from the summits. The valley of Montanvert appears to be peculiarly romantic. "Here (says M. Bourrit) we behold a spacious icy plain entirely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. Upon this there rose a mountain all of ice, with steps ascending to the top, which seemed the throne of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. It likewise took the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> facade, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> was beyond conception beautiful; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which shone upon it, gave a sparkling brilliance to the whole. The valley on our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand was ornamented with prodigious glaciers, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> up to an immeasurable height between the mountains, blend their colours with the skies, which they appear to reach." Alps, besides its proper signification, by which it denotes a certain chain of mountains which separate Italy from France and Germany, is frequently used as an appellative to denote any mountains of extraordinary height or extensive range. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, Aulonius and others call the Pyrenean mountains Alps; and Gellius the Spanish Alps, Alpini Hispani. Hence also we say, the British Alps, the Asiatic Alps, the Alps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. The Scottish Alps terminate in a most sublime and abrupt manner, at the great promontory, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTA">Alta</a> Ripa of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, the Ord or Aird, i.e. the Height of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a>. The upper part is covered with gloomy heath; the lower is a stupendous precipice, excavated into vast caverns, the haunt of seals and different sea fowl. On the eastern side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, this is the striking termination of the vast mountains of Scotland which form its Highlands, the habitation of the original inhabitants, driven from their ancient seats by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of Lowland Scots, descendants of Saxons, French, and Normans; congeners with the English, yet absurdly and invincibly distinguished from them. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">Language</a>, as well as striking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> boundaries, mark their place. Their mountains <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> on the west the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> along the west of Caithness; among which Morven and Scaraben, Ben Hop, and Ben Lugal, arise pre-eminent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUTHERLAND">Sutherland</a> is entirely alpine, as are Rossshire and Invernessshire. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">Summer</a> Alps are, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">Meal</a>-Fourvounich, the Corvarill, Benewich, and Benevich near Fort William; the last of which is reported to be 14,59 yards in height. Great part of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABERDEENSHIRE">Aberdeenshire</a> lies in this tract. It boasts of another Morven, roaring far beyond the others. This is the centre of the Grampian hills, and perhaps the highest from the sea of any in Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. They again comprehend the eastern part of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol6.html#article-PERTHSHIRE">Perthshire</a>, and finish on the magnificent shores of Lochlomond; on the western side of which Benlomond rises, distinguished among its fellows. From hence the rest of North Britain forms a chain of humbler hills; but in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, part of Westmorland, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, the Alps resume their former majesty. A long and tame <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> succeeds. The long sublime tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> arises, the ancient possession of the ancient British <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. From the Ord, the great mountains recede inland, and leave a vast flat between their bales and the sea, frouting the waves with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of lofty rocky precipices, as far as the little creek of Staxigo; the whole a bold, but most inhospitable shore for shipping. Wick and Staxigo have indeed their creeks, or rather chasms, which open between the cliffs, and may accidentally prove a retreat, unless in an eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALE">gale</a>. The Asiatic Alps are described under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> Altai Chain and Wentarian Mountains.
