The American Alps are, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a> or Cordilleras, in South America; and the Appalachian or Alleghany mountains in North America. The highest ground in North America is placed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Carver in lat 47° W. Long, from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> 68°, between a lake from which the Oregon flows, and another called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a>-bear Lake, from which arises the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. This exalted situation is part of the Shining Mountains, which are branches of the vast chain which pervades the whole continent of America. It may be fairly taken from the southern extremity, where Staten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">Land</a> and Terra del <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a> rise out of the sea as insulated links to an immense height, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, rocky, and marked with rugged spiny tops, frequently covered with snow. New <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a> may be added as another horribly congenial, rising detached farther to the east. The mountains about the straits of Magellan soar to an amazing height, and infinitely superior to those of the northern hemisphere under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude. From the north side of the straits of Magellan, Ian, they form a continued chain through the kingdoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, preserving a course not remote from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>. The summits, in many places, are the highest in the world. There are not less than 12, which are from 2400 toises high to above 3000. Pichincha, which impends over Quito, is about 35 leagues from the sea; and its summit is 2430 toises above the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. Cayambe, immediately under the equator, is above 3000; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIMBORAZO">Chimborazo</a> higher than the last by 200. Most of them have been volcanic, and in different ages marked with eruptions far more horrible than have been known in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the globe. They extend from the equator through Chili; in which kingdom is a range of volcanoes, from lat. 26. south, to 45. 30. and possibly from thence into Terra del Fuego itself; which, forming the straits of Magellan, may have been rent from the continent by some great convulsion, occasioned by their labours, and New Georgia forced up from the same cause. An unparalleled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of plain appears on their eastern side. The river of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMAZON">Amazon</a> runs along a level clothed with forests, after it bursts from its confinement at the Pongo de Berjas, till it reaches its sea-like discharge into the Atlantic ocean. In the northern hemisphere, the Andes pass through the narrow isthmus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> into the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, and preserve a majestic height and their volcanic disposition. The mountain Popocatepec made a violent eruption during the expedition of Cortez, which is most beautifully described by his historian Antonio de Solis. This is probably the same with the volcano observed by the Abbé d'Auteroche, in his way from Vera Cruz to Mexico; which, from the nakedness of the lavas, he conjectured to have been but lately extinguished. From the kingdom of Mexico, this chain is continued northward, and to the east of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>; then verges so greatly towards the west, as to leave a very inconsiderable space between it and the Pacific ocean; and frequently detached branches jut into the sea, and form promontories; which, with parts of the chain itself, were often seen by our navigators in the course of their voyage. Some branches, as we have before observed, extend towards the east, but not to any great distance. A plain, rich in woods and savannahs, swarming with bisons or buffaloes, flags, and Virginian deer, with bears, and a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>, occupies an amazing tract, from the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, as low as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of Mexico; and eastward to the other great chain of mountains, the Appalachian, which are the Alps of that side of northern America. Its commencement is supposed to be about Lake Champlain and Lake George, with branches pointing obliquely to the river St Lawrence eastward, and rising on its opposite coasts; others extending as far as <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-NOVA_SCOTIA">Nova Scotia</a>, but in their progress eastward diminish in height. The main chain passes through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEW_YORK">New <a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, where it is distinguished by the name of the Highlands, and lies within 40 miles of the Atlantic. From thence it recedes from the sea, in proportion as it advances southward; and near its extremity in South Carolina is 300 miles distant from the water. It consists of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> ridges divided by most enchanting valleys, and generally clothed with variety of woods. These ridges rise gradually from the east, one above the other, to the central; from which they gradually fall to the west, into the vast plains of the Mississippi. The middle ridge is of an enormous bulk and height. The whole extends in breadth about 70 miles; and in many places leaves great chasms for the discharge of the vast and numerous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which rise in the bottoms of the mountains, and empty themselves into the Atlantic ocean, after yielding a matchless <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> to the provinces they water. Beyond the branch of the Appalachian mountains called The Endless, is another of amazing extent, nearly as high as the mountains themselves. This plain (called the Upper Plains) is exceedingly rich land; begins at the Mohocks river; reaches to within a small distance of Lake <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ONTARIO">Ontario</a>; and to the westward forms part of the extensive plains of the Ohio, and reaches to an unknown distance beyond the Mississippi. Vast rivers take their rise, and fall to every point of the compass; into Lake Ontario, into Hudson's river, and into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> and Susquehanna. The tide of Hudson's river flows through its deep-worn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> far up, even to within a small distance of the head of the Delaware; which, after a furious course down a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, interrupted with rapids, meets the tide not very remote from its discharge into the ocean. Lower Alps, Department of, in France. This department is one of four into which the former Provence is divided. It is bounded on the north by the department of the Upper Alps; on the east by Piedmont, and the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">Maritime</a> Alps; on the south, by the department of the Var, and the northeast extremity of that of the Mouths of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a>; and on the west, by the departments of Vaucluse and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROME">Drome</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> town is Digne; its superficies is about 1,459,699 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> acres; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> 144,436 individuals. It is divided into five communal districts. Upper Alps, Department of. This department makes a part of Dauphiné, which contains three. It is bounded on the north by the departments of Mont Blanc and Isere; on the east by Piedmont; on the south, by the department of the Lower Alps; on the west, by that of the Drome, and part of that of Isere; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBRUN">Embrun</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town; its superficies is about 1,084,614 square acres; population 116,754 individuals. It is divided into three communal districts. Maritime Alps, Department of. This department is formed of the county of Nice. It is bounded on the north by the Apennines and the department of the Lower Alps; on the east, by the republic of Genoa; on the south, by the Mediterranean; and on the west, by the departments of the Var and Lower Alps: the principal town is Nice; its superficies is about 632,619 square acres; population 93,366 souls. It is divided into three communal districts. Alpujarras, or Alpaxares, mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the province of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the Mediterranean sea. They are about 17 leagues in length and 11 in breadth, reaching from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Velez to <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMERIA">Almeria</a>. They are inhabited by Moors, who are the remains of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> and ruin of their empire. They embraced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; but preserve their own manner of living, and their language, though much corrupted. Here is a rivulet between Pitros Pitros and Portugos, which dyes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> that is dipped in it black in an instant. Near this rivulet is a cavern, from which proceeds so malignant a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, that it destroys such animals as come near it. The Morifcos cultivate the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> extremely well, and plant fruit trees; some of which grow to a prodigious height and thickness, and give the mountains a very agreeable aspect.

ALQUIER

Pages 371-371

a liquid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a> to measure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, two of which make an almond. See ALMOND.

ALQUIFOU

Pages 371-371
or ARQUIFOU, is a sort of lead ore, which, when broken, looks like antimony. It is used by the potters to give a green varnish to their works, and thence is called potters ore. It is met with in Cornwall, &c. The potters mix a small portion of manganese with the alquifou, and then the varnish or glazing on their ware is of a blackish hue.

ALREDUS

Pages 371-371

ALURED, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ALREDUS, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEVERLEY">Beverley</a>, one of the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English historians, was born at Beverley in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>. He wrote in the reign of Henry I. There are no circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> known with any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of certainty. It is generally believed that he was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, and that he afterwards became one of the canons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of St John's at Beverley. And we learn in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> of Bishop Tanner's, that, for the sake of improvement, he travelled through France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and at Rome became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> chaplain to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Othoboni. He died in the year 1128 or 1129, leaving behind him the following works: 1. The Annals of Alured of Beverley; which was published at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1716, by Mr Hearne, from a manuscript which belonged to Thomas Rawlinson, Esq. It contains an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> from Brutus to Henry I., written in Latin, and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> accuracy, elegance, and perspicuity. 2. Libertates ecclesiae S. Johannis de Beverlac, &c. a manuscript in the Cottonian library. It is a collection of records relative to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Beverley, translated from the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. These are the only works which were written by Alredus. (Biog. Dict.)

ALRESFORD

Pages 371-371

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> to Southampton, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> by the river Itching, which feeds a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pond to the left of the town. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> of a Roman highway runs from hence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>. It consists of about 200 houses; has one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> streets, which are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and has a small manufacture of linens. It is 57 miles distant from London.

ALSACE

Pages 371-372

formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of France, bounded on the east by the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, on the west by Lorraine, and on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of the Rhine. It was formerly a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Germany, but was given to France by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of Münster. It is one of the most fruitful and plentiful provinces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, abounding in corn, wine, wood, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which divide it from Lorraine are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and generally covered with fir, beech, oak, and hornbeam. Those on the side of Switzerland are less high; and are furnished with all sorts of wood, as well for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a> as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> itself is diversified with rising hills and fertile vales, besides <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> forests; but that between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Ill, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HART">Hart</a>, and the Rhine, as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, is inferior to the rest, on account of the frequent overflowing of the Rhine. In High Alsace there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of silver, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. They however <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> none but those of Giromany, from which are annually drawn 1600 marks of silver, each mark being eight ounces; and 24,000 pounds of copper; but the expense of working them is almost equal to the profit. There are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> works in several parts of Alsace, and particularly at Betzendorf. There is a mineral <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> at Sulzbach, near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, in High Alsace; which is in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation for the palsy, weakness of the nerves, and the gravel.—The original inhabitants of Alsace are honest and good natured, but wedded to their own manners and customs. The fruitfulness of their country renders them indolent and inactive; for the Swiss make their hay and reap their corn, as well as manage the vintage of High Alsace, which sends a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> out of the province. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is the German; but the better sort of people in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> speak French; and, even in the country, they speak French well enough to be understood. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants was formerly computed at about half a million, who are mostly Lutherans and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. By the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of France this province forms two departments, viz. those of the Upper and Lower Rhine; the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the former being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLMAR">Colmar</a>, and that of the latter Strasbourg; but formerly it was divided into Upper and Lower Alsace, the former contained 32 large and small towns, and the latter 39, and in both there are upwards of 1000 market towns and villages. The Rauraci, Sequani, and Mediomatrici, were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitants of this province. Under the Merovingian kings its name first occurs in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of France, and it most probably is derived from the river Ill <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ill, the inhabitants on the borders of which were called Elsassen, from whom the country itself was afterwards denominated Elsass, in Latin Elsafia, Alsfatia, and Alsatia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> wrested it from the Celts; from them it passed into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Germans; and after the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Tolbiac, gained by Clovis in 496, it passed into the possession of the Franks. It was incorporated at a future <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Austrasia; and, in 1752, it was subjected, like the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, to the laws of Pepin and his successors. Lotharius, the eldest son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Debonnaire, at the decease of his father in 840, obtained it and united it to that part of the empire of the Franks which fell to him, and was generally known by the name of Lotharingia, or Lorraine. Afterwards it fell to his youngest son Lotharius by inheritance; and after him, in 869, it became a province of Germany, and was governed by dukes. About a century before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of dukes was abolished, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> counts who governed under them in Alsace, assumed the title of Landgraver, and the countries over which they presided, obtained the name of Landgravate, the one superior and the other inferior. The best part of the inferior was conveyed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of Strasbourg in 1375, who assumed the title title of Landgrave of Alsace. In after times, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was given by the emperors to several families, until at last Ferdinand I. bestowed it upon the German line of his own family, and consequently it remained in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the town of Brisac, the landgrave of the Upper and Lower Alsace, Sundgau, and the districts of the ten united imperial cities in Alsace, with the whole sovereignty belonging to them, was for ever ceded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of France, at the peace of Munster in 1648. The perpetual sovereignty of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Strasbourg, together with all its dependencies on the left of the Rhine, were ceded to France by the peace of Ryswick in 1697.

ALSEN

Pages 372-372

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, situated in the Lefter Belt, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entrance into the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, between Sleiwick and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNEN">Funen</a>, 100 miles west of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>. It extends in length six leagues, and about two in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile, producing abundance of fruit and variety of grain, with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> crops of aniseeds, a carminative much used in feasting the food and mixing with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> all over the Danish dominions. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 10. 12. N. Lat. 55. 12.

ALSFIELD

Pages 372-372

a town of Germany, in the landgraviate of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESSE">Hesse</a> Cassel, ten miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Marpurg, and 35 south of Hesse Cassel. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town, and well built; and the inhabitants were the first of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> who embraced the Reformation. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 5. N. Lat. 50. 40.

ALSHASH

Pages 372-372

a very beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> in Bucharia, supposed to be the same with that which is now called Taibacant, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Turkestan, policed by the Kaffirs. It is situated on the river Sichun, now Sir, and had a well watered garden for every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; but was ruined by Jenghiz Khan, who took the city, and caused a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of its inhabitants to be massacred.

ALSHEIDA

Pages 372-372

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Smaland, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, where a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> mine was discovered in 1738.

ALSINA

Pages 372-372

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a synonyme of the theligonum. See Theligonum, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALSINASTRUM

Pages 372-372

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, the trivial name of the elatine. See Elatine, Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALSINE

Pages 372-372
or Chickweed. See Botany Index. The common chickweed affords a remarkable instance of what is called the sleep of plants; for, every night, the leaves approach in pairs, so as to include within their upper surfaces the tender rudiments of the new shoots; and the uppermost pair but one at the end of the stalk are furnished with longer leaf-blades than the others; so that they can close upon the terminating pair, and protect the end of the branch.

ALSIRAT

Pages 372-372

in the Mahometan <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> laid over the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, finer than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and sharper than the edge of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, over which people are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, after their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of judgement. To add to the difficulty of the passage, Mahomet affirms, that the alfarat, narrow as it is, is befit with briars and thorns; none of which, however, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be any impediment to the good, who shall fly over it like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, Mahomet and his Mussulmans leading the way; whereas the wicked, by the narrowness of the path, the entangling of the thorns, and extinction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> which directed the former to paradise, will soon miss their footing, and tumble headlong into hell, which is gaping beneath to receive them.

ALSIVM

Pages 372-372

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of ancient Etruria, occupying (according to Cluverius) the spot on which Pala now stands. We are told by Dionysius Halicarnassensis, that Alium was built by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABORIGINES">Aborigines</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the Tyrrhenians invaded <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it must have been founded not long after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> in the days of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELEG">Peleg</a>. Its founder is said to have been one Alafus, Alafus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Alifa; whom some conjecture to have been Alifah, or Eliha, the son of Javan, mentioned in Scripture.

ALSOP

Pages 372-373

Anthony, an English divine and poet, was educated at Westminster school, and from thence elected to Christ-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1666, and of B.D. in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1726. On his coming to the university, he was very soon distinguished by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Aldrich, and published Fabularum Aesopicarum Defectus, Oxon. 1698, 8vo, with a poetical dedication to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Wicount Scudamore, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a> in which he took <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> against Dr Bentley in the famous dispute with Mr Boyle. He passed through the usual offices in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> to that of censor with considerable reputation; and for some years had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> noblemen and gentlemen belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> committed to his care. In this employment he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his merit recommended him to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JONATHAN">Jonathan</a> Trelawney, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, who appointed him his chaplain, and soon after gave him a prebend in his own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>, together with the rectory of Brightwell in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Berks, which afforded him ample provision for a learned retirement, from which he could not be drawn by the repeated solicitations of those who thought him qualified for a more public character and a higher station. In 1717 an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> was brought against him by Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Astley of Oxford, for a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>; and a verdict obtained against him for 200l., which probably occasioned him to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 10. 1726, was occasioned by his falling into a ditch that led to his garden door. A quarto volume was published in 1752, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Antonii Allop, Aedis Chrifli olim Alumni, Odorum libri duo. Four English poems of his are in Dodley's Collection, one in Peach's, several in the early volumes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a>, and some in "The Student." Mr Allop is respectfully mentioned by the facetious Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> of the Commons (Vol. I. p. 236), as having enriched the commonwealth of learning, by "Translations of Fables from Greek, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, and Arabic;" and not least detractingly by Dr Bentley, under the name of "Tony Allop, a late editor of the Aesopian Fables." (Biog. Dict.) Alsop, Vincent, an English nonconformist divine, was born in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTONSHIRE">Northamptonshire</a>, and educated at St John's college, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he took the degree of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of Arts. When he received deacon's orders, he went to Rutlandshire, and settled at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol13.html#article-OAKHAM">Oakham</a>, where he was an assistant to the master of the free-school. As he was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a sprightly turn, he fell into indifferent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; but was reclaimed by the frequent admonitions of the Reverend Mr Benjamin King. He afterwards married that gentleman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and becoming a convert to his principles, received ed ordination in the Presbyterian way, not being satisfied with that which he had from the bishop. He was settled at Wilbee in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHAMPTON">Northampton</a>, whence he was ejected in 1662, for nonconformity. After this he ventured to preach sometimes at Oakham, and at Wellingborough where he lived, and was once six months in prison for praying by a sick person. A book he wrote against Dr Sherlock in a humorous style, made him well known to the world, and induced Mr Cawton, an eminent nonconformist in Westminster, to recommend him to his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> for his successor. On receiving this call he quitted Northamptonshire, and came to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he preached constantly, and wrote several pieces which were extremely well received by the public. His living in the neighbourhood of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> exposed him to many inconveniences; but these ended with the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least in the beginning of the next reign, when Mr Allop's son engaging in treasonable practices was freely pardoned by King James. After this our divine went frequently to court, and is generally supposed to have been the person who drew the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> to that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> for his general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. After the Revolution, Mr Allop gave public testimonies of his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; yet upon all occasions he spoke very respectfully of King James and retained a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLEMENCY">clemency</a> in sparing his only son. The remainder of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> he spent in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his ministry, preaching once every Lord's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; besides which he had a Thursday lecture, and was one of the lecturers at Pinner's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. He lived to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and preserving his spirits to the last, died in May 1793. On <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> subjects he wrote with a becoming seriousness; but where <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> might properly be shown, he displayed it to great advantage. His funeral sermon was preached by Mr Slater, and his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be always preserved by his own learned and elegant writings. Of these the most remarkable, besides his sermons, are, 1. Antipozzo; in vindication of some great truths opposed by Dr William Sherlock, 8vo, 1675. 2. Melius Inquirendum; in answer to Dr Goodman's Compartmental Inquiry, 8vo, 1679. 3. The Mischief of Impolitions; in answer to Dr Stillingtonfleet's Mischief of Separation, 1680. 4. A Faithful Reproof to a False Report, with reference to the Differences among the United Ministers in London, 8vo. (Biog. Brit.)

ALSTEDIUS

Pages 373-373

JOHN HENRY, a German Protestant divine, and one of the most indefatigable writers of the 17th century. He was some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> at Herborn in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>; from thence he went into Transylvania, to be professor at <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALBA">Alba</a> Julia; where he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1638, in the 50th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. His Encyclopaedia has been much esteemed even by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; it was printed at Lyons, and sold very well throughout all France. His Theaurus Chronologicus is by some considered as one of his best works, and has gone through several editions. He also wrote Triumphus Bibliicus, to show that the principles of all arts and sciences are to be found in the scriptures. He was a Millenarian; and published, in 1627, a treatise De milie annis, in which he asserted that the reign of the saints on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> was to begin in 1694.

ALSTON

Pages 373-373
CHARLES, M.D., a botanical and medical writer, was born in the west of Scotland in the year 1683. He began his studies at the university of Glasgow, and about this period he had the good fortune to be taken under the patronage of the duchess of Hamilton, which afforded him an opportunity of pursuing the bent of his inclination, by attaching himself to the study of physic. About the age of 33, along with his friend and companion the celebrated Alexander Monro, he went to Leyden, and studied three years under Boerhaave. On their return to their native country, they, in conjunction with Rutherford, Sinclair, and Plummer, undertook departments in the college of Edinburgh, and by their abilities and industry, laid the foundation of that school of physic. The branches of botany and materia medica, were long the favourite studies of his life, consequently he undertook that department, and continued to lecture on them with increasing reputation until his death, which happened in November 1760, at the age of 77 years. His talents appear to have been naturally strong, which he improved and strengthened with great affluency and industry, and employed them successfully in the service of science. In the year 1753, his dissertation on the sexes of plants, in which he combats the doctrine of Linnaeus, was published in the first volume of the Edinburgh Physical and Literary Essays. The general plan of the work is conducted with much ingenuity, supported by some strong experiments, and although in the opinion of the learned, it has failed in its principal design, yet it must be acknowledged to be one of the best argued pieces on that side of the question. An asperity of language is sometimes used, very unsuitable to a scientific topic; but, however, it is proper to remark, that Linnaeus had given some reasons for this conduct by the nature of some of his descriptions. In the fifth volume of the Edinburgh Medical Essays, we have a short paper by Dr Alston on the efficacy of the powder of tin, to destroy or expel worms from the bowels. He informs us, that he received the prescription from an empiric, who was renowned for his skill in curing persons afflicted with that disease. The patient received the first morning one ounce of tin reduced to powder, and half an ounce each of the two following mornings, and was then purged with the infusion of senna and manna. He speaks with great certainty upon the efficacy of this medicine, which certainly has considerable power in these cases, and may be given to the most delicate subjects with perfect safety. Dr Alston also engaged in a chemical controversy respecting quicklime with Dr Whytt. But the most valuable of all his works, are his lectures on the Materia Medica, which were published in the year 1770, in two volumes 4to. The number of curious and useful facts contained in this book, will tend to secure its reputation, although considerable additions and improvements have been made, since that period, in this branch of science. (Gen. Biog.)

ALSTON-MOOR

Pages 373-373

a town in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, situated on a hill, at the bottom of which runs the river Tyne, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> over it. Near this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 4. N. Lat 54. 45. ALSTONIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALT-RANSTADT

Pages 381-381

a town in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, famous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> XII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a> and Augustus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of Saxony, in 1706, wherein the latter resigned the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>.

ALTAI MOUNTAINS

Pages 374-374

an extensive range of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> in the northern parts of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It begins at the vast mountain Bogdo, passes above the head of the Irtish, and then takes a course rugged, precipitous, clothed with snow, and rich in minerals, between the Irtish and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBY">Oby</a>; then proceeds by the lake Teleskoi, the rift of the Oby; after which it retires, in order to comprehend the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which form the Jenesei, and are locked up in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> mountains; finally under the name of the Saimir, it is uninterruptedly <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAIKAL">Baikal</a>. A branch infatuates itself between the sources of the rivers <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ONON">Onon</a> and Ingoda, and those of Ichikoi, accompanied with very high mountains, running without interruption to the northeast, and dividing the river Amur, which discharges itself into the east, in the Chinese dominions, from the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENA">Lena</a> and lake Baikal. Another branch stretches along the Olecma, croffles the Lena below Jakoutsk, and is continued between the two rivers Tougoufka to the Jenesei, where it is lost in wooded and marshy plains. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> chain, rugged with sharp-pointed rocks, approaches and keeps near the shores of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Ochotz, and passing by the sources of the rivers Outh, Aldan, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAIA">Maia</a>, is distributed in small branches, which range between the eastern rivers which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into the Icy Sea; besides two principal branches, one of which, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> south, runs through all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, and is broken, from the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Lopatka, into the numerous Kurile isles, and to the east forms another marine chain, in the Aleutian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> which range from Kamtschatka to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; most of them, as well as Kamtschatka itself, distinguished by volcanoes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the traces of volcanic fires. The last chain forms chiefly the great Cape Tschutki, with its promontories and rocky broken shores. The summits of the highest of the Altai mountains are covered with perpetual snow. The loftiest range of this extensive chain, is composed of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>. Another range of inferior height consists of thiftus, which lies on the sides of the granite mountains. Beside these rocks, there are <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of chalkstone, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, and marble. The Altai mountains abound in metallic ores. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, silver, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, have been discovered in them, with great abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The two latter have been wrought to a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, and have been found productive.

ALTAMONT

Pages 374-374

a very handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, and in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Citerior, 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of Bagniano. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 22. N. Lat. 39. 40.

ALTAMURA

Pages 374-374

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of a principality, seated on the foot of the Apennine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 16. 54. N. Lat. 41. 0.

ALTAR

Pages 374-377

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> upon which sacrifices were anciently offered to some deity. The heathens at first made their altars only of turf; afterwards they were made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, of marble, of wood, and even of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">horn</a>, as that of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> in Delos. Altars differed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> as well as in materials. Some were round, others <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and others triangular. All of them were turned towards the east, and stood lower than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the gods; and were generally adorned with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, representing either the gods to whom they were erected, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> their symbols. See the PAGAN ALTARS represented on Plate XVII. Upon the sides of fig. 1, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a> and two dolphins are exhibited, which denote it to have been dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. Fig. 2, a four-square altar, was dedicated to the Nymphs, as the inscription imports. Fig. 3, exhibits a Bacchanal holding a thyrsus in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, a mark of the altar's being built to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>: it had two other sides, which made it appear triangular. Of fig. 4, which was also triangular, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> or side exhibited a genius, one of whom (on the side represented) carries an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a> upon his neck, which seems to denote it an altar of Neptune. Fig. 5, an altar of a round shape, is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARA">Ara</a> Neptuni: the god himself is there represented, all naked, having the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLIUM">pallium</a> upon his shoulder; and holding in his left hand a trident, and in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> a dolphin. The height of altars also differed according to the different gods to whom they sacrificed. According to Servius, those altars set apart for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the celestial gods, and gods of the higher clasps, were placed on some pretty tall pile of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; and for that reason were called altaria, from the words alia and ara, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> elevated altar." Those appointed for the terrestrial gods were laid on the surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and called arae. And, on the contrary, they dug into the earth and opened a pit for those of the infernal gods, which they called ἀνακάλυψις, ἀνακάλυψις. But this distinction is not everywhere observed: the best authors frequently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> ara as a general word, under which are included the altars of the celestial and infernal, as well as those of the terrestrial gods. Witness <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Eccl. 5. En quatuor aras, where arae plainly includes altaria; for whatever we make of Daphnis, Phoebus was certainly a celestial god. So Cicero, pro Quint. Aras delubraque Hecate in Graecia vidimus. The Greeks also distinguished two sorts of altars; that whereon they sacrificed to the gods was called βωμός, and was a real altar, different from the other whereon they sacrificed to the heroes, which was smaller, and called εὐχεία. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> makes this distinction of altars in his Onomasticum; he adds, however, that some poets used the word εὐχεία for the altar whereon sacrifice was offered to the gods. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> version does sometimes also use the word εὐχεία for a sort of little low altar, which may be expressed in Latin by craticula; being a hearth rather than an altar. Before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> were in use, altars were erected sometimes in groves, sometimes in the highways, and sometimes on the tops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>; and it was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to engrave upon them the name, ensign, or character of the deity to whom they were consecrated. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> temples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome there were ordinarily three altars: The first was placed in the sanctuary, at the foot of the statue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, upon which incense was burnt and libations offered; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> was before the gate of the temple, and upon it they sacrificed the victims; and the third was a portable altar, upon which were placed the offering and the sacred vessels. Besides Besides these uses of altars, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> swore upon them, and swore by them, in making alliances, confirming treaties of peace, and other solemn occasions. Altars also served as places of refuge to all those who fled to them, whatever crime they had committed. Altars are doubtless as ancient as sacrifices themselves; consequently their origin is not much later than that of the world, Gen. ch. iv. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> their origin to the Egyptians; others to the Jews; others to the patriarchs before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. Some carry them as far back as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, whose altar is much spoken of by Jewish, and even Christian writers. Others are contented to make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> Enoch the first who consecrated a public altar. Be this as it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, the earliest altars we find any express testimony of are those erected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a>. Altars, in the patriarchal times, were very rude. The altar which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> set up at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BETHEL">Bethel</a> was nothing but a stone, which served him instead of a bolster; that of Gideon, a stone before his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and the first which God commanded Moses to erect was probably of earth or unpolished <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, without any <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any use was made of that metal, the altar was declared impure. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> altars of the Jews were, The altar of incense; that of burnt-offering; and the altar, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, for the shew-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>. The altar of incense was a small table of shittim wood, covered with plates of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUBIT">cubit</a> in length, another in width, and two in height. At the four corners were four kinds of horns, and all round a little border or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> over it. This was the altar hidden by Jeremiah before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>; and upon it the officiating <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> offered, every morning and evening, incense of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. See Plate XVII. The altar of burnt-offerings was made of shittim wood, and carried upon the shoulders of the priests by slaves of the same wood overlaid with bras. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Moses, this altar was five cubits square and three high; but in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>'s temple it was much larger, being twenty cubits square and ten in height. It was covered with bras; and at each corner was a horn or spire, wrought out of the same wood with the altar, to which the sacrifices were tied. Within the hollow was a grate of bras, on which the fire was made; through it fell the ashes, which were received in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a> below. At the four corners of the grate were four rings and four chains, which kept it up at the horns. This altar was placed in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of the burnt-offerings might not fully the inside of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABERNACLE">tabernacle</a>. See Plate XVII. The altar or table for the shew-bread was likewise of shittim wood, covered with plates of gold, having a little border round it, adorned with sculpture. It was two cubits <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, one wide, and one and a half in height. Upon this table, which stood in the holy of holies, were put, every Sabbath <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, twelve loaves, with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and incense. The Jewish altars, after their return from the captivity, and the building of the second temple, were in some respects different from those described above. That of burnt offerings was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pile, built of unhewn stone, thirty cubits square at the bottom, and twenty-four square at the top. The ascent was by a gentle rising, thirty-two cubits in length, and sixteen in breadth. Altar, is also used among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>-table. In the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, the altars were only of wood; as being frequently to be removed from place to place. But the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 509, decreed that no altar should be built but of stone. At first there was but one altar in each church; but the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> soon increased; and from the writings of Gregory the Great, who lived in the fifth century, we learn, that there were sometimes in the same church twelve or thirteen. In the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGDEBURG">Magdeburg</a> there are no less than forty-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> altars. The altar is sometimes sustained on a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, as in the subterranean chapels of St Cecilia, at Rome, &c.; and sometimes by four columns, as the altar of St Sebastian of Crypta Arenaria; but the customary form is, to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASSIVE">massive</a> of stone <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, sustaining the altar table. These altars bear a resemblance to tombs; to this purpose, we read in church-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that the primitive Christians chiefly held their meetings at the tombs of the martyrs, and celebrated the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> upon them: for which reason, it is a standing rule to this day in the church of Rome, never to build an altar, without including the relics of some saint in it.

ALTAR-THANE

Pages 377-377
or ALTARIST, in old Law-books, an appellation given to the priest or parson of a parish, to whom the altarage belonged. See ALTARAGE.

ALTARAGE

Pages 377-377

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, altars erected in virtue of donations, before the Reformation, within a parochial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, for the purpose of singing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> for deceased friends.

ALTARAGE LIKEWISE

Pages 377-377

E likewise signifies the profits arising to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> on account of the altar.

ALTDORF

Pages 377-377

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handsome town in Swisserland, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of Uri. It is situated below the lake of the Four Cantons, in a plain, at the foot of a mountain whose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are difficult, and serve instead of fortifications. It has four churches and two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; St Martin's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and that of the Holy <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">Cross</a> are the finest. The town-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> and the arsenal are also worth seeing. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 30'. N. Lat. 46° 30'.

ALTEA

Pages 377-377

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. It was taken in 1705, in favour of the archduke <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a>; but lost after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Almanza. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 0° 15'. N. Lat. 46° 34'.

ALTEMBURG

Pages 377-377

a town of Transylvania, fifteen miles south-west of Wilemburg, and thirty-five south of Clausenbourg. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 5'. N. Lat. 46° 25'.

ALTENA

Pages 377-377
or ALTONA, a sea-port town of Germany, in the duchy of Holstein in Lower Saxony. It is a modern town, built by the king of Denmark, and was burnt by the Swedes in 1712; but has since been beautifully rebuilt. The merchandise brought from Asia by the Danish East India Company is sold here. E. Long. 10° 0'. N. Lat. 53° 51'.

ALTERNATION

Pages 377-378

in its primary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes Alternation a succession by turns. ALTERNATION is sometimes used to express the different changes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> alterations of orders in any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things proposed. This is also called permutation, &c., and is easily found by a continual multiplication of all the numbers, beginning at unity. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be required to know how many changes or alternations can be rung on five bells, multiply the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, continually into one another; and the last product gives the number of changes.

ALTERNATIVE

Pages 378-378

is particularly used for the choice of two things proposed. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> we say, to take the alternative of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a>.

ALTHAEA

Pages 378-378

Marshmallow. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ALTHAEA Frutex. See Hibiscus, Botany Index.

ALTIMETRY

Pages 378-378

the art of measuring altitudes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heights, whether accessible or inaccessible. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>.

ALTIN

Pages 378-378

a lake in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, from whence flows the river Ob, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBY">Oby</a>, in N. Lat. 52°. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 85°. 55'. This lake is called by the Russians Telekhoi Ozero, from the Teleffi, a Tartarian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, who inhabit the borders of it, and who give it the name of Altin-Kul. By the Calmucks it is called Altinmor. It is near 90 miles long and 50 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with a rocky bottom. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it is sometimes frozen so hard as to be passable on foot, but the southern part is never covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the Altin lake, as well as in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which run through the adjacent places, only rises in the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when the snows on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are melted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>.

ALTINCAR

Pages 378-378

among Mineralists, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of factitious <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> used in the fusion and purification of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. The altincar is a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> powder. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">Divers</a> ways of preparing it are given by Libavius.

ALTING

Pages 378-381

Henry, a German divine, was born at Embden, in 1583. His father was minister of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Embden, and early destined his son to the same profession. In the year 1602, after a grammatical course he was sent to the university of Herborn: there he studied with so much assiduity and success, that he soon had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being a preceptor. Qualified by the vigorous exertions of his talents, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the three young counts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, Solms, and Hessenberg, who studied with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> palatine, first at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, and afterwards at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a>. A proper discharge of the duties of a lower station generally paves the way for a higher. For he was appointed preceptor to the prince in 1608: and in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of his assiduity and success, he was chosen to accompany the elector into England. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of celebrated men to whose acquaintance he was introduced in England, was the famous Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a>, archbishop of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>. In 1613, Alting returning to Heidelberg after the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the elector with the princess of England, received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, and was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a>. The increased knowledge and invigorated talents of Alting, were always receiving renewed opportunities of exertion; thus his eloquence quence and learning obtained full scope in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DORT">Dort</a>, to which he had been deputed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>, along with two other divines. It was but reasonable for Alting to expect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> prettiment and high advantages from the avowed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of the elector; but in this he was greatly disappointed, and he had only to participate in his misfortunes. In 1622, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Tilly took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Heidelberg, and devoted it to plunder. In order to escape the fury of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, Alting endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by a back door into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which was put under a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; but the officer who guarded the house, as he was entering said to him, "With this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>-axe I have today killed ten men, and Alting, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> I knew where to find him, should be the eleventh: who are you?" Alting with a singular presence of mind returned an evasive answer, which saved his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. "I am (said he) a teacher in the college of Wismar." The officer took him under his protection, but the Jesuits unfortunately taking possession of the house, the next <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, left the generous officer no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> at his departure to take care of the teacher of the college of Wismar. Alting evaded the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Jesuits, by hiding himself in a garret, and a cook of the electoral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> supplied him with food, who happened to be employed by Count Tilly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> occupied by him in the chancellor's house. In this perilous situation he remained until an opportunity offered of making his escape to Heilbronn, whither his family had been conducted before. But <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> intolerance harassed Alting, as much as he was formerly endangered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> hostility. With the permission of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Wirtemberg he retired for a few months to Schorndorf after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of the Palatinate by the victorious forces of Count Tilly. It was reasonable to expect that a welcome and hospitable reception might have been given, among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, to one who had <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> escaped the flames of a Popish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. But the doctrine of mutual forbearance and candour seems to have been little attended to by the Protestants at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, whatever was their progress in the knowledge of the other doctrines of Christianity. The palatinate being in the vicinity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Wirtemberg, the professors of Tubingen and Heidelberg frequently attacked each other in polemic writings and theological disputations. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> consequence was, that a settled jealousy and enmity existed between the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and their respective vicinities. The injuries which Alting had suffered from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy were not sufficient to secure him a friendly reception among the Lutheran ministers of Schorndorf, who were involved in these feuds, and therefore murmured at the permission which the duke had given to a professor of Heidelberg to reside there. The mischievous effects of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> divisions have been universally felt. In 1623, Alting retired with his family to Embrden, and afterwards followed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> his late pupil, now <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>. Such was the unfeigned <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to him, that he still retained him as a preceptor to his eldest son; and prevented him from accepting the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the church at Embrden, and likewise of a professorship at the university of Franeker. In 1627 his importance prevailed upon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, and he obtained leave to remove to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a>, and there ascended the divinity <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to lecture with increasing reputation until the day of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. The ardent desire and repeated endeavours of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> to appropriate to themselves the honour and benefit of his services, is the most unequivocal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the general esteem in which his character was held. The states of Groningen positively refused to give their consent to his removal, when the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> solicited him to come and labour among them. But some time after, the prospect of extensive usefulness in re-establishing the university of Heidelberg, and restoring the churches of the Palatinate, determined him to accept the office of professor of divinity and ecclesiastical senator, presented to him by Prince <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>. In the year 1634, amidst numerous hardships, to which the existing war exposed him, he set out for Heidelberg, and pursued his journey as far as Frankfort; when the battle of Nördlingen, in which the imperialists were victorious, rendered his farther progress impracticable, and therefore with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> difficulty he returned to Groningen. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">Domestic</a> affection and personal sufferings embittered the remaining years of this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s life. Deprived of his eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> by death, such was his great affection for her that it brought on a settled melancholy, attended with a bodily <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> which was with great difficulty removed; but after an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of four years a settled and irrecoverable melancholy seized him, in consequence of the loss of an amiable and beloved wife, which, together with the return of his bodily disease, in a few months put a period to his useful life in the year 1644. Alting was a man of eminent talents and extensive learning, possessed of amiable dispositions, which induced him to be more solicitous to serve the public than to benefit himself. The amiable character and extensive learning of Alting, cannot fail deeply to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> every reader, in consequence of his misfortunes. He was adverse to quarrels and disputes about trifles, although no friend to the innovations introduced at this period by the Socinians. According to his own judgment, adhering to the plain doctrine of Scripture, he was equally desirous to avoid fanatical scrupulosity and sophistical subtlety. The productions of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> are: *Notes in Decadum Problematum, Johannis Beom, Heidelbergae, 1618*; *Notes on a Decad of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Behmen's Problems.* Loci Communes; *Common places.* Problema; *Problems.* Explicatio Catachese Palaatinat.; *Explanation of the Palatine Catechism.* Exegetis Augustana Confessionis, &c., Amst. 1647; *<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the Augsburg Confession.* Methodus Theologiae Didactica et Catachetica, Amst. 1650; *A method of Didactic and Catechetical <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>.* The Medulla Historiae Prophezea, *Marrow of Profane <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>,* published under the name of Pareus, was written by Alting. (Gen. Biog.) Alting, James, son of Henry Alting, was born at Heidelberg in 1618. After the usual course of grammatical studies he became a student, and soon after professor of divinity in the university of Groningen. The Oriental languages were his favourite studies at an early period of his life; and in 1638 he put himself under the tuition of a Jewish rabbi at Embrden. Determining to take up his residence in England, he arrived there in 1640, and was admitted to clerical orders by Doctor Prideaux bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a>. By Altig, an offer of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> professorship in the university of Groningen, he was soon induced to alter his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of life, and consequently again returned to Germany in 1643. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> affability in these languages, and his knowledge in other sciences, procured him universal esteem, and great reputation as a scholar. About this time he received many academic honours; he was admitted doctor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, academic preacher, and at last, in conjunction with a colleague, Samuel des Marets, was chosen professor of divinity. These professors followed different methods of teaching, and adopted different systems. Des Marets was an admirer and follower of the subtleties of the scholastics; and by the ingenuity with which he purified the scholastic plan of instruction had acquired great reputation and considerable influence. Altig spent his time in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Scriptures, and in the pursuit of Rabbinical learning; and he delivered a course of lectures on divinity, which gained him great popularity. As it might naturally be expected, a mutual jealousy arose between the two professors; and their respective partisans in the university carried their animosity to an undue height. Established <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of authority, marshalled on the side of Des Marets.
