By the permission of the curators of the university he appeared as public accuser of Altig, and produced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of erroneous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> to the divines of Leyden for their opinion. The judgment of the divines upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a> shows a great degree of moderation and good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>: they pronounced Altig innocent of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, but imprudently fond of innovation; and they declared Des Marets deficient in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> and candour. If the superiors had not prohibited the farther discussion of these subjects in the confectories, classes, and synods, they would have occasioned as much mischief as they had excited general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. Such was the protection given to Altig, that whenever any of the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> proposed any further <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> against him, they were immediately rejected by the civil power; nay, the penalty of deprivation was decreed against those clergy who should revive the Marso-Altigian controversy. Whatever might be the advantages resulting to Altig from this protection, the magistrates certainly did wrong in proceeding so far in prohibiting a free discussion from the prelfs, either for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> against the judgments of the divines of Leyden. Although a kind of reconciliation was attempted by their common friends while Des Marets lay upon his death-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between Des Marets and Altig was never perfectly healed. Dr Altig died of a fever in 1679. The fondness which he showed for Rabbinical learning gave birth to the general report, that he was inclined to become a Jew. His opinions which seem to have excited more general attention than they deserve, may be seen at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in his writings, which were collected a few years after his death, and published in five volumes folio by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Menlo Altig, who wrote a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Low Countries, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Notitia Germaniae Inferioris. (Gen. Biog.) **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">Altitude</a>**, accessible and inaccessible. See <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>. The method of taking considerable terrestrial altitudes, of which those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are the greatest, by means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, is very easy and expeditious. Is done by observing, on the top of the mountain, how much the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> has fallen below what it was at the foot of the mountain. See Barometer. **Altitude of the Eye**, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">Perspective</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from the eye, perpendicular to the geometrical <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>. **Altitude**, in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, is the distance of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>, or other point, in the mundane sphere, from the horizon. This altitude may be either true or apparent. If it be taken from the rational or real horizon, the altitude is said to be true or real; if from the apparent or sensible horizon, the altitude is apparent. Or rather, the apparent altitude is such as it appears to our observation; and the true is that from which the refraction has been subtracted. The true altitudes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, fixed stars, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, differ but very little from their apparent altitudes; because of their great distance from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and the smallness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> semidiameter, when compared thereto. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the true and apparent altitude of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is about 52. This subject is further explained under Astronomy. **Altitude <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">Instrument</a>**, or Equal Altitude Instrument, is that used to observe a celestial object when it has the same altitude on the east and west sides of the meridian. See Astronomy. **Altrkirch**, a town of France, in the department of the Upper <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, situated on the river Ill, in N. Lat. 47° 40', E. Long. 7° 15'. **<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ALTMORE">Altmore</a>**, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRONE">Tyrone</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Ulster, situated in N. Lat. 54° 34', W. Long. 7° 2'. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTON">Alton</a>**, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMPSHIRE">Hampshire</a>, seated on the river Wey; W. Long. 0° 46', N. Lat. 51° 5'. It is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>; and consists of about 300 houses, indifferently built, chiefly laid out in one pretty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> street. It has one church, a Presbyterian, and a Quaker's meeting, a famous free school, a large manufacture of plain and figured baragons, ribbed druggets, and serges de Nimes; and round the town is a large plantation of hops. **Alton**, or **Avelton**, a village in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORDSHIRE">Staffordshire</a>, five miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UTTOXETER">Uttoxeter</a>. There are the ruins of a castle here, which some would have to be built before the Norman conquest; but Dr Plott is pretty certain that it was erected by Theobald de Verdun, in the beginning of the reign of Edward II. A great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the walls are still standing, but they are in a very ruinous condition. **ALTO et Basso**, or in Alto et in Basso, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> reference of all differences, small and great, high and low, to some arbitrator or indifferent person. Patent universis per presentem, quod Wilhelmus Tyler de Ketton, et Thomas Gower de Almefre, poiverunt se in Alto et in Basso, in arbitrio quattuor hominum; viz. de quadam querela pendente inter eos in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>. Nos et terram nostram altè et basè ipsius domini Regis supponimus voluntati. **Alto-Relieve**, See Relieve. **Alto-Relievo**, in Music, the tenor of the great chorus, which sings and plays only now and then in some particular places. **<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTORF">Altorf</a>**, a town of the circle of Franconia, in Germany. Germany. It has a botanical garden, with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, an anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, and a handsome library. It is subject to the house of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>; and is seated on the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, 15 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a>. E. Long. 11° 7'. N. Lat. 49° 25'.

ALTRINGHAM

a town of Cheshire in England, upon the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANCHESTER">Manchester</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1° 30'. N. Lat. 53° 25'.

ALUDELS

in the older and more complicated chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, were earthen pots without bottoms, inserted into each other, and used in sublimations.

ALUM

Pages 385-387

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, a clear and transparent saline <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, usually sold in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, of a very austere and astringent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, useful in medicine and in various arts. Most of the alum to be met with is artificially prepared by the methods related in their proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under the article Chemistry, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> by others similar to them: though sometimes a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is produced naturally. This native alum is mixed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HETEROGENEOUS">heterogeneous</a> matters, or effloresces in various forms upon the ores during calcination. It rarely occurs in a crystallized state, though thus it is said to be met with in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDINIA">Sardinia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and other places. It is also found in waters impregnated with fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, but very seldom in fountains or hot medicated waters. There are several kinds of alum to be met with; but these differ from one another only in being mixed with some salts which are not of the aluminous kinds. That called the Roman alum has been considered as preferable to any other. This is usually met with in small crystals, and has a reddish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, most probably owing to a small quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CALX">calx</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which, however, does not in the least impair its qualities. The other kinds of alum contain a portion either of vitriolated tartar or sal ammoniac, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the alkali used in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>. Mr Bergman informs us, that the vegetable alkali, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> pure, does not hurt the alum, though it be added in the preparation; but that the volatile alkali, by adulterating it with a portion of vitriolic sal ammoniac, renders it unfit for some purposes. The alum, made by adding a portion of clay to the liquor at the beginning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, he considers as equal, if not superior, to Roman alum. He informs us also, that a kind of alum some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> ago began to be manufactured at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>, which was equal in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to the Roman alum. On a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of this alum he found it mixed with cobalt. This <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is extremely useful in the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a>; as by means of it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of colours are fixed and rendered permanent upon cloth, which otherwise would either not adhere in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, or only for a very short time. In what manner this is accomplished, we are very much ignorant; the conjectures and theories on this subject are related under the article Dying. It constitutes the basis of crayons, which generally consist of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> of alum finely powdered and tinged for the purpose. In the preparation of Prussian blue, it prevents the basis of martial vitriol, which is soluble in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, from being precipitated by the superfluous alkali employed in the preparation of that pigment; that is, the alkali which is not saturated by the colouring matter. As this basis adheres more strongly than the clay to the vitriolic acid, and would form a green by the mixture of its yellowness, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> earth of alum likewise according to its quantity, dilutes the darker colours, even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> itself, and produces an infinite number of shades. It is also of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in the making of candles: for being mixed with the tallow, it gives it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and consistence which it has not naturally. Wood sufficiently soaked in a solution of alum does not easily take fire; and the same is true of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> impregnated with it; which, for that reason, is very properly employed in preserving <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, as it also excludes the moisture of the air. Paper impregnated with alum is useful in whitening silver, and silvering <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. Alum is also of use in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TANNING">tanning</a>, where it assists in restoring the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the skins almost entirely destroyed by the lime. Vintners fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their wines, &c., with alum; fishers use it to dry cod fish with; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a> have mixed it with the flour to make their <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and white: to this last use of it great objections have been made; but unjustly, for it is entirely innocent. It is now seldom used. In medicine it is of considerable use as an astringent and tonic. It is reckoned particularly serviceable for restraining hemorrhages, and immoderate secretions from the blood; but less proper in intestinal fluxes. In violent hemorrhages, it may be given in doses of 15 or 20 grains, and repeated every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> or half hour till the bleeding abates: in other <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, smaller doses are more advisable; large ones being apt to nauseate the stomach, and occasion violent constrictions of the bowels. It is used also externally, in astringent and repellent lotions and collyria. Burnt alum taken internally has been highly extolled in cases of colic. In such instances, when taken to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of a scruple for a dose, it has been said gently to move the belly, and give very great relief from the severe pain. Its officinal preparations are, for internal use, pulvis stypticus, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> styptica; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> applications, the aqua aluminis, and coagulum aluminis et alumen stypticum; which last is no other than the alum dried by fire, or freed from the watery moisture, which, like other salts, it always retains in its crystalline form. By this loss of its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> it becomes sharper, so as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a slight escharotic; and it is chiefly with this intention that it is employed in medicine, being very rarely taken internally. For these preparations, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>. Alum <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> are said to have been first found in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the year 1460; and in 1506 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VII. made a monopolizing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of this commodity to Augustine Chigi, a merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>. In the year 1608, the manufacture of alum was first invented, and successively practised in England, meeting with great encouragement in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where it was first made, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>, and the other gentlemen of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>. King James I. by advice of his ministry, assumed the monopoly of it to himself, and therefore prohibited the importation of foreign alum; and in 1625 the importation of it was further prohibited by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. Alum Works, places where alum is prepared, and manufactured in quantities for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. They differ from Alypius, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Greek writers on music, which Meibomius has industriously collected and published, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> and explanatory notes. The time in which he flourished cannot be precisely determined. He is said to have wrote before Euclid and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>; and Caffiodorus arranges his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled "Introduction to Music," between that of Nicomachus and Gaudensius. In this work is to be found the most complete nomenclature of all the sounds of the different scales and modes of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek music, which have escaped the wreck of time. So complex was the science of music in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> used for sounds were 1620 in number. The twenty-four letters of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPHABET">alphabet</a> furnished these notes, sometimes in an entire, sometimes in a mutilated, and sometimes in an altered form; and numerous discriminations of these took place by means of the accents and varied positions of letters. From the MS. of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Scaliger, Meursius first published this tract in 1616; but according to the testimony of Fabricius, it is by no means correct. Extracts have been published from Alypius, by Kircher, in his Musurgia, 1650, alleging that he translated the whole into Latin; but this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of ancient musical notation is so inaccurate, which he has inferred from him, that Meibomius, who consulted not only the Greek MS. of Scaliger, but that of Belejanus, Barocci, Barberitti, and Selden, affirms, that he found in it more than 200 errors. The learned Meibomius, with incredible industry, deciphered those characters, which previous to his time were so much confounded, disfigured, and corrupted, either through the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> or inattention of the transcribers of ancient MSS. This advantage resulted to the science of music, chiefly by his commentaries on Greek musicians, and particularly on the works of Alypius. Alypius of Tagaste, a Christian divine who flourished in the fourth century. In the year 388, he was baptized along with Augustine, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a similarity of dispositions and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sentiments, they became strongly attached to each other. In quest of information and improvement, he took a journey into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a>; and returning home, he soon acquired such general esteem, that he was appointed bishop of his native <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. He had adopted in the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the opinions of the Maniches; but in consequence of farther information and matured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, he became a powerful advocate for the Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DONATISTS">Donatists</a> flourished about this period, and arrogantly claimed the exclusive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but he, along with his friend Augustine, united his exertions in opposing the tenets of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> in the year 403, the erudition and talents of Alypius, along with several other eminent divines, were unsuccessfully employed in endeavouring to reclaim them, and to bring them again into the bosom of the church. In 411 Alypius was one of the seven who held a friendly and theological conference with seven of the Donatist <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. But all the eloquence and strength of argument made use of by these divines, although seconded by the penal decrees of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Honorius, were unsuccessful in producing a recantation of their errors, or a peaceful union with their brethren. In support of the Catholic faith, Alypius appears to have vigorously ex- Alyssum ered his talents; and it is much to be regretted that the means he employed for that purpose were not at all times the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>; for in the violence of his zeal he went as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> from the churches of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> to the emperor Honorius, in order to obtain severe decrees against the sect of the Pelagians. Although Alypius failed in his attempt to reclaim the Donatists from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a>, yet he was successful with the emperor in obtaining penal decrees against the Pelagians; in consequence of which their ministers were banished, their churches demolished, and their assemblies discontinued. Alypius died about the year 432, and his dispositions appear to have participated more of the violence of zeal, than of the meekness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a>. (Gen. Biog.)

ALUS LOCUTIUS

Pages 171-172

the name of a deity to whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> erected an altar. The words are Latin, and signify "a speaking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>." The following accident gave occasion to the Romans erecting an altar to Aius Ajutage, Aius Locutius. One M. Sedilius, a plebeian, acquainted the tribunes, that, in walking the streets by night, he had heard a voice over the temple of Veja, giving the Romans notice that the Gauls were coming against them. This intimation was, however, neglected; but after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> was confirmed by the event, Camillus acknowledged this voice to be a new deity, and erected an altar to it under the name of Aius Locutius.

ALVA

Pages 381-383

Ferdinand Alvarez of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOLEDO">Toledo</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of, was born in 1508, and descended from one of the most illustrious families of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. His grandfather, Frederick de Toledo, was his preceptor in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> arts, and he displayed his valour at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a> and at the siege of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TUNIS">Tunis</a>. The ambitious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. selected Alva as a proper <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for conducting his military enterprises, and he made him his general in 1538; and, after several operations, in which he both displayed his valour and military knowledge, in 1542 he successfully defended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERPIGNAN">Perpignan</a> against the dauphin of France. In 1546, Alva was made general in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which marched against the German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, who were marshalled under the banners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>. Francis, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of France, died at Rambouillet, and by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> a considerable change was made in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Instantly, therefore, Charles began his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> from Egra on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, and entered the southern frontier of Saxony, and attacked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTORF">Altorf</a> upon the Elster. Incessantly pushing forward, he arrived the evening of the 23rd of April on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELBE">Elbe</a>, opposite to Mühlberg. The river, at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, was three hundred paces in breadth, about four feet in depth; its current rapid; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> possessed by the Saxons was higher than that which he occupied. In opposition to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the duke of Alva and his other officers, Charles, with undaunted courage, and with inexplicable difficulties, led his army through the river, and engaged the Saxons. The elector displayed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> personal courage and military knowledge, but having received a wound in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, he at last surrendered himself prisoner. When he approached the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, he said, "The fortune of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> has made me your prisoner, most gracious emperor, and I hope to be treated." Here Charles hardly interrupted him, "And am I then at last acknowledged to be emperor? Charles of Ghent was the only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> you lately allowed me. You shall be treated as you deserve." The elector made no reply; but, with an unaltered countenance, which discovered neither astonishment nor dejection, accompanied the Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> appointed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> him. The emperor proceeded towards Wittemberg, whither the remains of the Saxon army had fled, carrying along with him the captive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, as a spectacle of consternation and amazement to his own subjects. But when he approached the town, he found it defended by the vigorous efforts of the elector's wife, along with the inhabitants. He summoned Sibylla once and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> to open the gates, informing her, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she persisted in her obstinacy, the elector should answer for it with his head. Accordingly he brought his prisoner to an immediate <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>. The proceedings against him were as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> as the stratagem was barbarous. Instead of consulting the states of the empire, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> remitting the cause to any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, which, according to the German <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, might have legally taken cognizance of the elector's crime, he subjected the greatest prince in the empire to the jurisdiction of a court martial. The emperor selected the unrelenting duke of Alva as a proper instrument to carry into effect any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of violence and oppression, and therefore made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of that court, composed of Spanish and Italian officers. Moved more by the entreaties of his wife than by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of his own danger, the elector submitted to all the rigorous and unjust <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> that were proposed in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; but when it was added, that he should also renounce the Protestant <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and become a Roman Catholic, he refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> in opposition to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>, and bravely fell a sacrifice to the cause of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. In 1552, Alva was intrusted with the command of the army intended to invade France, and was constrained by the opinion and authority of the emperor to lay siege to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, in opposition to his own military knowledge; but notwithstanding all his valour and abilities, the duke of Guise successfully defended the place. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the success of the French arms in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, he was made commander in chief of all the emperor's forces in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and at the same time invested with unlimited power. Success did not, however, attend his first attempts, and after several unfortunate attacks, he was obliged to retire into winter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. The next year he was sent into the pope's territories, and, had he not been restrained by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, he would have taken possession of all his fortified places, and deterred Henry from entering into any new connexion with him, and have thereby prevented the renewal of the war. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> was strongly inclined to peace, but Alva was inclined to severe measures: he however yielded to the instructions of his master, until being deluded, and sometimes haughtily answered, he at length sent Pino de Loffredo with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of cardinals, and another to Paul, in which, after enumerating the various injuries which his master had received, and renewing his former offers of peace and friendship, he concluded with protesting that, if his offers were again rejected, the pope should be chargeable with all the calamities that might follow. The pope threw Loffredo into prison; and, had not the college of cardinals interfered, he would have even put him to death; and on account of Philip's failing to pay tribute for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, he deprived him of the sovereignty of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. This violent conduct of Paul gave great offence throughout all Europe, and greatly lessened his influence in Italy; but Philip, though a young, ambitious, powerful monarch, and of a temper of mind impatient of injuries and affronts, moved moved with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> veneration, discovered an amazing reluctance against proceeding to extremities. After much time spent in negotiation, Philip was at last forced to give orders for Alva to take the field. He cheerfully obeyed, and began his march in the beginning of September 1556, with a well disciplined army, which reducing several <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma, he pursued his conquests to the very gates of Rome. The circumstances, however, in which Alva found his army, induced him to make a truce of 40 days, and, after several negotiations, he yielded to peace. One of its terms was, that the duke of Alva should in person ask forgiveness of the haughty pontiff whom he had conquered. Proud as the duke was by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and accustomed to treat with persons of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, yet such was the superstitious veneration then entertained for the papal character, that he confessed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> failed him at the interview, and his presence of mind forbore him. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> after this, he was sent at the head of a splendid embassy to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, to espouse, in the name of his master, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Henry king of France. Philip II., his new master, being strongly devoted to the Roman see, and determined to reclaim rebels to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and dissenters from his faith, by the most unrelenting severity and unbounded cruelty, he pitched upon Alva as the fittest person to carry this system into practice; with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, therefore, he was sent into the Low Countries in 1567. Having received his orders, armed with such power as left only the shadow of authority to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> governor, and provided with 10,000 veterans, he marched towards that devoted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. When he arrived, he soon shewed how much he merited the confidence which his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> repose in him, and instantly erected a bloody tribunal, to try all persons who had been engaged in the late commotions which the civil and the religious tyranny of Philip had excited. The depraved enormities of the mind of Alva raged with unexampled violence. He imprisoned the counts Egmont and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, the two popular leaders of the Protestants, and soon brought them to an unjust trial, and condemned them to death. In a little time he totally annihilated every privilege of the people, and with uncontrolled fury and cruelty, put multitudes of them to death. Beholding herself deprived of all authority, and her subjects devoted to destruction, the duchess of Parma resigned her office, disdaining to hold the nominal, while the actual reins of power were in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of Alva. This event increased the general tide of wretchedness, and every place was filled with scenes of horror and dismay. Unable for the present to administer the least aid, the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> saved his life by flight. This noble prince suddenly collected an army in Germany, and returned to the relief of his countrymen; and at the same time Prince <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, marched with an army into Friesland. Although success at first attended Lewis, yet the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> of Alva prevailed, and he was totally defeated. The prince of Orange proved a more formidable foe; and it gave exertion to the united talents of Alva, and his son Frederick of Toledo, to prevent the prince from making a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>. But notwithstanding all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and military skill of the prince of Orange, this was effected; and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> remained to Alva to baffle that great leader, and to compel him, after great loss of men, to disband the remainder of his army. Now the cruelty of Alva had unrestrained vent. Instantly the executioner was employed in removing all those friends of freedom whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> had spared. Uncontrolled, the base and unrelenting heart of Alva began to reduce all the provinces to utter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, and to extirpate Protestantism in that country. In most of the considerable towns, Alva built citadels. He erected a statue of himself, which was no less a monument of his vanity than his tyranny, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a>: he was figured trampling on the necks of two smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, representing the two estates of the Low Countries. By his unusual and arbitrary requisition of new supplies from the states, he greatly aggravated this haughty insult. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind displays unusual vigour when rendered desperate by oppression. The exiles from the Low Countries, roused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, fitted out a kind of piratical fleet, and, after strengthening themselves by successful depredations, ventured upon the bold exploit of seizing the town of Brielle. Thus, unattended by him, the cruelty of Alva was the instrument of the future independence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> Dutch provinces. The fleet of the exiles having met the Spanish fleet, totally defeated it, and reduced <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> and Mons; and numbers of cities hastened to throw off the yoke; while the states-general assembling at Dordrecht, openly declared against Alva's government, and marshalled under the banners of the prince of Orange. This situation of affairs opened the eyes of Alva to behold the instability of a power founded on terror and oppression; he therefore began in vain to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> more lenient measures. He prepared, however, with vigour to oppose the gathering storm, and afterwards recovered Mons, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MECHLIN">Mechlin</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, under the conduct of his son Frederick, where his soldiers more than retaliated upon the prince of Orange. With the exception of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a> and Holland, he regained all the provinces; and at last his son stormed Woerden, and, massacring its inhabitants with the most <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> cruelty, he then proceeded to invest the city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAARLEM">Haarlem</a>. Fully convinced of the miseries that waited their surrender, this city stood an obstinate siege; and nothing less than the inflexible and persevering spirit of Alva could have opposed difficulties almost insurmountable. Dispairing of success, Frederick was at one time disposed to raise the siege, but the stern reproaches of his father urged him on; and at length the inhabitants, overcome with fatigue and resistance, surrendered. The victorious Frederick gave tolerable conditions to the town; but his cruel father arriving on the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> after the surrender, sacrificed numerous victims, who had been led to expect mercy, and satiated his vengeance to the full. Their next attack was upon Alkmaar; but the spirit of desperate resistance was raised to such a height in the breasts of the Hollanders, that the Spanish veterans were repulsed with great loss, and Frederick constrained reluctantly to retire. Alva now resolved to try his fortune by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and with great labour and expense fitted out a powerful fleet, and proceeded to attack the Zeelanders, but was entirely defeated, and the commander taken prisoner. About the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the prince of Orange proceeded to attack the town of Gertruydenburg. Alva's feeble state state of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> disasters induced him to solicit his recall from the government of the Low Countries; a measure which, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, was not displeasing to Philip, who was now resolved to make trial of a milder administration. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1573, that devoted country was freed from the presence and oppressions of the duke of Alva, who, accompanied by his son, returning home, gave out the inglorious boast, that he had, during the course of six years, besides the multitudes destroyed in battle and massacred after victory, configned 18,000 persons to the executioner. Requiem, who succeeded him in the command, in his first act of administration, pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his insolent effigies at Antwerp, so that nothing might remain of him in that much injured country but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of his injustice and cruelty. Returning from this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of oppression and blood, he was treated for some time with great distinction by his master. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, however, soon overtook the crimes of Alva: for his son having debauched one of the king's attendants, under <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, he was committed to prison; and being aided in his escape by his father, and married by him to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> of his own, this procured Alva's banishment from court, and confinement in the castle of Uzeda. He remained two years in this disgraceful situation, until the success of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a> Antonio, in assuring the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, determined Philip to turn his eyes towards a person, in whose fidelity and abilities he could on this occasion most confide. A secretary was instantly despatched to Alva, to make inquiries concerning the state of his health, and whether or not it was sufficiently vigorous to undertake the command of an army. The aged chief returned an answer full of loyal zeal, and was immediately appointed to the supreme command in Portugal. It is a singular fact, however, that the enlargement and elevation of Alva was not followed by forgiveness. It is a characteristic mark of the unrelenting temper of Philip, and, at the same time, a noble testimony to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and loyalty of Alva, that although placed in this important trust, he did not procure his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>. In 1581, Alva entered Portugal, defeated Antonio, drove him from the kingdom, and soon reduced the whole under the subjection of Philip. Entering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, he seized an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and with their accumulated violence and rapacity, he suffered his soldiers to sack the suburbs and vicinity. It is reported, that Alva being requested to give an account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> expended on that occasion, he sternly replied, "If the king asks me for an account, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> make him a statement of kingdoms preferred or conquered, of signal victories, of successful sieges, and of sixty years <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>." Philip deemed it proper to make no farther inquiries. Alva, however, did not enjoy the honours and rewards of his last expedition, for in 1582, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 74, he was removed by death to the impartial tribunal of heaven, to receive the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> rewards of his iniquitous life. The actions already enumerated give such an ample idea of his character, that little more is necessary to complete it. In him a variety of extremes concentrated. Some of the best qualities of a commander were blended with some of the worst that ever existed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or in a general. The Spanish severity, little tempered by the spirit of generosity, appeared in all its horrible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFORMITY">deformity</a> in Alva. A strict impartial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> was his greatest military virtue, and vanity was his greatest weakness. In consequence of this strict discipline, he sometimes punished the unlicensed barbarities of his soldiers; and there is an instance recorded, that when his favourite son Frederick, thinking he could attack the prince of Orange with advantage, sent a request to his father for permission, he received a stern reprimand, for presuming to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his judgment on a point already determined by his superior, with a threatening in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of repetition. (Gen. Bage.)

ALVA DE TORMES

Pages 381-381

a considerable town in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Leon, and territory of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a>, with a very handsome castle. It is seated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Tormes. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 1'. N. Lat. 41° 0'.

ALVAH

Pages 383-383

the wood wherewith Moses sweetened the waters of Marah, Exod. ch. xv. ver. 25.—The name of this wood is not found in Scripture; but the Mahometans give it that of akab, and pretend to trace its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> from the patriarchs before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. Josephus on the contrary, says, that Moses used the wood which he found next lying before him.

ALVARES DE LUNA

Pages 383-384
treasurer, and a great favourite of John II. king of Castile, was famous for the prodigious ascendancy he gained over this prince, and for the punishment which at length overtook him. He was a natural son of Don Alvaro de Luna, lord of Canete in Arragon, and of a woman of infamous character. He was born in 1388, and named Peter; but Pope Benedict XIII., who was charmed with his wit though yet a child, changed Peter to Alvares. He was introduced to court in 1408, and made a gentleman of the bedchamber to King John, with whom he grew into the highest favour. In 1427 he was obliged to retire: the courtiers exerted all their endeavours to ruin him: they complained, that a man of no military skill, of no virtues whatever, should by mere artifice and dissimulation, be advanced to the highest authority; and they could not bear, that by the affluence of a few upstart men, whom he had raised and fixed to his interest, he should reign as absolutely as if he were king. They prevailed against him, and Alvares was banished from court a year and a half: but this was the greatest affliction imaginable to the king; who showed all marks of distress the moment he was removed from his presence, and now thought and spoke of nothing but Alvares. He was therefore recalled; and, being invested with his usual authority, revenged himself severely upon his enemies, by persuading the king to banish them. Of the 45 years he spent at court, he enjoyed for 30 of them to entire an ascendancy over the king, that nothing could be done without his express orders: nay, it is related by Mariana, that the king could not change an officer or servant, or even his clothes or diet, without the approbation of Alvares. In short he wanted nothing to complete his grandeur but the name of king: he had all the places in the kingdom at his disposal; he was master of the treasury, and by bounties had so gained the hearts of the subjects, that the king, though his eyes were now opened, and his affections sufficiently turned against him, durst not complain. But the day of reckoning was approaching, and at length he was seized; yet not directly, openly, and violently, but with some of that management which upon a similar occasion was formerly employed by Tiberius against Sejanus. During his confinement, he made several Alvares, several attempts to speak to the king in person; but not being able to effect this, he sent the following letter, from which, as well as from the rest of Alvarez's history, all court favourites may draw abundant matter for edification and instruction. "Sir, it is five and forty years since I was admitted into your service. I do not complain of the rewards I have received: they were greater than my merits or expectation, as I shall not deny. There was but one thing wanting to complete my happiness; and that was, to have fixed proper limits in time to this great fortune of mine. While, instead of choosing retirement, after the example of the greatest men, I still continued in the employment, which I thought not only my duty, but necessary for your interest, I fell into this misfortune. It is very hard that I should be deprived of liberty, when I have risked life and fortune more than once to restore it to you. Grief prevents me from laying more. I know that the Deity is provoked against me by my fins; but it will be sufficient for me, if his anger is appeased by the calamities I now suffer. I can no longer bear that prodigious mass of riches, which it was wrong in me to have heaped together. I should willingly resign them, but that every thing I have is in your power; and I am denied the opportunity of showing mankind, that you have raised a person to the height of greatness, who can contain wealth as well as procure it, and give it back to him from whom he received it. But I desire you in the strongest terms, that, as I was obliged, by the laws of the treasury, to raise 10,000 or 12,000 crowns by methods I ought not to have taken, you will restore them to the persons from whom they were extorted. If you will not grant this on account of the services I have done, yet I think it necessary to be done from the reason of the thing." This letter, however, produced no effect in his favour: Alvares was tried, and condemned to lose his head. After condemnation, he was removed to Valladolid; and having confessed himself, and received the sacrament, he was carried upon a mule to the market-place, in the middle of which a large scaffold was erected. Mounting the scaffold, he paid reverence to the cross, and presently gave his hat and signet to his page, saying, "These are the last gifts you will ever receive from me." He then submitted himself to the axe with the utmost intrepidity.

ALVAREZ

Pages 384-384

Francis, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and almoner to Emanuel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, flourished about the beginning of the 16th century. He was sent <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from Portugal to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>; and after a residence of six years in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, returned with letters of friendship from David to Juan, who had succeeded Emanuel, and of submission to Pope Clement VII. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, in the year 1523, he gave a narrative of his expedition to the pope, in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. In the year 1540, he published the relation of his journey in one volume folio, in the Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. He gives a plain and accurate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this empire; and we are indebted to him for the first of the kind that ever published. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was translated into Latin, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of De Fide, Regione, Moribus Ethiopum, by Damien Goez, a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and it has often been reprinted and translated into other languages. The information of Alvares is not, however, to be received with implicit <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, because he does not always speak from his own observation, and he frequently exaggerates. (Dict. Hist.)

ALVEARIUM

Pages 384-384

in Anatomy, the bottom of the concha, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hollow of the outer <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>.

ALVEARIUM ALSO

Pages 384-384

M also signifies a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a>-hive. The word is formed of alveus, "a channel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> cavity;" in allusion to the alveoli or cells in bee-hives. Some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> also the word alvearium for a bee-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, more usually called among us apiary. ALVEARIUM is sometimes also used figuratively, to denote a collection; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, alvearium amounts to much the same with what we otherwise called the faurus, cornucopia, or the like. Vinc. Boreus has published an alvearium of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

ALVEOLUS

Pages 384-384

in Anatomy, the sockets in the jaws wherein the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are fixed. Some writers speak of teeth growing without alveoli. Pliny mentions a person who had a tooth in his palate. Eustachius relates, that he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who at 60 had a tooth growing out of the middle of his fauces. Holler gives an instance of a person whose teeth were of a piece with his jaws, without any insertion into alveoli.

ALVIANO

Pages 384-385

Bartholomew, a Venetian general, flourished in the beginning of the 16th century. His talents were well calculated for the conduct of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> affairs, and in an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, raised him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation. In the year 1508, he gained such signal victories over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Maximilian, that he was decreed triumphal honours by the republic. During the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, he was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in command along with <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Pritigliano. It was, however, unfavourable to the cause in which they had engaged, that the tempers of the two commanders were very different. The commander in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> was hesitating and cautious; the other was bold and intrepid. Alviano commanded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REAR_GUARD">rear-<a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> at the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Aignadel, and after displaying the greatest exertions of valour, was wounded, overpowered, and at last taken prisoner. An increasing tribute was paid to the military talents of Alviano; for after the Venetians had become the allies of France, he was intrusted with the command of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. When the emperor attacked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, he defended it against him, and displayed numerous acts of valour in repelling the imperial troops. But the current of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> life runs unequally smooth on its attendance upon any character; for he lost the great battle of La Motte, in which, however, his exertions were so conspicuous, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> gave him the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> assurance of the continuance of their esteem. Fortune, however, soon became propitious to this great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and he defeated the enemy in Friuli. In the desperate battle of Marignano, he afforded such timely aid to Francis I. that it greatly contributed to his success. But the most vigorous gorous <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> must one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> yield to the force of constant exertions, and the most incessant fatigue; he had incurred such hardships in superintending the works at the siege of Brescia, that he was seized with a fever, of which he died at the advanced <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of sixty. His character stands <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the annals of military fame. By strict observance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, and a profuse liberality to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, he secured their esteem. As an unequivocal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this, they kept his body unburied twenty-five days, carrying it about with them during their marches, with all funeral pomp. His loss was deeply regretted by the state, and, as a proof thereof, his body was buried at the public <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, his unprovided family was supported by a liberal pension, and his daughters were portioned by the state. (Gen. Biog.)

ALYSSUM

Pages 387-387

Alyssom, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Alysoides, Madwort; (from ἀλεύω, to be mad; because it was believed to have the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of curing madness). See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ALYTARCHA

Pages 387-387

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Antioch in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, who, in the games instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods, presided over the officers who carried rods to clear away the crowd and keep order. In the Olympic games, the aytarches had the same command, and obliged every person to preserve order and decency.

ALZIRA

Pages 387-387

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALENCIA">Valencia</a>, seated on the river Xucar. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 20. N. Lat. 39. 10.

AMABYR

Pages 387-387

a barbarous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which formerly prevailed in several parts of England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, being a sum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> paid to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> when a maid was married within his lordship. The word is old British, and signifies "the price of virginity." AMACK. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMAK">Amak</a>.

AMADABAT

Pages 387-387

a corruption from Ahmedabad, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ahmed's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> (so called from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of that name); a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous city of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guzerat. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72. 12. N. Lat. 23. 0. Amadabat was formerly called Guzerat; and by Shah Jehan nicknamed Gheraluddin, or "the habitation of dust," because it was much incommode therewith. It was the seat of the Guzerat kings, as it is now of the Mogul governor. The city stands in a beautiful plain, and is watered by the little river Sabremetti, which, though not deep, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of rains overflows the plains prodigiously. The walls are built with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> and brick, flanked at certain distances with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> round towers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>. It has twelve gates; and, including the suburbs, is about four miles and a half long. The streets are wide. The Meydan Shah, or king's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, is 700 paces long, and 400 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, planted round with trees. On the west side is the castle, well walled with free stone, and as spacious as a little city; but its inward appearance is not conformable to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> magnificence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANSERAI">caravanserai</a> is on the south of the square, and its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornament. Near the Meydan also is the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, whose apartments are richly ornamented; and in the midst of the city is the English <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-FACTORY">factory</a>, where they purchase fine chintz, calicoes, and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> merchandise. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is so full of gardens flooded with fruit trees, that from an eminence it looks like a wood. The Hindoos have here an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> for sick beasts, and another for sick birds, which they take great care of. According to some late accounts, this city is little inferior to the best in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and is thought to yield ten times as much revenue as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURAT">Surat</a>.

AMADAN

Pages 387-387
or Hamadan, a town of Persia, between Taurus and Ilpahan. E. Long. 47. 4. N. Lat. 35. 15. It is seated at the foot of a mountain, where there are a great many springs, which water the adjacent country. The extent of the city is very large; but there are a great many waste spots within it, as well as cultivated land. The houses are built of brick hardened in the sun, and have but a very indifferent aspect. There is but one tolerable street; and that is where stuffs, garments, and the like, are exposed to sale: it is straight, long, and wide; and the shops are very well furnished. The adjacent parts are fruitful in corn and rice, insomuch that the neighbouring provinces are supplied from hence. It is said to enjoy a very salubrious air; but the cold in winter is intense. The Armenians have a church in this town; but it is a very ill contrived structure. The Jews have a synagogue near a tomb, where they pretend Esther and Mordecai lie interred. To this place they come in pilgrimage from several parts of the Levant. About a league from Amadan, there is a mountain called Nalliana, which abounds with all sorts of curious herbs. In the spring, people flock to this mountain from all parts to recover their health, by sucking in the salutary effluvia with their breath. Amadan is a very ancient city. It is said to have been destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, and rebuilt by Darius, who brought hither all his riches. The kings of Persia frequently retired to this place on account of its delightful situation; for which reason it obtained the name of the Royal City. It was conquered by the caliph Othman, and narrowly escaped being destroyed by Jenghiz Khan in 1220. It had then strong walls and a good castle, which are now in ruins. Its present beauty consists in its gardens and springs.

AMADEUS IX.

Pages 389-389

Amadeus and his successors, in memory of this signal victory. The explanation of this motto is said to be Fortitudo ejus Rhodium tenuit.—"His valour kept Rhodes." For this important service the grand master conferred on him the grant of a palace at Lyons. Andronicus the emperor of the east had married his daughter; and in order to promote the views of his son-in-law, Amadeus took a journey to Avignon to persuade Pope John XXII. to preach a crusade in favour of Andronicus. In the year 1323 the famous Amadeus died at that place. Deep penetration, keen discernment, consummate prudence, great valour, together with no small portion of the religious superstition of his time, appear to have been the reigning features in his character. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) Amadeus VIII. count of Savoy, in 1391, succeeded his father Amadeus VII. With the large sum of 4,000 florins of gold he purchased the country of Genevois from its last earl. Anxious to extend his territories, he purchased the city of Rumilly, upon the lake of Geneva, from the widow of the count of Genevois, and thus the house of Savoy became so illustrious that the emperor Sigismund erected Savoy into a duchy in the year 1426. Historians relate, that he assisted John Paleologus against the duke of Milan, who endeavoured to wrest from him the duchy of Montferrat. Deeply sensible of the services which he had received, Paleologus not only resigned to the duke, Chivas, Brandis, and several other estates, but submitted to hold all the marquisate of Montferrat as a fief from the house of Savoy. These fortunate acquisitions of territory were not yet limited; for upon the marriage of his daughter with Philip Maria, duke of Milan, he received Vercelli, and about the same time the count of Crefcentino submitted to become his feudatory. In his ambitious pursuit, he laid claim to the sovereignty of the city of Geneva; but that claim, though enforced by the pope, was rejected by the citizens with disdain, and the emperor Sigismund taking it under his protection, declared it an imperial city. After such an extensive acquisition of dominion, and amassing such sums of money, he formed the singular scheme of abandoning his throne and family; and for that purpose retired to a religious house at a place called Ripaille. But although he resigned the dukedom of Savoy to his eldest son Lewis, and made his youngest son Philip, count of Genevois; yet their honours were merely nominal, for he constrained them to live on a very scanty allowance, while he in his retirement received all the revenues, and collected such sums of money that he is said to have purchased the papal honours. During the previous part of his life having adopted great sanctity of manners, the motives for his retirement were generally reckoned religious; but what was the astonishment of mankind to behold the seat of his hermitage become the habitation of every rare delicacy, and of the most refined luxury. The local situation of the place was truly delightful, and was enriched with every thing that could afford gratification to the senses; and his residence confirmed some of his most intimate friends, along with 20 faithful servants, who were the guardians of his voluptuous secrets. Neither did he assume a religious habit, but wore purple robes, and upon his mantle was embroidered a golden cross. His table groaned under the weight of luxurious dainties, and the most excellent music cheered the daily feast; in short, such was the voluptuousness of that place, that in the French language the phrase, faire ripaille, signifies to make exquisite good cheer. He instituted a secular knighthood in that place under the appellation of St Maurice. The brethren assumed the name of hermits, wore beards, and excluded women from their community; and in other respects composed the character of decent epicures. When he obtained the papal dignity, and was crowned by the cardinal of Arles at Basil, all Europe was filled with astonishment in consequence of his elevation; for he had never entered into holy orders. But he had found means to remove every objection, the council confirmed his election, and with pretended reluctance he put on the pontifical ornaments, and was consecrated in the church of St Maurice. It seemed good to Amadeus to assume the title of Felix V. As might naturally be expected in such circumstances, the papal dignity was severely contested between him and Eugenius; and notwithstanding all the importunities of the council, the emperor refused to acknowledge his elevation. This religious dispute involved all Europe in contention. Historians relate that Germany remained neutral, and France, England, Italy, Spain, and Hungary, declared for Eugenius; but Arragon, Poland, and Bretagne recognized the council only; at the same time that Savoy, Switzerland, Basil, Strasbourg, Pomerania, and one of the duchies of Bavaria, recognized Felix. The emperor Frederick III. held a council at Frankfort, before which both the popes urged their respective rights by means of deputies. This attempt, however, to regain peace to Europe was unsuccessful; therefore the emperor repaired to the vicinity of Basil, and had a personal interview with Felix. The mind of Amadeus was now so confirmed in the enjoyment of pleasure, that he had again returned to his favourite retreat; and after the fathers of the council had frequently solicited him in vain to reside at Basil, he prevailed upon them to remove to Lyons, which was near the seat of his pleasures. During the contest, Eugenius had excommunicated Felix, the council, and several of the German princes, so that the whole church was then filled with confusion and disorder. The death of Eugenius, however, terminated the struggle; for upon his death the cardinals at Rome elected Thomas de Sarzan, who assumed the name of Nicholas V. In this situation of affairs, Amadeus deemed it prudent to enter into a negotiation for the resignation of his papal crown. In this transaction he displayed the profoundest policy and address, which induced Nicholas to annul all that Eugenius had done to his dishonour, or that of his associates; to confirm the determination of the council of Basil to appoint him perpetual apostolical legate in Savoy, Piedmont, and the other places of his own dominions, and even added to these the honour of being bishop of Basil, Lausanne, Strasbourg, Amadeus Strasburg, and Constance. Nor did his vanity forsake him even in this political transaction, for he provided that he should continue to wear the pontifical dress unless in very few particulars. In order to gratify the same haughty disposition, he stipulated that he should not be obliged to go to Rome, to attend any general council; and that when he had occasion to approach the pope, he should rise to receive him, and instead of kissing his toe, he should be permitted to kiss his cheek. Amadeus retired to Lausanne, and died there at the age of 60, in the year 1451. As the time in which he lived is fertile in memorable events, so the character of Amadeus was one of the most distinguished of his time. The versatility of his genius has led writers to differ in the delineation of his character. Some have represented him as a person of singular sanctity of manners, and possessed of uncommon moderation and virtue; others have represented him as a confirmed bigot, and a violent enthusiast; and a third class of authors have magnified his talents far above the general standard, and extolled him as one of the most accomplished princes in Europe. His real character appears to be a compound of extravagancies, in which virtue, genius, caprice, and vanity were blended. (Mod. Univ. Hist.) AMADEUS IX., count of Savoy, succeeded his father Lewis, in his dominion and honours. The prince who exerts his talents to promote the happiness of his subjects, is worthy of more fame than the prince who increases the number of his subjects by unjust and unnecessary wars. In this view Amadeus IX. deserves a place in the annals of his nation. His bodily constitution was weak, and he was afflicted with the falling-sickness, yet, in consequence of his piety, virtue, benevolence, and justice, he was named the Happy. The clemency of his temper was such that he readily pardoned those who offended him, and in few instances was he induced to punish. In his character, however, the virtue of benevolence shone with peculiar splendour among the other virtues of the Christian. A foreign minister one day used the freedom to inquire at Amadeus, if he kept any hounds. The duke replied, "a great number, and you shall see them to-morrow at noon." The minister attended at that hour in expectation of seeing a numerous pack of hounds; but the duke led him to a window which looked into an extensive square, and directing his view to a multitude of poor people eating and drinking, he exclaimed, "These are my hounds with whom I go in chase of heaven." In all these pious and benevolent labours he was seconded by his wife Isolande of France. When one of his parsimonious courtiers reminded him that he would spend all his revenues, he generously replied, "Here is the collar of my order, let them sell it and relieve my people." In the seventh year of his reign, and the thirty-seventh of his life, he died universally lamented by all his loyal subjects, in the year 1472. In high esteem for his virtuous qualities, his subjects conferred on him the appellation of The Blest. (Mod. Univ. Hist.)

AMADIA

Pages 389-389

AMADIA, a trading town of Asia, in Cilicia, belonging to the Turks; seated on a high mountain. E. Long. 43. 1. N. Lat. 36. 25.

AMADOW

Pages 389-389

AMADOW, a kind of black match, tinder, or touchwood, which comes from Germany. It is made of a sort of large mushrooms or spongy excrescences,

AMADOWRY

Pages 389-389

Amadowry which commonly grow on old trees, especially oaks, ash, and firs. This substance being boiled in common water, and afterwards dried and well beaten, is then put into a strong ley prepared with saltpetre, after which it is again put to dry in an oven. The drug-gifts fell this match wholesale in France, and several hawkers retail it. Some give to the amadow the name of pyrotechnical sponge, because of its aptness to take fire. AMADOWRY, a kind of cotton which comes from Alexandria by the way of Marseilles.

AMAIN

Pages 389-389

AMAIN, in the Sea Language, a term importing to lower something at once. Thus, to strike amain, is to lower or let fall the topsails; to wave amain, is to make a signal, by waving a drawn sword, or the like, as a demand that the enemy strike their topsails.

AMAK

Pages 389-389

AMAK, a small island in the Baltic sea, near Copenhagen, from which it is separated by a canal over which there is a drawbridge. Amak is about four miles long and two broad; and is chiefly peopled by the descendants of a colony from East Friesland, to whom the island was configned by Christian II., at the request of his wife Elizabeth, sister of Charles V., for the purpose of supplying her with vegetables, cheese, and butter.
