At these feasts they sacrificed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a> a sow, a sheep, and a bull or heifer, whence they took

AMBASSADOR

Pages 401-402
or Embassador, a public minister sent from one sovereign prince, as a representative of his person, to another. Ambassadors are either ordinary or extraordinary. Ambassadors in ordinary, is he who constantly resides in the court of another prince, to maintain a good understanding, and look to the interest of his master. Till about two hundred years ago, ambassadors in ordinary were not heard of; all, till then, were ambassadors extraordinary; that is, such as are sent on some particular occasion, and who retire as soon as the affair is dispatched. By the law of nations, none under the quality of a sovereign prince can send or receive an ambassador. At Athens, ambassadors mounted the pulpit of the public orators, and there opened their commissions, acquainting the people with their errand. At Rome, they were introduced to the senate, and delivered their commissions to the fathers. Ambassadors should never attend any public solemnities, as marriages, funerals, &c. unless their matters have some interest therein; nor must they go into mourning on any occasions of their own, because they represent the person of their prince. By the civil law, the moveable goods of an ambassador, which are accounted an accession to his person, cannot be seized on, neither as a pledge, nor for payment of a debt, nor by order or execution of judgment, nor by the king's or state's leave where he resides, as some conceive; for all actions ought to be far from an ambassador, as well that which toucheth his necessities, as his person: if therefore, he hath contracted any debt, he is to be called upon kindly; and if he refuses, then letters of request are to go to his master. Nor can any of the ambassador's domestic servants that are registered in the secretaries of state's office be arrested in person or goods; if they are, the process shall be void, and the parties suing out and executing it shall suffer and be liable to such penalties and corporal punishment as the lord chancellor or either of the chief justices shall think fit to inflict. Yet ambassadors cannot be defended when they commit anything against that state, or the person of the prince, with whom they reside; and if they are guilty of treason, felony, &c. or any other crime against the law of nations, they lose the privilege of an ambassador, and may be subject to punishment as private aliens.

AMBER

Pages 402-404

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, hard, semipellucid, bituminous substance of a particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in medicine and in several of the arts. It has been called ambra by the Arabians, and eleostrum by the Greeks. Amber has been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute in the world from the earliest times. Many years before Christ it was in esteem as a medicine; and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, Aeschylus, and others, have commended its virtues. In the times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, it became in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> esteem as a gem; and in the luxurious reign of Nero, immense quantities of it were brought to Rome, and used for ornamenting works of various kinds. The most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this substance is, that when rubbed it draws <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attracts other bodies to it; and, this, it is observed, it does even to those substances which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> thought it had an antipathy to; as oily bodies, drops of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> sweat, &c. Add, that, by the friction it is brought to yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> pretty copiously in the dark; whence it is reckoned among the native phosphors. The property which amber possesses of attracting light bodies was very anciently observed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THALES">Thales</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILETUS">Miletus</a>, 600 years before Christ, concluded from hence, that it was animated. But the first person who expressly mentions this substance is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOPHRASTUS">Theophrastus</a>, about the year 300 before Christ. The attractive property of amber is likewise occasionally taken notice of by Pliny and other later naturalists, particularly by Gellius, Kemelm Digby, and Sir Thomas <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">Brown</a>; but it was generally apprehended that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> was peculiar to amber and jet, and perhaps <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, till Gilbert published his treatise de Magnete, in the year 1600. From ἀμβρόσια, the Greek name for amber, is derived the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, which is now very extensively applied, not only to the power of attracting light bodies inherent in amber, but to other similar powers, and their various effects in whatever bodies they reside, or to whatever bodies they may be communicated. Amber assumes all figures in the ground; that of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, an almond, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, &c. In amber there have been found to be letters found very well formed; and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> and Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>.—Within some pieces, leaves, insects, &c. have likewise been found included; which seems to indicate either that the amber was originally in a fluid state, or that having been exposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> it was once softened, and rendered susceptible of the leaves, insects, &c. which came in its way. The latter of these suppositions seems the more agreeable to the phenomenon; because those insects, &c. are never found in the centre of the pieces of amber, but always near the surface. It is observed by the inhabitants of those places where amber is produced, that all animals, whether terrestrial, aerial, or aquatic, are extremely fond of it, and that pieces of it are frequently found in their excrements. The bodies of insects, found buried in amber, are viewed with admiration by all the world; but of the most remarkable of these, many are to be suspected as counterfeit, the great price at which beautiful specimens of this kind fell, having tempted ingenious cheats to introduce animal bodies in such artful manners, into seemingly whole pieces of amber, that it is not easy to detect the fraud. Of those insects which have been originally enclosed in amber, some are plainly seen to have struggled hard for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, and even to have left their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> behind them in the attempt; it being no unusual thing to see, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of amber that contains a stout beetle, the animal wanting one, or perhaps two of its legs; and those legs left in different places, nearer that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the mass from which it has travelled. This also may account for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> accident of finding legs or or wings of flies, without the rest of their bodies, in pieces of amber; the insects having, when entangled in the yet soft and viscid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, escaped, at the expense of leaving those limbs behind them. Drops of clear water are sometimes also preserved into it while soft, and preserved by its hardening round them. Beautiful leaves of a pinnated structure, resembling some of the ferns, or maidenhairs, have been found in some pieces; but these are rare, and the specimens of great value. Mineral substances are also found at times lodged in masses of amber. Some of the pompous collections of the German princes boast of specimens of native <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver in masses of amber; but as there are many substances of the marcasite, and other kinds, that have all the glittering appearance of gold and silver, it is not to be too hastily concluded, that these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> are really lodged in these beds of amber. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> is found in various shapes immersed in amber; and as it is often seen eroded, and sometimes in the state of vitriol, it is not impossible but that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, and the other metals, may be also sometimes immersed in it in the same state; hence the bluish and greenish colours, frequently found in the recent pieces of amber, may be owing, like the particles of the gem colours, to these metals; but as the gems, by their dense texture, always retain their colours, this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> and more lax bitumen usually loses what it gets of this kind by keeping some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. Small pebbles, grains of sand, and fragments of other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, are also not unfrequently found immersed in amber. Naturalists have been greatly divided as to the origin of this substance, and what class of bodies it belongs to; some referring it to the vegetable, others to the mineral, and some even to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Pliny describes it as "a resinous juice, oozing from aged pines and firs (others say from poplars, whereof there are whole forests on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>), and discharged thence into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, where undergoing some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, it is thrown, in this form, upon the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> very low: he adds, that it was hence the ancients gave it the denomination succinum; from succus, juice. Some suppose amber a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> substance. Prussia, say they, and the other countries which produce amber, are moistened with a bituminous juice, which mixing with the vitriolic salts abounding in those places, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of these salts fix its fluidity, whence it congeals; and the result of that congelation makes what we call amber; which is more or less pure, transparent, and firm, as these parts of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and bitumen are more or less pure, and are mixed in this or that proportion. Mr Brydone, in his tour to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, says, that the river Gearetta, formerly celebrated by the poets under the name of Simetus, throws up near its mouth great quantities of amber. He mentions also a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> amber, not uncommon there, made, as he was told, from <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPAL">copal</a>, but very different from the natural. According to Hartman, amber is formed of a bitumen, mixed with vitriol and other salts. But though this were allowed him in regard to the fossil amber, many dispute whether the sea amber be so produced. It is, however, apparent, that all amber is of the same origin, and probably that which is found in the sea has been washed thither out of the cliffs; though Hartman thinks it very possible, that some of it may be formed in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> under the sea, and be washed up thence. The sea amber is usually finer to the eye than the fossil; but the reason is, that it is deprived of that coarse coat with which the other is covered while in the earth. Upon the whole, it seems generally agreed upon, that amber is a true bitumen of a fossil origin. In a late volume of the Journal de Physique, however, we find it affected by Dr Girtanner to be an animal product, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> or wax formed by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a> called by Linnaeus formica rufa. These ants, our author informs us, inhabit the old pine forests, where they sometimes form hills about six feet in diameter: and it is generally in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> forests, or in places where they have been, that fossil amber is found. This substance is not hard as that which is taken up in the sea at Prussia, and which is well known to naturalists. It has the consistence of honey or of half melted wax, but it is of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> like common amber; it gives the same product by chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a>, and it hardens like the other when it is suffered to remain some time in a solution of common salt. This accounts for the insects that are so often found inclosed in it. Among these insects ants are always the most prevailing; which tends farther, Mr Girtanner thinks, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>. Amber, then, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, is nothing but a vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> rendered concrete by the acid of ants, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as wax is nothing but an oil hardened by the acid of bees; a fact incontrovertibly proved, we are told, since Mr Metherie has been able to make artificial wax by mixing oil of olives with the nitrous acid, and which wax is not to be distinguished from the natural. There are several indications which discover where amber is to be found. The surface of the earth is there covered with a soft scaly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and vitriol in particular always abounds there, which is sometimes found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, sometimes reduced into a matter like melted glass, and sometimes figured like petrified wood. Amber of the finest kind has been found in England. It is frequently thrown on the shores of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, and many other places, and found even in our clay pits; the pits dug for tile-clay between Tyburn and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KENNINGTON">Kennington</a> gravel pits, and that behind St George's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a> at Hyde-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> corner, have afforded fine specimens. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILESIA">Silesia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, are famous for the amber dug up there at this time. Germany affords great quantities of amber, as well dug up from the bowels of the earth, as toiled about on the shores of the sea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> there. <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEISSEN">Meissen</a>, Sweden, and many other places in this tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, abound with it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> has afforded, at different times, several quantities of fossil amber; and the shores of the Baltic abound with it. But the countries lying on the Baltic afford it in the greatest abundance of all; and of these the most plentiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is Prussia, and the next is Pomerania. Prussia was, as early as the time of Theodoric the Goth, famous for amber; for this substance coming into great repute with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, some natives of Prussia, who were about his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, offered their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to go to their own country, where that substance, they said, was produced, and bring back great stores of it. They accordingly did so; and from this time Prussia had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to be called the country of amber, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, which had before undeservedly that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. This article alone brings his Prussian majesty a revenue of $26,000 dollars annually. The amber of Prussia is not only found on the sea coasts, but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGGING">digging</a>; and though that of Pomerania is generally brought from the shores, yet people who dig, on different occasions, in the very heart of the country, at times find amber. Junker describes, after Neumann, the Prussian amber <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, which are the richest known. First, At the surface of the earth is found a stratum of sand. Immediately under this sand is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of clay, filled with small flints of about an inch diameter each. Under this clay lies a stratum of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> earth or turf, filled with fossil wood, half decomposed and bituminous; this stratum is extended upon a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of minerals, containing little metal except iron, which are consequently pyrites. Lastly, Under this bed the amber is found scattered about in pieces, or sometimes accumulated in heaps. Amber has a subacid resinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and fragrant aromatic smell, especially when distilled. It differs from the other bituminous substances in this, that it yields by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> a volatile acid salt, which none of the others do; otherwise it affords the same sort of principles as them, viz. an acid phlegm, an oil which gradually becomes thicker as the distillation is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; and when the operation is finished, there remains a black caput mortuum in the retort. When boiled in water, it neither softens nor undergoes any sensible alteration. Exposed to the fire in an open vessel, it melts into a black mass very like a bitumen: It is partly soluble in spirit of wine, and likewise in some essential oils; but it is with difficulty that the expressed ones are brought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon it. The stronger sorts of fixed alkaline lixivias almost totally dissolve it. This substance is principally of two colours, white and yellow. The white is the most esteemed for medicinal purposes, as being the most odoriferous, and containing the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of volatile salt; though the yellow is most valued by those who manufacture beads and other toys with it, by reason of its transparency. Amber is the basis of all varnishes, by solution in the ways described under the article <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">Varnish</a>. Amber, when it has once been melted, irrecoverably loses its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>. There have been some, however, who pretended they had an art of melting some small pieces of amber into a mass, and constituting large ones of them: but this seems such another undertaking as the making of gold; all the trials that have yet been made by the most curious experimenters, proving, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> which is necessary to melt amber is sufficient to destroy it. (Phil. Trans. No 248. p. 25.) Could amber indeed be distilled without impairing its transparency, or one large mass be made of it by uniting several small ones, it is easy to see what would be the advantages of such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. The art of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a> might possibly be also carried to a great height by this, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we could preserve the human corpse in a transparent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of amber, as the bodies of flies, spiders, grasshoppers, &c. are to a great perfection. Something of a substitute of this kind we have in fine rosin; which being distilled by heat, and the bodies of Ambertigris, small animals several times dipped in it, they are thus coated with colophony, that in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> resembles amber; but this must be kept from dust. Amber in substance has been much recommended as a nervous and cordial medicine; and alleged to be very efficacious in promoting the menstrual discharge, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the foetus and secundines in labour: but as in its crude state it is quite insoluble by our juices, it certainly can have very little effect on the animal system, and therefore it is now seldom given in substance. The forms in which amber is prepared are, A tincture, a salve, and an oil; the preparations and uses of which are described in the proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> under the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>. AMBER-Tree, the English name of a species of ANTHOSPERMUM.

AMBERG

Pages 404-404

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, with a good castle, ramparts, bastions, and deep ditches. It is seated near the confines of Franconia, on the river Wils. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> trade in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, which are found in the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. O. N. Lat. 49. 25. Anberg, a lofty mountain of East Gothland in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>. Near the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-WETTER">Wetter</a> lake on this mountain, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> has been found. On its top is the burying <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> kings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The spot is marked by a flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>.

AMBERGRIS

Pages 404-407

AMBERGREASE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> GREY-<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">AMBER</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, opaque, ash-coloured, fatty, inflammable substance, variegated like marble, remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, rugged, and uneven in its surface, and has a fragrant odour when heated. It does not effervescence with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>: it melts freely over the fire into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> rosin; and is hardly soluble in spirit of wine. It is found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, or the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, or in the sand near the sea coast; especially in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, on the sea coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, and that of Madagascar; on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, of the East Indies, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a>, and the Molucca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>: but most of the ambergris which is brought to England comes from the Bahama islands, from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>, &c. where it is found on the coast. It is also sometimes found in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of whales by the whale fisherman, always in lumps of various shapes and sizes, weighing from half an ounce to an hundred and more pounds. The piece which the Dutch East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> bought from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of Tydore, weighed 182 pounds. An American fisherman from Antigua found some years ago, about fifty-two leagues south-east from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDWARD">Windward</a> islands, a piece of ambergris in a whale which weighed about a hundred and thirty pounds, and sold for 500l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. There have been many different opinions concerning the origin of this substance. It has been supposed to be a fossil bitumen or naphtha, exuding out of the bowels of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> in a fluid form, and diffusing into the sea, where it hardens and floats on the surface. But having been frequently found in the bellies of whales, it has by others been considered as entirely an animal production. Clusius asserted it to be a phlegmatic secretion, or indurated Ambergris, indurated indigestible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the food, collected and found in the stomach of the whale, in the same manner as the Bezoars are found in the stomachs of other animals. In an account communicated by Paul <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUDLEY">Dudley</a>, Esq., in the 23rd volume of the Philosophical Transactions, the ambergris found in whales is represented as a kind of animal product, like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, and cafforeum, &c., secreted and collected in a particular bag or bladder, which is furnished with an excretory duct or canal, the spout of which runs tapering into and through the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENIS">penis</a>; and that this bag, which lies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> over the testicles, is almost full of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>-colored liquor, not quite so thick as <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, of the same smell as the balls of ambergris, which float and swim loofe in it; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and liquor may also be found in the canal of the penis; and that therefore ambergris is never to be found in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> only. But these circumstances are not only destitute of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, but also contrary to the laws of the animal economy: For, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, ambergris is frequently found in females as well as males; although that found in females is never in such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces, nor of so good a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, as what is found in males. Secondly, No person who has the least knowledge in anatomy or physiology, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ever believe that organized bodies, such as the beaks of the sepia, which are constantly found in ambergris taken out of the whale, can have been absorbed from the intestines by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACTEALS">lacteals</a> or lymphatics, and collected with the ambergris in the precluded bag above mentioned. Kämpfer, who has given us so many other faithful accounts in natural history, seems to come nearer the truth with regard to the origin of ambergris, when he says, that it is the dung of the whale; and that the Japanese for this reason call it kufira no fuu, i.e. whale's dung. This account, however, though founded on observation, has never obtained <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>; but has been considered rather as a fabulous story, with which the Japanese imposed upon him, who had himself no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> observation to prove the fact. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, therefore, remained a subject of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> doubt; and it was generally thought to be more probable, that ambergris, after having been swallowed and somehow or other changed in the stomach and bowels of the whale, was found among its excrements. But the most satisfactory account of the real origin of ambergris, is that given by Dr Swedlaur in the 73rd volume of the Philosophical Transactions, art. 15. We are told by all writers on ambergris, that sometimes claws and beaks of birds, feathers of birds, parts of vegetables, shells, fish, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of fish, are found in the middle of it, or variously mixed with it. Of a very large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pieces, however, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> examined, he found none that contained any such thing; though he allows that such substances may sometimes be found in it: but in all the pieces of any considerable size, whether found on the sea or in the whale, he constantly found a considerable quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spots, which, after the most careful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, appeared to be the beaks of the Sepia Ophiodon; and these beaks, he thinks, might be the substances which have hitherto been always mistaken for claws or beaks of birds, or for shells. The presence of these beaks in ambergris proves evi- Vol. I. Part II. Ambregris hook a whale of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, torpid, sickly, emaciated, or one that does not dung on being hooked, they immediately either cut up the above-mentioned protuberance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there be any, or they rip open its bowels from the orifice of the anus, and find the ambergris sometimes in one sometimes in different lumps, of generally from three to twelve and more inches in diameter, and from one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> to twenty or thirty pounds in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, at the distance of two, but most frequently of about six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> feet from the anus, and never higher up in the intestinal canal; which, according to their description, is in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the intestinum cæcum, hitherto mistaken for a peculiar bag made by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for the secretion and collection of this singular substance. That the part they cut open to come at the ambergris is no other than the intestinal canal is certain, because they constantly begin their incision at the anus, and find the cavity everywhere filled with the faeces of the whale, which from their colour and smell it is impossible for them to mistake. The ambergris found in the intestinal canal is not so hard as that which is found on the sea or sea coast, but soon grows hard in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>: when first taken out it has nearly the same colour, and the same disagreeable smell, though not so strong, as the more liquid dung of the whale has; but on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to the air, it by degrees not only grows grayish, and its surface is covered with a grayish dust like old chocolate, but it also loses its disagreeable smell, and, when kept for a certain length of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, acquires the peculiar odour which is so agreeable to most people. The gentlemen the Doctor conversed with confessed, that if they knew not from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> that ambergris thus found will in time acquire the above-mentioned qualities, they would by no means be able to distinguish ambergris from hard indurated faeces. This is so true, that whenever a whale voids its faeces upon being hooked, they look carefully to see if they cannot discover among the more liquid excrements (of which the whale discharges several barrels) some pieces floating on the sea, of a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> substance than the rest. These they take up and wash, knowing them to be ambergris. In considering whether there be any material <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the ambergris found upon the sea or sea coast, and that found in the bowels or among the dung of the whale, the Doctor refutes the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that all ambergris found in whales is of an inferior quality, and therefore much less in price. Ambergris, he observes, is only valued for its purity, lightness, compactness, colour, and smell. There are pieces of ambergris found on different coasts, which are of a very inferior quality; whereas there are often found in whales pieces of it of the first value; nay, several pieces found in the same whale, according to the above-mentioned qualities, are more or less valuable. All ambergris found in whales has at first, when taken out of the intestines, very near the same smell as the liquid excrements of that animal have; it has then also nearly the same blackish colour: they find it in the whale sometimes quite hard, sometimes rather softish, but never so liquid as the natural faeces of that animal. And it is a matter of fact, that after being taken out and kept in the air, all ambergris grows not only harder and whiter, but also loses by degrees its smell, and attains such an agreeable one, as that in general has which is found swimming upon the sea; therefore the goodness of ambergris seems rather to depend on its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. By being accumulated after a certain length of time in the intestinal canal, it seems even then to become of a whiter colour, and less ponderous, and to acquire its agreeable smell. The only reason why ambergris found floating on the sea generally possesses the above-mentioned qualities in a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, is because it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> older, and has been longer exposed to the air. It is more frequently found in males than females; the pieces found in females are in general smaller, and those found in males seem constantly to be larger and of a better quality; and therefore the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price in proportion to the size is not merely imaginary, but the rarity's sake, but in some respects well founded, because such large pieces appear to be of a greater age and possess the above-mentioned qualities in general in a higher degree of perfection than smaller pieces. It is known, that the sepia octopodia, or cuttle-fish, is the constant and natural food of the spermaceti whale, or phyceter macrocephalus. Of this the fishermen are so well persuaded, that whenever they discover any recent relics of it swimming on the sea, they conclude that a whale of this kind is, or has been, in that part. Another circumstance which corroborates the fact is, that the spermaceti whale on being hooked generally vomits up some remains of the sepia. Hence it is easy to account for the many beaks, or pieces of beaks, of the sepia found in all ambergris. The beak of the sepia is a black horny substance, and therefore passes undigested through the stomach into the intestinal canal, where it is mixed with the faeces; after which it is either evacuated with them, or if these latter be preternaturally retained, forms concretions with them, which render the animal sick and torpid, and produce an obilatation, which ends either in an abscess of the abdomen, as has been frequently observed, or becomes fatal to the animal; whence, in both the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, on the bursting of its belly, that hardened substance known under the name of ambergris, is found swimming on the sea or thrown upon the coast. From the preceding account, and his having constantly found the above-mentioned beaks of the sepia in all pieces of ambergris of any considerable size, Dr Swediaur concludes with great probability, that all ambergris is <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the bowels of the phyceter macrocephalus or spermaceti whale; and there mixed with the beaks of the sepia octopodia, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of that whale. He therefore defines ambergris to be the preternaturally hardened dung or faeces of the phyceter macrocephalus, mixed with some indigestible relics of its food. The opinion of Dr Swediaur, with regard to the origin of ambergris, has been confirmed by the information of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> J. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COFFIN">Coffin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of a ship employed in the southern whale fishery, given to a committee of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> in the year 1791. According to Mr Coffin's information, American ships had sometimes found small quantities of ambergris; but none, that he knew of, had ever been found by British ships. The quantity which he had brought home amounted to 362 ounces; and it was taken from the body of a female spermaceti whale on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, which was Ambergris was lean, sickly, and old; and yielded but a small proportion of oil. While the people were employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> up the blubber, ambergris was discovered coming from the fundament of the whale, and a piece of it was seen floating on the surface of the sea. More was observed in the same passage, and the rest was found in a bag a little below the passage and communicating with it. Mr Coffin supposes, that the sperm whale feeds almost wholly on the sepia or squid; for when the whale is dying a quantity of this fish, sometimes whole, sometimes in pieces, is thrown up. The bills of the squid were found, some on the outside adhering to it, and some mixed with it. The sperm whale, when struck, generally voids her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCREMENT">excrement</a>, and if she does not, Mr Coffin conjectures, that she has no ambergris; for he supposes, that the production of it is the cause or the effect of some disorder; and that it is most likely to be found in a sickly fish. The ambergris of the whale taken by Mr Coffin was mostly sold at 19s. 9d. per ounce; and a small part of it, when it was scarce, at 25s. It was bought partly for home consumption, and partly for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, Germany, and France. (Phil. Trans., vol. lxxxii.) The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of ambergris in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is now nearly confined to perfumery, though it has formerly been recommended in medicine by several eminent physicians. Hence the Effentia Ambrae Hoffmanni, Tinctura Regia Cod. Parisini, Trochisci de Ambra Ph. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WURTEMBERG">Wurtemberg</a>, &c. If we wish to see any medicinal effects from this substance, the Doctor observes, we must certainly not expect them from two or three grains, but give rather as many scruples of it for a dose; though even then, he thinks, there would not be reason to expect much effect from it, as he had himself taken of pure unadulterated ambergris in powder 30 grains at once without observing the least sensible effect from it. A sailor, however, who had the curiosity to try the effect of recent ambergris upon himself, took half an ounce of it melted upon the fire, and found it a good purgative; which proves that it is not quite an inert substance. In <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and part of Africa ambergris is not only used as a medicine and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>; but considerable use is also made of it in cookery, by adding it to several dishes as a spice. A great quantity of it is also constantly bought by the pilgrims who travel to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>; probably to offer it there, and make use of it in fumigations, in the same manner as frankincense is used in Catholic countries. The Turks make use of it as an aphrodisiac. Our perfumers add it to scented pills, candles, balls, bottles, gloves, and hairpowder; and its essence is mixed with pomatums, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, either alone or mixed with musk, &c. though its smell is to some persons extremely offensive. Ambergris may be known to be genuine by its fragrant scent when a hot <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> is thrust into it, and its melting like fat of an uniform consistence; whereas the counterfeit will not yield such a smell, nor prove of such a fat texture. One thing, however, is very remarkable, that this drug, which is the most sweet of all the perfumes, should be capable of being resembled in smell by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of one of the most odious of all stinks. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> found, that a vessel in which he had made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> digestion of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> faeces, acquired a very strong and perfect smell of ambergris, in so much that any one would have thought a great quantity of essence of ambergris had been made in it. The perfume was so strong and offensive, that the vessel was forced to be removed out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>.

AMBERT

Pages 407-407

a small town of France, in the department of Puy de <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">Dome</a>, formerly Lower Auvergne. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a small territory called Livradois. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">Paper</a> and playing <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, gambles, and woollen stuffs are manufactured here. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 15'. N. Lat. 45° 38'.

AMBETTUWAY

Pages 407-407

a barbarous name of a tree, the leaves of which, when boiled in wine, are said to create an appetite, and are used by the people in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> with that intention.

AMBIANI

Pages 407-407
or AMBIANENSIS CIVITAS, now Amiens, a city of Picardy. It is called Samarobriva by Caesar and Cicero: which, according to Valerius, signifies the bridge of the Samara, or Somme. Ambiani is a later name, taken from that of the people, after the usual manner of the lower age. This people, according to Caesar, furnished 5000 men for the siege of Alecia.

AMBIDENTER

Pages 407-407

among English Lawyers, a juror <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> embracer, who accepts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of both parties, for giving his verdict: an offence for which he is liable to be imprisoned, for ever excluded from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, and to pay ten times the sum he accepted.

AMBIDEXTER

Pages 407-407

a person who can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> both <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> with the same facility, and for the same purposes, that the generality of people do their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hands. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, some, as Hoffer, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> it to an extraordinary supply of blood and spirits from the heart and brain, which furnishes both hands with the necessary strength and agility; others, as Nicholas <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASSA">Massa</a>, to an erect situation of the heart, inclining neither to the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> nor left; and others to the right and left subclavian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> being of the same height, and the same distance from the heart, by which the blood is propelled with equal force to both hands. But these are only conjectures, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather chimeras. Many think, that were it not for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, all mankind would be ambidexters; and in fact, we frequently find nurses obliged to be at a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of pains before they can bring children to forego the use of their left hands. How far it may be an advantage to be deprived of half our natural dexterity, may be doubted. It is certain, there are infinite occasions in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, when it would be better to have the equal use of both hands. Surgeons and occultists are of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> obliged to be ambidexters; bleeding, &c. in the left arm or left ankle, and operations on the left eye, cannot be well performed but with the left hand. —Various instances occur in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, where the left hand has been exercised preferably to the right. But by the laws of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scythians, people were enjoined to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> both hands alike; and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> enjoins ambidexterity to be observed and encouraged in his republic.

AMBIENT

Pages 407-408

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used for such bodies, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, Ambient fluids, as compass others on all sides; thus, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is frequently called an ambient fluid, because it is diffused round the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>.

AMBIERLE

Pages 408-408

a town of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RHONE">Rhone</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> in a district of Roanne. AMBIGENÆ OVES, in the Heathen Sacrifices, an appellation given to such <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> as, having brought forth twins, were sacrificed, together with their two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, one on each side. We find them mentioned among other sacrifices to Juno.

AMBIGENAL HYPERBOLA

Pages 408-408

a name given by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton to one of the triple hyperbolas of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> order, having one of its infinite legs falling within an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> formed by the asymptotes, and the other without.

AMBIGUITY

Pages 408-408

a defect of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, whereby words are rendered ambiguous. See the next article.

AMBIGUOUS

Pages 408-408

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a word <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> which may be taken in different senses. An anonymous writer has published a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a> of ambiguous words: Lexicon Philosophicum de Ambiguitate Vocabulorum, Francof. 1597, 4to.—The responses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a> were always ambiguous.

AMBIT

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, is the same with what is otherwise called the perimeter of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. See PERIMETER. AMBIT was particularly used, in antiquity, to denote a space of ground to be left vacant betwixt one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> and another. By the laws of the twelve tables, houses were not to be built contiguous, but an ambit <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> space of 2½ feet was to be left about each for fear of fire.—The <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBITUS">ambitus</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> or monument denoted a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of feet, in length and breadth, around the same, within which the sanctity assigned to it was limited. The whole ground wherein a tomb was erected was not to be secreted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> uses; for this reason, it was frequent to inscribe the ambit on it, that it might be known how far its sanctity extended: thus, in fronte pedes tot, in agrum pedes tot. AMBITION (ambitio) is generally used in a bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, for an inordinate or illegal pursuit of power. In the strict meaning, however, of the word, it signifies the same with the ambitus of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. See the next article. Ambition, in the former and more usual sense, is one of those passions that is never to be satisfied. It swells gradually with success; and every acquisition serves but as a spur to further attempts. "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> (it has been well observed) could at once accomplish all his desires, he would be a miserable creature; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> is to wish and desire. Upon this account, every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> who aspires to be despotic aspires to die of weariness. Searching every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> for the man who has the least comfort in life, Where is he to be found?—In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>.—What! his Majesty? Yes, especially if he be despotic."

AMBITUS

Pages 408-408

in Roman Antiquity, the setting up for some magistracy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> office, and formally going round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> to solicit the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> and votes of the people. Ambitus differed from ambition, as the former lies in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, the latter in the mind. Ambitus was of two kinds; one lawful, the other infamous. The first, called also ambitus popularis, was when a person offered his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the republic frankly, leaving it to every body to judge of his pretensions as they found reasonable. The means and instruments here made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of were various. 1. Amici, or friends, under different relations, including cognati, affines, necessarii, familiares, vicini, tribules, clientes, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNICIPES">municipes</a>, sodales, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. 2. Nomenclatura, or the calling and saluting every person by his name; to which purpose, the candidates were attended by an officer, under the denomination of interpret, or nomenclator. 3. Blanditia, or obliging persons, by serving them, or their friends, patrons, or the like, with their vote and interest on other occasions. 4. Prehensio, the shaking every person by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, offering him his service, friendship, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind was that wherein force, cajoling, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, or other extraordinary influence, was made use of. This was held infamous, and severely punished, as a source of corruption and other mischiefs. Ambitus was practised, not only at Rome, and in the forum, but in the meetings and assemblies of other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, where numbers of citizens were usually found, on account of trade and business. The practice ceased in the city from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the emperors, by reason poets were not then to be had by courting the people, but by favour from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>. Persons who had causes depending practised the same, going about among the judges to implore their favour and mercy. They who practised this were called Ambitiosi. Hence we also meet with ambitiosa decreta, and ambitiosa justa, used for such sentences and decrees as were thus procured from the judges, contrary to reason and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, either gratuitously or for money.

AMBLE

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">Horsemanship</a>, a peculiar pace by which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s two legs of the same side move at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See HORSEMANSHIP.

AMBLESIDE

Pages 408-408

a town in Westmorland, seated at one end of Windermere. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. o. 49. N. Lat. 54° 30'.

AMBLETEUSE

Pages 408-408

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-port town of France, in the department of the Straits of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALAIS">Calais</a>, in the English Channel, twelve miles south-west from Calais, and eight <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOULOGNE">Boulogne</a>. At this port Caesar embarked his cavalry when he invaded England; and James II., when he abdicated the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> landed. It is defended with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERY">battery</a> of cannon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. I. 37°. N. Lat. 50° 48'.

AMBLYGON

Pages 408-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a>, denotes an obtuse-angled triangle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a triangle one of whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> consists of more than 90 degrees.

AMBLYOPY

Pages 408-408

among Physicians, signifies an obscuration of the sight, so that objects at a distance cannot be clearly distinguished.

AMBO

Pages 408-409
or AMBON, a kind of pulpit or desk, in the ancient churches, where the priests and deacons stood to read or sing part of the service, and preach to the people; called also Analogium. The term is derived from ἀναβάω, "to mount." The ambo was mounted upon two sides; whence some also derive the appellation from the Latin ambo, "both." The ambo was ascended by steps; which occasioned that AMB Ambohisi—that part of the office performed there to be called the Gradual. See Gradual. Besides the gospel, which was read at the top of the ambo, and the epistle, which was read a step lower, they likewise published from this place the acts of the martyrs, the commemoration of departed saints, and the letters of peace and communion sent by one church to another; here, too, converts made a public profession of their faith; and bishops their defence, when accused: treaties also were sometimes concluded, and the coronations of emperors and kings performed, in the same place. The modern reading-desks and pulpits have been generally substituted for the ancient ambos; though, in some churches, remains of the ambos are still seen. In that of St John de Lateran at Rome, there are two moveable ambos.

AMBOHISME

Pages 409-409
or Vohitsanghombe, a province of the island of Madagascar, so called from some red mountains of the same name, lying in S. Lat. 20°. These mountains are very high, resembling the Tafelberg of the Cape of Good Hope. On one side of this ridge the sea extends into the country for fifteen leagues; on the other is a flat country, abounding in ponds and marshes. Here is also a lake 15 leagues in length, and the same in breadth, containing many small islands. The inhabitants of the mountains are called Zaferabongs; and have plenty of gold, iron, cattle, silk, &c.

AMBOISE

Pages 409-410

D', George, a French <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> and minister of state, was born in the year 1460. His father was a descendant of the renowned <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Amboise, and, through the influence of his powerful connexions, he beheld the path of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> preferment open before his son; therefore he destined him to the clerical order. In these languishing expectations he was not disappointed; for he had sufficient influence to procure for him the bishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTAUBAN">Montauban</a> at the early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fourteen. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XI. appointed him one of his almoners; and in the course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> events, he became strongly attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, and suffered imprisonment in his cause. When this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, however, had regained his favour at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he was elevated to the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARBONNE">Narbonne</a>. After he had remained there for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he changed that station for the archbishopric of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a>. When the duke of Orleans was governor of Normandy, he made him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> general; and in that situation he was of essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, in restoring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and order. When the duke of Orleans became Louis XII., Amboise was suddenly raised to the elevated station of first minister and one of the cardinals. The same regard to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a>, which characterized his conduct when lieutenant general induced him to diminish the imposts, which rendered him very popular as first minister of France. In 1499, by his advice, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> undertook the conquest of the Milanese, and, on their revolt, the first minister was sent to quell the rebellion. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> confidence which Louis had reposed in him, induced the pope to make him his legate in France; and, in that station, he piously laboured to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> orders. He enforced his doctrine by precept, not only in setting them an example of holding no more benefices than one at a time, but also by devoting two-thirds of the revenue of the same to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, and to the repair of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> edifices. According to his own account he was ambitious of the papal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, "merely for the purpose of effecting the reformation of abuses and the correction of manners." It is reported that, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Pius III., he would have been elected pope had he not been deceived by the Italian cardinals. Disappointed in his views with regard to the papal honours, he persuaded his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to declare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Venetians, to whose influence he supposed his failure was owing. But this imprudent undertaking was suddenly interrupted; for in the prosecution of his journey for the Venetian war, he was seized with an illness, and confined in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Lyons. Affliction robs the reflecting powers of the mind, and calls to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> the past actions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. From the confidanthefs of his past errors and faults he was induced to express his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRITION">contrition</a> to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the infirmary who attended him at the convent of the Celestines. In the year 1510, and in the 50th of his age, he breathed his last in that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Industry, readiness, and good intention, characterized his conduct as a prime minister. He shone with peculiar brightness as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of literature. By his liberality and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, the arts and sciences flourished under his administration. It may be proper to add, that, assisted by some <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBOULE">Amboule</a>, of the ablest lawyers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; he formed a code of laws to reform the reigning abuses in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. Thus, by steadily pursuing the general welfare, he obtained the appellation of the "father of the people." (Gener. Biog.)

AMBOULE

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Madagascar, somewhat to the northward of S. Lat. 23°. It is a fertile and agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, watered by the river Manampani, whose mouth lies in S. Lat. 23° 36'. The country produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> in plenty. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a> are also found here. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle are extremely fat, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> excellent. In this province stands a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> town of the same name; near which is a fountain of hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, within 20 feet of a small river whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is almost <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. The water of the fountain is said to boil an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> hard in two hours; and the inhabitants affirm it to be a sovereign remedy against the gout. The people here are employed in different preparations of iron and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, which they have from their own mines, and forge several instruments with tolerable skill. Their governor is honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Roberlau, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. He exercises sovereign authority and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> power; but is frequently, in times of distress, surprised by his subjects, who assemble in great numbers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> his person, and threaten him with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> unless they are relieved. To extricate himself from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILEMMA">dilemma</a> he is instantly obliged to issue orders for distributing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> among them; but is usually repaid with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, a quadruple return being made in a plentiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>. The people of Amboule live in great licentiousness with their superiors, and their country is generally a retreat for the rough and lazy.

AMBOYNA

Pages 410-411

one of the Molucca <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the East Indies. It lies in S. Lat. 3° 36' and E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 126° 20', and is remarkable for being the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> for nutmegs and cloves, which is entirely monopolized by the Dutch East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>. It is about 24 leagues in circumference. Besides cloves, it likewise abounds in most of the tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and fish; nor is there here any deficiency of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is very scarce. This scarcity, however, proceeds more from the policy of the Dutch than either the intemperance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the barrenness of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>: For, excepting cloves, they have in Amboyna, as well as the Moluccas, industriously discouraged the cultivation of every edulent commodity, with the view of withholding subsistence from those who might be tempted to invade them. Of the natives, the men wear <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> whiskers, but leave little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> upon the chin; and have only a slight piece of stuff wrapped round their middle. The women tie their hair in knots: the maids are bought of their fathers before they are married; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the wife proves barren, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> is dissolved. Some of the natives are Mahometans, and some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>: but they are all said to be lazy, deceitful, and treacherous. They make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with small swift vessels, in shape like dragons with regard to the head and tail. Their houses are built of bamboo canes and fago trees. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on mats. Their weapons are bows and arrows, javelins, scimitars, and targets. Amboyna was first discovered by the Portuguese, who built a fort upon it, which was taken from them by the Dutch in 1605. They did not, however, become masters of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> at once. The English had here five factors, who lived under the protection of the Dutch cattle; holding themselves safe, in respect of the friendship between the two nations. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> differences had arisen between the Dutch and English colonists in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world; till at last, the English East India Company applying to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> James, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> was concluded in 1619, by which the concerns both of the English and Dutch were regulated, and certain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> agreed upon for preventing future disputes. This was an additional security to the English; and, by virtue of the treaty, they <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> two years in Amboyna, trading with the Dutch. During this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, several disputes happened; which occasioning mutual discontentments, the complaints were sent to Jacatra, in the island of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of both nations resident there: but they not agreeing, a state of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> was sent over to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, to be decided by the East India Companies of both nations; or, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they could not agree, by the king of England and the states of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, according to an article in the treaty of 1619.—But before these disputes could be decided in a legal way, the Dutch, in order to give the more specious colouring to the violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZURE">seizure</a> which they meditated of the island of Amboyna, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> being formed by the English and Japanese to dispossess them of one of their forts in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. The plot, it was alleged, had been confabulated by a Japanese and Portuguese in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, who were most unhappily tortured till they should answer in the affirmative such interrogatories as might favour the secret <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of those cruel inquisitors. Upon the injurious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of this constrained <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a>, they immediately accused the English factors of the pretended conspiracy. Some of them they imprisoned, and others they loaded with irons, and sent on board their ships; seizing at the same time all the English merchandise, with their writings and books. These acts of violence were followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of horror unexampled in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the most atrocious offenders. Some of the factors they tortured, by compelling them to swallow water till their bodies were distended to the utmost pitch; then taking the miserable victims <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the boards to which they had been fastened, and causing them to disgorge the water: if they did not acknowledge the imputed guilt, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of torture was repeated. Others of the English they consumed by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> them gradually from the feet upwards, in order to extort the confession of a conspiracy, which was only pretended by the internal policy of those <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> tormentors. Some had the nails of the fingers and toes torn off; and in some they made holes in their breasts, filling the cavities with inflammable materials, to which they afterwards put fire. Those who did not expire under the agonies of torture were confined to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the executioner. The allegation of this pretended conspiracy was equally void of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The Dutch had a garrison of 300 men in the fort, besides the burghers in the town, and several other forts and garrisons in the island, while the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the English did not amount to 20 men; nor were even those provided with arms or ammunition to effect such a design as that with which they were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>. There likewise was not one Amboyna. English vessel in the harbour, whereas the Dutch had eight ships riding near the town; neither, when the Dutch broke open the desks and trunks of the factors, was there found a single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> which could be construed into the most distant relation to any conspiracy. Add to all this, that each of the unhappy sufferers as could speak to be heard, declared in the most solemn manner their innocence of the plot with which they were charged. The whole of the transaction affords the most irrefragable testimony, that it was founded entirely upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> fiction of the Hollander, who had themselves formed the design of monopolizing the trade of the Spice Islands; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> of which they perpetrated, about the same time, a singular tragedy at Pooleon, where they put to the torture 162 of the natives, whom they likewise charged with a pretended conspiracy. It may justly be reckoned singular in the fortune of this commercial republic, that they have ever since been permitted to enjoy in peace those invaluable islands, which were originally obtained by such atrocious infringements of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and the laws of nations, as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stain the Dutch annals, to the latest ages, with indelible infamy. The more effectually to preserve this trade, the Dutch have had all the clove trees in the adjacent islands grubbed up. Sometimes also, when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> is very large, part of the produce of Amboyna itself is burnt. To prevent the rearing of cloves in any of the neighbouring islands, or the inhabitants from selling them to strangers, the governor of Amboyna makes the tour of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> with a fleet of curriculuses, confining sometimes of 20, and at others of 30, 40, or 50 sail. This expedition is made with all the pomp imaginable, in order to gratify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and folly of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> chiefs.
