The true reason of their taking all this pains is, because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> has shown, that no contracts, however solemn, can prevent the inhabitants of those islands from selling their spice to strangers: and even now, frauds are frequently practised by the Dutch themselves, though the Company is inexorable in punishing them, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people call the cloves galgen-bruid, that is, the gallows spice. Besides the cloves, coffee is also cultivated here by the Dutch, and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> mine has been lately found out. This was discovered by the quantities of gold dust that were washed from some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> by the torrents. Here also grow several kinds of valuable wood, of which they make tables, chairs, escritoires, &c. for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> persons in the government; and the rest is sold all over the Indies at a very extravagant rate. Amboyna is divided into two parts, viz. a greater and lesser <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>. The former, called Hilton, is 12 leagues in length, and two and a half <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. In this the Dutch have no less than five forts, or rather strong redoubts, mounted with cannon. The other is called Leytimor, five leagues in length, and one and a half broad, which is the southern part of the island; on this stands the fort of Victoria, which is the residence of the governor and his council, composed of 15 gentlemen or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. The fortress is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, the ramparts mounted with 60 pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> cannon, and the garrison usually composed of 600 men. It is so strong by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art, as to be in a manner impregnable; and so effectually does it command the harbour, that no vessel could come in or go out without being sunk by the cannon, if the governor chose. The inhabitants of Amboyna are computed at 70 or 80,000, of whom but a small number are Dutch; and this obliges the latter to be continually upon their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, and to keep a competent number of troops in each of their forts, particularly in that of Middleburgh, which stands upon the isthmus that connects these peninsulas. There are also redoubts and garrisons in all the islands of this government.

AMBRACIA

Pages 411-411

one of the most considerable cities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Epirus, situated on the river Arachthus, at a small distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. At first it was a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; but was afterwards reduced by the Aetolian kings of Epirus, who chose it for the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their residence. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the Aetolians made themselves masters of it, and held it till the year before Christ 189, when it fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. At this time Ambracia was a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength. It was defended on one side by the river Arachthus, and on the other by steep and craggy hills; and surrounded with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and thick wall, above three miles in compass. The Roman <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> Fulvius began the siege by forming two <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, separated by the river, but with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between them; the Romans were posted in one, and the Epirots their allies in the other. He then threw up two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, one of circumvallation, the other of contravallation; and built a wooden tower in form of a castle, over against the citadel, which stood on a hill. The Aetolians, however, before the lines were quite finished, found means to throw about 1000 men into the place. The lines being completed, the city was attacked in five different places at once. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTERING">battering</a> rams shook the walls on all sides: and the Romans, from their moveable towers, pulled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a> with a kind of scythes, which they fastened to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> beams. The besieged made a vigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. They were night and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> on the walls, and indefatigable in preventing the effects of the rams and scythes. The strokes of the former they deadened, by letting down beams, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, lumps of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, &c. by means of pulleys, upon them when they were in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: the others they rendered useless, by pulling the beams to which they were fastened into the city with hooks contrived for the purpose. While Fulvius was carrying on the siege, Nicander the Aetolian praetor, found means to throw 500 men into the city, under the command of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NICODAMUS">Nicodamus</a>, with whom Nicander agreed to attack the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> in the night time; not doubting, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the garrison from within, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> from without, fell upon them at the same time, they would be obliged to raise the siege. Nicodamus narrowly watched the time at which he was ordered to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; and though Nicander did not appear, marched out at the head of the garrison, armed with firebrands and torches. The Roman sentinels, surprized at this sight, ran to wake the legionaries, and soon spread a general alarm all over the camp. The legionaries marched in small bodies as they happened to meet, to repulse the enemy, whom they engaged in three different places. Two parties of the garrison were driven back; but the third, commanded

AMBRESBURY

Pages 411-412
or Amesbury, a market town in Wiltshire, about six miles north of Salisbury, and situated in W. Long. 1° 40' and N. Lat. 51° 20'.

AMBRONES

Pages 412-412

a Gaulish people who lived near the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> and Provence. They invaded the Roman territories in conjunction with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIMBRI">Cimbri</a> and Teutones; but were defeated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter by Marius, about 101 years before Christ. Their women, who had fled during the engagement in a kind of fortification made with their carts, on seeing their husbands dying, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> at their heels, armed themselves with axes, and gnawing with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, fell with fury on the pursuers and the pursued. Their first rage being spent, they desired to surrender themselves, upon the single condition, that their chastity should not be violated; but this equitable request being denied, they first killed their children, and then themselves, not one remaining alive out of the whole multitude.

AMBROSE

Pages 412-416

Saint, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the South <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific ocean</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, four <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> five leagues due west from St Felix island. At first view, it appears like two small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but after a nearer approach, it is found they are joined by a reef. It lies in S. Lat. 26° 13'. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80° 55' from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENWICH">Greenwich</a>. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rock 4 miles to the northward of the island, called, from its appearance, Sail-rock. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Roberts, who was here in 1792, found St Felix island inaccessible. On St Ambroise island, his crew killed and cured 13,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> skins of the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> weeks. The island has little else to recommend it. Fish and crawfish abound. The best season for sealing is from the 1st of April to the 1st of August. Ambrose of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, lived in the beginning of the third century, and was the intimate friend of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>. Jerome and Eusebius differ in the account they give of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. One denominates him a Marcionite, the other a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALENTINIAN">Valentinian</a>; but they both agree that he was converted to the orthodox <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, through means of the preaching of Origen. As is generally the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with new proselytes, he became very zealous, and was appointed deacon either at Alexandria, or at Caesarea, where Protecletus was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESBYTER">presbyter</a>. Origen dedicated many of his works, and among others his book on martyrdom, to Ambrose; at whose desire and expense they were published. Origen and Ambrose were alike indefatigable in their application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and lived in terms of the most intimate friendship. Origen being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, Ambrose assisted him, by providing notaries and amanuenses to copy his works. In that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, when the increase of copies was a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of immense labour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> expense, there were not only instances of private friendship, but of public utility. Ambrose is thus justly entitled to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the patrons of learning. Ambrose has been blamed by some, for having made no provision at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> for the poor infant Origen. The friends of Ambrose excuse this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his conduct, by saying, that Origen chose to live poor, and daily dependant on Ambrose, a divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a>. According to some historians, Ambrose died as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>, along with his friend Pro- tectetus, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> under Maximin, about the year 236; but the dedication of Origen's eight books against Celsus shows, that though he died before Ori-gen, yet he lived to the year 250, or near that period. Origen speaks of him as a man of great piety, and much devoted to the study of the sacred Scriptures. (Ambrose, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, was one of the most eminent fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the fourth century. He was a citizen of Rome, and born in France; some historians say in the year 334, but others say in the year 340. The birth of Ambrose is said to have been attended with a remarkable prefiguration of his future eloquence, by a swarm of bees coming and settling upon his mouth as he lay in his cradle. At the period of his birth, his father was Praetorian prefect of Gallia Narbonensis; but upon his death, the widow repaired to Rome with her family. Ambrose received a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and was reared in the habits of virtuous conduct by his mother, who was an accomplished woman, and eminent for piety. The names of those masters who instructed him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the Greek and Roman literature have not been transmitted to posterity: but in these branches he made early proficiency; and, having directed his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, he employed his eloquence with such reputation in the Praetorian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Anicius Probus, that he was soon deemed worthy of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. After he had <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in this station for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, Probus appointed him <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> of Liguria and Emilia, comprehending the territories of Milan, Liguria, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. Milan was chosen for the place of his residence, and by the prudent and gentle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his power, he conducted the affairs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> with general approbation and growing popularity. In the year 374, Auxentius the bishop of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> died, and his death gave a sudden change to the fortune and literary pursuits of Ambrose. At that period, the tide of religious contention ran <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> between the Catholics and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a>, and there ensued a strong contest concerning the choice of a new bishop. When the people assembled in the church to elect Ambrose, in the character of governor of the place, went into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, and, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, eloquent, and pathetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, admonished the multitude to lay aside their contentions, and, in the spirit of religious meekness, to proceed to the important work of choosing a bishop. It is reported, that when Ambrose had finished his address, a child cried out, "Ambrose is bishop." The agitated multitude suddenly caught the superstitious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, and regarding this as a miraculous intimation, they unanimously elected Ambrose bishop of Milan. Some suppose that this was entirely a device of Ambrose or his friends, and others ascribe it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accident. Ambrose strongly affected reluctance, and even pretended to fly from the city in order to avoid the intended <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. It is, however, unfortunate for the artifice of the governor that the place of his concealment was soon discovered, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> was known concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a>. Finding it inconvenient any longer to reflect the public choice, he exchanged the ensigns of civil for those of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; and, after being baptized, he was ordained bishop of Milan, about the end of the year 374. But whatever may be the sentiments of mankind concerning the singular conduct of Ambrose in accepting an office for which he was certainly unqualified in respect of previous studies, habits, and employments, yet it must be admitted, that he immediately betook himself to the necessary studies, and with ability, boldness, and integrity, acquitted himself in his new elevation. Having appropriated his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> to the poor, settled his lands upon the church, with the exception of making his foster tenant during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and having committed the care of his family to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, he entered upon a regular course of theological study, under the care of Simplician, a presbyter of Rome, and devoted himself to the labours of the church. Compelled by the irruption of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a> and the northern barbarians, who rushed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the Roman empire, spreading terror and desolation all around, Ambrose, along with several others, fled to Illyricum; but he remained only a short period in exile, for the northern invaders were quickly defeated by the forces of the emperor, and driven back with considerable loss into their own dominions; therefore, he and his companions returned to their respective habitations. After he returned to his ecclesiastical station, the eloquence and abilities of that zealous bishop found ample scope in the dispute between the Arians and the Catholics. About this era, the doctrine of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARIUS">Arius</a> concerning the person of Christ had been extensively received, and had many powerful defenders, both among the clergy and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people. Ambrose espoused the cause of the Catholics. Gratian, the son of the elder Valentinian, marshalled on the same side. But the younger Valentinian, who was now become his colleague in the empire, adopted the opinions of the Arians; and all the arguments and eloquence of Ambrose were insufficient to reclaim the young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> to the orthodox faith. Theodosius, the emperor of the east, also professed the orthodox faith, yet there were numerous adherents to Arius scattered throughout his dominions. In this general state of religious opinions in the empire, two leaders of the Arians, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALLADIUS">Palladius</a> and Secundianus, confident of numbers, prevailed upon Gratian to call a general council from all parts of the empire. This request appeared so equitable that he complied without hesitation, but Ambrose, aware of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, had the eloquence to persuade the emperor that a general council was improper, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> could be determined by a council of the western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>. The result was, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a>, composed of 32 bishops, was held at Aquileia in the year 381. Ambrose was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and Palladius being called upon to defend his opinions, declined; insisting that the meeting was a partial one, and that the whole bishops of the empire not being present, the feme of the Christian church could not be obtained concerning the question in dispute. Ambrose mentioned several precedents in favour of the authority of the court, and added, that the oriental bishops being acquainted with the place and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the meeting, might have been present, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had deemed the matter in difficulty. Ambrose. fion worthy of their attention; therefore, the court, although Palladius persisted in his refusal to plead his cause, put the vote, and he, along with his associate Secundianus, was ejected from the episcopal office. If Ambrose displayed great zeal in opposing the errors of Arius, he displayed equal zeal in opposing the heathen superstitions. Many of the senators remaining strongly attached to the heathen idolatry, upon Valentinian II. ascending the throne, they made a vigorous effort to restore the worship of the heathen deities. Symmachus, a very opulent man, and a great orator, who was at that time prefect of the city, was entrusted with the management of the pagan cause, and drew up a petition, praying that the altar of Victory might be restored to its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> station in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and for the proper support of seven veiled virgins, and the regular observance of the other pagan ceremonies. Great eloquence and peculiar infirmation characterized the petition. He argued that this form of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> had long been profitable to the Roman state, reminded the emperor how much Rome had been indebted to victory, and that it had been the uniform <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of the senators to swear fidelity to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> upon that altar. He likewise produced many facts to prove the advantages derived to the state from its ancient religious institutions, and intimated that it was one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> that all men worshipped under different forms, so that ancient practice should not be rashly laid aside. He even proceeded so far as to state the injustice of increasing the public revenue by robbing the church, and attributed the late famine which had overtaken the empire to the neglect of the ancient worship. To this petition, Ambrose replied in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Valentinian, arguing that the devoted worshippers of idols had often been forsaken by their deities; that the native valour of the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> had gained her victories, and not the pretended influence of pagan priests; that these idolatrous worshippers requested for themselves what they refused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>; that willing virginity was more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> than that procured by the public money; that as the Christian ministers declined taking temporal emoluments, they should also be denied to pagan priests; that it was absurd to suppose that God would send a famine upon the empire for neglecting to support a religious system contrary to his revealed will in the Scriptures; that the whole proceeds of nature encouraged innovations; and that all nations had permitted these, even in religion; that heathen sacrifices were exceedingly offensive to Christians; and that every Christian prince should suppress these pagan ceremonies. In the epistles of Symmachus and of Ambrose, both the petition and the reply are preserved, in which folly, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> argument, are strangely blended. It is scarcely necessary to add that the petition was unsuccessful. The increasing strength of the Arians proved too formidable for the zealous Ambrose. The young emperor and Justina, along with a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of clergy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a> professing the Arian faith, requested from the bishop the use of two churches, one in the city, the other in the suburbs of Milan. The prelate believing the bishops to be the guardians, both of the temporal and spiritual interests of the church, and that the religious edifices were the unquestionable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the church, positively refused to deliver up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> into the impious <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of heretics. Filled with indignation, Justina resolved to employ the imperial authority of her son in procuring by force what she could not by persuasion. Ambrose was required to answer for his conduct before the council. He went, attended by a numerous crowd of people, whose impetuous zeal so overawed the ministers of Valentinian, that he was permitted to retire without making the surrender of the churches. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> following, when he was performing divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in the Basilica, the prefect of the city came to persuade him to give up at least the Portian church in the suburbs. Still continuing obstinate, the court proceeded to violent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. The officers of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> were commanded to prepare the Basilica and the Portian churches to celebrate divine service upon the arrival of the emperor and his mother at the ensuing festival of Easter. The order respecting one of them was carried into effect, but the court perceiving the growing strength of the prelate's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, deemed it prudent to use softer measures; but all measures proved in vain: the bishop boldly replied, "If you demand my person, I am ready to submit: carry me to prison or to death, I will not resist; but I will never betray the church of Christ. I will not call upon the people to succour me; I will die at the foot of the altar, rather than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> it. The tumult of the people I will not encourage, but God alone can appease." This strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> was followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TORRENT">torrent</a> of eloquence from the pulpit, pursuing his scheme with the most violent zeal. But the court remained unconvinced, and another attempt being made, under a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> of ferocious Goths, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the church of Basilica; when they were about to enter, Ambrose thundered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCOMMUNICATION">excommunication</a> against them, and so overawed them that they retired; and Ambrose and his friends remained in possession of the churches. About this time, also, an Arian bishop challenged Ambrose to a dispute before the emperor; but he declined, saying that matters of faith should be determined by a council of bishops. Many circumstances in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Ambrose are strongly characteristic of the general spirit of the times. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> causes of his victory over his opponents were, his great popularity, and the superstitious reverence paid to the episcopal character at that period of society. But it must also be admitted, that he used several indirect means to obtain and support his popular authority. Many indigent persons were supported by his liberal bounty; in his explanations of Scripture he made constant and severe allusions to existing and public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of singing had no small effect upon the minds of the vulgar. At a time when the influence of Ambrose required vigorous support, he fortunately was admonished in a dream to search for the remains of Gervasius and Protasius, two martyrs who had quietly repose under the pavement of the church. The skeletons were found entire, were stained with blood, and the head of one of them separated from the body. The vulgar crowded in thousands to behold these venerable relics. According to report, Ambrose report, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> man was restored to sight, several demons were expelled, and sick persons healed by touching these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. Ambrose exulted in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, and appealed to them in his eloquent sermons; whilst the court derided and called in question their existence. The bishop continued firm in his opinions; the people believed; and the existence of the miracles was established. And it is a very singular fact, that there, and many other miracles, obtained current <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> among the Christian historians of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, third, and fourth centuries. Dr Cave in speaking of them says, "I make no doubt but God suffered them to be wrought, at this time, on purpose to confront the Arian imposters." Although the court were displeased with the religious principles and conduct of Ambrose, yet they respected his great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> talents; and when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> required, they solicited his aid, which he generously granted. When Maxentius usurped the supreme power in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, and was meditating a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, Valentinian sent Ambrose to him, who prevailed upon him to desist from the undertaking. On a second attempt of the same kind Ambrose was employed; and, although he was unsuccessful, yet, if his advice had been followed upon his return, the schemes of the usurper would have proved abortive; but indifferent to his counsels, the enemy was permitted to enter Italy, and Milan was taken. Jutina and her son fled; but Ambrose remained in his station, and proved beneficial to many of the sufferers, by causing the plate of the church to be melted for their relief. Theodosius, the emperor of the East, espoused the cause of Jutina, and by force of arms regained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. In the year 392, a tumult happened at Thessalonica, in which Botheric, one of the officers of Theodosius was slain; and he was so greatly enraged, that he issued a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> mandate for the promiscuous massacre of the inhabitants of that place: and about seven thousand persons were assassinated, without distinction or mercy. The courageous Ambrose, informed of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, wrote to the emperor a severe reproof, and an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> admonition, charging him not to approach the holy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with his hands stained with innocent blood. When the emperor was about to enter the church of Milan to attend upon the service, the bishop met him, and with a stern countenance prohibited him from approaching the temple of God. The emperor reminded him that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> had been guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>. The bishop replied, You have "imitated David in his guilt; go and imitate him in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>." The prince obeyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, and, by a course of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENITENTIAL">penitential</a> sorrow, during the space of eight months, he laboured to regain the favour of the church. After the termination of this period, he was absolved, but at the same time was made to sign an edict that an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of thirty days should intervene before the sentence of death or confiscation should be put in execution. When the mind reflects upon the numerous bad effects of instant and violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> was certainly fraught with policy and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>. If the reader laments the weakness which subjected the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the clerical power, he must be gratified that a moderate use was made of that authority. The undaunted courage of Ambrose received another severe <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> in the year 392, after the assassination of Valentinian, and the base Eugenius had usurped the empire of the west. Rather than join the standard of the usurper, he fled from Milan. But after the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of Theodosius was victorious, he generously supplicated the emperor for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> of those who had supported the cause of Eugenius. Theodosius, soon after he had acquired the uncontrolled possession of the Roman empire, died at Milan. The bishop did not long survive the emperor; but died in the year 397. In his last illness he preserved perfect composure of mind, informing his friends that he had endeavoured so to conduct himself that he might neither be ashamed to live nor to die. On many accounts the character of the bishop of Milan stands high among the fathers of the ancient church. With unvarying steadfastness he delivered his religious sentiments on all occasions; with unwearied assiduity he discharged the duties of his office; with unabated zeal and boldness he defended the orthodox cause, in opposition to the Arians; with a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> he fed the numerous poor who flocked to his dwelling; with uncommon generosity he manifested kindness to his adversaries; and with Christian affection he sought the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of all men. His general habits were amiable and virtuous, and his powers of mind were uncommonly vigorous and persevering. Ambition and bigotry were the chief blemishes in his character. The writings of Ambrose are voluminous, although little more than adulterated editions of Origen and other Greek fathers. The great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of his writings was to defend and propagate the Catholic faith. In some of these he recommends perpetual celibacy as the perfection of Christian virtue. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">Modern</a> judgment and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> may perhaps induce some to esteem the writings of Ambrose absurd, trivial, and even ludicrous; but there is a freshness and vigour in his style, and there are excellent sentiments interspersed, which render the writings of the bishop of Milan worthy of a perusal. With his usual severity and acrimony, Gibbons too severely censures this prelate. "Ambrose (says he) could <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> better than he could write; his compositions are destitute of taste or genius, without the spirit of Tertullian, the copious elegance of Lactantius, the lively <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> of Jerome, or the grave energy of Augustin." The most accurate and complete edition of his works, is that published by the Benedictine monks printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in two volumes in 1682. (Gen. Biog.) Ambrose, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a>, an eminent Presbyterian minister, was educated at Brazen-nose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, where he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts, and became minister of Preston, and afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARSTANG">Garstang</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANCASHIRE">Lancashire</a>, whence he was in 1662 ejected for nonconformity. It was usual for him to retire every year for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> into a little hut in a wood, where he shunned all society, and devoted himself to religious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a>. Dr Calamy observes, that he had a very strong impulse on his mind of the approach of death, and took a formal leave of his friends at their houses a little before his departure; and the last night of his life he sent his discourse concerning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> to the press. The next day he shut himself up in his parlour, where to the great surprize and regret of all who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him, he Ambrose was found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> expiring. He died in 1663-4, in the 72d year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He wrote several other books; as the Prima, Media, et Ultima, or the First, Middle, and Last Things; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a> with Devils; Looking unto <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, &c. Ambrose, or St Ambrose in the Wood, an order of religious, who use the Ambrosian office, and wear an image of that saint engraven on a little plate: in other respects they conform to the rule of the Augustins. See Ambrosian Office and Augustins.

AMBROSIAN OFFICE OF RITE

Pages 416-416

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a particular formula of worship in the church of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, which takes its name from St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a>, who instituted that office in the fourth century. Each church originally had its particular office; and when the Pope, in after times, took upon him to impose the Roman office upon all the western churches, that of Milan sheltered itself under the name and authority of St Ambrose; from which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the Ambrosian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> has prevailed.

AMBROSIN

Pages 416-416

in middle-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> writers, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a> struck by the lords <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, wherein was represented St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> on horseback, with a whip in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. The occasion of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COINAGE">coinage</a> is said to have been a vision of that saint, who appeared to the Milanese general in 1339, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. AMBROSINIA. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

AMBROSIUS AURELIANUS

Pages 416-416
or Aurelius Ambrosius, a famous general of the ancient Britons, of Roman extraction. He was educated at the court of Aldroen of Armorica: who, at the request of the Britons, sent him over with 10,000 men, to assist them against the Saxons, whom Vortigern had invited into Britain. Ambrosius had such success against the Saxons, that the Britons chose him for their king, and compelled Vortigern to give up to him all the western part of the kingdom divided by the Roman highway called Watling-street. Some time after, the Britons being discontented with Vortigern, and having withdrawn their allegiance from him, he retired to a castle in Wales, where being besieged by Ambrosius, and the castle taking fire, he perished in the flames, and left his rival sole monarch of Britain; who now took upon him the imperial purple, after the manner of the Roman emperors. Geoffrey of Monmouth tells us, that Ambrosius built Stonehenge near Salisbury in Wiltshire. Ambrosius, according to this historian, coming to a monastery near Caercaradoc, now Salisbury, where three hundred British lords, massacred by Hengist, lay buried, and resolving to perpetuate the memory of this action, he ordered his workmen to prepare a large quantity of stones and other materials. But having, at the instigation of Tremounus archbishop of Caerleon, consulted the famous Merlin, this magician advised him to send over to Ireland for certain great stones, called eborea gigantum, the giant's dance, placed in a circle on a hill called Killair, which were brought thither by giants from the farthest borders of Africa. A body of forces was accordingly sent into Ireland, under Pendragon, Ambrosius's brother, to fetch these stones; but were opposed in their attempt by Gilliomanus king of the country, who derided the folly of the Britons in undertaking so ridiculous an expedition. Nevertheless, the Britons having vanquished this prince in battle, brought away the stones; and by the direction and affluence of Merlin, who had accompanied them, these wonderful stones, by order of Ambrosius, were placed over the graves of the British lords, and are now what is called Stonehenge. Alexander Mechain celebrates this fable in his poem De divina sapientiae landibus. Polydore Virgil affirms another origin of Stonehenge: he tells us it was erected by the Britons as a monument to their general Ambrosius, on the place where he fell in battle, to perpetuate the memory of his glorious actions and services done to his country. Both these stories are rejected by our best antiquaries; who, however, are by no means agreed as to the true origin of this famous piece of antiquity. See Stonehenge. After the Britons had defeated the Saxons, and obliged them to retire northward, Ambrosius is said to have convened the princes and great men at York, where he gave orders for repairing the churches destroyed by the Saxons, and restoring the exercise of religion to its former lustre. This is confirmed by Matthew of Wellminster; who highly applauds the great zeal of Ambrosius in repairing the churches, encouraging the clergy, and restoring the honour of religion. The Monmouth historian gives this prince a very high character. "He was a man (says he) of such bravery and courage, that when he was in Gaul no one durst enter the lists with him; for he was sure to unhorse his antagonist, or to break his spear into shivers. He was, moreover, generous in bestowing, careful in performing religious duties, moderate in all things, and more especially abhorred a lie. He was strong on foot, stronger on horseback, and perfectly qualified to command an army." The same author tells us he was poisoned at Winchester by one Eopa a Saxon, disguised as a physician, and hired for that purpose by Pafcentius one of the sons of Vortigern: but the generally received opinion is, that he was killed in a battle which he lost in the year 508, against Cerdic, one of the Saxon generals.

AMBRY

Pages 416-416

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in which are deposited all utensils necessary for housekeeping. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> abbeys and priories, there was an office under this denomination, wherein were laid up all charities for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>.

AMBUBAJE

Pages 416-417

in Roman Antiquity, were immodest women, who came from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> to Rome, where they lived by prostitution, and by playing on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>: the word is derived from the Syriac abu, which signifies a flute; although others make it come from am and Bais, because these prostitutes often retired to Baiae. According According to Cruquius, these women used likewise to sell paint for ornamenting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>, &c.

AMBULANT

Pages 417-417
or **AMBULATORY**. They gave in France the name of Ambulant commissioners to those commissioners, or clerks of the king's farms, who had no fixed office; but visited all the offices within a certain district, to see that nothing was done in them against the king's right and the interest of the farm. Ambulant is also used to denote those brokers at Amsterdam, or exchange agents, who have not been sworn before the magistrates. They transact brokerage business, but their testimony is not received in the courts of justice.

AMBULATORY

Pages 417-417

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> anciently applied to such courts, &c., as were not fixed to any certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; but held sometimes in one place, and sometimes in another; in opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATIONARY">stationary</a> courts.—The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> was anciently ambulatory; so also were the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a>, &c.

AMBURBIUM

Pages 417-417

in Roman Antiquity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> made by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> and pomerium, in which they led a victim, and afterwards sacrificed it, in order to avert some calamity that threatened the city.

AMBURY

Pages 417-417
or **ANBURY**, among Farriers, denotes a tumour, wart, or swelling, which is soft to the touch, and full of blood. This disorder of horses is cured by tying a horse-hair very hard about its root: and, when it has fallen off, which commonly happens in about eight days, strewing some powder of verdigris upon the part, to prevent the return of the complaint. If the tumour be so low that nothing can be tied about it, they cut it out with a knife, or else burn it off with a sharp hot iron; and, in finewy parts, where a hot iron is improper, they eat it away with oil of vitriol, or white sulphur. Many of our farriers boast of a secret which infallibly cures all protuberances of this kind; the preparation of which is this: Take three ounces of green vitriol and one ounce of white arsenic; beat them to a coarse powder, and put them into a crucible; place the crucible in the midst of a charcoal fire, stirring the substance, but carefully avoiding the poisonous fumes: when the whole grows reddish, take the crucible out of the fire, and when cool, break it and take out the matter at the bottom; beat this to powder in a mortar, and add to four ounces of this powder five ounces of album rubris; make the whole into an ointment, and let it be applied cold to warts; rubbing them with it every day. They will by this means fall off gently and easily, without leaving any swellings. It is best to keep the horse quiet, and without working, during the cure. What sores remain on the parts from which the swellings fall off, may be cured with the common application called the countess's ointment.

AMBUSCADE

Pages 417-417
or **AMBUSH**, in the Military Art, properly denotes a place where soldiers may lie concealed till they find an opportunity to surprise the enemy. In the language of Scripture, these terms are not always taken in their proper signification, for laying ambushes for any one, attacking him in secret, laying shares for him. They sometimes signify no more than attacking a man who has no distrust of such a thing; attacking one behind, concealing one's self in some particular place in order to surprise any one. See the book of Judges, ch. ix. 25, 32, 34, 35. Abimelech, who lay lurking with his people in the heights of Sichem, so, however, as to rob and treat those who passed that way very ill, came and attacked the city of Sichem with his troops divided into three bodies: "Tetendit infidias juxta Sichimam in quatuor locis." Literally, according to the Hebrew, "They prepared ambuscades against Sichem in four heads or companies." And a little farther, verse 43. "Abimelech, being informed that the Sichemites had marched, took his army and divided it into three bodies, and laid wait for them in the field." It seems certain, that in these parages ambushes, properly so called, were not the things in question. In the first book of Samuel, Saul complains that David laid ambuscades for him: "Infidiator usque bodie permanentis." Now nothing could be worse grounded than this accusation, if we understand the word infidari in its proper signification; but he might say, though unjustly, that David was his secret enemy. And in the Chronicles it is said, that God turned the ambushes laid by the enemies of Israel upon themselves; that is to say, their endeavours, their malice, their arms, he turned against themselves; for the enemies there mentioned came not in private or by stratagem; they marched openly in arms against Israel.

AMEDIANS

Pages 417-417

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, so called from their professing themselves amantes Deum, "lovers of God;" <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather amati Deo, "beloved of God." They wore a gray <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and wooden shoes, had no breeches, and girt themselves with a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. They had 28 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>; and were united by Pope Pius V. partly with the Cistercian order, and partly with that of the Scolastici, or wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a> wearers.

AMELIA

Pages 417-417

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, situated between the Blue-ridge and the tide waters, having <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> county on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> George county on the east, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNENBURG">Lunenburg</a> county on the south and west. Amelia, including Nottaway, a new county, contains 18,097 inhabitants, of whom 11,037 are slaves. **AMELIA Ile**, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, lies about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues north of St Augustine, and very near Talbot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> on the south, at the mouth of St John's river. It is 13 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 2 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, is very fertile, and has an excellent harbour. Its north end lies opposite Cumberland island, between which and Amelia ile is the entry into St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s river, in N. Lat. 30° 52', W. Long. 67° 23'.

AMELOT DE LA HOUSSAI

Pages 417-418

Nicholas, born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> in 1634, was much esteemed at the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of France, and... and appointed secretary of an embassy which that court sent to the commonwealth of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, as appears by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his Translation of Father Paul's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>; but he afterwards published writings which gave such offence, that he was imprisoned in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>. The first works he printed were the History of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a> of Venice, and that of the Ulcoks, a people of Croatia. In 1683 he published his translations into French of Machiavel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, and Father Paul's History of the Council of Trent, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">Political</a> Discourses of his own upon Tacitus. These performances were well received by the public. He did not prefix his own name to the two last-mentioned works, but concealed himself under that of La Mothe Joffeau. His translation of Father Paul was attacked by the partisans of the pope's unbounded power and authority. In France, however, it met with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success; all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of the Gallican <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> promoting the success of it to the utmost of their power, though at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> there were three memorials presented to have it suppressed. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of this translation was published, it was violently attacked by the Abbé St Real, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> he wrote to Mr Bayle, dated October 17, 1685. Amelot defended himself in a letter to the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>. In 1684, he printed, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, a French translation of Baltasar Gracián's Oracula <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">Manual</a>, with the title of l'Homme de Cour. In 1686, he printed La Morale de Tacite de la Flatterie; in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> he collected several particular facts and maxims, which represent in a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> the artifices of court flatterers, and the mischievous effect of their poisonous discourses. Frederick Leonard, a bookseller at Paris, having proposed, in the year 1692, to print a collection of all the treaties of peace between the kings of France and all the other princes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, since the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VII. to the year 1690, Amelot published a small volume in duodecimo, containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRELIMINARY">preliminary</a> discourse upon these treaties; wherein he endeavours to show, that most princes, when they enter into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, think more how to evade than how to perform the terms they subscribe to. He published also an edition of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> d'Ollat's letters in 1697, with several observations of his own; which, as he tells us in his advertisement, may serve as a supplement to the history of the reigns of Henry III. and Henry IV., kings of France. He wrote several other works; and died at Paris in 1706, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 73. Amelot was at one time confined in the Bastille, probably on account of his political writings. AMELOTTE Denis, a celebrated French writer, was born at Saintonge in 1606. He maintained a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> correspondence with the fathers of the Oratory, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of priests founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Neri. He wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Charles de Gendron, second superior of this congregation, and published it at Paris in 1643. In this work he said something of the famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">Abbot</a> of St Cyran, which greatly displeased the gentlemen of Port <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, who, out of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, published a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a> against him, entitled Idée générale de l'esprit et de livre de P. Amelotte. He was so much provoked by this satire, that he did all in his power to injure them. They had finished a translation of the New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, and were desirous to have it published; for which purpose they endeavoured to procure an approbation from the doctors of the Sorbonne, and a privilege from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. But Amelotte, by his influence with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a>, prevented them from succeeding. In this he had also a view to his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; for he was about to publish a translation of his own. Amelotte's translation with annotations, in 4 volumes octavo, was printed in the years 1666, 1667, and 1668. It is not very accurate, according to F. Simon, who tells us that it contains some very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> blunders. Amelotte wrote also an Abridgement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>, a Catechism for the Jubilee, and a kind of Christian Manual for every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Towards the end of his life, he entered into the congregation of the Oratory in 1650; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> amongst them till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened in 1678.

AMEN

Pages 418-418

εγενόμητε τρεῖς, faithful, certain. It is made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of likewise to affirm any thing, and was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> used often by our Saviour: Amen, ἐγενόμητε τρεῖς, i.e. Vertly, verify, I say unto you. Lastly, It is understood as expressing a wish: as Amen, So be it, (Numb. v. 22.) <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> an affirmation, Amen, yes I believe it, 1 Cor. xiv. 16. The Hebrews end the five books of Psalms, according to their way of distributing them, with the words Amen, amen; which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEPTUAGINT">Septuagint</a> have translated γένοιτο, γένοιτο; and the Latin, Fiat, fiat. The Greek and Latin churches have preserved this word in their prayers, as well as alleluia and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HALLELUJAH">hallelujah</a>; because they observed more energy in them than in any terms which they could use in their own languages. At the conclusion of the public prayers, the people answered with a loud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, Amen; and St Jerome says, that at Rome, when the people answered Amen, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of their voices was like a clap of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>: In similitudinem celestis tonitruit Amen reboat. The Jews assert, that the gates of heaven are opened to him who answers Amen with all his might.

AMEND

Pages 418-418
or AMENDE, in the French Customs, a pecuniary punishment imposed by a judge for any crime, false prosecution, or groundless appeal. AMENDE Honorable, a species of punishment formerly inflicted in France upon traitors, parricides, or sacrilegious persons, in the following manner: The offender being delivered into the hands of the hangman, his shirt is stripped off, a rope put about his neck, and a taper in his hand; then he is led into court, where he must beg pardon of God, the king, the court, and his country. Sometimes the punishment ends here; but sometimes it is only a prelude to death, or banishment to the galleys. AMENDE Honorable, is a term also used for making recantation in open court, or in presence of the person injured.

AMENDMENT

Pages 418-418

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the correction of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> committed in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, which may be amended after judgment, unless the error lies in giving judgment; for in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it is not amendable, but the party must bring a writ of error. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> may be amended on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a> at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">plea</a> is pleaded; but not afterwards, without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> and leave of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. AMENDMENT of a Bill, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, is some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> made in the first draught of it.

AMENTUM

Pages 419-419

in Roman Antiquity, a thong tied about the middle of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dart, and fastened to the fore finger, in order to recover the weapon as soon as it was discharged. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the amentum, thinking it helped to enforce the blow. It also denotes a latchet that bound their sandals.

AMERADE

Pages 419-419

a kind of officers among the Sara- cens, answering to the governors of provinces among the Europeans. The name is originally the same with that of Emir.

AMERCEMENT

Pages 419-419
or **AMERICIAMENT**, in Law, a pecuniary punishment imposed on offenders at the mer- cy of the court. It differs from a fine in being impos- ed arbitrarily, in proportion to the fault; whereas a fine is a certain punishment settled expressly by some statute. HERESY OF ALMARIC

Pages 336-336

a tenet broached in France by one Almaric, in the year 1209. It consisted in affirming, that every Christian was actually a member of Christ; and that without this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> no one could be saved. His followers went farther, and affirmed, that the power of the Father lasted only during the continuance of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSAIC_LAW">Mosaic <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; that the coming of Christ introduced a new law; that at the end of this began the reign of the Holy Ghost; and that now confession and the sacraments were at an end, and that every one is to be saved by the internal operations of the Holy Spirit alone, without any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.—Their morals were as infamous as their doctrine was absurd. Their tenets were condemned by a public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENS">Sens</a>, in the year 1209.

WEST'S PINDAR

Pages 359-359

Pausanias adds, that the Eleans had a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which condemned any woman to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> that should either appear at the Olympic games, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> this river during that solemnity: and the Eleans add, that the only woman who transgressed it, had disguised herself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> or keeper of the games, and conducted her son thither; but when she <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him come off victorious, her joy made her forget her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, so that her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> was discovered. She was pardoned; but from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> a law was made that the keepers should appear there naked.
